10356-travels-in-morocco-volume-2:
James Richardson, who died before this book appeared, wrote these travels in Morocco, edited by his widow and issued in two volumes. This second volume carries the journey deeper into Moroccan towns, courts, and peoples. Richardson had already written on Central Africa and the Sahara, and he brought the same curious eye here.

Chapters treat Jewish communities in Mogador and the Atlas, the sharifian dynasty, slave-trade talks with Britain, and the limits and peoples of the empire. Anecdotes lighten the learned detail. Readers get a rich, Victorian-era portrait of Morocco on the edge of European pressure.
10562-friends-in-need-ship-s-company-par:
W. W. Jacobs published this comic tale as the second part of Ship's Company, opening in the private bar of the Red Lion. Joseph Gibbs finishes his half-pint slowly, unable to see where the next will come from, and asks only for work, not slavery. His friends, George Brown and Bob Kidd, cheer him with grim jokes.

Gibbs wonders what it would feel like to make a hole in the water, while his friends note that wives often gain from a Friendly Lead after a death. The joke turns dark, then comic, in Jacobs's salty style. Readers get a short, funny tale of sailors, poverty, and friends in need.
10656-a-collection-of-old-english-plays-:
A. H. Bullen edited A Collection of Old English Plays in four volumes between 1882 and 1889, rescuing Elizabethan and Jacobean dramas that had gone unreprinted. This second volume opens with a play of Spanish gentlemen, fathers and sons, lovers and partings, as Don Pedro prepares to leave for France. The old spelling is kept, giving the text its period flavor.

Bullen chose plays that readers could hardly find elsewhere, and his editions helped revive interest in the lesser dramatists of Shakespeare's age. The volume suits students of early drama and lovers of old plays. It offers comedy, intrigue, and formal verse from a theater richer than its famous names alone.
1068-personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-volum:
Ulysses S. Grant, dying of cancer and writing to save his family from debt, carries his memoirs through the second half of the Civil War in this volume. He tells of the Wilderness, Spotsylvania, Cold Harbor, and the long siege of Petersburg, then of Appomattox and Lee's surrender. Mark Twain published the book.

Grant's prose is plain, modest, and exact, with a soldier's eye for ground, supply, and error. He praises foes and owns his own mistakes with the same calm. The memoirs, finished days before his death, became a classic of American letters and the standard soldier's account of the war.
10782-homeward-bound-sailor-s-knots-part:
W. W. Jacobs's "Homeward Bound," the second tale in Sailors' Knots from 1909, turns on a husband's campaign against his wife's spending. Mr. Hatchard answers extravagance with a week of fault-finding and grunts, a treatment that once worked but now fails. Two huge pink vases on the mantelpiece prove it, bought while he was out.

The comedy lies in the war over the vases, as Hatchard demands who gave them and his wife calmly owns the purchase. Jacobs tells it in plain, funny dialogue. Readers get a domestic farce complete in itself, needing no other tale from the book.
10797-the-wits-and-beaux-of-society-volu:
Grace and Philip Wharton wrote Wits and Beaux of Society as lively lives of fashionable men and women. This second volume, edited by Justin Huntly McCarthy in 1890, carries the series onward. Its contents open with Horace Walpole: his mother, his school days with Gray, his letters, his father's house at Houghton, and his place in London society.

The Whartons mix anecdote, gossip, and portraiture, with original pictures by H. K. Browne and James Godwin. Their subjects are the talkers and beauties of eighteenth-century England. Readers get entertaining social history, told through the people who made the drawing rooms sparkle.
1101-king-henry-vi-part-2:
William Shakespeare's history play follows the weak King Henry VI as his realm slides toward civil war. His queen, Margaret, and her favorite, Suffolk, scheme for power, while the Duke of York nurses his claim to the throne and Jack Cade raises a rebels' army in Kent. Plots, murders, and battles crowd the stage.

Good men fall, bad men rise, and the king prays while his kingdom burns. The play's rough energy and its famous line about lawyers show Shakespeare still learning his craft. It opens the Wars of the Roses sequence that runs through the Henry VI plays to Richard III.
11010-the-spectator-volume-2:
Henry Morley edited this second volume of The Spectator, reproducing Addison and Steele's essays as first issued and as corrected by their authors, with introduction, notes, and index. Number 203, for Tuesday, October 23, 1711, warns against a loose tribe of men who seduce women across London and father children on churchwardens, a satire on rake culture.

Later essays discuss Milton's Paradise Lost, including Mammon, architect of Pandemonium, and the infernal assembly's debate. The Spectator's daily papers, on manners, literature, and morals, shaped English prose and public taste. Morley's edition helps modern readers follow references and enjoy Addison and Steele's wit, irony, and humane observation of city life.
1117-king-henry-iv-part-2:
King Henry IV lies dying while his son Hal still haunts the taverns with Falstaff, and the rebellion smolders on after Shrewsbury. William Shakespeare's sequel follows Hal's slow turn toward duty, the king's sleepless nights, and Falstaff's schemes, until Hal takes the crown as Henry V and casts his old friend off.

The play is darker and sadder than its predecessor, with Justice Shallow's country scenes and the famous rejection scene as its poles. Falstaff's fall still stings audiences. The play completes Hal's education and sets up the triumph of Henry V.
11182-the-boatswain-s-mate-captains-all-:
W. W. Jacobs wrote this short comic tale, The Boatswain's Mate, second in the Captains All series. Mr. George Benn, retired boatswain, sighs at the door of Mrs. Waters's bar, declaring his feelings will never change. Mrs. Waters replies sharply that he always asks her to marry him after the third mug, and Benn promises next time to ask before a drop, to prove he is in earnest.

Refused five times in a fortnight, Benn walks two miles deep in thought, naps on a shady bank, and meets a tall old soldier carrying a bundle. Later, a burglar creeps into a bedroom, hides in a cupboard, and is confronted by a woman with a candle and a double-barrelled gun. Jacobs's humour turns courtship, burglary, and seafaring talk into a tidy comic plot.
11419-the-love-affairs-of-great-musician:
Rupert Hughes's Love Affairs of Great Musicians, volume two from 1903, treats Franz Liszt, Richard Wagner, Tchaikovsky the woman-dreader, a violinist's heart, Robert Schumann and Clara Wieck, and musicians as lovers generally. Liszt's chapter opens with Nietzsche's phrase, Liszt or the art of running after women. noting that his letters to his last love alone fill four volumes, though he began piano only at six and gave his first concert at nine.

Hughes writes gossipy, informed biography, with illustrations of Liszt, Wagner and Cosima, Paganini, Berlioz, Verdi, Schubert, and the Schumanns. The book's premise is that love shaped music, for better and worse. Music lovers will enjoy its anecdotes, even where modern biography has corrected them.
11472-paying-off-deep-waters-part-2:
W. W. Jacobs's Deep Waters story Paying Off opens with the night-watchman gloomily confessing good nature as his biggest fault, having spent his life doing fellow creatures good turns and getting ingratitude. A man he once helped arrives with grinning companions to remind him, sitting on a barrel that feels like red-hot cinders after two minutes. Captain Mellun, a foolish, soft-headed man who somehow keeps his job, pretends to ask after the watchman's health while upsetting him for amusement.

The story's comedy lies in the watchman's self-pity and sharp tongue. Jacobs keeps the tale short, a single yarn told on a wharf. Readers of his sea humor will recognize the pattern: a favor remembered, a score settled in talk.
11700-j-s-le-fanu-s-ghostly-tales-volume:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu's second volume of ghostly tales pairs two works. An Authentic Narrative of a Haunted House is dated 1862. Ultor de Lacy is dated 1861. The editor of the University Magazine vouches for the haunted house account.

He says every witness was respectable and would have sworn to each incident on oath. Ultor de Lacy opens in a large room with a turf fire. An old woman works there with a wooden spoon. Two ladies in red drugget cloaks appear, like Munster peasant girls. The tales keep Le Fanu's method: plain testimony, a strange house, and dread that grows from detail.
11952-a-popular-history-of-france-from-t:
Volume 2 of Guizot's History of France continues from the Crusades to the Hundred Years' War. Chapters treat the decline and end of the Crusades, the kingship in France. The communes and the third estate, with a frontispiece of the bridge of Toulouse and an engraving of preaching the Second Crusade.

The Hundred Years' War occupies the later chapters: Philip VI and John II, the States-General of the fourteenth century, and Charles V. Guizot follows the growth of royal power, the rise of towns. The long war with England as interlocking stories, in which institutions, not battles alone, decide the fate of a kingdom.
11972-dialstone-lane-part-2:
Part 2 of W. W. Jacobs's Dialstone Lane continues the comic tale of Mr. Chalk's expedition to the Southern Seas, which has become a standing joke with the captain. The captain waylays Chalk to ask after his progress and to offer advice for emergencies at sea, known and unknown, until even Chalk tires of the pleasantries.

In this portion the captain, jovially, admits burning a map to ashes, calling it a load off his mind, while Chalk stares in speechless dismay. A girl faces round to prompt a hesitating captain about a crow's-nest. The comedy turns on matchmaking, treasure maps, and seafaring men trying, with misplaced confidence, to manage life ashore.
12077-the-philippines-past-and-present-v:
Dean C. Worcester, interior chief of the Philippines from 1901 to 1913, put out this first volume in 1914. A former member of the Philippine Commission, he writes as a defender of American rule after the war against Filipino freedom forces.

Worcester claims that freedom was never pledged, that rebel rule was harsh and split, and that the war conduct of American troops has been judged unfairly. Later chapters cover civil rule, the civil service, the police force, courts, and health work. The book is openly one-sided, and modern readers will read it against Filipino accounts. As a record, it shows how American officials backed colonial rule at its height.
12122-the-monkey-s-paw-the-lady-of-the-b:
First published in 1902, The Monkey Paw is the most famous story in W. W. Jacobs book The Lady of the Barge. Set in a modest English home on a cold, wet night, it turns a soldier souvenir into a lesson about wishes.

Mr. and Mrs. White and their son Herbert receive a dried monkey paw said to grant three wishes, with a warning that fate rules men lives to punish interference. They wish for two hundred pounds to clear their house debt, and the money arrives as compensation after Herbert dies at work. Later wishes bring worse horror. Jacobs builds dread from small domestic detail, and the tale has become a byword for wishes that backfire.
12152-keeping-watch-night-watches-part-2:
A pretty girl in a passing skiff sets the night watchman moralizing in Keeping Watch, the second tale in W. W. Jacobs Night Watches. Human nature, he sighs, is the same on water as on land: lovers pretend, and pretence keeps love alive.

The girl reminds him of one he knew years before, who came weekly to the wharf on her father schooner, the Belle. Captain Butt watched his daughter closely, yet she found ways to meet the watchman, walk the jetty, and talk of life and might-have-beens. The story follows their cautious courtship and its quiet end. Jacobs comedy is bittersweet here, mixing dockside humor with the knowledge that youth and its chances pass quickly.
12202-the-castaway-odd-craft-part-2:
Mrs. John Boxer keeps a small sweet shop in the seaside town of Shinglesea when her husband, lost with the North Star three years before, walks back through the door. That return opens The Castaway, a comic story from W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft.

Boxer tells tall tales of survival, shows a cut on his head as proof, and settles back into married life with gusto. His mother-in-law, Mrs. Gimpson, suspects the stories, and the household soon fills with neighbors eager to hear more. Jacobs comedy rests on a man who enjoys his own legend too much, and on women who see through it. The story ends with the returned sailor caught between his yarns and his audience.
12397-the-star-chamber-an-historical-rom:
W. Harrison Ainsworth's historical romance, second volume of a Leipzig edition dated 1854, follows intrigue at the Stuart court. Contents promise poison and counter-poison, a forged confession, a wager between the Spanish envoy Gondomar and the Marquis of Buckingham, and a tilting match in the old palace yard at Westminster.

Sir Giles Mompesson, Prince Charles and Whitehall intrigue anchor the action, as Clement Lanyere's story and Sir Jocelyn's rupture with Gondomar push toward disgrace. Ainsworth mixes court pageantry with conspiracy, letting secret cabinets and tiltyard display carry the plot. The volume reads as Victorian historical romance at full stretch, colourful, crowded and fond of court scandal.
12410-the-travels-of-marco-polo-volume-2:
The Travels of Marco Polo, volume two, presents the complete Yule-Cordier edition. It includes the unabridged third edition of Henry Yule annotated translation, revised by Henri Cordier, with Cordier later notes and addenda of 1920. The frontispiece copies a painting inscribed Marcus Polus, Venetian, first traveler of the whole world and India.

Volume two continues Polo account of Asia, with notes on trade, manufacture, and courts. A mid-book note describes indigo making by fermentation: branches cut, placed stem upwards in a vat, loaded, and filled with water until fermentation begins. Yule and Cordier notes weigh Polo truth against legend. The edition remains the standard scholarly Marco Polo in English, rich in geography and history.
12471-what-i-remember-volume-2:
Thomas Adolphus Trollope's second volume of memoirs, published in 1887, ranges from northern England and Brittany to Paris, Ireland and Florence. Chapters recall Dickens, Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Garibaldi, Walter Savage Landor, and Mr. and Mrs. Lewes, alongside letters from friends and memories of his mother and his first marriage.

Trollope writes as a long resident of Florence looking back, mixing travel, literary gossip and family history in an easy, anecdotal voice. The volume's charm lies in proximity: famous names appear as dinner guests and neighbours, not as monuments. For readers of Victorian letters it offers first-hand glimpses of writers and exiles who shaped the age from Italy.
1252-le-morte-d-arthur-volume-2:
Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur continues in this second volume, opening with Book Ten and the deeds of Sir Tristram. Tristram jousts with Arthur, saves Palomides, and meets Launcelot in combat, unknown to each other. Malory wrote Le Morte d'Arthur in prison in the fifteenth century, drawing on French romance.

Launcelot brings Tristram to court amid great joy, and the knights' rivalries and loves drive the tale onward. Malory's prose, in this classic retelling, remains the great English source for Arthurian legend. Book Ten, with Tristram's deeds, is the longest and most romantic section of the work.
12538-account-of-a-tour-in-normandy-volu:
Dawson Turner's second volume of letters from Normandy, addressed to the Reverend James Layton of Catfield, investigates the architectural antiquities of the duchy. Letters run from Ducler and St. Georges de Bocherville through Jumièges, Gournay, Gisors, Andelys, Evreux and Harfleur, with observations on history, country and inhabitants.

Engravings illustrate abbeys, castles, tombs and churches, including the tombs of Agnes Sorel and the Enervés at Jumièges, and Château Gaillard at Andelys. Turner writes as a learned antiquary, fond of detail and local lore. The volume offers a rich, illustrated tour of Norman architecture for readers who travelled, in print, before photographs took over.
12668-an-account-of-the-english-colony-i:
Lieutenant-Colonel David Collins, of the Royal Marines, continues his account of the English colony in New South Wales in this second volume, from first settlement in 1788 to August 1801. Remarks on native inhabitants follow, with particulars of New Zealand from Lieutenant-Governor King's manuscripts.

An account of the voyage by Captain Flinders and Mr. Bass, by which a strait separating Van Diemen's Land from New Holland was found, is abstracted from Bass's journal. Collins writes as an official historian of a penal colony becoming a settlement. The volume is a key source for early Australia, Tasmania and New Zealand, detailed and administrative in tone.
12964-melbourne-house-volume-2:
Melbourne House, volume two, continues the story of Daisy Randolph in this 1865 New York edition by the author of The Wide, Wide World. Daisy, a young girl under a doctor's care, travels with her father and Dr. Sandford after a tender parting from Juanita. Her illness and her quiet faith shape the home scenes that follow.

At table and in company, Daisy watches the bright scene from her quiet corner, glad of the doctor's thoughtful care. She keeps her habit of giving thanks, even when her mother's interference makes her pause. The book suits readers who want a gentle domestic novel about a child's conscience, manners, and trust in God.
12985-eugene-field-a-study-in-heredity-a:
Slason Thompson's Eugene Field: A Study in Heredity and Contradictions, volume two of 1901, continues the life of the Chicago poet and humorist. A frontispiece prints Little Boy Blue in Field's own hand, with the dusty toy dog and rust-red soldier awaiting the child who kissed them and put them there. Portraits, views, and facsimiles enrich the volume.

A subscription passage shows Field's friends rallying to fund a two-volume edition of his original work, sending money orders to Thompson as custodian. Thompson argues that heredity and contradiction shaped Field's charm. The book suits readers of American humour and newspaper poetry.
13018-the-letters-of-elizabeth-barrett-b:
Frederic G. Kenyon edited The Letters of Elizabeth Barrett Browning, volume one, third edition of 1898, with portraits and biographical additions. Chapters span 1806 to 1851: birth and Hope End, London magazine poems, Torquay and her brother Edward's death, Wimpole Street, the Poems of 1844, friendship with Robert Browning, marriage, and Florence life. Casa Guidi fronts the volume.

A letter on her Masque shows the young poet in deep despondency, ready to burn the manuscript. Kenyon took it home, confessed a prejudice against sacred subjects and a prejudice for her, and returned it with counsel. The letters reveal a poet's mind at work. The volume is essential for Browning readers.
13148-peter-simple-and-the-three-cutters:
Captain Marryat's Peter Simple, in this 1895 Dent edition bound with The Three Cutters, follows a young midshipman through naval life. A biographical introduction and a prefatory note open volume one, then chapters run from Peter's first days at sea onward. Marryat, himself a naval officer, writes from service knowledge, not library research.

One comic passage wheels a drunken third lieutenant about in a wheelbarrow, while a sentry challenges each new arrival in turn. Later, Peter seeks his grandfather, Lord Privilege, at Eagle Park, and is met coldly in the library. The novel mixes humor, hardship, and sea adventure, and it remains one of Marryat's most loved boys' books.
13162-coralie-everyday-life-library-no-2:
Charlotte M. Braeme's Coralie, number two in the Everyday Life Library, is a romance by the author of Dora Thorne. Its narrator opens on eighty pounds a year, a sum that buys few gloves or cigars and often no good dinner, yet leaves him passing rich. His father, Captain Trevelyan, died when he was a child, and his mother followed some years later.

Later, Edgar learns he is heir to Crown Anstey, its title, and a vast fortune, since Sir Barnard and his only son died together. Coralie herself appears in black crape, white neck and arms bare, with heliotrope sprays in bodice and hair, seated in a velvet chair. Braeme's tale is a melodrama of poverty, inheritance, and love, written for a wide popular audience.
13272-beethoven-s-letters-1790-1826-volu:
Volume two of Beethoven's Letters, translated by Lady Wallace from Nohl and Köchel, continues the second part, Life's Mission, from 1815 to 1822. Letters run from Steiner and Company to Haslinger, Baroness Ertmann, Zmeskall, and Czerny, numbered from 216 onward. The volume closes the composer's later correspondence with publishers, pupils, and friends.

Beethoven argues over guardianship, calling one candidate unfit for want of time and credit, and barred by a court from acting. He also bargains over quartets, offering a new work and swearing on his honor as an artist that it ranks among his best. The letters show a proud, exacting master, fighting for money, art, and control of his own work.
13621-the-poems-of-jonathan-swift-d-d-vo:
William Ernst Browning edits volume two of Jonathan Swift's poems, published by G. Bell and Sons in 1910, with a frontispiece of Hester Vanhomrigh, Vanessa, from a picture owned by G. Villiers Brinus. Contents run from Cadenus and Vanessa and To Love through Stella's birthdays, Stella at Wood-Park, and verses by Stella herself.

Swift addresses a monarch as defender of the faith and nursing mother to church and family, praying for profound and lasting peace. A poem on Humphry contrasts Agamemnon's ten years' war, unsung and lost in endless night, with a friend whom tuneful songs will save from dark oblivion. The volume gathers Swift's wit, affection, and satire in verse.
1370-autobiography-of-andrew-dickson-whi:
Andrew Dickson White, first president of Cornell University and author of A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology, continues his autobiography in this second volume. Diplomacy, education, and reform fill its pages. White served as minister to Germany from 1879 to 1881, and to Russia in the 1890s.

White recalls service as minister to Germany and Russia, the founding of Cornell, and battles for free inquiry. The volume gives an insider view of American higher education and foreign service in the Gilded Age. His second volume covers Cornell's growth and his diplomatic years in detail.
13720-mardi-and-a-voyage-thither-vol-1-o:
The first volume of Herman Melville's Mardi, published in 1864, opens a voyage that soon leaves realism behind. A sailor deserts his whaler at Ravavai, an island near the tropic of Capricorn. He sets out with companions across the South Seas in search of a lost maiden, drifting from island to island in a strange archipelago.

Along the way the travellers meet envoys from Hautia, bearing a moss-rose bud and a Venus-car as tokens, and the talk turns to philosophy, kingship, and human folly. Melville mixes sea adventure with allegory and satire, and the book's long meditations puzzled readers who wanted another Typee. It stands as his most ambitious and most uneven romance, a bridge between his sea tales and later work.
13721-mardi-and-a-voyage-thither-vol-2-o:
Herman Melville's Mardi, second volume, continues a voyage that began as a South Seas tale and grew into philosophy. Sailors reach the imagined archipelago of Mardi and travel from island to island. They visit temples, meet pilgrims, and debate gods, kings, and human nature. Braid-Beard, Mohi, and Babbalanja trade stories and arguments.

Melville uses the voyage to satirise politics, religion, and philosophy. Each island stands for an idea or a nation, and talk often matters more than action. The prose shifts between adventure, poetry, and essay. Readers who want a straight sea story may find it strange. Those who enjoy Melville's later depths will find Mardi a bold experiment.
1382-poems-volume-2:
George Meredith's second volume of poems gathers his later lyric and meditative verse in the Surrey edition of 1912. The poems move between nature, love, and the life of the mind, with the same close watch of seasons, birds. Country walks that marks his novels, but in tighter, more musical form.

Some pieces are short songs, others are longer reflections on age, loss, and the spirit's growth. Meredith's diction can be dense, yet his images stay vivid and his feeling direct. The volume offers a good entry to a poet better known as a novelist, in his most personal voice.
14052-rousseau-volume-1-and-2:
John Morley wrote Rousseau in two volumes, first printed in 1886 and reprinted through 1905. Morley offers a continuous personal history, noting no full English life of Rousseau existed. France, he says, had nothing more complete than Musset-Pathay's history of Rousseau's life and works. Morley's study pairs with his Voltaire.

Morley traces Rousseau from Geneva to Paris, from music to philosophy, from fame to paranoia. He weighs the Social Contract, Emile, and Confessions with Victorian liberal judgment. A passage on energy and principles saving progress between the Seven Years' War and the States General shows his scope. The biography suits students of the Enlightenment. It remains a classic English Rousseau.
14289-the-life-of-napoleon-i-volume-1-of:
John Holland Rose's Life of Napoleon I, first published in 1901 and revised through 1910, draws on new materials from British official records. Dedicated to Lord Acton, the volume follows Bonaparte from early promise to imperial power, with Napoleon's own advice to his son as motto: read history, since history is the only true philosophy.

Debate scenes reveal the man beneath the legend. Bonaparte spars with philosophizing atheists who prize mental dexterity over Socratic truth, then looks to a midnight sky and asks who made all that. Carlyle's phrases fit the moment, Rose argues: instinct for nature and ineradicable feeling for reality. Louisiana diplomacy follows, as American protests stir Washington and Talleyrand blandly denies any transfer. Scholarship and drama combine throughout.
14290-the-life-of-napoleon-i-volume-2-of:
John Holland Rose wrote this second volume of his life of Napoleon, built on British official records. It runs from Ulm and Trafalgar through Austerlitz, the fall of Prussia, and the wars that wore France down. Rose weighs Napoleon's statecraft against the strain of campaigns. The volume first appeared in 1901 and was revised through 1910. Its chapters move at the pace of marches, treaties, and battles.

Rose shows a France tired of glory, where Paris crowds jeered the Emperor in lampoons yet bore the drain of men and money. Protectionists cheered his trade policy, while Girondin voices praised him as a friend of farm freedom. After Elba, 180,000 troops stood under his eagles, and he hoped for half a million by June. Marshals failed him: some stayed loyal to Louis, one went mad, and others were too old or ill. The volume judges a ruler at the edge of his power.
1494-the-legends-of-the-jews-volume-2:
Louis Ginzberg's second volume carries the legends from Joseph to the Exodus, again translated by Henrietta Szold. Joseph the favourite son, hated by his brothers, cast into a pit, and sold into Egypt, opens the book. The tale runs through Judah and his sons to Moses and the flight from Egypt.

As in the first volume, Ginzberg weaves rabbinic tale and commentary into a flowing narrative, with notes pointing to sources. The legends fill gaps in the biblical text with wonder and moral weight. The volume is a rich treasury for readers of folklore, faith, and the Jewish tradition.
14973-essays-on-wit-no-2:
Essays on Wit number two, from the Augustan Reprint Society in November 1946, gathers short Augustan pieces on wit with an introduction by Edward N. Hooker. An essay on wit from 1748 stands beside Richard Flecknoe on one that zanies the good companion and on a bold abusive wit, from 1665.

Joseph Warton's Adventurer numbers 127 and 133, from 1754, and Of Wit from the Weekly Register of 1732 complete the set. Membership in the society brought six publications a year for two dollars fifty. Together the pieces show wit as a social art: quick, cutting and praised when it pleases, blamed when it wounds, in coffeehouse and print.
1501-king-henry-vi-part-2:
The second part of Henry VI follows the king's weak rule as his court splits between Gloucester, the lord protector, and the ambitious York, Suffolk, and Margaret of Anjou. From the palace to Gloucester's garden, St Albans, and a hall of justice, intrigue hardens into the first open moves of civil war.

Gloucester's fall, Suffolk's murder, and Jack Cade's rebellion crowd the play, and York's claim to the throne grows bolder by the act. Henry watches, pious and helpless, as his realm unravels. It is a darker, tighter history than Part 1, and the true start of the Wars of the Roses.
15098-diderot-and-the-encyclop-dists-vol:
John Morley's study of Denis Diderot, first published in 1878 and reprinted in 1905, traces the French thinker who led the great Encyclopédie. This first volume follows Diderot from his birth in 1713 through his Paris struggles, his marriage, and his early writings. Morley sets him among Voltaire, Rousseau, and their circle.

Long passages of summary and close reading lay out Diderot's ideas on religion, morals, and society, and explain why his work mattered on the eve of revolution. Morley argues that the encyclopedists gave France a new way of thinking, not mere clever talk. The book still serves as a clear guide to a key mind of the Enlightenment.
1518-king-henry-iv-part-2:
The second part of Henry IV follows the ailing king, the lingering rebellion, and Prince Hal's slow turn from tavern life toward the crown. Falstaff still blusters through Eastcheap and Gloucestershire, recruiting ragged soldiers and dodging the law, while the king's counsellors weigh war and justice.

Hal's rejection of Falstaff at his coronation closes the comedy with a chill, as the new Henry V takes up the weight of kingship. The play is darker and more reflective than its predecessor. It meditates on age, friendship, and the price of power with deep, autumnal feeling.
15869-a-voyage-towards-the-south-pole-an:
The second volume of Captain James Cook's account of his second voyage, in the Resolution and Adventure, during 1772 to 1775. Printed in London for Strahan and Cadell in 1777, it carries maps, charts, and views drawn by Hodges. Cook writes as commander, with Furneaux's narrative of the Adventure added. The volume completes a landmark of exploration.

Book Three follows the passage from Ulietea to New Zealand, with island peoples, winds, and anchorages noted in detail. Later books press round the world through southern seas. Cook's prose stays plain, careful, and honest about ice, distance, and doubt. The volume matters for geography and seamanship: a great voyage, told by the man who sailed it.
1589-tamburlaine-the-great-part-2:
Marlowe's second part of Tamburlaine follows the Scythian shepherd turned emperor as his conquests grow wider and his pride grows harder. From his sons' failures to the burning of a holy book and the death of his beloved Zenocrate, the conqueror's triumphs curdle into grief and rage.

Tamburlaine's mighty line still rolls through battles, courts, and funeral marches, and the play ends with his own death and a son unworthy of his crown. The sequel is darker than Part 1. It is a grand, brutal study of power that outlives its purpose and its man.
15998-alfred-russel-wallace-letters-and-:
The second volume of Alfred Russel Wallace's letters and reminiscences, by James Marchant, issued by Cassell and Company in London, New York, Toronto, and Melbourne in 1916. Two photogravures and eight half-tone plates join the text, with a portrait of Wallace from 1913. Marchant gathers the naturalist's own words and friends' memories. Wallace, co-discoverer of natural selection, speaks here in old age.

Part Three treats Wallace's works on biology and geographical distribution, with correspondence to match. Letters show his thought on evolution, islands, and the distribution of life. The tone stays modest and curious. The volume serves students of science: a great naturalist, remembered by his letters, at full stretch.
16350-curiosities-of-literature-vol-2:
Isaac Disraeli fills this second volume with short essays on odd corners of literary history. Charles I, the Duke of Buckingham, royal promotions, modes of greeting, fireworks, banned Bibles, and the early drama all get brief, lively pieces. Literary friendships, solitude, and the Jews of York appear alongside notes on Massinger, Milton, and the Italian stage.

Edited by his son, the Earl of Beaconsfield, the volume invites browsing rather than straight reading. Each piece is short and packed with anecdote. For lovers of books about books, it is a treasure chest of curious facts, first gathered in the early 1800s and still fresh.
16546-hinduism-and-buddhism-an-historica:
This second volume of the historical sketch of Hinduism and Buddhism opens with the Mahayana: its main features, bodhisattvas, Buddhas, metaphysics, scriptures, and chronology. Indian Buddhism as seen by Chinese pilgrims and its decadence follow, then Hinduism proper: Siva and Vishnu, ritual, caste, sect, Sankara, and later Vishnuism north and south.

The writer's preface notes the hard task of transcribing many Eastern tongues, using each language's standard English system. The volume is scholarly and wide-ranging. Students of Eastern religion will find a solid, old-style survey, careful with names, schools, and dates.
16556-short-story-classics-american-vol-:
William Patten edited this 1905 second volume of American short story classics, with introduction and notes. De Forest's Brigade Commander leads, followed by Bayard Taylor, Thomas Bailey Aldrich, Harold Frederic, Bret Harte's Idyl of Red Gulch, Thomas Nelson Page, and a dozen more. Every story was cleared with its author or estate.

The set spans Civil War tales, humor, mystery, and local color, showing American short fiction at its nineteenth-century peak. Each piece stands alone, and Patten's notes place each writer. Readers who want the best American stories in one book will find this a strong, varied sampler.
16646-the-letters-of-elizabeth-barrett-b:
Frederic G. Kenyon edited this second volume of Elizabeth Barrett Browning's letters, third edition, issued by Smith, Elder in London in 1898 with portraits. It covers 1851 onward, from Casa Guidi Windows through Venice, Milan, Paris, and London, to Florence, Rome, and the Crimean War years. Later chapters take up Tennyson, spiritualism, and her last years.

Kenyon adds short life notes between letter groups, so the reader can track moves, friends, and books as they come. The letters show a poet at home abroad: wife, mother, invalid, and keen watcher of politics and verse. The volume is a rich, first-hand record of a famous literary marriage and of Europe in the 1850s.
16680-the-onlooker-volume-1-part-2:
Alfred Henry Lewis edited this May 28, 1902 number of The Onlooker, volume one, part two, sold weekly in New York for five cents. Contents mix the Casual Club on Tammany and its lost funds, verse, a play column, Lady Betty's comment, drift of the day, and a tale of smuggled silk by the Old Lobbyist. The Observer firm held the copyright.

Lewis packs city politics, stage talk, and gossip into a small, sharp weekly. Tammany bosses, failed men, and club talk fill its pages with bite. The issue gives a lively peek at New York in 1902, best read for its snap judgments and its view of a city run by machines, money, and talk.
16894-oscar-wilde-his-life-and-confessio:
Frank Harris wrote this first volume of Oscar Wilde's life and confessions, printed and issued by the author in New York in 1918, with copyright in 1916. Chapters move from Wilde's father and mother on trial into schoolboy days and Trinity Dublin and Magdalen Oxford. Formative influences and poems, a quarrel with Whistler, and marriage follow. Faith and practice, reputation, and growth to originality about 1890 appear. A first play, a meeting with Lord Alfred Douglas, and the threatening cloud close the volume.

Harris tells Wilde's rise with a friend's heat, mixing memoir, gossip, and praise for wit. The volume ends as danger gathers, before the trials. Readers should weigh Harris with care, as he shapes tales to his own ends. Yet the book gives a vivid, close portrait of Wilde in his brilliant years.
16895-oscar-wilde-his-life-and-confessio:
Frank Harris wrote this second volume of Oscar Wilde's life and confessions, printed and issued by the author in New York in 1918, with copyright in 1916. Book two, chapter seventeen, opens in prison, where Wilde faced bad food and soul-degrading routine for two years' hard labor in a lonely cell. Harris asks whether Wilde would be conquered by prison or conquer it.

Harris mixes memoir, gossip, and judgment, praising Wilde's wit while mourning his fall. The volume tracks prison, release, and last years with a friend's heat. Readers should weigh Harris with care, as he shapes tales to his own ends, but the book gives a vivid, close portrait of Wilde in ruin and after.
16896-corinne-or-italy-volume-1-of-2:
Mme. de Stael wrote this novel Corinne, or Italy, volume one, issued by J. M. Dent in London in 1894 with an introduction by George Saintsbury and pictures by H. S. Greig. Saintsbury notes that Sainte-Beuve said with Corinne, Mme. de Stael ascended the Capitol, a phrase from his Coppet-and-Weimar talks on an idol of his youth he never renounced. A frontispiece shows crowds breaking ranks as horses pass.

De Stael sets a gifted woman poet against Italy's art, ruins, and love, with Oswald as her English counterpart. The novel mixes travel, art, and romance in a grand, emotional style. Readers who love Romantic fiction will find a landmark tale of a woman artist, famous in its day for its Italian scenes and its heroine's fire.
1700-the-life-of-charlotte-bronte-volume:
Charlotte Brontë's father goes blind, undergoes a cataract operation, and watches his daughter write The Professor and then Jane Eyre — the years this second volume covers. Gaskell draws on letters and on friends who knew Charlotte, and she writes as both biographer and mourner.

The volume follows Charlotte through fame, the deaths of her brother and sisters, and her marriage, and it keeps returning to Haworth parsonage as the place that formed her. It remains the first full life of Brontë, valuable for its closeness to its subject even where later research has corrected its details.
1706-a-history-of-science-volume-2:
Henry Smith Williams, assisted by Edward H. Williams, carries his history through the Middle Ages and into the new cosmology. Chapters cover science in the Dark Age, the work of Arab scholars who kept Greek learning alive, and medieval science in the West. They end with the turn brought by Copernicus and his successors.

The trial of Galileo gets careful treatment, as does the slow change from a closed cosmos to an open one. Written for general readers, the volume shows how knowledge survived a thousand years of neglect and then moved fast, once observers began to trust their instruments more than inherited authority.
17375-the-works-of-guy-de-maupassant-vol:
Volume two of Guy de Maupassant's works, copyright 1909, gathers Monsieur Parent and other stories. The title tale opens in a small public garden, where little George builds sand hills and tops one with a chestnut leaf while his father watches with concentrated love. Other tales include The Father, A Vagabond, Useless Beauty, Fly, The Mad Woman, That Pig of a Morin, and Mademoiselle Fifi.

Maupassant's prose is sharp, ironic, and exact, with Normandy peasants, Paris folk, and soldiers in turn. The set shows his range: comedy, cruelty, and pity in short frames. Short story lovers will find a rich volume from a master of the form, best read a tale or two at a time.
17722-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-3-no-:
The Bay State Monthly, a Massachusetts magazine, issued this number as volume three, number two, in May 1885. Its opening piece, by Charles Carleton Coffin, profiles Sylvester Marsh, projector of the Mount Washington Railroad. Coffin begins in the Pemigewasset Valley, where few settlers lived. John Marsh of East Haddam, Connecticut, travelled up the Merrimack valley with his wife Mehitable at the close of the last century.

As a monthly number, the magazine mixes Massachusetts biography, history, and literature. Readers get a snapshot of Bay State letters in 1885, through a railroad pioneer's life. The issue suits readers of New Hampshire and Massachusetts history.
1866-north-america-volume-2:
Ports where a hundred vessels once lay with double funnels, towns emptied by war, and Americans arguing their cause with heat fill this second volume of Trollope's travels. The book is partly a travel journal and partly an argument about the Civil War, written while the war was still undecided.

Trollope describes harbors that once held a hundred double-funnelled vessels, towns emptied by war, and Americans pleading their cause with heat. His judgments are blunt and sometimes unfair. That bluntness is the book's value: a famous English novelist reporting a country at war, in real time, without knowing how it would end.
18827-the-poetical-works-of-edward-young:
Little, Brown and Company issued this second volume of Edward Young's poems in Boston in 1859. It gathers work from across Young's career as a poet and clergyman of the eighteenth century. The contents run from long religious poems to satire, odes, and short occasional pieces written for friends and public events.

Readers will find The Last Day in three books, The Force of Religion, and the seven satires of Love of Fame, the Universal Passion, including two on women. An ode on the sea service, a paraphrase from Job, epitaphs, and letters in verse round out the volume. The collection shows Young's range, from grave meditation on death and faith to sharp comment on ambition and society.
18906-history-of-english-humour-vol-2:
The Reverend A. G. L'Estrange wrote this second volume of his History of English Humour, published in London in 1878 by Hurst and Blackett. An introduction on ancient humor precedes the history proper. L'Estrange, author of lives and travel books, treats humor as a subject worthy of serious, chronological study.

The second volume opens with burlesque and parody, including the Splendid Shilling, and moves through later writers and forms. A printer's error left no chapter fifteen, though no chapter is missing, a point the transcriber notes. Readers get a Victorian survey of English wit, useful for its examples and for its view of what counted as humor across centuries of writing.
19488-the-life-of-joan-of-arc-vol-1-and-:
Anatole France wrote this life of Joan of Arc, translated by Winifred Stephens and published in London and New York in the early nineteen hundreds in two volumes. France prides himself on following the rules of historical research, and scholars praised the work's care.

Scenes follow Joan from her village to the court, where a friar preaches that God has sent a holy maid to lead the king to his anointing. The biography weighs faith, politics, and war with a skeptic's fairness, and it remains a major literary life of the Maid.
19548-autobiography-of-seventy-years-vol:
George F. Hoar, longtime senator from Massachusetts, wrote this autobiography of seventy years, put out in New York in the early nineteen hundreds in two volumes. The first volume runs from his Concord boyhood and Harvard days through the founding of the Republican Party and the politics of Massachusetts.

Portraits of famous men fill the pages, from Roger Sherman's family to Daniel Webster and the lawyer-diplomat William Evarts. Hoar writes as a participant, not a bystander, and the book remains a first-hand guide to American public life across the nineteenth century.
19613-history-of-dogma-volume-2:
Adolf Harnack wrote this second volume of his history of dogma, translated from the third German edition and published in Boston in the early nineteen hundreds. It surveys how the old and new elements formed the Catholic Church, fixing what counted as apostolic.

Rule of faith, collected writings, organization, and worship each get a chapter, with Irenaeus, Tertullian, Hippolytus, Clement, and Origen as guides. Harnack traces how a living faith hardened into church order, a story still central to church history. Harnack traces how living faith hardened into church order, step by step. Harnack argues that titles first honoring Rome's temporary occupant gained a deeper truth when applied to its Church.
19938-recreations-of-christopher-north-v:
Christopher North was the pen name of John Wilson, Edinburgh professor and magazinist. His Recreations gather tales, essays, and sporting sketches. Volume two holds a child singing at a holy hour. She was as full of life as the star above her was of lustre. The hour tamed them both, the narrator says. At the party's bidding she renewed the strain. Wilson's lyric sentiment runs at full tide here.

Wilson co-created Blackwood's famous Noctes Ambrosianae dialogues. The Recreations collect his gentler, rural side. Angling, cottages, and Scottish scenery fill their pages. His prose influenced a generation of magazine writers. Volume two shows the sentiment Scots readers loved. Modern taste finds it lush; the craft is undeniable.
19973-the-mabinogion-vol-2:
Volume two of The Mabinogion continues Lady Charlotte Guest's Welsh tales. A great king's court assembles here in full splendor. Nine crowned kings, his tributaries, attend his high festivals. Earls and barons join them as invited guests. Such feasts mark Arthur's court in the Welsh telling. His dominion runs both by sea and by land. The Welsh Arthur is an emperor, not merely a king.

Guest's translation carried these tales to world readers in the 1840s. Volume two holds branches of the Mabinogi and native romances. Giants, hounds, and otherworld journeys crowd its pages. The prose keeps a bardic, formula-rich music. These stories are the deep source of much modern fantasy. Reading them is visiting the wellhead.
20109-reminiscences-of-sixty-years-in-pu:
George S. Boutwell published volume two of his Reminiscences of Sixty Years in Public Affairs in 1902. Boutwell served in Congress and in Grant's cabinet during stormy years. He recalls the Thirty-seventh Congress and its failed plans for compromise. Those fights split both parties before and during the Civil War.

One rival drew Democratic support as the People's Party candidate. Boutwell's own radical stand cost him backing from cautious Republicans. Such inside detail is the value of a long public memoir. Readers get war-era politics told by a man who voted, spoke, and served through it.
20539-letters-of-edward-fitzgerald-in-tw:
The second volume of Edward FitzGerald's letters carries his correspondence into his later years. The talk turns often to his famous translation of Omar Khayyam. Friends sent him copies, versions, and questions about the Persian poet he had made an English classic.

FitzGerald asks after a lithograph copy of Omar that a friend mentioned. My translation has its merit, he writes, but it misses a main one in Omar, which he will leave the friend to find out. He jokes in the same breath about Latin versions needing correction. The letters show his modesty, humor, and endless tinkering.
20646-the-nabob-vol-1-of-2:
The Nabob is the English version of Alphonse Daudet's great French novel Le Nabab, issued here in two volumes in 1898. It tells of a Tunisian adventurer who arrives in Paris with a fortune and buys his way toward power. This first volume opens with high praise for its author.

Henry James declared that Daudet stood at the head of his profession, and called him an admirable genius. Robert Louis Stevenson thought the same of Daudet's gift. The introduction gathers such verdicts before the story starts. Daudet's Paris of money, newspapers, and bought honors then unfolds in his bright, ironic style.
20778-sylva-or-a-discourse-of-forest-tre:
John Evelyn stands high among prose writers of the late seventeenth century, this edition notes. His Sylva, a discourse of forest trees, first came out in 1664. Volume one opens a work born of worry for England's shrinking woods.

Evelyn urges landowners to plant oaks and other trees for future fleets and homes. He mixes lore, craft, and sound growing advice for each kind. Sylva counts as an early call to care for forests as a public good. Gardeners and woodland lovers still read Evelyn for his zest and his deep store of tree craft.
20827-traditions-of-the-north-american-i:
Between two stormy seas lives young Chappewee in volume two of Traditions of the North American Indians. His father, the first of men, found a world rich in food and pleasant things. That first landing lay near the Dog-rib people's hunting grounds.

Creation tales and hero stories fill this second set of camp-fire traditions. James Athearn Jones took them from native tellers and early sources alike. Each tale shows how a people explained the world's start and shape. Read with care for its age, the volume keeps lore that oral memory alone once carried across long centuries of change.
20835-the-monctons-a-novel-volume-1-of-2:
Geoffrey Moncton, youngest son of a rich Yorkshire baronet, tells his family's tale. His father's hopes all centered on the first-born son, as custom ruled. Junior sons counted for little, yet Geoffrey still needed a gentleman's start in life.

An army commission, bought by Sir Robert, launches the young man's path. Volume one of The Monctons builds a world of rank, money, and family pride. The novel probes what younger sons did when birth order shut most doors. Its calm, period voice suits readers who like old family sagas told from inside the great house.
2088-life-and-letters-of-charles-darwin-:
Francis Darwin edits the second volume of his father's life and letters, covering the years after the Origin of Species appeared in 1859. Letters and notes trace the spread of evolution through the 1860s and 1870s. Francis Darwin chose letters that show his father's humour and modesty beside his science.

Chapters follow the Variation of Animals and Plants, the Descent of Man, and the Expression of the Emotions, with side work on coral reefs, earthworms, and geology. The volume lets Darwin speak for himself, in letters that are warm, candid, and often funny. The volume covers the fierce debates after 1859, when evolution divided churches, universities, and homes.
2092-the-writings-of-samuel-adams-volume:
Harry Alonzo Cushing edits the second volume of Samuel Adams's writings, covering 1770 to 1773, the years when resistance to Britain hardened into revolution. Adams writes letters, resolves, and appeals. Adams's letters of 1770 to 1773 cover the Boston Massacre and the Tea Party's approach.

The volume follows the Boston Massacre, the committees of correspondence, and the growing quarrel over tea and taxes. It gives Adams the organiser in his own words, urgent, plain, and fixed on colonial rights. Cushing's notes identify correspondents, so readers can follow Adams's network of patriots. Adams's plain, urgent letters show a man who trusted committees more than crowds.
20934-the-natural-history-of-selborne-vo:
A full spring called the Well Head gave Selborne its name and its start, says volume two. Constant water drew the village to its side across the ages. Its rivulet grows, by Oakhanger, into a fair stream of the parish.

Gilbert White's second volume adds letters on fossils, weather, and rural lore. His Hampshire parish stays the whole stage, yet the world feels vast there. White notes swallows, tortoises, echoes, and old customs with one keen eye. Read with volume one, it completes a classic of close looking that made one small place stand for all nature.
21260-canada-and-the-canadians-vol-2:
Sir Richard Henry Bonnycastle, a lieutenant-colonel of Royal Engineers in Canada West, published this two-volume account of Canada in 1849. Volume Two returns to Toronto after a flight to Lake Superior, then travels to Hamilton by fast steamer. Loons, diving bells, and birds caught with hooks at Niagara fill the road.

Bonnycastle meets Peter Jones, the Ojibwe chief and missionary, and weighs the Family Compact, church quarrels, and the new university. He argues for the value of Canada's union with Britain against repeal talk. Public works spending and President Polk's Oregon claims also catch his engineer's eye. The book mixes travel, politics, and natural history.
21329-the-nabob-vol-2-of-2:
Alphonse Daudet's novel of Parisian money and manners closes in this second volume, translated by George Burnham Ives with an introduction by Brander Matthews. Chapters resume at A Day of Spleen and move through an exhibition, a public man, and the affair of the Jenkins pearls. The nabob of the title is a rich outsider buying his way into Paris society.

A clerk's memoirs appear twice, framing the great man's rise and ruin from inside his household. The first night of a play called Revolte, scenes at Bordighera, and the obsequies fill the closing movements. Daudet drew the tale from real Paris scandals of wealth, politics, and newspapers in the early Third Republic.
21513-the-life-and-adventures-of-peter-w:
Robert Paltock's Life and Adventures of Peter Wilkins first appeared in 1751, and volume one is given here. A. H. Bullen's preface, from the 1884 edition, praises the tale as a fine voyage of the imagination. Bullen laments how little is known of Paltock himself.

Wilkins is cast away and finds a strange land reached by flight, in the manner of a dream voyage. Winged folk and a new world test the hero's wits and heart. The tale stands near Robinson Crusoe and Gulliver in kind, yet has a charm all its own. Hazlitt and fame open Bullen's essay on why writers seek lasting names.
21665-a-brief-history-of-the-english-lan:
J. M. D. Meiklejohn compresses English studies in volume two of his Brief History of the English Language and Literature. The set covers grammar, word history, and the history of letters. Each part alone, the notice says, makes a good one year's course.

This part suits high schools and colleges, where the first suits high schools alone. Meiklejohn aims at the utmost clearness and simplicity throughout. He sets syntax out as firm rules, so young learners have solid ground. Pupil-teachers in England used the book through four years of study and a first college year, with verse grammar held for the fifth.
2168-miscellaneous-writings-and-speeches:
Macaulay's second volume of miscellaneous writings gathers his contributions to the Edinburgh Review, from Dryden in 1828 to Barere in 1844. Essays on history, Mill on government, and Sadler on population follow. Macaulay's Edinburgh Review essays, written from 1828, made him famous before his History.

Macaulay writes with his usual vigour, judging books and politics in long, balanced periods. The volume shows the young reviewer becoming the historian of England, and it remains a model of critical prose. His Dryden essay, opening the volume, judges a poet he both admired and criticised. Sadler and Mirabeau pieces show Macaulay judging population and revolution with equal vigour.
2182-the-marble-faun-or-the-romance-of-m:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Roman romance continues in this second volume, where four friends in Rome face guilt, love, and a crime that will not stay buried. Miriam, Hilda, Kenyon, and the faun-like Donatello move through studios, shrines, and catacombs, each carrying a secret that shapes the others. The city itself, with its art and ruins, mirrors their inner lives.

Hawthorne dwells on conscience and on whether a wrong act can lead to deeper moral knowledge. The prose is rich and slow, full of art, Catholic ritual, and shadowed streets. Readers who enjoy a brooding, thoughtful novel will find this volume deepens the mystery and the moral questions of the first.
21851-history-of-the-negro-race-in-ameri:
Black Americans from 1800 to 1880 fill this second volume of George W. Williams's History of the Negro Race in America, published in 1883. Williams was the first Black member of the Ohio legislature and a judge advocate of the Grand Army of the Republic. His note says slavery grew with the Republic's growth until the sword parted them. He promises honest, impartial inquiry into the whole struggle over slavery's spread.

Six parts and twenty-nine chapters cover Black people as slaves, as soldiers, and as citizens. The wider work opens with the unity of mankind, a sketch of Africa, and the Black governments of Sierra Leone and Liberia. It was a landmark: a full history of Black America by a Black historian, built on records.
22021-gallipoli-diary-volume-2:
General Sir Ian Hamilton commanded the Allied force sent against Turkey at Gallipoli in 1915. His Gallipoli Diary, published in 1920, prints the journal he kept during the campaign. Volume II covers the last, hardest months. It begins with Lord Kitchener's advice and a visit from the Prime Minister's envoy.

Hamilton describes the August attacks at Sari Bair and Suvla, and how the Suvla landing collapsed. He argues with London, weighs the French plan, and watches the case for evacuation grow. Artillery reports fill the appendices. The diary is both a record and a defence, written by the man who carried the blame for a failed campaign.
22022-aunt-jo-s-scrap-bag-volume-2:
Louisa May Alcott, the author of Little Women, issued Shawl-Straps as the second series of Aunt Jo's Scrap-Bag. Alcott jokes in her opening pages that travel books are a fate no writer escapes. She had sworn never to write one, yet here it is. The book grew out of her tour of Europe in 1870 and 1871.

Alcott travelled with a younger companion through Brittany, Switzerland, Italy, and London. She writes about inns, peasants, pictures, and the small disasters of the road. Her tone is brisk, funny, and unsentimental. American readers at home got Europe through the eyes of "Aunt Jo," and the scrap-bag format let her mix sketches, stories, and chat.
2227-soldiers-three-part-2:
Rudyard Kipling returns to his three private soldiers of the British army in India for a second round of barrack-room tales. Soldiers Three, Part 2 follows Mulvaney, Ortheris, and Learoyd through scrapes, loves, and mischief, told largely in their own vivid slang. The stories swing between comedy and sudden sadness.

Kipling knew army life from the inside, and his soldiers feel real: loyal to each other, careless with officers, and tender in unexpected moments. The collection captures the color and hardship of India under the Raj. Readers get Kipling's early genius in short, punchy form.
22421-the-hesperides-noble-numbers-vol-1:
The Hesperides and Noble Numbers collect the poems of Robert Herrick in two volumes. An introduction notes a singular fact of English poetry. The first great age of lyric poetry matched the great age of drama.

The lyric school advanced steadily as the dramatic school declined. It declined from the bright promise of its dawn. Herrick stands near the center of that lyric flowering. His Hesperides holds secular songs of love, flowers, and country life. Noble Numbers adds his sacred poems to the set. Readers get a Cavalier poet's full range in one place. Short, musical lyrics make the volumes easy to dip into anywhere.
2252-king-henry-iv-part-2:
Old Falstaff and the ailing Henry IV dominate this darker sequel, in which rebellion simmers and the prince grows distant from his tavern friends. King Henry IV, Part 2 revisits Eastcheap with less laughter. Falstaff recruits ragged soldiers, Justice Shallow recalls past glories, and the king dies urging his son to busy his mind with foreign wars. Shakespeare deepens the history's shadows.

The play ends with Hal's coronation and his public rejection of Falstaff, a moment as cold as it is famous. Grief, age, and the price of power run through every scene. Together with Part 1 it forms Shakespeare's fullest portrait of England in transition.
2255-king-henry-vi-part-2:
England slides toward civil war in this middle panel of Shakespeare's Henry VI sequence, as the weak king loses France and his nobles scheme around him. Part 2 stages the fall of Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, the rebellion of Jack Cade, and the first clash of York and Lancaster. The commons rise, the court rots, and murder becomes policy.

Cade's Kentish rebels promise a topsy-turvy world, and Shakespeare gives their grievances real bite. York's ambition sharpens toward open claim. The play's violence and political cynicism anticipate the Wars of the Roses to come.
22567-history-of-the-united-states-volum:
E. Benjamin Andrews wrote a multi-volume History of the United States. Volume two's contents show the young nation forged by war. Military experience gained stands among its listed lessons and themes.

Nothing but war, Andrews argues, could have done this work. The population then was scattered across a vast country thinly. Difficulties of communication made unity harder still for the colonies. Other centrifugal influences pulled the states apart from one another. France was no longer a menace to the colonies after independence. Instead she became a natural friend and ally of America. Such themes carry the narrative through the Confederation and Constitution. Readers get scholarly nineteenth-century history with its arguments laid out plainly.
22689-the-confessions-of-a-caricaturist-:
The Confessions of a Caricaturist, volume 2, is the second half of Harry Furniss's memoir of life as a leading comic artist of Victorian London. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Furniss drew for Punch and illustrated books by Dickens and Carroll, and his confessions are stuffed with the famous faces he sketched.

The sample recalls a man who in 1887 startled the town with an artistic joke: a bold, full-scale parody of a Royal Academy exhibition, years in the making. Anecdotes of artists, actors, and politicians crowd the volume in that spirit. Furniss writes as an insider who loved the bohemian art world even while laughing at it. His memoir remains a rich source on the making of celebrity images.
22797-diderot-and-the-encyclop-dists-vol:
John Morley wrote Diderot and the Encyclopaedists, whose second volume completes his study of Denis Diderot and the men who made the great French Encyclopaedia. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Morley, a leading Victorian man of letters, treated the philosophes as heroes of free thought.

The sample turns to Diderot's own writings. It praises a dialogue Diderot published in 1773, the Conversation of a Father with His Children. The dialogue shows his taste for putting moral questions in an interesting way. The little dialogue, perfect in its simple, realistic form, asks a sharp question. May a man set his own judgment of special circumstances above the law of the land? Morley's second volume weighs such works one by one. The book remains a lucid English road into Enlightenment France.
2304-legends-and-lyrics-part-2:
Adelaide Anne Procter, one of Victorian England's most popular poets, continues her collection of legends and lyrics in this second part. The poems retell saints' lives, ballads, and moral tales in smooth, singable verse, with a strong undercurrent of charity and faith. Procter's gift was for the lyric that ordinary readers could carry in memory.

Dickens admired her work and published much of it, and her verses reached a wide audience in their day. The poems now read as period pieces, sincere and musical. Lovers of Victorian poetry will find a representative voice here.
2318-droll-stories-volume-2:
Honore de Balzac's Droll Stories, in this second volume of ten tales, retells ribald legends supposedly gathered from the abbeys of Touraine. The stories celebrate clever wives, lusty clerks, foolish husbands, and kings caught in their own traps, all in a mock-Renaissance French that the English keeps earthy and direct. Balzac wrote them as a holiday from his great realistic novels.

The tales are bawdy, funny, and sometimes cruel, with a storyteller's delight in human appetite. They show Balzac's range beyond the Comedie Humaine. Readers who enjoy Rabelaisian humor will find this volume a treat.
2333-critical-and-historical-essays-volu:
Macaulay's second volume of essays continues his triumphant run through history and literature, with pieces on figures such as Warren Hastings and Lord Clive. Critical and Historical Essays, Volume 2 shows the historian as advocate, defending and damning with equal vigor. His India essays in particular shaped British views of empire for generations.

The prose remains magnificent, even where modern readers will challenge his conclusions. The volume pairs well with the first for a full view of Macaulay's mind. History lovers will find it hard to put down. His essay on Warren Hastings remains the most debated piece in the volume.
23991-mission-furniture-how-to-make-it-p:
H. H. Windsor's Mission Furniture, How to Make It, Part Two, appeared in Chicago in 1910 as a Popular Mechanics handbook. Like the magazine, the handbooks were written so you can understand it, with texts and illustrations prepared expressly for the series by experts and revised by the magazine's editor.

Part two gives plans for an oak buffet, a plain oak hall clock, a rocking chair, and a curved back arm chair. A plate rack, a magazine table, and a waste paper basket follow. An oak writing desk and an oak couch with cushions follow, with oak stain and a tool for marking dowel holes. Stock lists specify wood already planed, sanded, and cut, in the plain, sturdy Mission style.
24215-the-comedies-of-william-congreve-v:
This first volume of William Congreve's comedies was transcribed from the 1895 Methuen and Company edition, part of the English Classics series edited by W. E. Henley. Its introduction first takes up the life of Congreve and how his four comedies differ in quality. It then turns to two wider questions, beginning with the charge of grossness of language against Restoration comedy.

The editor argues that grossness is a matter of time and place, not of fixed habit. A later age may reject a word from flatness and repetition rather than stricter morals. No word in Congreve, he holds, lacks an equivalent in contemporary writing. Readers get Congreve's comedies framed by a spirited defense of his wit and diction.
2469-repertory-of-the-comedie-humaine-pa:
The second part of the Repertory of the Comedie Humaine continues the guide to Balzac's characters and their appearances across his novels. Where Part 1 maps the major figures, this volume extends the census further, helping readers trace minor characters and family lines through the Human Comedy. The repertory's thoroughness is its point.

For readers deep in Balzac, the two parts together form an indispensable companion. Scholars still consult such guides to untangle his web. The volume rewards the patient Balzac traveler. The repertory was compiled to help readers track Balzac's returning characters.
24781-the-birth-of-yugoslavia-volume-2:
Henry Baerlein published this second volume in London in 1922, covering Yugoslavia from the autumn of 1918 to 1921. It opens with the new state's first year of liberty, then follows further months of trial: border fights, the Italian occupation of Adriatic towns, and the struggle to set frontiers. A closing chapter sketches national traits of Croats, Serbs, and Slovenes.

Baerlein writes from close knowledge, naming towns like Pola, Zadar, and Rijeka and quoting orders that left civil servants unpaid for refusing Italian forms. The book gives a ground-level view of a new country finding its shape after empire. It pairs with volume one for readers tracing how Yugoslavia was born.
24939-the-nursery-august-1873-vol-xiv-no:
The August 1873 number of The Nursery, published in Boston by John L. Shorey, gathers stories, verses, and pictures for young children. The Mother's Prayer opens the issue in a gentle key, while Coosie and Carrie, Fourth of July Cake, and Prairie Dogs mix domestic scenes with small adventures. A Journey to California stretches the young reader's map a little wider.

The Blackberry Frolic closes the number with Amy, her dog Quilp, and a party of schoolboys gathering berries, a summer outing told in the magazine's plain, cheerful voice. These monthly numbers were meant to be read aloud at bedtime or in the nursery, and this one shows the formula at its friendliest. It survives as a charming sample of Victorian children's periodical writing.
25096-the-roman-traitor-vol-2:
The second volume of Herbert's Roman Traitor carries the conspiracy of Catiline toward its crisis in the Rome of Cicero and Cato. Published in Philadelphia in 1853 as the second half of a historical novel, it resumes the plots, loves, and betrayals set in motion in volume one.

Conspirators such as Lentulus weigh flight against defiance, wondering what proof Cicero holds and whether a consular of Rome can be touched. Herbert keeps the pace high with revels, whispered tidings, and mounting fear among men who know the net is closing. The volume completes a melodramatic portrait of a republic destroying itself from within.
25256-traditions-of-lancashire-volume-2:
John Roby's Traditions of Lancashire, volume two, in a fifth edition from Routledge in 1872, collects legends and ghostly tales from the English county. Roby, a Manchester writer, gathered stories that mixed folklore, family history, and local pride, illustrated with engravings on steel and wood.

Tales include the Fairies' Chapel, the Luck of Muncaster, the Peel of Fouldrey, a legend of Bewsey, Clegg Hall, the Mermaid of Martin Meer, and Mother Red-Cap. A poacher chasing a hare toward the Fairies' Chapel shows Roby's method: a local scene, a strange turn, and a moral left hanging in the mist.
25340-the-works-of-lord-byron-vol-2:
The Works of Lord Byron, volume two, is a scholarly edition rich in notes on Byron's poems, including material around Childe Harold. Notes by Byron himself and, after Canto IV, by J. C. Hobhouse follow each canto, while footnotes record manuscript variants and useful information.

Editorial matter traces Byron's dealings with his publisher Murray in 1816, over proofs, a fair copy that never arrived, and scraps that wandered to Geneva before reaching Mrs. Leigh. The edition's apparatus lets readers see how Byron's texts were made, revised, and preserved. It suits students who want Byron with his history attached.
2579-the-french-revolution-volume-2:
Hippolyte Taine continues his history of contemporary France with this second volume on the Revolution, subtitled The Jacobin Conquest. Where the first volume traced spontaneous anarchy, this one follows the rise of a disciplined party that seized the new political organs of France.

Taine studies the Jacobins themselves, their mentality, their promises, and the machinery by which they took power. His tone is hostile and forensic, and he piles up police reports, speeches, and local records. The volume stands as a powerful, partisan account of how a revolution devours its own moderates.
25819-buchanan-s-journal-of-man-march-18:
Buchanan's Journal of Man, volume one, number two for March 1887, gathers archtypal literature for the future, with a general plan of the brain and synopsis of cerebral science. A reply to Miss Phelps on superficial criticisms follows.

Spiritual phenomena fill much of the issue, from Abram James and Eglinton to spirit writing and mind reading. Miscellaneous intelligence covers pigmies in Africa, a human phenomenon, surviving superstition, and a spiritual test of death. Craniology and crime, morphiomania in France, psychometry, and progress of spiritualism show a journal mixing science, spiritualism, and reform.
2582-the-modern-regime-volume-2:
Hippolyte Taine closes his great history with this volume on the Church and public instruction under the modern regime. After Taine's death in March 1893, his nephew Andre Chevrillon arranged these last manuscripts and wrote the introduction that opens the book.

Taine traces moral institutions, schools, and the evolution of French life between 1814 and 1890. His theme is how a nation trains its conscience and its children after revolution. The volume is drier than his portraits of Napoleon, but it completes his argument about what the new France kept, lost, and built.
25912-sea-power-in-its-relations-to-the-:
Captain A. T. Mahan, of the United States Navy, studies sea power in the War of 1812 in this second volume, printed in 1899. Chapters follow Bainbridge's squadron through the winter of 1812 to 1813, with actions between Constitution and Java and between Hornet and Peacock, and the growing pressure on the Atlantic coast. Mahan weighs how fleets, trade, and blockade shaped the war.

Figures give the scale of the sea fight: from September 1813 to March 1814, Americans took two hundred and seventy prizes outside the Lakes, with eighty six tied to West Indies trade. Mahan judges that quite one third of all prizes belonged to that trade, and notes the saying that the West Indies swarmed with American privateers. The book is a careful naval history of a war fought largely at sea.
2594-the-forsyte-saga-volume-2:
John Galsworthy continues the Forsyte saga with In Chancery, opening with an Indian summer of an old Forsyte before the law takes center stage. Soames prepares to take steps against Irene, Jolyon watches his family from home, and the younger generation hears the old quarrels anew.

Divorce, trusteeship, and a new love tangle the clan, while Timothy's house and Soho rooms hold the older order. Galsworthy writes with the same cool irony, letting property law expose private feeling. This volume turns the saga from a portrait of wealth into a drama of marriage breaking apart.
25940-the-posthumous-works-of-thomas-de-:
Alexander H. Japp edits the second volume of Thomas De Quincey's posthumous works, printed by Heinemann in 1893. Subtitled Conversation and Coleridge, with other essays critical, historical, biographical, philosophical, imaginative, and humorous, the book gathers pieces left in manuscript. Japp thanks Mrs. Baird Smith and Miss De Quincey for aid, and J. R. McIlraith for reading proofs.

Contents run from conversation and Coleridge through Finlay's history of Greece, the assassination of Caesar, a supplement on Cicero, and a memorial chronology. Chrysomania, on the gold frenzy, and a defense of the English peerage follow, with more essays after. De Quincey argues for close approximations a memory can hold over letter perfect truth no mind can retain.
2617-memoirs-of-general-william-t-sherma:
William T. Sherman opens this second volume of his memoirs in March 1864, when he relieved Grant in command of the Military Division of the Mississippi at Nashville. His departments covered Ohio, Cumberland, Tennessee, and Arkansas, and the Atlanta campaign lay ahead.

Sherman writes of Nashville and Chattanooga, of marches, battles, and the hard choices of total war, in a soldier's blunt prose. The memoir is both a campaign history and a self defense, written by a general who knew his fame would be argued over. It remains a key firsthand account of the Civil War's western theater.
2620-the-home-book-of-verse-volume-2:
Burton Egbert Stevenson made this second volume of The Home Book of Verse the book of love poems, opening part two with Emerson's Eros. The sense of the world is short, Emerson writes, yet to love and be beloved remains a lesson men and gods have not outlearned.

The anthology gathers love lyrics across ages, from tender courtship to lasting devotion, chosen for reading aloud at home. Stevenson keeps the tone warm and varied, mixing famous names with quieter voices. The volume suits couples, families, and anyone who wants love poetry without academic apparatus.
26243-discovery-of-oxygen-part-2:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele's Chemical Treatise on Air and Fire, here in part two of the Discovery of Oxygen series, reprints his 1777 experiments for the Alembic Club. The Edinburgh reissue of 1964 presents the Swedish chemist's hunt for the nature of air and fire, a question he calls the chief business of chemistry. Scheele weighs rival views of elements, from earth and phlogiston to the older peripatetic set.

He insists that fire and heat must be grasped before any solvent can work, and he reports a multitude of trials. Later pages show how to catch and move airs, filling bladders from bottles and back again. The treatise gives modern readers a direct view of chemistry before oxygen won its name, with apparatus, patience, and close watching.
26327-casa-braccio-volumes-1-and-2:
F. Marion Crawford's Casa Braccio, his twenty-fifth novel, appeared in two volumes in 1895, dedicated to his wife at Sorrento. Part one is called Sister Maria Addolorata, and part two Gloria Dalrymple. Pictures by A. Castaigne show Nanna and Annetta, a veiled face, and a man looking long and sadly at a woman.

The story opens at Subiaco, beyond Tivoli in the Samnite mountains, a town crowned by a cardinal's palace and tied to Saint Benedict and Saint Scholastica. Convent life, Italian society, and old family feeling drive the plot. A later chapter notes that Il Trovatore was still fresh, before Wagner eclipsed melody with tone poetry. The novel gives Crawford's Italy in full colour.
26416-the-naval-history-of-the-united-st:
Willis J. Abbot's second volume of American naval history opens in June 1813, after the loss of the Chesapeake, and follows the coastal war while Captain Porter's Essex cruises the Pacific. Fifteen men in the little cutter Surveyor, with six twelve-pound carronades, face fifty boarders from the British frigate Narcissus in the York River. Gunboat flotillas, Chesapeake Bay raids, and the cruise of the Argus fill the early chapters.

Later chapters cover the battle of the Enterprise and the Boxer, and the close of 1813 at sea. Still later chapters turn to Civil War actions against river forts, where sailors cut barricades with axe and ketch while troops marched through woods and marsh. Illustrations by H. W. McVicar and W. C. Jackson accompany the narrative throughout.
26495-a-system-of-logic-ratiocinative-an:
John Stuart Mill's System of Logic, volume one of the third edition, sets out the principles of evidence and the methods of scientific investigation. Book One treats names and propositions, asking what names denote: feelings, substances, qualities, relations, and quantity, and how definitions and classification work. Book Two turns to reasoning, the syllogism, demonstration, and necessary truths.

Book Three, the heart of the volume, treats induction: its grounds, the law of universal causation, the composition of causes, and observation and experiment.
