Mill lays out his four methods of experimental inquiry, tests that compare cases to find causes, with examples, and weighs plurality of causes and the intermixture of effects. The volume closes with the deductive method and the explanation of laws of nature.
2669-the-life-and-adventures-of-baron-tr:
Thomas Holcroft translated this second volume of Baron Trenck's memoirs, issued by Cassell in 1886. Holcroft himself wrote some thirty plays, including The Road to Ruin, and he brings a dramatist's pace to Trenck's tale.

The volume carries the baron's adventures onward, through fresh imprisonments, escapes, and service in foreign armies. Trenck's voice stays bold and unrepentant, even as fortune turns against him. The book closes a memoir that reads like an adventure novel, yet claims to be true. Holcroft's translation keeps Trenck's swagger intact through every reversal of fortune. Trenck's tale ends as boldly as it began.
2672-the-complete-writings-of-charles-du:
Charles Dudley Warner's second volume of complete writings opens with Saunterings, and a note correcting misapprehensions. Warner jokes that he will not ask an idle public to saunter under a false idea, and promises to go somewhere without teaching anything about it.

The essays wander through travel, society, and daily life with a genial, observant eye. Warner writes for readers who like talk better than textbooks, and his humor stays light. The volume shows a popular Victorian essayist at ease, strolling rather than preaching. Saunterings sets the tone: curious, unhurried, and fond of company.
26849-the-works-of-mr-george-gillespie-v:
George Gillespie was minister of Edinburgh and one of Scotland's commissioners to the Westminster Assembly of 1644. His works were first collected in this two-volume Edinburgh edition of 1846, with a memoir by M. W. Hetherington. Volume one opens with that memoir and an appendix of extracts from Wodrow's Analecta, then gives Gillespie's great dispute against the English popish ceremonies forced upon the Church of Scotland.

Gillespie argues his case in three parts: first against the necessity of the ceremonies, then against their expediency, then against their lawfulness. Festival days, kneeling at communion, and private administration of the sacraments all come under fire, as ceremonies that bind conscience, breed scandal, and keep the marks of past idolatry. The volume is a systematic Presbyterian brief against imposed ritual.
27506-political-women-vol-2:
Sutherland Menzies, author of Royal Favourites, published this second volume of Political Women in London with Henry S. King in 1873. The book treats the women who shaped French politics in the age of the Fronde and of Mazarin, closing scenes as well as triumphs.

Book five, continued from volume one, covers the struggle between Condé and Turenne and the noble conduct of Mademoiselle de Montpensier. It also covers the fall of the Fronde, Beaufort killing the Duke de Nemours in a duel, and the triumph of Mazarin. Book six gives closing portraits of Madame de Longueville, Madame de Chevreuse, the Princess Palatine, and Madame de Montbazon. It is history told through its leading women.
27515-state-trials-political-and-social-:
H. L. Stephen selected and edited this first volume of State Trials, political and social, published by Duckworth in London and the Macmillan Company in New York in 1899. Stephen frames his few remarks as a letter to Gerald, the friend who suggested the book, and confesses almost an apology for his undertaking.

The trials chosen are Sir Walter Raleigh, Charles I, the regicides, Colonel Turner and others, the Suffolk witches, and Alice Lisle. Portraits of Raleigh and Lord Russell come from photographs of pictures in the National Portrait Gallery. The volume gives famous trials in readable form, with their political and human stakes intact.
27537-sentimental-education-or-the-histo:
Gustave Flaubert's Sentimental Education, or the History of a Young Man, appears here in volume two of a collected edition, with a critical introduction by Ferdinand Brunetiere of the French Academy. M. Walter Dunne printed the edition for subscribers in New York and London in 1904.

Volume two continues the story from chapter eleven onward. Its chapters include a dinner and a duel, little Louise growing up, Rosanette as a lovely Turk, the barricade, and a strange betrothal. An auction and a bitter-sweet reunion follow. Flaubert traces a young man's hopes and failures with cool, exact prose. The volume stands as a classic of the modern novel.
27575-madame-bovary-a-tale-of-provincial:
Gustave Flaubert's Madame Bovary, a tale of provincial life, appears here in its first volume of two, with a critical introduction by Ferdinand Brunetière and a biographical preface by Robert Arnot. Simon P. Magee published it in Chicago in 1904.

Part one follows the new boy, a good patient, a lonely widower, and consolation, through a new ménage, a maiden's yearnings, and disillusion, to glimpses of the world and idle dreams. Part two opens a new field, adds friends and cares, and moves through silent homage and smothered flames to a village festival, a woodland idyll, and lovers' vows. Brunetière begins by noting that Flaubert remained at home and wrote.
27799-holland-v-1-of-2:
Edmondo De Amicis wrote Holland, translated from the Italian edition by Helen Zimmern and published in Philadelphia in 1894 in two volumes, the first covering Holland, Zealand, Rotterdam, Delft, and The Hague. Photographs by Charles L. Mitchell illustrate the edition.

De Amicis opens by marveling at a map where land and water seem to contest the country, then travels by canal and road through Dutch towns, churches, and harbors. The book is a classic of nineteenth-century travel writing, warm, observant, and fond of a people who made land from the sea.
28072-a-history-of-art-in-chald-a-assyri:
Georges Perrot and Charles Chipiez wrote A History of Art in Chaldæa and Assyria, published in London by Chapman and Hall and in New York by A. C. Armstrong in 1884. The first volume carries four hundred and fifty-two engravings, with fifteen steel and coloured plates.

Chapters cover the general character of Chaldæo-Assyrian civilization, the principles of its architecture, and funerary architecture, with sections on materials, the column, the arch, decoration, and orientation. Perrot and Chipiez's history remains a foundational nineteenth-century survey of Mesopotamian art, built on excavation and comparative study.
28191-opening-ceremonies-of-the-new-york:
Opening Ceremonies of the New York and Brooklyn Bridge, May 24, 1883, preserves the programme and speeches of the bridge's first day. Trustees, mayors Seth Low of Brooklyn and Franklin Edson of New York, and chief engineer Washington A. Roebling head the official list. Bands, prayers, and addresses fill the order of exercises.

Orations by Abram S. Hewitt and Richard S. Storrs praise the bridge as a triumph of engineering and a bond between two cities. The pamphlet, printed by the Brooklyn Eagle, gives the names, order, and words of the day. It remains a primary record of one of America's great public openings.
2834-the-portrait-of-a-lady-volume-2:
Henry James continues the story of Isabel Archer in this second volume of The Portrait of a Lady, picking up at chapter twenty-eight. Isabel, an independent young American woman in Europe, now faces the results of her marriage to Gilbert Osmond. Friends such as Lord Warburton and Ralph Touchett watch her freedom narrow inside a polished but cold household.

James traces Isabel's slow recognition of her mistake through conversation, social visits, and quiet scenes rather than open confrontation. The drama lies in what she understands about Osmond, her stepdaughter Pansy, and her own choices. Readers value the volume for its close study of conscience, money, and the price of a decision that cannot easily be undone.
28721-the-esperantist-vol-1-no-2:
The Esperantist, number 2, for December 1903, edited by H. Bolingbroke Mudie, served as the Esperanto gazette for spreading the international language. Published by the Esperanto Club at 41 Outer Temple, London, it cost fourpence a copy and three shillings a year. Its contents mix movement news with literature in and about Esperanto.

Pieces include what Max Müller said, The Beggar Maid, a continued Tempest translated by A. Motteau, An Autumn Daisy, The Biter Bitten, and The Three Friends. Phonetic longhand Esperanto, comrades in other lands, two fables, correspondence, dictionary specimens, and a grammar synopsis follow. Secretaries from Bournemouth to Surbiton, and a Remington fitted for Esperanto, show a language organizing itself.
28742-memorials-of-old-london-volume-1-o:
Memorials of Old London, volume 1, edited by P. H. Ditchfield and published by Bemrose and Sons of London and Derby in 1908, surveys the ancient city. Ditchfield dedicates the memorials to Lord Mayor Sir John Charles Bell, and the frontispiece paints the Old Bell Inn, Holborn, in 1897. The volume belongs to the Memorials of the Counties of England series.

Chapters cover London in early times, Celtic, Roman, Saxon, and Norman, the Tower of London, St. Bartholomew the Great, and the London Charterhouse. Glimpses of medieval London, the Guildhall, the city companies, the Hanseatic League, and the city's arms follow. Illustrations show Roman tiles, pottery, sandals, city gates, and old London Bridge. Readers get London's past, building by building.
2875-personal-recollections-of-joan-of-a:
Mark Twain continues his life of Joan of Arc in this second volume, again through the voice of her page and secretary, the Sieur Louis de Conte. The chapters carry Joan from court and camp through Patay, the crowning of the heir of France, and her five great deeds, toward capture and trial. Twain presents the translation as drawn from an unpublished manuscript in the National Archives of France.

Battle scenes show armies hurling each other backward and forward, with panic spreading when soldiers fear Joan has been killed. The narrator's devotion keeps the history personal even as the stakes widen. The volume closes Joan's story, pairing the triumph of Reims with the doom she herself foretells.
29092-the-complete-poetical-works-of-sam:
This second volume of The Complete Poetical Works of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, edited by Ernest Hartley Coleridge, gathers the dramatic poems and versions now published for the first time. The volume carries textual and bibliographical notes, with the same careful system as volume one: Greek transliterated between plus signs, Hebrew between pound signs, and diacritics shown by breve and macron marks.

Coleridge's plays and dramatic fragments stand beside his lyric verse, showing a poet who worked in many forms. Ernest Hartley Coleridge, the poet's grandson, edited the set with scholarly care. Readers get the second half of a complete Coleridge, valuable for students of Romantic drama and for anyone who knows the Ancient Mariner and wants the rest.
29452-the-wings-of-the-dove-volume-1-of-:
Henry James's novel The Wings of the Dove, volume one of two, was printed in New York in 1902 by Charles Scribner's Sons. It opens with Kate Croy waiting for her father, pale with irritation, moving from a shabby sofa to a sticky armchair as she weighs whether to leave without seeing him. Fortune, honor, and love press on her from the first page.

James writes in his late, winding manner, tracing motives that shift like light in a room. This first volume sets the triangle that will test Kate, her lover, and a dying heiress. Readers of James will find the master's art at full stretch: subtle, dense, and deeply felt.
29716-the-harmsworth-magazine-v-1-1898-1:
Volume one, number two of the Harmsworth Monthly Pictorial Magazine, dated 1898 to 1899, opens with a complete story by Catherine Childar, My Travelling Companion, illustrated by Fred Pegram. It begins on a miserable November day, when splenetic Englishmen, the French say, flock to the Thames to drown themselves. The narrator sits over a dingy dining-room fire, finding fire more cheering than water.

Her eldest sister bursts in with a letter: Tommy, here is an invitation, from a schoolfellow named Mysie Sutherland, who lives near a place the narrator must visit. A picture asks, will he come, after Marcus Stone. Readers of Victorian magazines will find a lively, illustrated number from the age of the new pictorial press.
306-the-early-short-fiction-of-edith-wha:
Volume Two of Wharton's early short fiction gathers her best-known tales with early verse. Stories include Afterward, The Fulness of Life, Xingu, The Verdict, and The Reckoning, dated from 1893 to 1911. Poems like Botticelli's Madonna and Chartres follow.

Afterward, from January 1910, opens with a laughing claim about a ghost no one will ever know. Xingu satirizes a ladies' lunch club with a single mysterious word. The volume shows Wharton's wit sharpening into irony. It pairs with Volume One as a complete early survey. Wharton's early verse shows the poet she set aside for fiction.
30708-history-of-the-rise-of-the-hugueno:
Henry M. Baird, a professor at the University of the City of New York, wrote this second volume of his history of the Huguenots, printed in London in 1880. It covers the years from the Edict of January in 1562 to the death of Charles the Ninth in 1574. Baird treats French Protestants not as a sect alone, but as a force in the wars and courts of France.

Book two opens with the first civil war, the massacre of Vassy, and the pleas of Louis of Condé and Theodore Beza for justice. Later chapters follow court plots, the Guises, Jeanne d'Albret, and the shifting hopes of the Huguenot cause. It is a detailed, source-based history, best for readers who already know the outline of the French wars of religion and want the full political story.
31064-stories-by-american-authors-volume:
Held here is volume two of Stories by American Authors, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1896, with copyright in 1884. Its six stories are The Transferred Ghost by Frank R. Stockton, A Martyr to Science by Mary Putnam Jacobi, Mrs. Knollys by J. S. of Dale, A Dinner-Party by John Eddy, The Mount of Sorrow by Harriet Prescott Spofford, and Sister Silvia by Mary Agnes Tincker.

The opening story, first printed in Century Magazine in May 1882, begins at the country residence of Mr. John Hinckman, a place of broad, smooth-shaven lawns, towering oaks and elms, bosky shades, and a little quiet rill spanned by a rustic bridge. Fruits and flowers, people, endless chess, billiards, rides, walks, and fishing fill the house, yet none of them, nor all together, would have held the narrator long. It is an anthology of American short fiction.
31545-studies-in-spermatogenesis-part-1-:
N. M. Stevens's Studies in Spermatogenesis, with especial reference to the accessory chromosome, part one, was published by the Carnegie Institution of Washington in September 1905 as publication number thirty-six. Stevens opens with the problem of sex determination, noting that further investigation of the so-called accessory chromosome seemed necessary. According to McClung in 1902, the chromosome might be a sex determinant, a view supported by Sutton in 1902 in work on Brachystola magna.

The study examines sperm formation in insects, tracing chromosomes through cell division to test that hypothesis. Chromosomes are the small bodies in a cell that carry inherited traits. Cell division is the process by which one cell splits into new cells. In plain terms, it asks how the making of sperm cells decides the sex of the young. Stevens's work became a landmark in genetics, since the accessory chromosome proved to be the sex chromosome.
31546-studies-in-spermatogenesis-part-2-:
N. M. Stevens's Studies in Spermatogenesis, part two, is a comparative study of the heterochromosomes in certain species of Coleoptera, Hemiptera, and Lepidoptera, with especial reference to sex determination. It was published by the Carnegie Institution of Washington in October 1906, as publication number thirty-six, part two, pages 33 to 74, with plates eight to fifteen. Heterochromosomes are chromosomes that differ in appearance between the sexes, and Stevens compares them across beetles, true bugs, and butterflies and moths.

The study extends part one's work on the accessory chromosome, testing whether these differing chromosomes decide sex. Stevens's comparative method, setting species beside species, gave genetics some of its first firm evidence. Readers of the history of biology will find a technical but landmark paper, from the years when the chromosome theory of sex was taking shape.
32145-the-poetical-works-of-william-lisl:
Volume two of the poetical works of William Lisle Bowles, canon of St. Paul's Cathedral and rector of Bremhill, appeared in Edinburgh, London, and Dublin in 1855, with a memoir, critical dissertation, and explanatory notes by the Reverend George Gilfillan. The memoir opens with a claim about poetry and its age: the poetry of each age is vitally connected with its character and progress, as vividly as its politics or its religion.

Gilfillan pictures a garden's soil through flowers and herbs alike. He purposes to compare the brief course of Bowles's work with that standard. Readers get a mid-Victorian collected edition, pairing Bowles's verse with a critical life. The volume serves readers who want both the poems and the contemporary judgement on a poet of an earlier generation.
32186-tales-from-blackwood-volume-2:
Tales from Blackwood, volume 2, gathers magazine stories first printed in Blackwood's Magazine, published by William Blackwood and Sons in Edinburgh and London. Its contents mix adventure, humour, and the supernatural, with authors named for most pieces. The volume opens with Colonel E. B. Hamley's Lazaro's Legacy, a tale of the siege of Gibraltar, first printed in December 1851.

Hamley's tale draws on his grandfather Major Flinders's notebook, kept as an accurate journal of siege incidents under his own observation. Other tales include Dr. Maginn's A Story without a Tail, Faustus and Queen Elizabeth, Professor Aytoun's How I Became a Yeoman, Mrs. Southey's Devereux Hall, Dr. Robert Macnish's The Metempsychosis, and College Theatricals. Readers get a Victorian magazine miscellany, varied in tone and setting.
32330-a-struggle-for-rome-v-2:
Felix Dahn's historical novel appears here in volume two of three, translated from German by Lily Wolffsohn and published in London in 1878. The volume continues Book Three, opening with Theodahad and the arrival of a Gothic escort sent by Totila. At a villa evening meal, Valerius, Valeria, and Julius debate peace and war, with the old Roman dreading armed Greeks entering Italy and the young hero Totila full of ardour for war.

Valeria believes that war would teach her father to love Totila as he deserves, since Totila would defend both her and Italy. The novel sets personal loyalty against the fate of a kingdom, as Goths, Romans, and Byzantines struggle for Rome. This middle volume carries readers deep into Dahn's vast, dramatic account of a collapsing empire and the leaders who fought over its future.
32341-davenport-dunn-a-man-of-our-day-vo:
Charles Lever's Davenport Dunn, A Man of Our Day, volume one of two, with illustrations by Phiz, was published in London by Chapman and Hall in 1862. Its first chapter, Hydropathic Acquaintances, starts at Como beside the lake, a haunt dear to opera dancers, a fancy of prima donnas, a haven for retired barytones. Lever wonders why this spot should rank as heaven for all who have lived, sighed, sung, and danced inside the footlights' magic ring.

Crystal waters mirror every cliff and crag with intense distinctness, vegetation runs variegated to the very verge of extravagance, orange-trees stand overloaded with fruit, and arbutus bespangled with red berries. Villas more coquettish than any scene-painter conceived, with terraces, statues, vases, fountains, and marble balconies steeped in balmy odours, complete a picture of brilliant colouring and variety. Readers get a Victorian novel opening at a fashionable spa.
32342-davenport-dunn-a-man-of-our-day-vo:
Charles Lever's novel continues in this second and final volume, with illustrations by Phiz. It opens with Davenport Dunn entering a drawing room before dinner to find Lady Augusta Arden alone, his heart beating fast as he wonders how she remembers their morning scene. Lady Augusta greets him with an affable smile, teasing him about the pressing despatch that called him away and about his talk of important business.

From that drawing-room meeting, the volume follows Dunn, a man of his day, through ambition, society, and the claims of love and reputation. Lever writes with wit about manners, money, and the gap between what people say and what they want. Readers who began the story in volume one will find its threads drawn together here in a brisk, social conclusion.
32489-stories-pictures-tell-book-2:
Flora L. Carpenter's Stories Pictures Tell, Book Two, published in Chicago and New York in 1918, continues her picture-study lessons for schools. Carpenter was formerly supervisor of drawing in Bloomington, Illinois, and instructor at Waite High School in Toledo. She again wrote for teachers who lacked time to gather material on pictures, though much could be found about artists. Half-tone photographs illustrate each lesson, with suggestions to teachers at the end.

Contents follow the school year, from Landseer's Shoeing the Bay Mare and Reynolds's Angels' Heads in September and October, through Millet's First Step and Madame Ronner's Fascinating Tale. Renouf's Helping Hand, Reynolds's Strawberry Girl, and Troyon's Return to the Farm close the year. A review of pictures and artists studied helps teachers and pupils recall the course.
32888-paris-from-the-earliest-period-to-:
William Walton continues his history of Paris in a second volume from George Barrie and Son of Philadelphia, copyright 1899. Its opening chapter treats national and municipal administration, above all the Parlement of Paris. The Parlement's history, Walton argues, would itself constitute a history of the capital.

The chapter follows the prévôts, the king's lieutenants who administered justice and commanded the watch. Its first official record is a charter of 1060, signed by Étienne, prévôt de Paris. Walton contrasts that Étienne, who advised plundering a treasury, with Étienne Boileau, chosen by Saint-Louis for straight justice. Later passages cover the charniers of the Cimetière des Innocents, where bones were stored to make room for new corpses.
33363-the-poetical-works-of-elizabeth-ba:
Elizabeth Barrett Browning's poetical works, in six volumes, reach volume two in this London edition of 1890. Its contents run from The Romaunt of Margret and Isobel's Child to The Lay of the Brown Rosary, A Romance of the Ganges, and Lady Geraldine's Courtship. The volume also holds Bertha in the Lane and The Runaway Slave at Pilgrim's Point, showing Browning's range from romance to protest.

The poems suit readers who love Victorian verse at its most musical and earnest, with ballads, romances, and lyrics side by side. Browning's voice, at once tender and bold, carries each piece. For students of poetry, this volume is a rich slice of a major poet's work, best read slowly, poem by poem.
33472-with-the-world-s-great-travellers-:
With the World's Great Travellers, volume two, edited by Charles Morris and Oliver H. G. Leigh, gathers travel writing from many lands. Its contents move from New York, Washington, and Chicago to Winnipeg Lake, a fine scenic route, South Pass and Fremont's Park, and the Yellowstone Park, with authors from Leigh and W. F. Butler to John C. Fremont. The special edition was printed in Chicago in 1901.

The volume suits armchair travelers, offering first-hand accounts of American places in the words of those who saw them. Its tone is varied, from guidebook detail to personal adventure. For readers who love travel anthologies, it is a rich, old-fashioned collection, full of routes, wonders, and the voices of explorers.
3367-a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-volume-2:
William Dean Howells continues A Hazard of New Fortunes in its second part, with an apartment found. The volume opens on the evening March accepts a lower offer from Mrs Green and agrees to rent her flat. The widow, whose earlier lodgings March had turned down, sits with her daughter in a back room upstairs. Under a shaded lamp, the mother sews while the girl sketches beside her at one table.

As they chat, the girl pauses now and then, raising her head and cocking it slightly to examine her drawing. That quiet scene carries the novel's domestic weight: a household's fortunes decided in a parlor, not a boardroom. Readers mid-novel will find Howells's New York taking shape room by room, as the Marches settle and the magazine's world gathers around them.
3372-their-silver-wedding-journey-volume:
William Dean Howells continues the Marches' silver wedding journey in this second volume. Burnamy waits for them at Carlsbad station, and Mrs March chides him in a motherly way for going to such trouble to greet them. For now she hides any hint that she knows he spent an extra day with the Triscoes in Leipzig.

His warm delight at seeing both Marches matches everything she could have hoped for. Still, she wishes he had not tarried, and that small concealment tints their reunion. Howells writes the comedy of older travelers: a marriage of twenty-five years, a young man's romance, and a spa town where everyone watches everyone else.
33743-the-history-and-antiquities-of-the:
Karl Otfried Müller, professor at the University of Göttingen, wrote this history and antiquities of the Doric race. The work forms the second and third volumes of Müller's Histories of Greek Tribes and Cities, following a separate first volume on Orchomenos and the Minyae. This volume is the first of two.

Book One traces the Doric race from earliest times to the end of the Peloponnesian War. Müller's learned, systematic approach shaped nineteenth-century classical scholarship, and the history remains a landmark for students of ancient Greece.
3376-the-landlord-at-lion-s-head-volume-:
William Dean Howells continues The Landlord at Lion's Head in this second volume. Jackson writes to Westover as promised, and outdoes that promise with his mother, sending her a letter each week all winter. She once tells Cynthia, as the girl carries the mail in from the barn, that she feels she lives only between letters. It is ridiculous, she adds, in her own spelling.

The men leave the mail in the barn until their horses are stabled, having driven it over from Lovewell. That small routine carries the novel's feeling: a mountain hotel, a family apart, and letters as lifelines. Howells writes the second half of his Lion's Head story with patience, letting winter, work, and affection do the work of plot.
33798-sinister-street-vol-2:
Compton Mackenzie continues the education of Michael Fane in this second volume of Sinister Street, published in New York in 1919 with copyright from 1914. Book One, Dreaming Spires, opens with Michael glad to start the adventure of Oxford from Paddington, whose simplicity might faintly mitigate alarms no deliberation could disperse. Chapters follow his first day, week, and term, Cheyne Walk, youth's domination, gray and blue, and Venner's. They also follow the Oxford looking-glass, the lesson of Spain, Stella in Oxford, and his last term, week, and day.

Book Two, Romantic Education, moves through Ostia Ditis, Neptune Crescent, the Café d'Orange, Leppard Street, the innermost circle, and Tinderbox Lane. It also moves through the gates of ivory and horn, seeds of pomegranate, and the old world, closing with an epilogical letter. Mackenzie writes a rich, autobiographical novel of youth, Oxford, and London.
33801-the-mysteries-of-paris-illustrated:
Eugene Sue's vast Paris novel reaches its second volume in this Boston edition de luxe, illustrated with etchings. Volume two follows a ball, a rendezvous, an ambush, and a rectory house, then turns to Clemence d'Harville, misery, and a judgment and execution. Rigolette, a young working woman, enters the story near its close.

Sue moves between salons and back streets, letting rich and poor cross paths in a city of secrets. Etchings by Mercier, Bicknell, Poiteau, and Adrian Marcel mark key scenes. The volume shows why the novel gripped readers: fast incident, strong feeling, and a Paris that feels both grand and dangerous.
34010-the-history-and-antiquities-of-the:
Karl Otfried Muller, a professor at Gottingen, wrote this history of the Doric race, translated by Henry Tufnell and George Cornewall Lewis in a second, revised edition published in London in 1839. Volume two holds Book Three on the political institutions of the Dorians and Book Four on their domestic institutions, arts, and literature.

Chapters trace Greek states from royal aristocracy of the heroic age through timocracy, tyranny, and democracy, with the supposed laws of Lycurgus drawn from the Delphic oracle. Appendices treat the Doric dialect and chronological tables. The volume remains a classic of early Greek history.
34053-the-palace-of-pleasure-volume-2:
William Painter's Palace of Pleasure, Elizabethan versions of Italian and French novels, returns in this second volume, edited for a fourth time by Joseph Jacobs and published in London in 1890. Painter drew on Boccaccio, Bandello, Cinthio, Straparola, Queen Margaret of Navarre, and others, turning their tales into English.

Volume two continues the first tome from the forty-seventh novel, Galgano and Madonna Minoccia, through the Duke of Venice and Ricciardo, Filenio Sisterno, and a muleteer. Jacobs's edition gives the tales with scholarly care. The book offers a rich store of Renaissance storytelling in Tudor dress.
3406-ragged-lady-volume-2:
The second half of William Dean Howells's novel about Clementina Claxon, a young woman known to friends as a ragged lady, picks up her story. The volume picks her up as an adult moving through hotels, drawing rooms, and new acquaintances, still carrying the plain habits of her earlier life. A woman in mourning for her mother, a clerk who recalls her old rooms, and other small encounters mark how far she has come.

Howells keeps his eye on manners and money rather than on sudden twists. Clementina must judge suitors, friends, and her own pride as her prospects change. Readers who start here should know the story begins in volume one, but this half stands as a study of a woman learning to live in a richer world without losing herself.
34074-the-new-gresham-encyclopedia-amiel:
The New Gresham Encyclopedia, volume one, part two, runs from Amiel to Atrauli, published in London in 1922 by the Gresham Publishing Company. Plates in this part cover human anatomy, archaeology of the stone, bronze, and iron ages, and architecture, with a color map of Asia. A key to pronunciation opens the volume.

The encyclopedia gives short, ordered entries for a general reader, with guides to saying foreign names. Part two continues the first volume's alphabetical run. The book serves readers who want the reference knowledge of its age in handy parts.
3647-the-dwelling-place-of-light-volume-:
This second volume of Winston Churchill's industrial novel follows Janet Bumpus and her tangled tie to Ditmar, a powerful mill man. In the days after their first meetings, the tension of their relationship tests Janet's ingenuity and her powers of resistance. She feels shame at the feelings he arouses, yet a sense of mastery at holding such a man in leash pleases her vitality and spirit.

Churchill writes Janet's inner life with care, as she weighs pride, resentment, and desire. The excitement that the leash might break hangs over every scene. Readers who began the novel in volume one will find here its romantic and moral center, where a young woman in a mill town fights to keep her independence.
3682-mr-crewe-s-career-volume-2:
This second volume of Winston Churchill's political novel follows Mr Crewe into the legislative hall itself. The State Tribune gives column reports of hearings, with little editorial pushes beside them, and the hall must be lighted for evening gatherings drawn by Crewe's energy. Churchill notes that it is not the function of a romance to repeat House proceedings with journal exactness.

Instead he likens the state house to pioneer Kentucky, a dark and bloody ground where battles of selfish interests ebb and flow. Crewe, an innocent and unselfish bystander in this telling, desires only to make his state a utopia, while measures and men press against him. The volume suits readers following a reformer from rallies into the hard work of lawmaking.
3737-a-far-country-volume-2:
Winston Churchill sends Hugh Paret to the state capital in the second book of his novel of modern America. Hugh arrives by train and gazes at the state house dome. Then he walks into a lobby thick with lawmakers and tobacco smoke, where Colonel Paul Barney, generalissimo of the railroad, runs the legislative battle from his rooms. The young lawyer learns how votes are managed among farms and cities, and how principle bends under pressure.

Later scenes show a popular speaker working a crowd on prices, wages, and the cost of a wife's dress, while the audience laughs and nods. Churchill uses these set pieces to ask how a democracy talks itself into serving private wealth. Readers who like political novels will find this volume the most public part of Hugh's story, with back rooms and stump speeches in full view.
3839-memoirs-of-marguerite-de-valois-que:
Marguerite de Valois continues her memoirs in a second book dominated by the League and war against the Huguenots. Her brother returns to court with the Catholic nobility, and the king, pleased at first, soon turns his thoughts to destroying the Huguenots and to engaging her brother against them. Marguerite herself becomes a target, and the king works to keep her from her husband.

Her escape takes her through Flanders toward Spa, with gentlemen escorts seeing her safe to the frontier. At Cateau-Cambresis she sends a countess a black satin gown, curiously embroidered, that cost nine hundred crowns, while news arrives of Huguenot troops planning to attack her on the road. The book reads as a queen's flight through a kingdom at war with itself.
3848-memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-mo:
Madame de Montespan, maid of honor to Henrietta of England, recalls the second book of her court memoirs with gossip and statecraft intertwined. After six months of marriage Henrietta has grown so beautiful that the king himself draws attention to it, and Monsieur, indifferent to his wife, still takes offense on a point of honor. The Chevalier de Lorraine's revenge and the king's suspicions darken the comedy.

The king, planning a Dutch expedition that needs English help, sends Henrietta herself as negotiator to her brother Charles, since she is the king's pet. A Venetian embassy meanwhile congratulates Louis on Flanders and predicts triumphs for ambition. The volume mixes bedroom talk with diplomacy, and readers who like court memoirs will find it frank and fast moving.
3928-prince-zilah-volume-2:
Jules Claretie's second volume of Prince Zilah keeps its hero amid Paris fashion and chatter. A baroness rattles on about sabots she was told to wear, miserable things that nearly made her break her neck entering her carriage, yet something new that attracts attention. Everybody asks what they are, she says, and when one has pretty feet, not too large, the effect is worth the risk.

She moistens her red lips with lemonade, nibbles a cake, and hastily departs just as Prince Andras's carriage stops before the gate. The baroness waves a gay hand and will not take a minute of his time, since he has pleasanter business today. Readers who like Claretie's society novels will find a volume of gossip, fashion, and a prince pursued by talk.
3932-zibeline-volume-2:
Philippe de Massa's second volume of Zibeline moves among painters, generals, and actresses in Paris. A painter, asked what he pencilled on the back of his menu, answers with the profile of General de Prerolles. He proposes the general's mare Aida as a companion picture to Seaman, the famous horse that won the great steeplechase at Liverpool in 1882. The general himself would adorn a canvas hung opposite her at the next Salon.

The general interrupts in alarm, begging to be spared the honor of figuring in such an equestrian contradance. He pleads that he lacks the means to bequeath to posterity what his fair model possesses. The actress asks whether she is as rich as they say. Readers who like Massa's society romance will find a volume of art talk, horses, and money.
3936-a-woodland-queen-reine-des-bois-vol:
Andre Theuriet's second volume of A Woodland Queen turns from inheritance papers to the forest itself. Woodsmen set steel to a great oak, and the trunk trembles from base to summit like a living thing. Bark, sapwood, and core fly in shivers, yet the oak resumes an impassive attitude and bears the assaults stoically.

Looking upward at its proud and stately head, one would affirm it never could fall. Then the woodsmen fall back, a moment of solemn and terrible suspense passes, and the enormous trunk heaves and plunges down among brushwood with a crash of breaking branches. A sound of lamentation rumbles through the icy forest. Readers who like Theuriet's country writing will find a volume of work, wonder, and loss.
3940-the-confession-of-a-child-of-the-ce:
Alfred de Musset's second volume of The Confession of a Child of the Century studies a love grown cold. The narrator and his mistress keep a curious analysis of their past intercourse, and she treats him with kindness that he distrusts. They walk in the garden but no longer wander through woods and valleys, and she opens the piano when they are alone.

Her voice no longer awakens transports of joy like sobs inspired by hope. When they part, she gives him her hand, but he feels it lifeless, and effort marks their familiar ease. Sadness lies at the bottom of it all, and both feel a third party between them. Readers who like Musset's jealousy study will find a volume of estrangement told from inside.
3944-monsieur-de-camors-volume-2:
Octave Feuillet's second volume of Monsieur de Camors turns on a mother's hopes for her daughter. Madame de Tecle tells Camors, in confidence she will confess to God that night, that her daughter, when she has done all she can for her, will make him an excellent wife. The girl will benefit him and be an honor to him, and one day thank her mother with all her heart.

Madame de Tecle perceives already what her daughter wishes and loves, though Camors cannot know or even suspect it. There is already a woman in that child, she assures him, much more charming than her mother. Then the door opens, and Mademoiselle Marie enters brusquely holding a gigantic doll in each hand. Readers who like Feuillet's society drama will find a volume of matchmaking and innocence.
3948-cinq-mars-volume-2:
Alfred de Vigny's second volume of Cinq Mars turns to madness, devotion, and a hidden listener. A woman asks the young man whether he has said anything to afflict her, or whether he loves, and reassures him she will not tell his love. She calls herself mad but gentle, very gentle, and says three days ago she was beautiful, asking whether his love is beautiful too.

Then suddenly Jeanne begins to recite the service for the dead in a monotonous voice, with incredible rapidity, seated on the bed and turning the beads of a long rosary. The door opens, she looks up, and flees through another door in the partition, leaving a startled witness to wonder whether he saw an imp or an angel. Readers who like Vigny's romance will find a volume of mystery and foreboding.
3955-l-abbe-constantin-volume-2:
Ludovic Halevy's second volume of L'Abbe Constantin opens with a priest's evening prayer. The abbe prays God to bless Mrs Scott in her children, and to give Miss Percival a husband after her own heart. The prayer follows a sweet and happy day passed through the bounty of two women. Gratitude, not doctrine, frames the chapter.

The next chapter, titled The Fair Americans, turns to Paris itself. Formerly Paris was the Parisians' own, Halevy writes, as London is the Englishmen's and Madrid the Spaniards'. Those times are no more, and Paris has become an immense Babel, a universal and international city with no frontiers left to France. Readers who like Halevy's gentle comedy will find a volume of charity, visitors, and a changing capital.
3959-a-romance-of-youth-volume-2:
Francois Coppee's second volume of A Romance of Youth turns on a father's farewell counsel. Amedee sheds tears on his father's shoulder, while the old man softly strokes his son's hair with trembling hands. The boy sobs that he loves and respects his father with all his heart. He begs to dress quickly, go to the office together, return the same way, and dine like good friends.

He begs his father not to ask him to leave that day. But Monsieur Violette suddenly rises as if he has formed a resolution, and answers firmly that he has said what he had to say, and the boy will remember it. That is sufficient, he says, and bids Amedee go amuse himself with friends that evening. Readers who like Coppee's tender realism will find a volume of family love and parting.
3964-cosmopolis-volume-2:
Paul Bourget's novel of Rome in the late nineteenth century moves among rich travelers, artists, and schemers who form a small world of their own. The second volume turns to Countess Steno, a bold Venetian woman who faces danger with energy rather than fear.

Steno looks each threat in the face and acts, while those around her weigh risk, love, and gain in her shadow. Bourget uses her parties, talks, and private moments to show how a cosmopolitan set judges character and forgives scandal. The volume works as a portrait of high society and as a slow study of a woman who refuses to be ruled by fright.
3969-jacqueline-volume-2:
Th. Bentzon, writing as Madame Blanc, sets the second part of her French novel in the home of a deputy and his young daughter Jacqueline. Family tension has grown between Jacqueline and her stepmother, and a plan to take the girl to Italy brings that tension into the open.

Over breakfast, talk of the Italy trip startles everyone at the table and sharpens the watchful contest between stepmother and stepdaughter. Letters and guarded talk carry much of the strain, as Jacqueline tries to read the motives of the adults around her. The volume shows a bright young woman learning to guard her pride while her future is argued over by others.
3973-the-ink-stain-tache-d-encre-volume-:
Rene Bazin's diary novel continues in its second part, where a young scholar writes day by day about work, family pressure, and hope. His uncle Mouillard writes in fury, urging him to leave Paris at once for a law practice in Bourges after taking his degree.

The diarist answers with low spirits and dry humor, torn between duty to his family and love for his own studies. Friends such as Lampron break the gloom with visits and talk, while the young man weighs what a safe career would cost him. Readers get an intimate, dated record of a mind arguing with itself, one entry at a time.
3977-fromont-and-risler-volume-2:
Alphonse Daudet's Paris novel continues in its second volume around Risler, a kind brewer who has given up his old haunts after marrying Sidonie. She wants him among rich, well-dressed men, and feels shame at his evenings with old friends over pipe smoke.

Risler stops going to the brewery on the Rue Blondel, trading old company for his wife's social hopes. Daudet uses that small choice to show how marriage, money, and pride reshape a man's days. The volume also keeps the business house of Fromont in view, where work, family, and ambition meet and clash in daily Paris life.
3982-gerfaut-volume-2:
Charles de Bernard's novel continues in its second volume with a friend's sharp reproach. Marillac learns that Gerfaut led him off their agreed route at Strasbourg, through the Vosges, for a reason Gerfaut had kept hidden: the Baroness de Bergenheim.

The volume turns on trust between friends and the pull of a forbidden love. Marillac feels his confidence abused, while Gerfaut must own the detour and its motive. Bernard keeps the quarrel civil and pointed, letting honor, friendship, and desire argue in plain speech. Readers see how one secret journey can strain even a long bond.
3987-conscience-volume-2:
Hector Malot's novel of guilt and crime continues in its second volume with a night watch outside a door. A man waits near a porte-cochere across the street, hoping to watch the concierge without being seen by passersby.

The crucial moment turns on watching, waiting, and fear of notice, as the watcher weighs a safer plan against the risk of being marked. Malot keeps the tension close and plain, letting streets, doorways, and small choices carry the dread. Readers follow a man whose conscience has become his jailer, long before any court or judge takes up his case.
3992-madame-chrysantheme-volume-2:
Pierre Loti's Japan novel continues in its second volume among the officers' households on the suburban slopes. By July, four officers of the ship live in like fashion, married through the same agent, Kangourou, and on visiting terms with each other's wives.

The merry neighbor Madame Campanule leads a round of calls, small talk, and household scenes. Loti keeps his sailor's eye on gardens, rooms, and daily custom, showing how a set of brief marriages forms a small foreign colony. Readers get a warm, close view of port life, where charm and distance sit side by side in every visit.
3997-an-attic-philosopher-in-paris-volum:
Emile Souvestre's Paris journal continues in its second volume with dated notes from a top-floor room. On the first of July the writer marks the end of June, the month the Romans gave to Juno, and notes how Numa's reform kept old month names alive.

The volume mixes sky, season, and city life with short moral notes on power, fame, and daily conduct. Souvestre writes as a quiet watcher from the roofs, finding lessons in small sights. Readers get a gentle, thoughtful book, part diary and part essay, that invites slow reading and a second look at ordinary days.
4058-marius-the-epicurean-volume-2:
Walter Pater's philosophical romance continues in its second volume among the Stoics of Marcus Aurelius. The emperor's ideas of large generalization could chill the heart, yet Aurelius joined them to kindness, humor, and the popular religion with its many gods.

A chapter called The Ceremony of the Dart marks the volume's ritual and reflective pace. Marius tests Stoic calm against Epicurean pleasure and the pull of early Christian faith, in prose of great beauty. Readers who stayed with the first volume will find the second deeper and graver, as Marius nears his life's turning point.
4102-the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1:
Azel Ames's Mayflower history continues in its second volume with the ship herself. Early chroniclers left neither picture nor general description of the Mayflower, and few data from which to rebuild her lines and details.

Tradition places her among the merchant craft of her day, and Ames works from that tradition with care, weighing tonnage, rig, and build. The volume suits readers who love ships, as it rebuilds a famous vessel from scraps. It gives the Pilgrim story its wooden stage, plank by plank. Ship lovers will linger over every guess and measure.
4234-correspondence-of-wagner-and-liszt-:
The second volume of the Wagner-Liszt correspondence carries the two composers' letters through triumphs and quarrels. One letter notes that a call to Berlin for Tannhauser has by no means been frustrated, though the theater intendant cannot decide the matter.

The king alone can suspend the usual order, and his decision stands independent of the intendant's authority. Wagner argues his case with passion and pride, while Liszt answers as friend, champion, and critic. Readers who love music history will find genius and ego in every letter. Genius, pride, and friendship sound through every page.
4236-dynevor-terrace-or-the-clue-of-life:
The second volume of Dynevor Terrace, a Victorian domestic novel, opens its fifth chapter on a new world of emigration. Prayers for emigrants sing of southern skies, new stars, and fresh hues where pearl and coral hide, tokens of grace ever fresh and new.

Early-year days, devoid of spring brilliance but full of soft, heavy fragrance, foster tender growth in grey air. The novel follows a family through separation, faith, and the clue of life itself. Readers who enjoy Yonge-era domestic fiction will find a gentle, earnest continuation.
4258-andersonville-a-story-of-rebel-mili:
The second volume of John McElroy's prison narrative opens in the spring of 1864. New prisoners began to reach Andersonville after a quiet winter. A first lot of about seven hundred men had been captured at Olustee in Florida. They joined older prisoners taken at Gettysburg, Chickamauga, and Mine Run.

McElroy records the arrival of Black soldiers and harsh treatment of officers of colored regiments. He records the killing of a sergeant of a Negro squad, and the rough justice of the camp. The volume keeps the private soldier's viewpoint of the first volume. Names, regiments, and small scenes make the prison's growth concrete.
4263-the-golden-bowl-volume-2:
Henry James published The Golden Bowl in 1904, and this second volume carries the second half of the novel, Book Second: The Princess. The story centers on Maggie Verver, her father Adam, her husband the Prince, and Charlotte, whose close ties and hidden pasts create a quiet crisis inside a wealthy, polished marriage.

James tells the tale largely through Maggie's slowly widening awareness, as she begins to accept what she has sensed and to act on it. The famous golden bowl itself, a flawed object bought in a London shop, becomes the emblem of a marriage that looks perfect and is not. This volume completes the arc begun in Volume I.
4402-the-shaving-of-shagpat-an-arabian-e:
George Meredith wrote this Arabian entertainment around Shibli Bagarag, nephew of a barber, whose task is to shave the enchanted Shagpat. This second volume opens with the betrothal of Shibli to Noorna bin Noorka, daughter of the vizier Feshnavat, who smiles gravely at the bargain. Noorna declares herself content with her fair youth of flowing speech.

Later tales in the volume include the punishment of Shahpesh the Persian, the genie Karaz, the well of Paravid, the horse Garraveen, and the talking hawk. Meredith tells the whole in a rich, mock-oriental prose, full of nested stories. The volume carries the quest forward, with magic, wit, and betrothal at its heart.
4407-the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-volum:
Book Two of George Meredith's Ordeal of Richard Feverel opens with a public duty: the laying of ghosts. The mystery of the apparition that frightened little Clare was never solved at Raynham, where dread walked the abbey. Meredith takes up the ghost as a figure for the fears haunting his hero's youth.

The book's chapters run from the blossoming season and the magnetic age through an attraction, Ferdinand and Miranda, and the unmasking of Master Ripton Thompson. Good wine and good blood follow, with the system encountering the wild oats. Richard's boyhood ends here, and the ordeal of love begins.
4414-sandra-belloni-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Sandra Belloni opens on a memorable evening at half past nine, when five-and-twenty stout young fellows of the Hillford Club march to Ipley Common. Prize-winners, wrestlers, boxers, and topers set out together, and the scene gives Meredith's comedy its rough, male chorus.

The book's chapters promise the magnanimity in beer, sentiment and passion taking the disease of love, a short discourse on puppets, the Besworth question, and Wilfrid's exhibition of treachery. Emilia, the singer at the novel's heart, moves among the ladies of Brookfield toward resolve. This volume deepens the love plot and the social satire.
4422-rhoda-fleming-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Rhoda Fleming opens at the theatre, where Edward's club engagement that evening was with his unlucky cousin Algernon. He wants a dinner and five pounds or so, a hazy margin that shows a borrower dancing on fortune's edge. The scene sets the novel's money worries in motion.

The book's chapters follow the farmer speaking, Rhoda and Robert, a visit to Wrexby Hall, Fairly Park, and a yeoman of the old breed. An assembly at the Pilot Inn and Robert smitten low follow, with Mrs. Lovell showing a tame brute. Rhoda's steadfastness anchors a story of sisters, seduction, and the price of honor.
4428-evan-harrington-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Evan Harrington opens at the Aurora, a rare old tavern with the smell of good food and long custom. The house, born when taverns served as clubs for steady men, has lived on its bachelor regulars. For a month it has known dismay and sorrow over its most constant patron.

The book's chapters introduce an eccentric, place the countess in low society, and send the gentleman on the road again. Doings at an inn, ale shown to have one quality of wine, and the match of Fallowfield against Beckley follow. Evan, son of a tailor, moves among gentry who do not know his birth, and comedy follows.
4436-vittoria-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Vittoria opens in Verona, where a lieutenant reads a letter as he clatters through quiet streets toward the Porta Tosa. The writer is glad their old affection is not dead, yet she cannot consent to meet him yet. She would rather they should not meet, and the letter breaks into reproach.

The book's chapters follow the Pope's mouth, Laura Piaveni, the bronze butterfly, and the plot of Signor Antonio. Vittoria, singer and patriot in the Italian revolt against Austria, moves between love and conspiracy. This volume carries her from Verona's streets toward the larger drama of revolution.
4445-the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-vo:
Book Two of George Meredith's Adventures of Harry Richmond opens with a free life on the road. Harry wakes very early, kindly taken to his pillow, with an arm round his rest. The boy's adventures widen from Dipwell Farm to the highway. Janet Ilchester and an evening with Captain Bulsted come along the way.

An expedition follows, with the great fog and the fire at midnight. A voyage bound on the Priscilla follows that. Harry conducts learned arguments with the captain and meets old friends. His father, the adventurer, draws nearer through these chapters, and the novel's comedy of fortune gathers speed.
4454-beauchamp-s-career-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career opens with Captain Baskelett, while England bustles over an extinguished war and counts its cost. Nevil Beauchamp, naval officer turned radical, moves through a country arguing about empire, honor, and the price of glory. His career will test every loyalty he holds.

The book's chapters bring an interview with the infamous Dr. Shrapnel, a superfine conscience, and the leading article of Mr. Timothy Turbot. Cecilia Halkett appears, with a partial display of Beauchamp in his colours, his friend and foe, and the act of canvassing. Politics, love, and principle collide in Meredith's most political novel.
4462-the-tragic-comedians-a-study-in-a-w:
Book Two of George Meredith's Tragic Comedians opens on the plains, where the hero comes down to his love on the second day. As usual when they meet, it seems they have not parted, and his animation makes it so. His warmth, like summer morning sunlight, strikes through her blood and disperses her hesitating strangeness.

The novel studies a well-known story, the love of Ferdinand Lassalle and Helene von Donniges, retold as comedy and tragedy together. Meredith watches two strong wills, girlish dread, and the steps taken and regretted. This volume deepens the courtship, as messages from a distance give way to meetings that thrill and unsettle.
4466-diana-of-the-crossways-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Diana of the Crossways opens with Redworth laughing for gladness of heart. A position of delicacy for a lady and gentleman is met in simple fashion, without hurt to either. The conflict of the night follows, with a journey in a chariot. Dialogue and a small incident on the road fill the ride.

Between Emma and Diana, the first days of her probation follow. Glimpses of Diana under her cloud before the world follow those. Percy Dacier is introduced, with a midnight bell and a scene of early morning. The Princess Egeria closes the book. Diana, witty heroine and novelist, moves through London society toward scandal and survival.
4472-one-of-our-conquerors-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's One of Our Conquerors opens on the dumbness possible in a household with one heart. Two who live in union are expected to share everything, Meredith notes, especially when they love one another and share a cause. Yet reserves on important matters persist, and the chapter probes that silence.

Later chapters bring the latest of Mrs. Burman, a stage on the drive to Paris, and a patriot abroad. Skepsey's misconduct and its effect on Nataly follow, with a young maid's imaginings and suitors for the hand of Nesta Victoria. Victor Radnor, the conqueror of the title, and Nataly move through London toward a reckoning.
4478-lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Lord Ormont and His Aminta opens in Aminta's amber dressing-room, in a mood of languor. Mrs. Nargett Pagnell sadly notes a long month of separation, and begs her niece for an exact statement of the situation, items will do. Then she slips into prattle and holds the field, a worthy, good, intolerable woman.

The book's chapters show effects of a prattler's doses, Mrs. Lawrence Finchley, and a flash of the bruised warrior. A short passage in the game played by two follows, with the secretary taken as an antidote. Lord Ormont, old soldier, and Aminta, his young wife, play their marriage game under society's eyes.
4484-the-amazing-marriage-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Amazing Marriage opens with small causes, as a clock sounds a late morning hour of the night. Gower Woodseer stands at his hotel door, after parting from Fleetwood and his merry company, under stars low over a ridge of pines. Beneath the roof lies the household whose fortunes the novel follows.

The book's chapters follow the prisoner of his word, Henrietta's letter on the great event, and an irruption of Mistress Gossip. A pendant, the opening stage of the honeymoon, and a bride from foreign parts tasting old England follow. Down Whitechapel way and the girl Madge close the book, as marriage, gossip, and money entangle.
4490-celt-and-saxon-volume-2:
Book Two of George Meredith's Celt and Saxon opens with Miss Mattock, as Mrs. Adister O'Donnell faces the task of composing epistles. She dislikes letter writing, Meredith notes, because she cannot conceive an idea disconnected from her letter's main theme, and she regards words independent of ideas as conjuring. Her native superiority despises the art.

The book's chapters follow a dinner party, Rockney, and the Mattock family, with the great Mr. Bull and Celtic and Saxon views of him. Something of Richard Rockney follows, with crossing the Rubicon, Captain Con's letter, and Mars convalescent. Meredith's unfinished novel of nations continues its witty comparison of Irish and English minds.
4535-sylvia-s-lovers-volume-2:
Elizabeth Gaskell's Sylvia's Lovers continues in this second volume, covering chapters fifteen through twenty-nine. Philip Hepburn, who went to bed with humble, penitent gratitude after a sudden turn from despair to hope, now faces a difficult question, an engagement, and rejected warnings. Chapters trace an eddy in love's current, an important mission, love and loss, a rejected suitor, and deepening shadows.

Retaliation, brief rejoicing, coming troubles, a dreary vigil, gloomy days, an ordeal, and wedding raiment follow in quick succession. Readers of this middle volume watch Sylvia's courtship tighten and darken, as promises made in hope meet the hard facts of war, work, and pride. It should be read after volume one, since its power depends on knowing Monkshaven, Sylvia, and the rivals already in play.
4610-the-letters-of-horace-walpole-earl-:
Horace Walpole's letters continue in this second volume, covering 1749 to 1759, with letters now first collected marked in the contents. The volume opens in 1749 with letters to Sir Horace Mann on proceedings in Parliament. They cover a formidable minority headed by the Prince, Lord Egmont, innovations in the Mutiny Bill, and a new Navy Bill. Later letters report debates, a jar at Leicester House, King Theodore of Corsica, and the spread of Methodism.

May letters describe rejoicings for the peace, a jubilee masquerade, and fireworks. They add English credulity, a projected chastisement of Oxford, union between the Prince's party and Jacobites, and the disgrace of Maurepas. Walpole's eye for gossip, epigram, and bon-mot never flags. Readers get a vivid, gossipy record of mid-century politics and society, best read in sequence with volume one.
466-the-gaming-table-its-votaries-and-vi:
Andrew Steinmetz surveys gambling across ages and lands in the first of two volumes. He opens with gaming as a world-wide passion, then traces dice and cards among Hindus, Egyptians, Greeks, and Roman emperors. France, England, Brighton, German spas, and America each get their turn.

Steinmetz, a barrister, writes from fact and anecdote, naming lords, poets, and sharpers ruined at the table. Lotteries, lady gamesters, and laws against play fill later chapters. The volume reads as a vivid social history of a vice that, in his day, still cleaned out noblemen and clerks alike.
4720-wacousta-a-tale-of-the-pontiac-cons:
John Richardson's Wacousta, or The Prophecy, continues in this second volume of three, opening on the evening of a day fertile in melancholy incident, to which the first volume was devoted. That evening the drawbridge of Detroit is lowered for the third time since the garrison was invested. It moves not with a disregard shown by rattling chains, but with caution attesting secrecy of purpose. No array of armed men denotes a hostile expedition.

Most troops, overcome by the day's harassing duties, have retired to rest. A few guards walk their posts, apparently to check midnight drowsiness, but really to witness preparations going on by torchlight. Richardson writes the Pontiac conspiracy as frontier romance, with siege, prophecy, and divided loyalties. Readers should start with volume one, since this volume carries its plot, characters, and secrets forward without retelling them.
4726-john-lothrop-motley-a-memoir-volume:
Oliver Wendell Holmes, Sr., continues his memoir of John Lothrop Motley in this second volume, covering 1860 to 1866, when Motley was forty-six to fifty-two. It opens with residence in England, the outbreak of the Civil War, and letters to the London Times. A visit to America follows, with appointment as minister to Austria, Lady Harcourt's letter, and Miss Motley's memorandum.

The winter of 1859 to 1860 was passed chiefly at Oatlands Hotel, Walton-on-Thames. In 1860 Motley hired a house at 31 Hertford Street, May Fair, London, having just published the first two volumes of his History of the Netherlands. When civil war threatened and broke out at home, his love of country would not let him stay silent. Readers should start with volume one, since this volume carries Motley's middle years forward without retelling his youth.
4798-the-complete-poetical-works-of-perc:
The Complete Poetical Works of Percy Bysshe Shelley, volume two, is the Oxford edition of 1914, edited by Thomas Hutchinson. It includes materials never before printed in any edition of the poems. Its contents open with early poems of 1814 and 1815, including a stanza written at Bracknell. Stanzas of April 1814, poems to Harriet and to Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin, Yet Look on Me, and Mutability follow.

On Death, A Summer Evening Churchyard, and a poem to Wordsworth follow, with Feelings of a Republican on the Fall of Bonaparte and a note on the early poems by Mrs. Shelley. Poems of 1816 include The Sunset, Hymn to Intellectual Beauty, and Mont Blanc, with a cancelled passage, a fragment called Home, and a fragment of a ghost story. Poems of 1817 open with Marianne's Dream and poems to Constantia singing. Readers get Shelley's early verse in a scholarly Oxford text.
4965-waverley-or-tis-sixty-years-since-v:
Walter Scott's Waverley, subtitled Tis Sixty Years Since, continues in this second volume with Mr. Gilfillan marching his prisoner toward Stirling on a delightful autumn afternoon. Dinner hour in Scotland sixty years since was two o'clock, so by four Gilfillan leads his followers stoutly along, eyeing his hero and longing for controversy.

The march becomes a debate, as the Presbyterian minister cannot resist arguing with his captive. Scott sets the Jacobite rising of 1745 against such small human encounters. Readers following Edward Waverley's adventures get the novel's middle movement, where romance meets the hard politics of rebellion.
4972-frederick-chopin-as-a-man-and-music:
Frederick Niecks's second volume on Chopin turns to the composer's loves and his life with George Sand. Various accounts tell of their first meeting. Chopin's first impression of her is weighed. The two characters are compared. Portraits of both follow, with an account of her power of pleasing.

The volume also covers Chopin's publications in 1837 and 1838 and his playing at court and at concerts in Paris. Niecks weighs gossip against evidence throughout, asking why an artist's choice of partner so often puzzles outsiders. Readers get a careful biography of Chopin's middle years, grounded in letters and contemporary report.
4999-the-notebooks-of-leonardo-da-vinci-:
Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks, in this second volume, gather the master's notes on sculpture and related arts. The editor notes with surprise that the horse statue of Francesco Sforza appears only in passing. Leonardo worked on it for years. Yet thirteen notes in his hand throw light on that famous work's strange history.

Earlier writers knew only a few of the passages, numbered 712, 719, and others. The volume arranges the new material to show Leonardo thinking through sculpture. No editor is named in the record. Readers get Leonardo at work in fragments: practical, curious, and endlessly observant about making things stand and move.
510-the-purcell-papers-volume-2:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu gathers Irish tales in this second volume of the Purcell Papers, framed as a priest's legacy. A countess's secret history opens the set, followed by the bridal of Carrigvarah, a strange event in the life of Schalken the painter, and scraps of Irish ballads. Names are changed where the living might be hurt.

Le Fanu writes in rich, eerie prose, mixing family pride, ghostly dread, and country talk. The painter's tale, of a devilish visitor, ranks among his most famed. The volume preserves his early mastery of Irish gothic, where old houses keep old sins.
5144-my-life-volume-2:
Richard Wagner's autobiography, in its English translation of 1911, continues his life story in its second volume. Part Three covers the years 1850 to 1861, opening with his wife Minna finding quarters near Zurich, in the parish of Enge, while Wagner lived in exile after the Dresden rising.

The volume follows the composer's work, friendships, and restless moves through those years, as he planned the great operas that would define his career. Readers interested in Wagner will find here his own account, candid and self-justifying, of the middle period in which his art and his legend took shape.
5226-life-and-letters-of-thomas-henry-hu:
Leonard Huxley's Life and Letters of Thomas Henry Huxley continues in this second volume, covering the years 1870 through the mid-1880s. Its chapters follow Huxley year by year, through his work in science, education, and public debate, with letters that show his friendships, controversies, and family life.

The volume presents Huxley, Darwin's great defender, in his most active middle period, lecturing, writing, and shaping British science. Readers get a portrait built from Huxley's own words, and a detailed record of Victorian science at the moment it became a public force.
5235-the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-:
Charles James Lever's Harry Lorrequer continues in this second volume, covering chapters eleven through seventeen. Harry tries his hand at making love for a friend at Cheltenham, and revisits Dublin and Tom O'Flaherty. He samples boarding-house society and joins a chase. He recalls the Peninsula, with a repeated chapter number in the print copy noted by the editors.

The volume holds only this middle stretch of Harry's confessions, and its comedy moves between England and Ireland. Readers following the novel in order will find matrimonial adventures, theatricals, and regimental anecdotes that complete the set, told with Lever's usual high spirits.
531-the-gaming-table-its-votaries-and-vi:
Andrew Steinmetz closes his history of gambling in this second volume, turning from nations to sharpers and clubs. Polite cheats, professional gamesters, duels, suicides, and gaming houses fill the chapters. Dice, cards, piquet, faro, hazard, cockfights, and the turf each get a turn, with odds explained.

Steinmetz, a barrister, mixes anecdote with moral warning, showing how fraud, passion, and chance ruin men of all ranks. Fortune-telling by cards and card tricks close the book on a lighter note. The volume serves as a vivid record of Victorian gaming life at its sharpest.
5462-the-sisters-volume-2:
Georg Ebers continues his ancient Egyptian romance The Sisters in this second volume at Memphis. The chapter opens inside the city's white walls, where the old palace of the kings stands amid bastions and ramparts. Built of plastered brick, it holds courts, corridors, chambers, and halls without number, with painted wooden outbuildings and a pillared banqueting hall in the Greek style.

The palace setting prepares the volume's court scenes, where Greek and Egyptian worlds meet in one royal household. Ebers describes the buildings with an archaeologist's care, making place part of the story. Readers get a richly detailed stretch of historical romance, set in a Memphis of stone, color, and ceremony.
5468-joshua-volume-2:
A chamberlain ushers Hosea into the audience chamber in the second volume of Georg Ebers's Joshua. Subjects summoned before the king usually waited for hours, but the Hebrew's patience is not tried long. The palace, normally full of a gay and noisy crowd, lies hushed in the deepest mourning, with slaves and warders silent.

The audience takes place against that mourning, giving the volume a solemn, courtly tone. Hosea, the figure later known as Joshua, stands before Egyptian power at a moment of grief and decision. Readers get a biblical-era romance told through palace ceremony, restraint, and waiting.
5751-st-george-and-st-michael-volume-2:
Volume two of St George and St Michael picks up the romance at chapter seventeen, with a fire engine, moonlight and apple blossoms, and an enchanted chair. Molly and a white horse follow, with a damsel who falls sick. A cataract comes next, with Amanda, Dorothy, and Lord Herbert. A great mogul, Richard Heywood, a witch's cottage, and the moat of the keep carry the tale toward Raglan stables and an apparition.

The second volume deepens the Civil War romance, as lovers, marquises, and household folk navigate siege, loyalty, and rumor. Readers who finished the first volume will find the same blend of history, mystery, and domestic feeling, now with higher stakes. The story rewards reading in order, since its charms and dangers grow from choices made in earlier chapters.
5796-journeys-through-bookland-vol-2:
Volume two of Journeys Through Bookland, edited by Sylvester for children, opens with a little chimney sweep from the days of open fireplaces. A footnote explains that houses once held a network of huge chimneys through which a small boy could work his way, brushing soot as he went. From that working child's story, the volume leads young readers through further tales, poems, and lessons.

The collection is built for family reading, mixing classic stories with guidance for parents and teachers. Children meet adventure, fancy, and moral tales in short, manageable pieces, while adults get a structured path through children's literature. The volume suits homeschooling, bedtime reading, and anyone building a young reader's library one journey at a time.
5809-following-the-equator-a-journey-aro:
Part two of Mark Twain's Following the Equator covers chapters nine through nineteen, on the way to Australia and beyond. Chapter nine opens with a Pudd'nhead Wilson maxim that human environment makes climate, then notes a September night close to Australia, with Sydney fifty miles distant. Passengers are called to the bow to see a fine sight in the dark, where the sea's surface escapes the eye.

We travel with Twain through ports, lectures, and colonial encounters, hearing his jokes about climate, custom, and empire. The part balances shipboard life with shore excursions, as Twain tests guidebook claims against what he sees. It suits readers following Twain around the world in order, and it stands alone as vivid travel writing from the age of steam.
5819-the-gilded-age-part-2:
Part two of The Gilded Age, by Twain and Charles Dudley Warner, covers chapters ten through eighteen, and it opens days after a funeral. Something happens that will change the drift of Laura's life and shape her character in greater or lesser degree. Major Lackland, once a man of note in his state, a man of extraordinary natural ability and learning, enters the story as Laura's fortunes turn.

Readers follow the novel's satire of speculation, politics, and social climbing through Laura's widening world. The part balances Washington schemes with personal choices, showing how money and reputation tempt even strong characters. It suits readers following the Gilded Age in order, since Laura's decisions here set much of the later novel in motion.
5837-sketches-new-and-old-part-2:
Part two of Mark Twain's Sketches New and Old opens with Answers to Correspondents, written about 1865. Addressing a moral statistician, Twain declares he wants none of the man's statistics, having lit his pipe with the whole batch. He hates such people, he says, always ciphering how much a man's health is injured and his intellect impaired by this or that habit.

Twain offers his epistolary comedy at its sharpest, as fake letters invite real jokes about reformers, numbers, and human folly. The part gathers further sketches in the same vein, each answering a correspondent with wit rather than patience. It suits readers who enjoy Twain's early newspaper humor, and anyone who has ever wanted to answer a scold with a laugh.
5855-personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-vo:
Volume one, part two of Sheridan's Personal Memoirs covers chapters nine through fifteen, opening with an expedition to Booneville. Headings treat destroying supplies, Confederate stragglers, success of the expedition, a reconnaissance, and the importance of bodily sustenance, before the Battle of Booneville and a recommendation for appointment as brigadier general. The expedition, Sheridan notes, was composed of the Second Michigan and other troops.

Readers get Sheridan as a rising cavalry commander, learning raiding, supply, and battle in the western theater. The memoir favors brisk operational detail, with hunger and horses mattering as much as heroics. It suits Civil War readers following Sheridan's early career, and it bridges his cadet years and his later fame as an army commander.
5861-personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-:
Part two of Grant's Personal Memoirs covers chapters fourteen through twenty-five, from the Mexican War's lessons to the Pacific Coast. Chapter fourteen opens with return of the army, marriage, orders to the Pacific Coast, crossing the Isthmus, and arrival at San Francisco. Grant notes that his Mexican War experience advantaged him afterward, teaching practical lessons and bringing regular officers into personal acquaintance.

We follow a young officer between wars, as peacetime service, travel, and separation shape the future general. The memoir's plain narrative favors marching, posts, and duties over romance, letting routine reveal character. It suits Civil War readers tracing Grant's formation, and it bridges his Mexican service and his later return to command.
5899-the-physiology-of-marriage-part-2:
Balzac continues The Physiology of Marriage in its second part, on means of defence, interior and exterior. A Hamlet epigraph asks to be or not to be, and Meditation Ten opens a treatise on marital policy, supposing a man has reached the position described in the first part. From there, Balzac weighs how husbands may guard a marriage, and what such guarding costs.

Readers get Balzac's witty, provocative analysis at full stretch, mixing maxims, cases, and social observation. The second part favors strategy and irony, treating marriage as a field of maneuver as much as a bond of love. It suits readers who finished the first part, and anyone curious about Balzac's famously unsentimental view of Parisian married life.
5967-what-s-mine-s-mine-volume-2:
George MacDonald opens the second volume with a story told by Ian, about a widow left poor after a well-to-do husband's death. Work is hard to find, hard to do, and hardly paid, yet the woman trusts in God and holds that whatever he pleases must be right. Only hearts of grace, Ian says, grasp such struggles.

The volume's chapters continue with Rob of the Angels, a new house, the brothers, the princess, the stag's head, Annie of the shop, and an encounter. Love allodial, a tomb, and Mercy calling on Grannie follow.
6022-stories-by-foreign-authors-german-v:
Four German tales fill this volume, each in translation arranged with copyright owners or made fresh for the series. Berthold Auerbach gives Christian Gellert's Last Christmas, Leopold Kompert a Ghetto Violet, Wilhelm Hauff The Severed Hand, and Adelbert von Chamisso the famous Peter Schlemihl.

Auerbach opens on 22 December 1768, as three o'clock strikes from St. Nicholas tower in Leipzig and a gentle man in a loose overcoat leaves the university, followed by a troop of students. The collection samples German storytelling from sentiment to the uncanny, with a scholar, a ghetto flower, a severed hand, and a man who sells his shadow.
6042-the-diary-and-letters-of-madame-d-a:
Frances Burney, Madame d'Arblay, covers the years 1787 to 1792 in this second volume of diary and letters, with notes by W. C. Ward and Lord Macaulay's essay prefixed. The pages open on court duties at St. James's and Windsor, with the Queen's birthday drawing room and a serious dilemma.

Counsels of a court official, Mr. Turbulent's anxiety to introduce Mr. Wellbred, eccentric Mr. Bryant, bantering a princess, and the Duchess de Polignac at Windsor fill the early entries.
