Burney writes as an insider watching royalty at close range, noting manners, mishaps, and the small theater of court life.
6096-amelia-volume-2:
Henry Fielding's Amelia, volume two, opens its fifth book with an old acquaintance, a brace of doctors, and much physical matter. Booth pays a visit to a noble lord, affairs of Sergeant Atkinson unfold, and matters requiring no preface give way to heroic matter and the heroic behavior of Colonel Bath.

The sixth book adds panegyrics on beauty, a history looking a little backwards, and an extraordinary turn. Fielding keeps Booth and Amelia amid doctors, lords, and soldiers, testing marriage under debt and temptation. The middle instalment alone holds the focus of this account, and neither its predecessor nor its successor enters the discussion.
6147-narrative-and-miscellaneous-papers-:
Thomas De Quincey opens his second volume with the heavens as revealed by Lord Rosse's telescopes. Modern superstition, Coleridge and opium-eating, the temperance movement, on war, and the last days of Immanuel Kant follow. A footnote credits J. P. Nichol's thoughts on the system of the world.

De Quincey recalls publishing, some years earlier, a paper from the German of Kant on the age of the earth. Kant wished not to count the earth's years, since a million more or less mattered little to him, but to settle a deeper question.
6170-memorials-and-other-papers-volume-2:
De Quincey's second volume of Memorials opens with Klosterheim, The Sphinx's Riddle, and The Templars' Dialogues. Klosterheim begins in the winter of 1633, set in with unusual severity across Suabia and Bavaria, though scarcely past the first week of November.

The tale opens on 8 November, or 18 November by modern reckoning, when winter campaigns had become policy in the war sweeping Germany. Blooming Edens of peace and prosperity threatened to turn to howling wilderness, and vast tracts already had. Only the second collection is treated in this entry, with the first collection set aside for its own entry. War turns Eden-like lands into a howling waste.
6175-pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-:
A Prairie Vagabond opens Parker's second volume, with Little Hammer, a disappointment to missionaries, Hudson's Bay officials, Mounted Police, Crees, Blackfeet, and half-breeds alike. Oblivious to depreciation, he loves the Company's post at Yellow Quill and ranges Red Deer River hospitality.

Little Hammer salutes Sergeant Gellatly with a familiar How, borrows tobacco of half-breed women, and strangely pays it back with other tobacco. She of the Triple Chevron and Three Outlaws complete the volume. This account follows the second set of tales alone, leaving the other sets to be covered elsewhere. The volume keeps its humor dry and its north cold.
6187-northern-lights-volume-2:
To-Morrow opens Parker's second Northern Lights volume. A woman ironing a white petticoat lifts her head and says nothing is the matter with the world today, it is so good it almost hurts. Snow-tipped mountains, fir and cedar foothills, and maple and ash woods in autumn tints merge to one soft red tone.

A stream roars down a ravine, air braces nerves, and the passion of life answers the passion of living in her. She lays her iron on a hot stove and takes another, touching it with care. Qu'Appelle and The Stake and the Plumb-Line complete the volume.
6193-mrs-falchion-volume-2:
Mrs. Falchion, book two, opens on the slope of the Pacific, among hills of God, as a servant brings letters on the last evening of the college year. Examinations are over, and the narrator wonders where to spend holidays, choosing between Muskoka lakes and Yosemite Valley.

Because it is his first year in Canada, he prefers not to go beyond the Dominion. The first two letters, tradesmen's bills, do not interest him, but the third brings a thumping pleasure, though not from Miss Treherne. A weekly letter from her already came that morning.
6207-the-trail-of-the-sword-volume-2:
Friends in Council opens the second epoch of The Trail of the Sword. Montreal and Quebec stand as cheerful in still iron winter as any city under a more cordial sky. Men loved, hated, made and broke bargains, lied to women, kept foolish honour with each other, and did deeds of valour for a song.

Through nature's stern soul ran men with hearts of summer. On a notable day in Iberville's life, a window in a low stone house on Notre Dame Street, Montreal, might show a priest joyously playing violin. Parker sets New France winter alight with talk, honour, and music.
6212-the-translation-of-a-savage-volume-:
The Passing of the Years opens Parker's second volume of The Translation of a Savage, with Lali's slow recovery and a change upon her. The strange ride has taken the last strong flicker of desire for savage life from her, and she now knows her position toward her husband.

He never loved her, she sees, and she served only as an instrument for unworthy retaliation. As soon as she can speak after her accident, she forbids writing to him of it and asks only that he hear she is well. Her new friends, caring for her herself, cannot refuse.
6216-the-pomp-of-the-lavilettes-volume-2:
Ferrol's recovery opens Parker's second volume of The Pomp of the Lavilettes, swifter than expected, with Christine as constant attendant and self-made nurse. No one seriously interferes, though the Cure protests, not vaguely, to Madame Lavilette, who now defies or evades him as convenient.

Linkage by marriage with nobility would justify Madame Lavilette's long-baffled hopes, while the parish gossips, little heard at Manor Casimbault. By and by the Cure stops visiting, but the regimental surgeon comes often and stays late, perhaps best placed to advise and warn. The second volume alone is the subject of this entry, and the first volume is not revisited here.
6220-the-trespasser-volume-2:
Strange Encounters opens Parker's second volume of The Trespasser, as Gaston sits on horseback in a quiet corner of grounds while his uncle sketches him. When Saracen will remain quiet no longer, the uncle holds up a sketch Gaston can scarcely believe possible in the time, full of force and imagination.

Gaston leaves his uncle with a nod, rides quietly through park into village and on to moor, and turns at the top to look down. The landscape's perfectness strikes him, as if the picture had grown there, with no suburban villa or modern cottage in sight.
6225-the-seats-of-the-mighty-volume-2:
Moray writes as though one Sunday afternoon had settled his whole story, then admits the making took many weeks of solitude. In that time he saw no face but Gabord's, the jailer who brought bread and water twice a day and answered no questions about Juste Duvarney or Voban. The chapters here bring the Chevalier de la Darante, an officer of marines, and the coming of Doltaire, with a boast and a poisoned point to follow.

This second volume deepens the intrigue around a prisoner who must think his way out of a cell. Gabord's watchful silence, the talk of wine and crumbs, and the slow passage of days build a mood of close confinement. Parker lets Moray's voice carry the suspense, as plans form in the dark and enemies gather just out of sight.
6231-the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-:
Philip d'Avranche, first lieutenant of the Narcissus, comes ashore at the Ecrehos under the pilotage of Jean Touzel, after Admiralty orders send the ship to take soundings there. The vessel twists through rock teeth into a cove, boats put off to explore, and Philip walks the shingle to a ruined chapel in no good humour with himself or the world. Ranulph, watching from the island, has guessed the ship aright.

This volume turns on meetings at the edge of the sea, where naval duty and island life collide. Carterette keeps her small counter with hot soup, coffee, and Jersey wonders fried on a charcoal fire, a homely counterpoint to ships and orders. Parker keeps the coast itself in view, a place of reefs, tides, and narrow coves that shapes every choice his people make.
6238-the-lane-that-had-no-turning-volume:
Five brothers live with their sister Louison three miles from Pontiac, and Medallion first meets them by selling them a slice of farm at auction. Taken into their house during a severe illness, he finds Louison guarded by a constant, reverent courtesy, her maiden dignity shielded by every brother. The volume holds four tales: Louison's absurd romance, a little bell of honour, a son of the wilderness, and a worker in stone.

Parker's Pontiac stories turn on French Canadian village life, where custom, pride, and affection rule daily conduct. Medallion, the auctioneer turned guest, watches a household built on respect and quiet feeling. These are short, warm tales of neighbours and kin, told with humour and a fond eye for the small ceremonies that hold a parish together.
6251-michel-and-angele-a-ladder-of-sword:
Lempriere of Rozel, butler to the Queen, sees a sight he tells to his dying day while Elizabeth is at chapel at Greenwich Palace. Gentlemen of the rod kneel to lay a cloth as if at an altar. Salt, plate, and bread are placed with ceremony, and a duke's daughter bears a tasting knife beautiful as a rose. Lempriere, given an office where others do the work, watches court ritual with a Jerseyman's plain astonishment.

This second volume moves between palace ceremony and the choice set before Michel de la Foret, sword or book, until Trinity Day. The Queen's word gives him that choice, while Leicester sees only the sword at his side and the gold-bound book under his arm, and storms off under the trees. Parker writes Elizabeth's court as theatre and trap, where a refugee's faith must pass inspection in public.
6257-donovan-pasha-and-some-people-of-eg:
Fielding's orderly is straight enough from behind, legs like pipe stems and body like a board. But his face gives little pleasure, with a nose like rubber and eyes of dull, sullen mongrel look. Those eyes turn brownish red when he is excited, a sign all know. Selamlik Pasha calls it hashish, Fielding calls it a cross of Sudanese and fellah blood, and little Dicky Donovan has his own view of Ibrahim the orderly.

This second volume holds five tales, from Fielding's orderly and the eye of a needle to a treaty of peace, mercy at Tiberius, and a world gone mad. A woman called a blasphemer faces sheikh and ulema, while one man's plea tries to save her by calling her favoured of God. Parker writes Egypt through soldiers, officials, and villagers, with humour and a sharp eye for how rumour turns into judgment.
6269-embers-volume-2:
King Rufus hunts the deer in springtime, calling to Dolly with a hey ho, in the first poem of this second volume of Parker's verse. Dolly stays coy, the greenwood fills with play, and a king learns that love is not won by a day's hunting. The volume runs on through life's sweet wages, a valley, a lily flower, love lying in a cold grave, and Granada called twice over.

Epitaphs follow for beggar, maid, fool, fighter, sea reapers, and watcher, with poems on waking, forgetting, waste places, and the twilight of love. A new Aphrodite, an ancient pledge, and a tribute of King Hath widen the range, and a little child closes the run. Parker writes short lyrics of loss and praise, where a name or a place can carry a whole life.
6273-a-lover-s-diary-volume-2:
Dreams open this second volume, and a bride, a wraith, and surrender follow, with a citadel, malfeasance, and an annunciation close behind. Vanished dreams give way to a divided life, yet life is sweet, and lost footsteps lead to a closed door and a chalice. A treasure, a decree, and a morning sacrifice carry the lover onward, through the sea, a chart, and a darkened way to reunion.

Parker's later lyrics turn from courtship to endurance, as the lover learns to live on after parting and to find the message in memory. Song was gone from him, the fight was good, and absolution comes at last, with a ghost told not to vex the living. These poems are graver than the first volume's, but they keep its music, and they end with a passing that still affirms life.
6276-the-money-master-volume-2:
Thirteen years after, the clerk of the court tells a story, and the parish must judge which man matters more, the New Cure or Jean Jacques Barbille. When the Old Cure died at eighty-five, after baptising, confirming, and comforting a whole people, his young successor could command obedience but not yet love. For a time Jean Jacques took the Old Cure's human place in the district, though in a vastly different way.

This second epoch follows Jean Jacques through a great day and waking from sleep. A gate in the wall, a claim to be a philosopher, and a shrug with a who knows for an answer follow. The clerk keeps a promise, and a master carpenter faces a problem. Parker writes parish life as a contest of influence, where mills, money, and kindness all buy a hearing, but none buys a heart outright.
6282-the-world-for-sale-volume-2:
Ingolby's square head jerks forward in stern inquiry as he warns Jowett the horse dealer to take care, for a proved charge could mean a penitentiary term. Jowett, shrewd, vain, and humorous, is a favourite in both towns, has money in the bank and corner lots, and keeps low company without apology. His constant companion is Fabian Osterhaut, common property of both towns, who does a little of everything from bill posting to insurance work.

This second book turns on a sultan, matter and mind and two men, and luck. The sentence of a patrin, light, a chain of the past, and a woman from Wind River follow. A mayor fills an office, a monseigneur meets a nomad, and beacons burn. Parker writes town rivalry as a contest of talk, law, and nerve, where a British town refuses to settle affairs by knife or gun.
6290-wild-youth-volume-2:
Out on the prairie under stars, Orlando has fought the first great battle of his life and emerged victorious, though no drawn battles exist in struggles of the soul. He is tortured by the thought that none will believe the truth tomorrow, and that penalty may follow where no crime was done. Louise, who could have returned defiant hand in hand with him, wakes at daybreak glad of the victory, yet shadowed by trouble to come.

This second volume runs from a moon not alone through Louise, man unnatural, and Orlando's warning, to Filion and Fiona, outward bound, cross trails, and a superior man. At Tralee, Louise must face Joel Mazarine, who distrusts every man and woman and will distrust her with sternness. Parker writes a night's victory and a morning's reckoning, where innocence without proof must still stand its trial.
6293-no-defense-volume-2:
Michael Clones stands before a prison asking if it is near the time. His friend sits on a stone in faded coverings, pinched with cold on a November day. Seven minutes, and Dyck Calhoun will be out, God bless him. He was condemned to eight years but freed after four, grey at the temples and broken in joy. His father's estate was swallowed by creditors, and he was perhaps freed for what he told the government about the French navy.

This second book sends Dyck into the world again, toward mutiny's hour, the West Indies, and the nick of time, with an admiral's say. Between prison exit and the ship Ariadne, months roughen but do not coarsen him, and among seamen he sets himself to become their leader. Parker writes a freed man's second start, where naval service must prove whether tragedy or success will fill his three years.
6297-carnac-s-folly-volume-2:
What has happened since I have been gone, mother, Carnac asks on his return, eight months after vanishing from Montreal. Late April sun melts snow on the hills, birds sing, and his mother answers sorrowfully that Junia has been away since last fall, nursing a sick aunt in the west. Carnac shakes his head: everything is all wrong, he blundered, and he is paying the price.

This second book holds Carnac's return, the house of the three trees, Carnac and Junta, a journey by John Grier, and the reading of a will. He found Luzanne Larue, but divorce proved impossible, for their names stood signed as man and wife in a hotel book. Parker writes a spring homecoming shadowed by a past bargain that will not release him.
6331-the-pillars-of-the-house-or-under-w:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Pillars of the House, subtitled Under Wode, Under Rode, opens its first volume in London in 1875 with a birthday gift. Four boys burst through a street door with book straps over their shoulders, shouting for Felix, while five voices within answer Jolly, and a pyramid of children crowds a narrow stair. Two handsome girls, a smaller girl and boy, and a creature rolling on the stair complete the household chorus.

The first volume follows a large family through picnic, birthday, and daily life, with Felix and Geraldine at its centre and a feeble, lame boy soothed by a mother's gentle talk. Yonge writes domestic life with close attention to children, manners, and faith, as a house holds together under strain. This is volume one of two, and its story stops where the second volume takes up the tale.
637-the-letters-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Sidney Colvin continues Stevenson's letters in this second volume, from Bournemouth through America to Samoa. Life at Bournemouth, a winter in the Adirondacks, Pacific voyages, and long Samoan years fill the sections. Letters to Mrs. de Mattos, friends, and family track work, illness, and island life.

Stevenson writes with the same wit and warmth as in volume one, now from a farther shore. His Samoan letters show a writer at home in a new world, yet still tied to old friends. The volume closes the set as a rich, moving record of a life lived largely by pen.
6660-theological-essays-and-other-papers:
Thomas De Quincey, author of Confessions of an English Opium-Eater, gathers theological essays and other papers in this second volume. Its contents run from secession from the Church of Scotland and a toilette of the Hebrew lady to Milton, Charlemagne, modern Greece, and Lord Carlisle on Pope. The opening essay, dated 1844, warns of a great revolution in Scotland.

De Quincey writes with his usual force and fancy, turning church politics into high drama. Lord Aberdeen's Act, he says, may calm the strife, but danger has not yet passed. Volume two shows De Quincey at his most learned and combative, on faith, letters, and nations.
6931-sunny-memories-of-foreign-lands-vol:
Harriet Beecher Stowe continues her sunny memories of foreign lands in this second volume, told in letters home. Letter nineteen opens with breakfast, Macaulay, Hallam, and Milman, then lunch at a Surrey parsonage and dinner at Sir Edward Buxton's. Later letters record dinner at Lord Shaftesbury's, an antislavery meeting at Exeter Hall, and visits to Windsor, Eton, and the poet Gray.

Further letters bring Kossuth, Pembroke Lodge, dinner at Lord John Russell's, and Lambeth Palace, with Clarkson, Joseph Sturge, Gladstone, and the Archbishop of Canterbury's sermon. Stowe writes as a famous American guest in England, warm, observant, and ever mindful of slavery's cause. The volume is a travel letter book of high society and reform.
6940-old-mortality-volume-2:
Walter Scott's Old Mortality continues in this second volume with a council of war in a shepherd's hut. A quarter of a mile from the field of battle, leaders of the Presbyterian army meet in a miserable cottage, the only enclosed spot near at hand. Burley guides Morton toward the hut, where a wild confusion of sounds greets them instead of the calm gravity fit for such a council.

Discord and loud uproar strike their new ally as an evil omen for measures to come. The volume follows Morton among the Covenanters after battle, as factions argue and the rising's fate hangs in the balance. Only this volume's own course is told here, from the hut council onward through the quarrels that shape the war.
6943-the-heart-of-mid-lothian-volume-2:
The second volume of Scott's Heart of Mid-Lothian opens in a darkened room of grief. Mrs Saddletree enters to find her guests sunk in misery, the old man laid in bed after a long swoon, curtains drawn, and Jeanie sitting motionless at his side. Kind but blunt, Mrs Saddletree opens the window, draws the curtain, and urges her kinsman to sit up and bear his sorrow like a good man and a Christian.

His hand falls lifeless as she lets it go, and the scene sets the volume's somber key. Only this volume's course is followed here, as the household bears its blow and Jeanie faces what must be done. Scott keeps the focus close on family feeling, even as the law's shadow hangs over the house.
7086-life-of-her-most-gracious-majesty-t:
Sarah Tytler's life of Queen Victoria continues in this second volume, edited with an introduction by Lord Ronald Gower. The contents open with royal progresses to Burghley, Stowe, and Strathfieldsaye, then the Queen's powder ball and her first visit to Germany. Railway speculation, failure of the potato crop, Peel's resolutions, the birth of Princess Helena, and a visit from Ibrahim Pasha follow.

Autumn yachting, Spanish marriages, and winter visits lead to Prince Albert's installation as chancellor of Cambridge and the Queen's visit to Scotland's western isles and Ardverikie. French fugitives, the People's Charter, a first stay at Balmoral, and fresh attacks on the Queen fill later chapters. Only this second volume's matter is described here.
7113-the-land-of-midian-revisited-volume:
Burton's second Midian volume continues the march through central and eastern Midian, from chapter eleven onward. The contents list unknown lands south of the Hisma, ruins of Shuwak and Shaghab, and a road from Shaghab to Ziba with ruins of El Khandaki and Umm Amil. A turquoise mine and a return to El Muwaylah follow, with a week around and upon the Sharr mountain.

Later chapters go down south to El Wijh with notes on quarantine and the Hutaym tribe, then to a southern sulphur hill and a cruise to El Haura. The last marches pass an inland fort, ruins of gold mines at Umm el Karayat and Umm el Harab, and the road to El Bada. Only this second volume's march is traced here.
713-memoirs-of-extraordinary-popular-del:
Charles Mackay devoted this second volume to four great follies that seized whole peoples. The Crusades sent armies east in the name of faith, with banners, spears, and vast loss of life. The Witch Mania then shows how fear of witchcraft led towns to hunt and burn the accused.

Two shorter studies close the book: the slow poisoners, who killed in secret for gain or hate, and haunted houses, where dread and rumour made empty rooms seem alive. Mackay's moral is plain: crowds can lose reason as fast as single minds. The volume remains a classic warning about panic, belief, and the power of a shared delusion.
7134-the-great-conspiracy-volume-2:
Logan's second part of The Great Conspiracy opens at chapter six, The Great Conspiracy Maturing, on November 6, 1860. That day came and passed, and by the seventh the conviction that Lincoln would be elected had become certainty, heralded the length and breadth of the Republic. Excitement ran unparalleled: Northern Republicans rejoiced that slavery at last stood where the people could believe it in course of ultimate extinction.

The Douglas Democracy, chagrined at their leader's defeat, filled with gloomy forebodings for the country. The Southern Democracy, or a large portion of it, openly exulted that the long wished revolt of the Slave Power and separation of Slave from Free States stood at hand. Especially in South Carolina, fire eaters led the cry. Only this second part's course is followed here.
7146-cecilia-or-memoirs-of-an-heiress-vo:
Frances Burney's Cecilia, memoirs of an heiress, continues in this second volume of three, edited by R Brimley Johnson. Book four continues with a chapter titled A Murmuring, and book five opens with a rout, a broad hint, and an accommodation. A detection, a sarcasm, and a surmise follow, with a bold stroke, a miser's mansion, and a declaration.

A gamester's conscience, a persecution, a man of business, and a solution close book five, while book six opens with a debate, a railing, and an antique mansion. A rattle, a storm, a mystery, and an anecdote lead to a conference, an attack, and a retreat. Only this second volume's course is followed here, as Cecilia's fortune entangles her in town manners and money plots.
7155-the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-2:
Part two of Twain's Prince and the Pauper opens at chapter five, Tom as a Patrician, with Tom Canty left alone in the prince's cabinet. He makes good use of his chance, turning this way and that before the great mirror and admiring his finery. Then he walks away imitating the prince's high bred carriage while watching results in the glass. Next he draws the beautiful sword, bows, and kisses the blade, laying it across his breast as he saw a noble knight salute.

That salute went to the Tower lieutenant five or six weeks before, when Norfolk and Surrey lords were delivered into captivity. Tom plays with the jewelled dagger at his thigh and examines costly ornaments. He tries each sumptuous chair, dreaming how proud he would be if the Offal Court herd could peep in. He wonders if they would believe his tale at home.
7180-handy-andy-a-tale-of-irish-life-vol:
Samuel Lover's Handy Andy continues in this second volume, opening late at night in pitch dark, where a whistle from Dick answers with wheels, hoofbeats, and the rattle of an unseen vehicle. The illustrations promise Andy's cooking, a crack shot, a challenge, a party at Killarney, and an abduction, all etched from Lover's own drawings. Volume Two carries the tale past its first half without pause.

Andy remains the well-meaning Irish servant whose blunders drive the comedy, and the new chapters keep him among masters, rivals, and festive crowds. Lover writes in a broad, good-humoured style that lets mishap follow mishap while affection for his people never fades. This volume alone holds the later turns of Andy's career.
7194-the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-2:
Part Two opens on a tranquil Sunday morning, with Aunt Polly leading family worship. Her prayer is built of solid courses of scriptural quotation, welded with a thin mortar of originality. From that summit she delivers a grim chapter of Mosaic Law, as if from Sinai itself, before Tom girds himself to get his verses.

Sid learned his lesson days before, but Tom bends all his energy to five short verses, choosing part of the Sermon on the Mount because he can find none shorter. The comedy lies in the gap between holy duty and a boy's cunning economy of effort. This part holds the Sunday-school scene alone, bright with Twain's eye for village ritual.
7243-a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur:
Part Two of Mark Twain's Connecticut Yankee finds the hero second personage in the kingdom for political power, dressed in silks, velvets, and cloth of gold that prove showy and most uncomfortable. He takes the choicest suite in the castle after the king's, aglow with loud-coloured hangings. Yet the stone floors hold only misfit rushes for carpet, and proper conveniences, he notes, simply do not exist.

Merlin's tower gives the part its centre, as magic and modern cunning face each other across a court of silk and stone. Twain mines the gap between splendour and squalor for comedy, letting the Yankee's plain talk puncture courtly pride. This part holds the rise to power and its gaudy, draughty rooms.
732-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
Edward Gibbon devoted this second volume, with notes by H. H. Milman, to Rome's turn toward Christianity and to Constantine. A long opening section traces how Roman rulers treated Christians, from Nero's cruelty to Constantine's favour. It weighs law, persecution, and the slow growth of the church within the empire.

The volume then tells of the founding of Constantinople, Constantine's new capital, and his political system. Gibbon's irony and learning are on full show, as he links faith, power, and city-building. The book is essential for readers who want to see how an empire changed its gods and its centre, and what that change cost.
7532-a-book-of-old-ballads-volume-2:
Beverley Nichols's second volume of old ballads begins with an invitation. Lithe and listen, gentlemen, to the tale of the Heir of Linne, who sells his broad lands for gold and spends it all. King Cophetua and the Beggar Maid follows, with Sir Andrew Barton, May Collin, and the Blind Beggar's Daughter of Bednall Green. Thomas the Rhymer, Young Beichan, and Brave Lord Willoughbey keep the sequence moving.

The Spanish Lady's Love and The Friar of Orders Gray close the book, and color plates show King Cophetua, May Collin, Thomas the Rhymer, Young Beichan, and the Heir of Linne. The volume mixes romance, sea fighting, and fairy lore, all in the direct speech of the ballads. It is the middle book of Nichols's set, and the most varied in mood.
7751-godolphin-volume-2:
Constance and Godolphin walk and ride together each day in the second volume of Lytton's Godolphin, and at evening he hangs over her chair to hear her rich, soft songs. Lady Erpingham watches with secret delight, sure a match grows between two handsome, gifted young people.

Prudence whispers they are poor, but the countess recalls a dowry saved from her jointure for Constance, which she would gladly give if Godolphin were the groom. Through rural scenes, omens, and a first shy confession, the volume traces love growing under a kind chaperone's eye.
7758-falkland-book-2:
Emily Mandeville, married to a man she cannot love, finds her feelings waking in Book Two of Lytton's Falkland. The narrator warns it is risky for women to sit still with their hearts, for pause reveals a hollow that worldly folly once hid. Her son's birth had filled that hollow with new joy.

Then Falkland comes, and no woman he wished to charm had ever resisted him. His ardor matches her tenderness, and from that meeting her life splits in two. The volume is a frank early tale of a married woman's love, told with pity for a heart caught between duty and desire.
7851-memoirs-of-aaron-burr-volume-2:
Matthew L Davis's Memoirs of Aaron Burr, volume two, opens with Burr's brief study of law. It gives his definition of the craft, his way of preparing cases, his maxim for sluggards, and his love of mystery and surprise against opponents. His choice of agents and his coolness in civil and military life follow.

An anecdote from the contested election of 1800 shows the same acuteness in politics, after a career begun at the Revolution's close under fair auspices. With a frontispiece of Theodosia and the motto of burying Caesar, not praising him, Davis offers a candid, close portrait of a divisive founder.
7877-passages-from-the-english-notebooks:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Passages from the English Note-Books, volume two, opens April 4, 1856, at a Milton Club dinner on Ludgate Hill. Hawthorne dines with Bennoch at a club for dissenters and nonconformists whose ideas sit uneasily with church and state, in a large reading room full of papers.

A tall white-haired gentleman and Mr. Tupper greet each other warmly, and Hawthorne steps forward with outstretched hand before his name can be spoken unheard. Through London dinners, travel, and talk, the notebooks record an American author's daily England with candor, humor, and watchful detail.
7880-passages-from-the-french-and-italia:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Passages from the French and Italian Note-Books, volume two, continues in Florence on June 8, with a morning at the Uffizi gallery. The entrance lies through a great palace court to the Arno at one end and the Grand Ducal Piazza at the other, with Medici busts in the vestibule.

Hawthorne walks the long gallery slowly, full of sculpture and pictures, a chronological run from Giotto and Cimabue through Botticelli, Fra Angelico, and Filippo Lippi. Though pictures face away from light, he calls it the most perfect series he has seen, haunted by masters in every church.
7975-memoirs-of-james-robert-hope-scott-:
Robert Ornsby, professor of Greek and Latin literature in the Catholic University of Ireland, wrote this second volume of memoirs of James Robert Hope-Scott of Abbotsford, with selections from his correspondence. The volume opens in 1841 and 1842 with Hope's pamphlet on the Jerusalem bishopric, his study of canon law. And his letters to John Henry Newman about a monastery and the Oxford Movement. Later chapters follow Pusey's consultation of Hope and the religious controversies of the time.

The memoir is built from letters, so Hope's mind and friendships emerge in his own words. Readers interested in the Oxford Movement, the road to Rome, and Victorian religious argument will find a detailed, insider account. Volume two stands on its own for the 1840s, though it gains depth read after the first.
8089-passages-from-the-american-notebook:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's second volume of passages from his American notebooks opens at Brook Farm on April 13, 1841, where he calls the snowy settlement a polar paradise. Comparing the community's stormy arrival to the Plymouth pilgrims stepping ashore on mountain snowdrifts, he insists that spring and summer will come in due season. Later extracts come from his private letters as well as his journals.

The notebooks show Hawthorne observing before he invented: landscapes, neighbours, and the daily life of the Brook Farm experiment. They are the raw material of his fiction, full of images that later grew into stories. For readers of The Scarlet Letter and The House of the Seven Gables, this volume is a revealing workshop, and a record of a writer watching America closely.
8167-gargantua-and-pantagruel-illustrate:
Book two of Rabelais's Gargantua and Pantagruel follows the giant Pantagruel, son of Gargantua, through his heroic deeds and sayings. The English text reprints Sir Thomas Urquhart of Cromarty's 1653 translation, with footnotes from the Maitland Club edition of 1838 and the translators. Urquhart's translation of book three appeared posthumously in 1693, and Peter Antony Motteux's rendering of books four and five followed in 1708. With some omitted passages restored from the 1738 edition edited by Ozell.

Rabelais's second book is a feast of learned comedy, bawdy humour, and satire on church, law, and learning. Pantagruel's Paris education and his battles remain famous. For readers new to Rabelais, this book offers his world at its most exuberant, in a translation that is itself a classic of English prose.
8459-marse-henry-an-autobiography-volume:
Volume 2 of Henry Watterson's autobiography, Marse Henry, continues the Louisville editor's story into Congress and wider circles. Contents list Charles Eames and Charles Sumner, Schurz and Lamar, and Watterson going to Congress. Stephen Foster and his songs, music and Theodore Thomas follow, then Henry Adams and his family, John Hay, and the three mousquetaires of culture, with Paris scenes.

Watterson writes as a man who knew the makers of post-Civil War America, and the volume mixes politics with music, letters, and friendship. Readers get a firsthand account of Washington and Louisville life, witty and partisan. It pairs with volume 1, and stands alone as a memoir of an editor among statesmen.
8461-memoirs-of-henry-hunt-esq-volume-2:
Henry Hunt wrote these memoirs himself, in His Majesty's jail at Ilchester, in Somerset, and volume 2 continues his story. Hunt, the radical orator known as Orator Hunt, was jailed after the Peterloo era. His memoirs mix self-defense, political argument, and prison life, with Pope's lines on faultless pieces as his epigraph.

Readers meet a leading voice of early nineteenth-century radicalism, writing from a cell about reform, crowds, and his own career. Hunt's memoirs are partisan and vivid, and they show how radicals told their own stories when the press attacked them. The volume suits readers of British political history, and of prison writing.
8472-life-on-the-mississippi-part-2:
Part 2 of Life on the Mississippi opens with chapter 6, A Cub-pilot's Experience, aboard the poor old Paul Jones. Delayed four days on rocks at Louisville, plus other delays, the boat fools away about two weeks going from Cincinnati to New Orleans. The young Twain gets acquainted with a pilot who teaches him to steer, deepening the fascination of river life.

This section shows the cub pilot's schooling, with steering lessons, river lore, and the slow growth of skill. Readers get Twain's apprenticeship in full, after the geography of part 1. It is the book's training montage, told with humor about a young man's eagerness to master a dangerous trade.
8512-the-three-cities-trilogy-lourdes-vo:
Émile Zola's Lourdes, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, continues in volume 2 with the second day of the pilgrimage. The train arrives at twenty minutes past three by the Lourdes station clock, its dial lit by a reflector. Shadowy forms move under the slanting roof of the platform, resignedly going to and fro, pilgrims and patients seeking a cure.

Zola, the naturalist novelist, studied Lourdes as a social phenomenon: faith, sickness, hope, and commerce around the grotto. Volume 2 follows Pierre and Marie through the second day's devotions and disappointments. Readers get a novel that is also reportage, skeptical and compassionate, about why crowds still come to Lourdes.
8527-eve-s-diary-part-2:
Part 2 of Mark Twain's Eve's Diary, illustrated by Lester Ralph, opens on Sunday, pleasant again, though heavy days came before. Eve writes that she tried to get Adam some of those apples, but cannot learn to throw straight, and failed, though she thinks the good intention pleased him. The apples are forbidden, Adam says she shall come to harm, but she is not so sure.

This middle part follows Eve's Eden life as she learns the garden, its creatures, and Adam's gruff ways. Readers get Twain's Eve in full curiosity, testing rules and charming her companion. The part suits readers following the diary in order, and those who want Eve's voice at its most playful.
8533-the-literary-remains-of-samuel-tayl:
Volume 2 of the Literary Remains of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, collected and edited by Henry Nelson Coleridge, continues the poet's unpublished writings. Contents open with an extract from a letter of February 1818 to a gentleman who attended Coleridge's spring lectures, and a letter to J. Britton, before moving into Shakespeare criticism and other remains.

Readers meet Coleridge as lecturer and critic, thinking aloud about Shakespeare and poetry in letters and fragments. The volume, like its companion, preserves what Coleridge's nephew judged worth saving from a vast, unfinished mind. For Coleridge students, it is a primary source; for general readers, a glimpse of Romantic criticism in the making.
8540-the-life-of-the-rt-hon-sir-charles-:
Stephen Gwynn began this life of Sir Charles W. Dilke, and Gertrude M. Tuckwell, Dilke's literary executrix, completed and edited it, in two volumes with portraits. Volume 2 opens with chapter 34, Home Affairs from October 1883 to December 1884. Egypt in 1884, and franchise and redistribution, follow, tracing Dilke's career through the great questions of late Victorian politics.

Dilke, a radical Liberal minister, fell from power over a divorce scandal, and the biography treats his later life with care. Readers get a political life from inside the Liberal Party, with documents and recollection. The volume suits readers of Victorian politics, and of reputations made and broken.
8552-the-seaboard-parish-volume-2:
George MacDonald continues The Seaboard Parish in volume 2, with contents including Another Sunday Evening, Niceboots, The Blacksmith, The Life-Boat, Mr. Percivale, The Shadow of Death, At the Farm, The Keeve, The Walk to Church, and The Old Castle, with Joe and his trouble and a small adventure.

MacDonald, the Scottish minister and fantasist who influenced C. S. Lewis, writes a parish novel as a series of sermons, stories, and seaside scenes. The narrator, a minister, reflects on his people, his family, and the shore. Readers get Victorian religious fiction at its gentlest, where sermons and daily life braid together by the sea.
8583-roughing-it-part-2:
Chapter 11 begins the second part of Mark Twain's Roughing It, published in 1880, by turning to frontier justice in Montana. There, local vigilantes hanged Slade, a notorious figure who had relocated to the territory from Rocky Ridge. Twain retells the episode using Dimsdale's history The Vigilantes of Montana as his source.

This section follows Twain's western years through the Slade story and frontier justice, with humor and horror mixed. Readers get the West as Twain lived it, where law was improvised and violence common. Part 2 suits readers following Roughing It in order, and those who want Twain's frontier at its rawest.
8594-normandy-the-scenery-romance-of-its:
This second part of Gordon Home's illustrated tour of Normandy opens at chapter four, in the cathedral city of Evreux at evening. The great bell tolls over cobbled streets, yellow light washes painted house fronts, and laurels in the courtyard of the Hotel du Grand Cerf catch the last sun. Home insists Evreux needs no fine evening to please, and the chapter sets out to prove it street by street.

From Evreux the road runs to Bernay and on through the towns covered in this middle stretch of the book, with Home's drawings and notes on churches, inns, and country roads. The pace stays slow and observant, built for a traveller on foot or by carriage rather than a hurried tourist. Readers get the companion volume to parts one and three, filling the map between Rouen and the western coast.
8674-charles-o-malley-the-irish-dragoon-:
Charles Lever continues the adventures of Charles O'Malley, the Irish dragoon, in this second volume, illustrated by Phiz. The Peninsular War provides the ground: skirmishes, the lines of Ciudad Rodrigo, the Coa, night marches, Lisbon, and the retreat of the French. Between battles come dinners, masquerades, villas, letters, confessions, and the hero's charger, Maurice, all told with Lever's high spirits.

Later chapters reach Fuentes d'Onoro, Almeida, and a night on the Azava, mixing real campaign history with comic scrapes and romantic entanglements. O'Malley's servant Mike and the regimental doctor add broad humour to the soldiering. The volume stands as a classic of Irish military fiction, best read after volume one, and still enjoyable for its pace, its jokes, and its picture of Wellington's army from inside.
8702-the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-2:
Gustave Dore's Bible illustrations reach their second volume with the patriarchs and the early judges. The text pairs each engraving with its Bible passage, beginning with the trial of Abraham's faith on Mount Moriah. Then the burial of Sarah, Eliezer finding Rebekah, Isaac blessing Jacob, and Jacob tending Laban's flocks. Joseph's story follows, from his sale into Egypt to his dreams for Pharaoh and his reunion with his brothers.

Moses in the bulrushes closes the patriarchal arc, before the volume turns to war against Gibeon and Jael slaying Sisera. Dore's dramatic engravings, all shadow, scale, and gesture, made the Bible visible for millions who could not afford the grand original edition. Readers can enjoy the pictures in the mind's eye through the passages, and follow a sweep of Genesis and Judges in short, powerful scenes.
8722-the-three-cities-trilogy-rome-volum:
Emile Zola's Rome, in Ernest A. Vizetelly's translation, follows Abbe Pierre Froment through the Eternal City in this second volume, which is Part II of the novel. Pierre, having leisure one afternoon, begins his wanderings with a visit he has set his heart on. Prompted by a letter from old Count Orlando Prada, hero of Italian independence and reunion. Prada wrote spontaneously after a hasty reading of Pierre's book New Rome, and his letter blazes with patriotic faith, accusing the priest of errors about Italy.

From that meeting, the volume opens Rome's two worlds: the Romans of the new Italy, the Pradas and Saccos, the Corso and the Pincio. The ancient city of palaces, forums, and catacombs. Zola piles up street life, art, and church politics as Pierre seeks a hearing for his book. Readers get the middle movement of a great naturalist novel about faith, Rome, and modern Italy.
8791-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
This second part of Dante's Purgatory, in Cary's translation, covers cantos five through ten. Canto five opens with Dante leaving spirits behind and following his conductor. When a soul points and cries out that light does not shine from Dante's left hand, since he, a living man, blocks it. The shades gaze in wonder, first at the marvel and then at Dante himself, until Virgil urges him on like a tower, unmoved by babbling crowds.

Later cantos climb the mountain's lower slopes, meeting the late repentant, the negligent rulers, and souls who sing as they wait. The mood softens from Hell's terror to hope: punishment here cleanses rather than merely torments. Readers moving from the Inferno will feel the change at once, in lighter air, music, and the promise that these souls will, in time, ascend. The part makes a gentle entry to Purgatory's middle cantos.
8797-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
Cary's Paradise continues in this second part, covering cantos fifteen through twenty-one, where Dante climbs through the heavens of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. Canto fifteen opens with true love showing itself clear in kindness, as sacred chords fall silent before righteous prayer, and a sudden trail of fire glides through the still, pure evening air. The imagery of light grows ever more intense as Dante meets his ancestor Cacciaguida.

Warriors of faith, just rulers formed into an eagle of light, and contemplatives on a golden ladder fill these cantos, testing Dante's understanding of history, justice, and prayer. Beatrice guides and explains, while Dante's questions grow bolder. Readers in the middle of Paradise will find its most political heavens here, where earthly fame and heavenly order are weighed against each other in shining, difficult poetry.
8824-poems-in-two-volumes-volume-2:
William Wordsworth's second volume of Poems in Two Volumes turns to Scotland and to moods of his own mind. Poems written during a tour in Scotland open with Rob Roy's Grave, The Solitary Reaper, Stepping Westward, Glen-Almain, the Matron of Jedborough, To a Highland Girl. An address to the sons of Burns after visiting their father's grave on August 14, 1803. Yarrow unvisited closes the Scottish group in the contents shown.

Moods of My Own Mind follows. To a Butterfly, Written in March while resting on the bridge at the foot of Brother's Water, The Small Celandine, and The Sparrow's Nest. The volume shows Wordsworth at his most intimate and musical, finding large feeling in small encounters. Readers who love the famous Reaper will find its companions here, and a book that rewards quiet, repeated reading.
891-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
In this second volume of Gibbon's history, Rome's story turns from emperors to faith and to a new capital. The opening chapters follow the Roman state's dealings with Christians, from Nero's reign to Constantine's favour, tracing persecution, growth, and the church's slow rise within the empire.

Gibbon then tells how Constantine founded Constantinople and remade the empire's government around it. Milman's notes guide the reader through the sources. The volume matters because it shows an empire changing its gods and its centre, a change that would shape Europe and the Near East for a thousand years.
8912-lyrical-ballads-with-other-poems-18:
William Wordsworth issued this second volume of Lyrical Ballads in 1800, the book that helped launch English Romantic poetry. It gathers short poems on farm folk, children, lost love, and quiet country scenes, told in plain speech rather than grand, high-flown verse. Wordsworth held that true feeling could live in simple words.

Here readers meet Lucy Gray, the shepherd boys of Dungeon-Gill, Ruth, and the boy who listens to owls, among many others. The poems prize memory, nature, and the inner life of plain people. For students of poetry, this volume is a key text, showing a new style at the very start of its life.
8929-adela-cathcart-volume-2:
George MacDonald's Adela Cathcart continues in this second volume with song, the curate and his wife. The shadows, an evening at the curate's, Percy and his mother, the broken swords, and my uncle Peter. The narrator confesses slight dismay at the solemn turn the club-stories have taken, lasting only a moment. Adela is deeply interested, again wearing the look of abstracted thought and feeling. He tells himself this mental fare differs greatly from what she is used to, yet she can mark, learn, and inwardly digest it.

Adela, an invalid young woman, is healed in part by stories told by a circle of friends, in MacDonald's frame-tale design. Fairy tales, parables, and sermons in story form do the work of medicine and ministry together. Readers who enjoy MacDonald's fantasy and his theology will find volume two deepening the first.
9095-the-life-and-letters-of-maria-edgew:
Augustus J. C. Hare edited this second volume of the life and letters of Maria Edgeworth, the Irish novelist. The letters, such as one from Coppet in September 1820, follow Edgeworth and her father through Switzerland, in low carriages over mountain roads, past glaciers, cascades, and the fair valley of Lauterbrunn. Her eye is quick and amused.

Through her own words, readers meet the Europe of her day, its writers, hosts, and scenes, and see how a working novelist watched the world she later wrote about. Hare's editing lets Edgeworth speak for herself. The volume is a delight for those who love letters as a form of travel and talk.
9165-the-three-cities-trilogy-paris-volu:
Émile Zola wrote Paris as the third book of his Three Cities trilogy, translated by Ernest Vizetelly. This volume holds Book Two of the novel. Its hero, Abbé Pierre Froment, a priest who has lost his faith, shelters his wounded brother Guillaume in a quiet house at Neuilly. Revolution brews in the streets outside.

Pierre tends Guillaume in silence, torn between love for his brother and dread of the plot around him. Zola sets private anguish against public strife. The volume carries the trilogy toward its close, where faith, reason, and life fight for Pierre's soul.
920-ethics-part-2:
Baruch Spinoza's Ethics continues in Part Two, on the nature and origin of the mind, translated by R. H. M. Elwes. Spinoza now explains the results that must follow from the essence of God, the eternal and infinite being, though not all of them, for the mind itself becomes his subject.

He argues that mind and body are one substance seen in two ways, and that ideas follow from God as surely as bodies do. His geometric method stays strict, with definitions, axioms, and proofs. Part Two is the bridge from God to man in Spinoza's system, and it is vital for readers following his argument whole.
9316-a-doctor-of-the-old-school-volume-2:
Ian Maclaren wrote this Scots tale of Dr. MacLure, the doctor of Drumtochty, in Book Two, Through the Flood. MacLure gives no grand speech from the hearthrug, as town doctors might. He speaks in the yard, one foot in the stirrup, or in silence. Leaving Annie Mitchell's sickbed, he says not one word, and her husband's heart sinks.

Tammas, dull of speech yet sharp in love, reads the doctor's face at once. Maclaren writes in Scots flavor with deep tenderness. The volume remains a moving portrait of a country doctor, plain, tireless, and loved.
9444-samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-:
A threshing machine arrives with no warning in this second part of Marietta Holley's Samantha Among the Brethren. Samantha knew nothing of it till half an hour before, and Josiah Allen was no more to blame. Solomon Gowdey fell bed sick, so the crew came straight to the Allens, driving past the parlor windows to the barn.

One horse falls down, and Steve Yerden's yelling at his team caps the din. Holley, as Josiah Allen's Wife, turns farm chaos into comedy with a moral edge. The part remains a funny, warm slice of rural church and farm life.
9601-the-poetical-works-of-alexander-pop:
Volume two of Alexander Pope's poetical works, edited by George Gilfillan in 1856, pairs Pope's verse with memoir and notes. Gilfillan's essay opens by noting Pope's strange fate: admired and abused at once, in life and after death. Critics fought over his body like Greeks over Patroclus, judging his manhood and his poetry together. His creed, politics, and ease fed the quarrel.

The volume presents Pope's poems with critical dissertation and explanatory notes, so a reader can follow his wit and craft. Satire, epistle, and mock epic show his range. A reader gets a Victorian edition of a master satirist, with guidance for modern eyes.
9609-joseph-andrews-vol-2:
Volume two of Henry Fielding's Joseph Andrews, edited by George Saintsbury, continues the comic novel's second book and opens its third. Parson Adams meets Parson Trulliber in a famed interview, then blunders through fresh adventures with honest simplicity. A dialogue with his host nearly ends in a quarrel, saved by the lovers' return. Book three opens with praise of biography.

Later chapters bring night scenes, strange adventures, and Mr. Wilson's life history, told at length. Fielding's humor stays broad and humane, with Adams as its innocent heart. A reader gets the middle stretch of a classic comic novel, rich in road, inn, and parsonage wit.
9751-night-and-morning-volume-2:
Volume two of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Night and Morning opens with Mr. Beaufort haunted on his way home. Gloomy terrors dog him, as Philip's denunciations seem aimed less at himself than at his son. He fears Arthur may meet a strange, exasperated scatterling at passion's height. After a scene with Arthur, he doubts he can rule the boy at all.

Book two carries the novel's feud forward, as fathers, sons, and outcasts collide. Lytton's prose favors polished dread and moral weight. A reader gets the second book of a Victorian tale of ambition, where a father's guilt shadows his son's path.
9821-a-writer-s-recollections-volume-2:
Volume two of Mrs. Humphry Ward's A Writer's Recollections, published in November 1918, recalls London in the 1880s and her rise as a novelist. Chapters follow London friends, the publication of Robert Elsmere, and first visits to Italy. Amalfi and Rome, Hampden and Marcella, and Helbeck of Bannisdale mark her path. Henry James and Roman friends fill later pages.

Ward opens with John Morley, Forster's critic in the press, met at a master's dinner in the late 1870s. Her memoir blends literary gossip with sober self-judgment. A reader gets a rich Victorian writer's life, told by one who knew James, Balfour, and Rome at first hand.
990-theologico-political-treatise-part-2:
Baruch Spinoza, a Dutch thinker of the seventeenth century, sets out a bold way to read the Bible in this part of his great treatise. He treats scripture as a human text shaped by its own time, and he tests claims about miracles, prophecy, and divine law by reason rather than by fear. His aim is to free both faith and thought.

The chapters press on to ask what scripture can truly teach: not physics or history, but love of God and care for one's neighbor. Spinoza argues that states gain peace when they let minds judge freely. The work shocked his age and still frames debates on scripture, faith, and free speech.
9921-the-works-of-lord-byron-letters-and:
This second volume of Byron's letters and journals, edited by Rowland E. Prothero, covers August 1811 to April 1814, the years of his sudden fame. It includes his letters to his publisher John Murray, his journal from November 1813, and his correspondence with Walter Scott.

Readers follow the making of Childe Harold's first cantos, The Giaour, and The Bride of Abydos, with parliamentary speeches and newspaper attacks in the appendices. Byron writes with wit, frankness, and sudden feeling. The volume is the best short road into the poet's mind at the height of his celebrity.
a-book-of-old-ballads-volume-2:
Volume 2 of Beverley Nichols's A Book of Old Ballads continues his selection from Percy's Reliques and the Child collection, in the same old-spelling dress as the first volume. It opens with 'The Heir of Linne,' whose unthrifty lord spends his gold on company, cards, and dice until nothing is left but the lesson his father buried for him.

The rest of the volume holds 'King Cophetua and the Beggar Maid,' 'Sir Andrew Barton,' 'May Collin,' and 'The Blind Beggar's Daughter of Bednall Green. ' 'Thomas the Rhymer' and 'Young Beichan' bring in fairyland bargains and rescues from across the sea. While 'Brave Lord Willoughbey,' 'The Spanish Lady's Love,' and 'The Friar of Orders Gray' close the set. Colour plates illustrate four of the ballads.
a-collection-of-old-english-plays-volume: The second volume of Arthur Henry Bullen's old English plays opens with Don Pedro Gusman and his sons. Its scenes move between Spain and France, with partings, love, and questions of honor. Like the first volume, it prints plays long out of reach of ordinary readers. Bullen's careful editing brings forgotten Renaissance drama back into print.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co:
Part 2 opens with Hank installed as the second man in the kingdom, lodged in silk and velvet and missing soap, matches, and a looking-glass. Merlin, whose tower Hank has marked for pulling down, plots against the upstart whose eclipse trick stole his fame and left his magic looking cheap.

As the Boss, Hank watches a tournament, plans schools, factories, and telegraph lines in secret, and calls it beginning civilization under cover of miracle. The part closes as he rides out in search of adventures with the talkative Sandy, in Twain's parody of the knight-errant tales he had been reading. The comedy runs on the gap between sixth-century manners and nineteenth-century know-how.
a-doctor-of-the-old-school-volume-2: In the second volume of Ian Maclaren's Doctor of the Old School, the doctor faces a sickbed crisis. He gives his opinion from the hearthrug in a solemn procession from sick room to dining room. When he leaves the room where Annie Mitchell's life ebbs away, he says not one word. Her husband reads trouble in his face, and the glen holds its breath.
a-far-country-volume-2:
Winston Churchill opens book two at the state capital, where Hugh Paret arrives by train to a broad, shallow river and the dome of the state house against the sky. The lobby of the Potts House is already full of lawmakers: heavy-jawed workers from the cities and moon-faced, astute countrymen who manipulate votes among farms and villages.

This middle volume deepens Paret's practice in railroad and corporation law and his education in how legislation is really bought and managed. Colonel Paul Barney and his kind teach the going rates. Success grows, and with it the compromises Paret once would have refused. Churchill writes politics from the cloakroom, in detail learned from his own years in public life.
a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-volume-2:
William Dean Howells opens the second part of his novel on the evening Basil March accepts a reduced offer and takes a New York apartment. In the house he rejected, a widow and her daughter sit sewing and drawing under a drop-light, talking of furnaces and lodgers. The two households, Marches and Leightons, will cross through the magazine that employs them both.

This volume settles the characters into the city: the search for rooms, the first numbers of Every Other Week, and the young artist Beaton's visits to both families. Howells renders the economics of genteel life — rents, dinners, dress — with fine exactness. The great strike and tragedy still wait ahead, in later volumes.
a-history-of-science-volume-2:
Henry Smith Williams covers the beginnings of modern science in the second volume of his five-volume history, assisted by Edward H. Williams. The contents start with science in the Dark Age and medieval science among the Arabs. Then the scene shifts west, and the pace of discovery quickens.

Chapters trace the new cosmology from Copernicus to Kepler and Galileo, Galileo's new physics, and the false sciences of alchemy and astrology. Medicine runs from Paracelsus to Harvey, and the volume closes with Newton's work on light and gravitation, instruments of precision, and natural history up to Linnaeus. Williams writes a clear, connected story for general readers.
a-lover-s-diary-volume-2: Gilbert Parker's A Lover's Diary, volume two, opens in dreams and shadows, where the lover lives year to year among warders of desire. A bride, a wraith, surrender and a citadel give way to divided life, lost footsteps, a chalice and a decree, then to morning, sacrifice and reunion. The volume ends with absolution, a benediction and an envoy bidding the ghost rest.
a-popular-history-of-france-from-the-ear: François Guizot carries his history of France through the decline and end of the Crusades into the growth of kingship, communes, and the third estate. The volume follows the Hundred Years' War under Philip the Sixth and John the Second, the States-General of the fourteenth century, and the reign of Charles the Fifth. Steel engravings of crusade preaching, Saint Louis administering justice, and the Sicilian Vespers accompany the narrative.
a-romance-of-youth-volume-2:
Francois Coppee continues a Paris childhood in A Romance of Youth, Volume 2 of the English edition. Little Amedee, a widow's son, spends his afternoons with the Gerard family next door. The father engraves copper plates on a high stool while his daughters play around him. Four rooms hold old furniture, comrades' pictures, and children's games.

Maria Gerard, a wild, inventive girl, makes Amedee her little husband in play. Her sister Louise, ten and very much a young lady, lends herself to the make-believe calls. A pasteboard doll serves as the baby they present to visitors. Madame Gerard rules the kitchen and scolds the noise that shakes her Rouen crockery. Coppee writes poverty without misery here: bacon smells, hide-and-seek, and first affection fill the rooms. Readers gathering the four volumes find the hero's heart formed in this one, long before youth tests it in earnest.
a-voyage-towards-the-south-pole-and-roun: James Cook continues his voyage towards the South Pole and round the world in this second volume, with book three running from Ulietea to New Zealand. The chapters pass the Friendly Isles, a reception at Anamocka with a robbery and its consequences, and the passage to the New Hebrides. Discovery of several islands, intercourse with the natives, departure from Tanna, and the survey and description of New Caledonia carry the voyage toward its close.
a-woodland-queen-reine-des-bois-volume-2:
André Theuriet continues his French pastoral in this second volume, which holds the fourth, fifth, and sixth chapters of the whole: The Dawn of Love, Love's Indiscretion, and Love by Proxy. The heir of Vivey, settled now in the woodland estate, finds his feelings engaged where his position forbids them to show. A go-between carries what he cannot say.

Theuriet lets the middle book ripen slowly, in walks, harvests, and village talk under the trees. The forest is refuge and temptation at once for his woodland queen. By the close, the love that began at dawn has committed the indiscretion of the chapter title, and a dark secret waits for the third volume to reveal it.
a-writer-s-recollections-volume-2: Mrs. Humphry Ward continues a writer's recollections in this second volume, published in November 1918. The contents run from London in the eighties and London friends through the publication of Robert Elsmere to first visits to Italy. Amalfi and Rome, Hampden and Marcella, and Helbeck of Bannisdale follow. The Villa Barberini, Henry James, Roman friends, and Eleanor lead to an epilogue, with recollections of Morley beginning at a Master's dinner table.
abigail-adams-letters-vol-2:
Volume Two of Abigail Adams's letters covers the presidency years and the early republic. John Adams was now in high office, and Abigail wrote from the center of the new nation's politics. The 1840 edition completes the set.

The letters treat the move to Washington, party fights, and the bitter Adams-Jefferson feud. Abigail judges public men with a dry wit and strong opinions of her own. Home and state business mix on every page, as they did in her life. Together the two volumes form America's most famous political correspondence between husband and wife. She also records the death of friends and the strain of public life.
account-of-a-tour-in-normandy-volume-2: Dawson Turner continues his account of a tour in Normandy in this second volume, moving from Ducler, Saint Georges de Bocherville, and Langlois to Jumièges. Its abbey history and the tombs of Agnes Sorel and Enervez follow, with Gournay, Neufmarché, Gisors, the Andelys, Château Gaillard, and Écouis after them. Évreux cathedral, Saint Taurinus, and the vicinity with Navarre, Cocherel, Pont-Audemer, Harfleur, and the Bec abbey close the tour.
adela-cathcart-volume-2: George MacDonald continues Adela Cathcart in this second volume, where the contents run from Song and The Curate and His Wife through The Shadows and The Evening at the Curate's. Percy and His Mother, The Broken Swords, and My Uncle Peter complete the volume. The first chapter confesses dismay at the solemn turn the club stories have taken, yet Adela is deeply interested. She wears a look of abstracted thought and feeling, and marks, learns, and inwardly digests the strange newness of her thoughts.
alfred-russel-wallace-letters-and-remini: Alfred Russel Wallace returns in a second volume of letters and reminiscences, this time centred on his works in biology and geographical distribution. Correspondence and memoir show the older naturalist defending, revising, and extending ideas formed on his great journeys. Together with the first volume, it forms a full, personal record of a life spent observing the living world.
amelia-volume-2:
Amelia, Volume 2, by Henry Fielding, continues his last novel in the Saintsbury edition of the Works, where it forms part of the eighth volume overall. George Saintsbury edited the set, with illustrations by Herbert Railton and E J Wheeler. This volume's contents open Book V with the reader meeting an old acquaintance, then a chapter containing a brace of doctors and much physical matter, Fielding's joking word for medical business.

Book V follows Captain Booth to a noble lord. The lord's favor might free Booth from his troubles. Serjeant Atkinson, his loyal friend from the Gibraltar days, carries much of the action. Amelia Booth, the most patient heroine Fielding ever wrote, holds the household together against debts, bailiffs, and her husband's weaknesses. Saintsbury's Amelia is a reading edition of a domestic epic: marriage under financial siege, told with the author's late, mellow irony.
amundsen-south-pole-vol-2:
The second volume of Roald Amundsen's The South Pole, in A. G. Chater's 1912 English translation, tells the dash itself. Five men with dogs set out from the Bay of Whales in October 1911. They reached the Pole on December 14, ahead of Scott's party.

Amundsen describes the climb onto the polar plateau, the careful marking of the pole site, and the fast run back. The party reached base in January with men and dogs in good shape. The volume also carries the voyage home and the scientific results. It is the winner's own telling of the race.
an-account-of-the-english-colony-in-new-: David Collins continues his account of the English colony in New South Wales in volume two, from its first settlement in 1788 to August 1801. Remarks on the native inhabitants and particulars of New Zealand recur, with an account of the voyage by Captain Flinders and Mr. Bass. The volume carries the colony's story through its hard early years.
an-attic-philosopher-in-paris-volume-2:
Morning in a Paris garret fills An Attic Philosopher in Paris, Volume 2, the second English portion of Emile Souvestre's journal of a poor scholar. The philosopher wakes in good humor and defends the first hour of the day against the world's habit of wasting it. Sleep, he argues, lies about a man's character; the waking hour tells the truth. His small room, his books, and the roofs of Paris supply his text.

Inside, the day's entries move from meditation to the street and back: workmen, neighbors, small kindnesses, and small shames. Souvestre's narrator measures wealth by attention rather than money, finding sermons in errands and weather. The poor around his attic appear as people, not scenery, each with a history the diary pauses to learn. Readers in the second volume get the book's method pure: a philosopher's day kept like an account book, with joy entered on the credit side.
ancient-records-egypt-breasted-1906-vol-:
Volume two of Breasted's Ancient Records of Egypt, published in 1906, is devoted to the eighteenth dynasty. That dynasty built Egypt's empire: Thutmose III's campaigns in Syria, Hatshepsut's famous expedition to Punt, and the wealth of Amenhotep III fill its inscriptions. Breasted translates the annals, hymns, and tomb records reign by reign.

The volume catches Egypt at its height, when its armies reached the Euphrates and its temples rose at Thebes. Court biographies and victory stelae give the human grain inside the royal boasts. Breasted's corpus made such texts usable by every historian of the ancient world. Volume two is often the most read of the five. Its records anchor the chronology of the whole region.
andersonville-a-story-of-rebel-military-:
Volume 2 of John McElroy's Andersonville opens at chapter twenty-three with a new lot of prisoners. Until now only the old captures, from Gettysburg, Chickamauga, and Mine Run, had come in. The armies were quiet all winter, preparing for the death grapple of spring. Then the Florida expedition's survivors arrive from the battle of Olustee, men McElroy says were sacrificed to a general's incompetency. With them comes a queer crowd, the prisons' character changing as numbers swell toward Andersonville itself.

Inside, the volume records the early Andersonville months and the cruelties with names attached. An officer of a colored regiment is mistreated; the sergeant of a Negro squad is killed, and McElroy prints it as evidence. Readers get the descent here: Richmond was a prison, but Georgia is a system, built around men too weak to leave.
ante-nicene-fathers-vol-2:
Volume two of the Ante-Nicene Fathers, edited by Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson in 1885, gathers the Fathers of the second century. The writers here are Hermas, Tatian, Athenagoras, Theophilus, and Clement of Alexandria. The set as a whole is the standard English home of the early church writers.

Hermas's Shepherd, a book of visions on repentance, opens the volume. Tatian and Athenagoras defend the faith against pagan charges, while Theophilus writes to a pagan friend. Clement of Alexandria closes it, wedding Greek learning to Christian teaching. The volume shows the young church arguing for its life in a hostile empire.
appian-roman-history-white-vol-2:
The second volume of Appian's Roman History, in Horace White's 1899 English version, turns from foreign wars to the wars Rome fought on itself. Appian wrote in Greek around 160 CE. His five books on the civil wars run from the Gracchi brothers to Sextus Pompeius, the last holdout after the death of Caesar.

Here are the land reforms that split the city, the march of Sulla, the rise of Pompey and Caesar, and the death lists that killed Cicero. Appian tells it as one long fall from republic to one-man rule. His is the only connected ancient account of these wars, and still the fullest source for the end of the republic.
arabian-nights-lane-1848-vol-2:
Edward William Lane made the Nights scholarly in his Thousand and One Nights, and Volume II here is the 1848 printing. Lane's version, first published from 1838 to 1840, filled the tales with notes on Egyptian life and custom. Volume II completes the library's Lane set alongside its mates.

Lane trimmed what Victorian families could not read, yet his learning gave the tales new weight. His notes turn stories into a window on Cairo's streets, homes, and beliefs. Readers who want the Nights with a guide beside them still choose Lane, and this volume carries his middle nights.
arabian-nights-payne-1882-vol-2:
Payne's second volume of the Thousand Nights and One Night, from 1882, keeps Shahrazad's nights unrolling. Tales of merchants, demons, and enchanted cities fill the Calcutta text that John Payne followed for his first complete English version. The frame holds: each dawn leaves a story hanging, and the king spares the teller one more day.

Victorian readers met in these pages a world of jinn and treasure that bowdlerized editions had hidden. Payne's plain, rich English let the Arabic storyteller's art speak without trimming. Volume II deepens the set's claim to completeness, night after marvelous night.
aristophanes-eleven-comedies-vol-2:
Volume two completes the eleven surviving comedies of Aristophanes, the master of Athenian Old Comedy. An anonymous English translation carries the set. The plays span the later years of his long career.

The Birds builds a city in the sky to escape Athenian folly. In Lysistrata, women end a war by withholding sex from their husbands. The Frogs stages a contest between dead tragedians in the underworld. Thesmophoriazusae, Ecclesiazusae, and Plutus round out the volume. Together they show comedy testing every Athenian institution, from the assembly to the gods. His last plays show comedy itself changing toward gentler, more domestic plots.
aristophanes-plays-rogers-loeb-1924-vol-:
Rogers's second Loeb volume of Aristophanes, published in 1924, holds The Peace, The Birds, and The Frogs. In The Peace a farmer flies to heaven on a dung beetle to rescue the goddess Peace from a pit. The Birds builds a city in the sky and starves the gods into terms.

The Frogs sends Dionysus to the underworld to fetch back a dead tragedian. There Aeschylus and Euripides contest in verse, weighed line by line like goods. Rogers renders the songs and slang in brisk rhyming verse. These three are among the most inventive comedies ever staged. The volume shows Aristophanes moving from topical satire toward pure fantasy.
arnold-history-rome-vol-2:
Rome strides toward world power in the second volume of Thomas Arnold's History of Rome, from 1843. The middle Republic fights the Punic Wars against Carthage. Victory at sea and in Spain and Africa makes Rome master of the western seas.

Arnold pairs firm learning with the moral eye of a great teacher. He asks what conquest did to the conquerors as well as the conquered. Generals and senates alike face his even judgment. The narrative carries readers from a city-state to an empire in the making, in prose that kept the work a Victorian classic for decades.
athenaeus-deipnosophists-yonge-vol-2:
Volume two of Yonge's Deipnosophists continues Athenaeus's banquet of the learned. The guests keep eating, drinking, and quoting lost books at length. Courses of fish, fowl, and wine structure the endless conversation.

Cooks, flute-girls, philosophers, and parasites all receive learned discussion. Athenaeus piles quotation upon quotation from authors otherwise vanished. Parasites and flatterers get a famous taxonomy of their types. The talk ranges from Homer to the price of fish in Athens. Yonge's English carries the feast's second helping steadily. Readers taste how much ancient learning survived only inside other men's dinner talk here.
ausonius-evelynwhite-loeb-vol-2:
The second Loeb volume of Ausonius, in Hugh G. Evelyn White's translation, completes the poems of the Bordeaux master. Ausonius wrote in the late fourth century, when Gaul was rich, Christian in name, and still steeped in the old classics. His letters and later poems fill this volume.

Verse letters to his friend Paulinus press the monk-poet to leave his Spanish retreat, a plea Paulinus famously refused. Riddles, epigrams, and a strange cento stitched from Virgil show the playful side of his craft. Read with the first volume, the set gives the full Ausonius. Few poets show so well how the Roman world turned toward the medieval one.
autobiography-of-andrew-dickson-white-vo:
Andrew Dickson White filled volume two of his autobiography largely with diplomacy, drawing on his years as an American envoy abroad. The volume opens with his service as minister to Russia from 1892 to 1894 under President Harrison. White describes presentation to Emperor Alexander the Third, talks with ministers and grand dukes, and a first sight of the heir, the future Nicholas the Second.

Railways, court ceremony, and the treatment of Russian Jews all enter his notes. White had helped found Cornell University before this second career, and he writes as a scholar watching empires at close range. Later chapters continue his diplomatic service. The tone stays curious, courteous, and quietly judgmental about power.
autobiography-of-seventy-years-vol-1-2:
George Frisbie Hoar, senator from Massachusetts, published this memoir with Scribner's in 1903, covering seventy years of American life. Portraits front the volumes, one showing Hoar in 1897. He dedicates the record to his wife and children. Ancestry comes first: Roger Sherman and his family, then Hoar's father Samuel, a Concord lawyer of national standing.

Boyhood in Concord among famous neighbours leads to Harvard sixty years before, then law at Worcester. Chapters trace the founding of the Republican Party, Daniel Webster, the Know Nothing party and its fall, and Hoar's election to Congress beside Sumner and Wilson. Quoting John Sherman on finance shows his method: public men are judged by their words in storms. The memoir is a participant's history of the Republican party's rise.
b09-zwingli-latin-works-2:
Volume two of Zwingli's Latin Works and Correspondence spans 1522 to 1528, the years when Zurich's reform took hold. William John Hinke edited the volume, published at Philadelphia in 1922 under the American Society of Church History. Translators Henry Preble, Walter Lichtenstein, and Lawrence A McLouth carried the Latin into English.

These are the years of open break: images removed, the mass set aside, and Zurich set on a new course. Zwingli's letters show him guiding a city through change while arguing with foes on every side. His treatises state the Swiss case in his own sharp terms. The volume forms the core of the English Zwingli set.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-2:
Volume two of Michael L. Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud finishes Tract Sabbath, begun in volume one. The 1918 edition carries the second half of the Sabbath discussions. Sabbath law was a daily test of faithfulness for observant Jews, and the rabbis treat it with care.

The talks turn to cooking, travel limits, and what may be moved or worn on the holy day. Case after case sharpens the line between rest and work. Rodkinson's plain English keeps the debates readable without flattening their logic. With volume one, it gives the full Sabbath tractate in English dress.
badauni-muntakhab-vol-2:
