Akbar's reign rolls on in the second volume of Badauni's chronicle, in W. H. Lowe's 1899 English version. Court intrigue thickens, and debates on faith grow bolder at court. Badauni's private scorn for the emperor's bold experiments sharpens page by page.

He records grants, quarrels, hunts, and heresies in one blunt stream. The gap between the public glory and his secret doubts fascinates modern readers. Few Mughal sources read with such spice and attitude. Lowe's translation keeps the chronicler's bite, giving English readers a history that entertains even as it informs about power, faith, and pride.
bancroft-history-us-vol-2:
Colonial America deepens in the second volume of Bancroft's History of the United States, in the 1866 printing. New colonies rise, assemblies claim their rights, and self-rule takes root. A distinct American character begins to form across the seaboard.

Bancroft writes as the nation's celebrant, tracing one long march toward freedom. Town meetings, charters, and quarrels with royal governors all point forward. He finds destiny at work in small, stubborn acts of self-government. The volume builds the base of his democratic epic, the long colonial prelude without which the Revolution, in his view, cannot be understood.
beauchamp-s-career-volume-2:
Volume two of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career covers chapters eleven to eighteen of Nevil Beauchamp's story. Nevil, a young naval commander turned radical candidate, has come home from war to public banquets and praise. Captain Baskelett, his worldly cousin, opens this portion. The infamous Dr. Shrapnel, Nevil's fiery mentor, receives a full interview.

Meredith follows the canvass for the borough of Bevisham, where votes must be begged door by door. A leading article and the journalist Timothy Turbot show the press at work. Nevil's superfine conscience troubles allies who want a quieter candidate. Friend and foe blur as the election nears. These chapters mix political satire with a portrait of a hero too honest for party management, in Meredith's densest and most allusive prose.
beethoven-s-letters-1790-1826-volume-2:
Ludwig van Beethoven's letters conclude in this second volume of Lady Wallace's translation, from the collections of Nohl and Köchel. The contents open on the second part, Life's Mission, covering 1815 to 1822 and beyond. Publishers Steiner and Haslinger, the faithful Zmeskall, the del Rio family, and the young Czerny receive letter after letter, numbered past two hundred and thirty.

Business and devotion share the pages. Writing to the Archduke Rudolph, Beethoven thanks him warmly for receiving Herr Drechsler, a candidate he had recommended, and begs the favour continue firm. Abbé Stadler, he hears, is angling for the same post. Guardianship wars, the nephew, money quarrels, and the late quartets all stand behind these notes. The voice stays urgent, funny, and imperious to the end of the correspondence in 1826.
bernal-diaz-vol-2:
Volume Two of Bernal Diaz's memoirs, in Lockhart's translation, brings the conquest of Mexico to its grim climax. Diaz, the old soldier, had set out to correct the grand histories with a ranker's memory. This volume holds his most harrowing chapters.

He describes the Spanish flight from Tenochtitlan on the Night of Sorrows and the long siege that followed. The city's fall, Cortes's later expeditions, and the conquerors' quarrels over spoils close the story. Diaz ends poor and unthanked in Guatemala, still proud of what the soldiers did. His eyewitness voice outlasted every official version of the conquest.
bibliotheca-chemica-a-catalogue-of-the-a:
John Ferguson's Bibliotheca Chemica concludes in this second volume, published at Glasgow by James MacLehose and Sons in 1906. The catalogue records the alchemical, chemical, and pharmaceutical books collected by James Young of Kelly and Durris. Young's family printed it for private distribution, following his instructions, after his death.

A long entry on the Nürnberg publisher Friedrich Roth-Scholtz shows the method. Roth-Scholtz married Tauber's youngest daughter in 1720, while Wedel married an elder, and the firm traded on as Tauber's heirs. He died at Nürnberg in January 1736, indefatigable as a collector of books, plates, coats of arms, coins, and printers' devices. Ferguson quotes Leupold's Prodromus and weighs merits like a judge: bibliography here is biography, imprint by imprint.
blackstone-commentaries-sharswood-vol-2:
Sir William Blackstone's Commentaries on the Laws of England appears here in Volume 2 of George Sharswood's edition, covering Books 3 and 4. Blackstone first published the Commentaries in the 1760s. Sharswood, an American judge, edited this 1893 form; the set's first volume, Books 1 and 2, is also live.

Book 3 treats private wrongs: how courts hear civil cases, juries work, and injuries are remedied. Book 4 treats public wrongs, the criminal law, from treason and murder to trial and punishment. Blackstone wrote English law as a clear, ordered whole that lay readers could grasp. The Commentaries taught generations of lawyers in Britain and America their first law.
brant-ship-of-fools-barclay-vol-2:
More fools board the ship in Volume Two of Barclay's English Ship of Fools, the 1874 Jamieson edition of Brant's satire. Flatterers, drunkards, and the learned-ignorant take their places among the crew. The remaining chapters of the 1494 original complete the voyage toward the land of fools.

Verse satire and woodcut portraits keep the moral medicine entertaining to the last page. Brant's targets, from corrupt clergy to vain scholars, rarely feel dated. Barclay's Tudor English adds a second layer of period charm for modern readers. Together the two volumes hold Renaissance Europe's most famous satire entire. The journey ends where it began, with human folly undefeated and oddly lovable.
bryce-american-commonwealth-vol-2:
State and local life fill the second volume of Bryce's American Commonwealth, from 1888. Bryce turns from Washington to governors, townships, parties, and the press. Public opinion, he argues, is the true sovereign of the republic.

He shows democracy at ground level, in caucuses, courts, and city halls. Parties appear as vast machines that both serve and strain the system. His eye for flaw and strength stays even throughout. The volume completes a classic study. It understood America from the bottom up as fully as from the top down, and it still rewards close reading today.
burton-pilgrimage-medinah-meccah-vol-2:
The second volume of Burton's Personal Narrative of a Pilgrimage to El-Medinah and Meccah completes his 1853 journey. Volume one reached Medina, the Prophet's city and burial place. Burton, still in disguise as a pilgrim, now presses on to Mecca itself. The Memorial edition text is used here.

He performs the rites of the Hajj among the crowds: circling the Kaaba, drinking from the well of Zamzam, and standing on the plain of Arafat. His notes on the rites remain among the fullest ever made by an outside observer. The volume closes with the return journey and his appendices. The pilgrimage book made Burton the most famous traveler of his age.
byron-letters-vol-2:
Volume Two of Byron's Letters and Journals, edited by Prothero in 1898, covers the years of marriage, scandal, and exile. Byron wed Annabella Milbanke in 1815, and the marriage collapsed within a year amid dark rumors. In 1816 he left England forever.

The letters follow him to Switzerland, where he met Shelley and wrote through a haunted summer, then on to Venice. He is by turns bitter, funny, tender, and reckless. Prothero prints the record with care, letting Byron's own voice dominate. Few letter writers of any age match his energy on the page. His letters to his publisher Murray mix business, gossip, and bravado.
carlyle-cromwell-letters-vol-2:
Civil War fills the second volume of Carlyle's Cromwell, in the 1904 Lomas edition. Letters from camp and council trace the revolution as it unfolds. Cromwell the soldier and statesman speaks in terse, godly, driven prose.

Battles, sieges, and hard choices crowd the years covered here. Carlyle's commentary blazes beside the texts he prints. Readers hear the war in the first person, from the man at its center. The volume gives history a rare texture. Orders, prayers, and reports were written in the press of events by a leader who felt God's hand in each turn.
carlyle-friedrich-vol-2:
War over the Austrian succession fills the second volume of Carlyle's life of Frederick the Great, from 1865. The young king gambles his new crown on bold marches and pitched battles. His triumph shocks the old courts of Europe.

Carlyle turns dry campaigns into epic poetry with sheer force of prose. He admires nerve, speed, and iron will above all virtues. Councils, camps, and freezing bivouacs pass in vivid rush. Readers feel war as the king's stern school, where Prussia's fate hung each season on one man's nerve and the loyalty of his hard-pressed troops.
carnac-s-folly-volume-2:
Carnac's Folly, Volume 2, by Gilbert Parker, is Book II of his Montreal novel. Parker brings Carnac Grier home in spring, eight months after he vanished. Snow melts on the hills. His mother has only sad news for him. Junia has been away since last fall, nursing an aunt in the West. Carnac shakes his head. Everything, he says, is all wrong. He blundered, and he is paying the price.

He found Luzanne Larue, the woman of his folly. Divorce, she told him, was impossible. They had signed a hotel book as man and wife. A year had passed besides. The House of the Three Trees and Carnac and Junta follow. John Grier makes a journey, and a will is read. Parker's Canada of lumber mills and French marriages traps his hero neatly. Carnac's mistake was made in a moment. Its papers will take a novel to burn.
cecilia-or-memoirs-of-an-heiress-volume-:
The second volume of Frances Burney's Cecilia, or Memoirs of an Heiress, continues the story of a young heiress in London society. Burney, edited here by R. Brimley Johnson, follows Cecilia through routs, hints, accommodations and detections as fortune-hunters circle her wealth.

Books Four through Seven move from a murmuring and a rout to a miser's mansion, a gamester's conscience, a persecution, a debate, a storm and a mystery. Cecilia's wit and virtue are tested by suitors, guardians and fashionable follies at every turn. Readers of eighteenth-century fiction will find Burney's comedy of manners sharp, lively and full of social observation.
celt-and-saxon-volume-2:
Volume two of George Meredith's Celt and Saxon covers chapters twelve to nineteen, ending the fragment. Miss Mattock watches a letter that she is sure will go. The dinner-party at Earlsfont tests Patrick O'Donnell among the Saxon Adisters. Talk of Rockney and the Mattock family fills the social middle.

Captain Con's letter arrives with its shoal of subterfuges and honest blundering. Mars convalescent closes the book, as a wounded officer recovers under Jane's care. Meredith never finished the novel, so this volume is a conclusion by accident. Patrick's love for Caroline hangs unresolved. The fragment's charm lies in its people and its theme: whether Celt and Saxon, Irish warmth and English reserve, can learn to honour what each lacks. It stops mid-conversation, like a visit cut short.
chambers-cyclopaedia-1728-vol-2:
The second volume of Chambers's Cyclopaedia followed the first in 1728, completing the universal dictionary of arts and sciences. Chambers had set out to gather all useful knowledge between two covers, in plain alphabetical order. With this volume, the design stood whole.

Volume 2 carries the alphabet to Z, treating the later sciences, trades, and terms of art with the same cross-referenced method. Readers could enter at any word and follow the links through the whole circle of learning. Two stout books changed how mankind keeps its knowledge, and every encyclopedia since has followed the model more or less closely. The pair also shaped the French Encyclopédie, which grew from a translation project into the Enlightenment's loudest voice. Chambers's own work remains the first great work of reference of that age.
charles-o-malley-the-irish-dragoon-volum:
Volume II of Charles Lever's novel, again illustrated by Phiz, takes O'Malley to war in earnest. Fifty-five chapters are listed. A doctor's tale opens the volume in a Loughrea barrack crowded with young officers. Skirmishes and the lines of Ciudad Rodrigo follow quickly, with Mickey Free, the hero's comic servant, never far away.

The middle chapters march through Lisbon, night marches, and a haunted lodging where a gorgeously dressed figure smiled from a niche. Patrick's Day in the Peninsula interrupts the fighting. Fuentes de Oñoro gets two chapters, and the storming of Ciudad Rodrigo two more. Brussels, the Duchess of Richmond's ball, Quatre Bras, and Waterloo close the soldier's road home.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100130006-2:
Memorandum from John H. Waller, Inspector General, to the Acting Deputy Director for Administration forwards a statement of work. Its subject is a study of the PATB, the agency's Professional Applicant Test Battery. The final version was being presented to a contractor, Waller writes, following a phone call the day before.

He points to page one, where the statement grounds the work in lawful selection and placement of staff. The contractor fully grasps the weight of the Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures, he states. Item F.3 asks the contractor to discuss possible test bias against any category of persons. Any racial or discriminatory aspects of the battery would thus be covered, he argues. The attached statement seeks an expert, independent critique of how the agency used the battery. Its tasks include judging the Strong-Campbell interest inventory, the foreign language test, and the writing test.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100040033-2:
J. Kenneth McDonald, Chief of the DCI History Staff, asked a records office to search for wartime facts in a memorandum dated 29 September 1982. The query came from the Army Center of Military History and began with a French lawyer. It concerns the escape of five German general officer prisoners of war in France in 1945.

McDonald encloses the Army letter and its attachments and asks whether the OSS Archives held by the CIA hold anything he can send to Maitre Guy Fleury. The Army had told the lawyer that his request was being referred to the Agency. The short file is a routing step in an outside research query, not an answer to it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01m00147r000100210002-2:
Security of United States government personnel in Panama is set out in National Security Directive 6, issued in March 1989. An Executive Secretariat routing slip dated 27 March 1989 and a National Security Council handling notice frame the copy. The directive answers harassment of American personnel in Panama.

Defense and the Joint Chiefs are told to keep, until after the May 7 elections, a policy of cutting posted military families by normal rotation and by holding back incoming dependents. The embassy would continue its own drawdown. A policy coordinating committee would watch the harassment, report big changes, and keep the treatment of private American citizens under review. The policy would be looked at again after the vote.
cia-crest-cia-rdp02-06298r000900060007-2:
Fisher Level-Trol controller and transmitter units of the 2500 and 2503 Series fill an instruction manual dated July 1980, Form 1013. A specification table sets out the input signal as liquid level, or the level between two liquids, taken as a share of displacer length. Standard displacer lengths are 14 or 32 inches.

Output for the basic controller and transmitter runs 3 to 15 or 6 to 30 pounds per square inch, with stated supply pressures and air use figures. Later pages work through calibration, including formulas that use displacer volume and the specific gravity of the process liquid. The manual thus serves fitters setting up level control on plant vessels.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100280001-2:
Jamaican Prime Minister Edward Seaga's hold on power is weighed in a Directorate of Intelligence memorandum dated 13 February 1984. The summary is direct: his hope of serving the full five-year term won in a snap election the previous December has been undercut by economic reverses.

The latest blow, the paper reports, is a threat by the head of the International Monetary Fund to break off talks on a key standby loan. Business backing for Seaga's austerity program is fading as tight money and high interest rates pinch firms. The paper warns that, without signs of recovery by May or June, pressure for a fresh election would grow, and Michael Manley could win it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000100560001-2:
Presidential succession in the Philippines is tested on paper in a secret intelligence assessment dated February 1985, EA 85-10022. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it, with help from the global issues office. It rests on information available as of 15 January 1985.

Key judgments say President Marcos keeps political bodies weak on purpose. The succession path is left vague as part of that design. That points to a rough road to new leadership if he dies in office, the paper warns. Later pages size up figures around the contest. A rich farm magnate could fund a bid. Acting armed forces chief Fidel Ramos is said to pledge that he will uphold the constitution.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000200730001-2:
New Zealand under Prime Minister David Lange is assessed in a confidential paper dated May 1985, EA 85-10086. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it with a contribution from the Office of Central Reference. It rests on information available as of 20 April 1985 and centers on economic problems.

Although the ANZUS dispute and the bar on American ship visits dominate the press, the paper turns to the home economy. Finance thinking quoted in the body blames part of the job shortage on a rigid work force: state pressure in wage setting has crowded out bargaining at firm level. High wage settlements in the 1970s left minimum wages too high for many jobs, one minister argues. Early reform wins are noted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201090001-2:
China's trade in the third quarter of 1984 is set out in a reference aid marked EA CIT 85-001, dated March 1985. Front matter explains that the publication is made for American government officials. Copies reach outsiders through the Library of Congress and the National Technical Information Service.

A method note says the latest quarterly estimates rest on about 75 percent of trade having been reported. Past patterns suggest final totals will differ by under 2 percent for exports and under 4 percent for imports. Long tables then break trade down by goods, with rows for chemicals such as carboxylic acids and dyes, and for soaps and other product groups.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201270001-2:
China has signed a wave of contracts for Western plants and gear, in a memorandum dated 21 February 1985. The subject is contracting for major projects under the Seventh Five-Year Plan, which runs from 1986 to 1990. The summary ties the timing to the planning cycle.

In three months, China signed over 10 billion dollars in contracts, the paper reports. Direct purchases top 4 billion, and joint ventures will bring about 6 billion in capital imports. Transport gear and plants take over half the total, and one nuclear power plant deal at Daya Bay alone takes 3 billion. American firms won almost 3 billion, twice the West German share, though that lead is not expected to hold.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201630001-2:
Japan news for April 1985 is gathered in a memorandum dated 30 April 1985, EA M 85-10092. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it, using information available that day. Trade friction with the United States leads the month.

Reaction to congressional threats of payback, and to Prime Minister Nakasone's 9 April message on opening Japan's markets, filled the news. Most press observers hold that the public, the ruling party, and many officials now accept they must heed his call, the summary reports. Some commentators call the 37 billion dollar trade surplus appalling. Other editorials cite the strong dollar and the American budget deficit as causes of the gap.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000301710001-2:
China's fiscal and monetary policy is revisited in a memorandum dated 6 June 1985. The opening matches a theme heard before: Beijing's direct grip on the economy has shrunk as decision power moved downward. The state has turned to Western demand tools in reply, rebuilding the banking system and using treasury bonds.

Last year's trial of the new tools failed badly, the summary reports. Bank credit and the money supply soared, state spending rose past plan, and the budget deficit widened. Beijing has given the central bank tighter control over credit and wages, and plans deep cuts in administrative spending. Steeper taxes on local investment projects are meant to curb off-budget outlays. Price reform remains the missing piece.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000301990001-2:
North Korea's new posture between Moscow and Beijing is analyzed in a memorandum dated 25 July 1985, EA M 85-10144. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it, using information available as of 23 July. Recent shifts in Pyongyang's conduct toward both powers drive the study.

The changes mark a basic rethink of strategic options, not mere tactical moves, the paper judges. New flexibility toward the South forms part of the shift. The clearest gain is hardware: Soviet MIG-23 jets arrived in recent months. Pyongyang's failure to win real benefit from thirteen years of Washington-Beijing warmth heads the list of motives for downgrading China. A stronger, more assertive Soviet Union also draws the North.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302250001-2:
Provincial leadership changes in China during 1985 are counted in a memorandum dated 18 November 1985. East Asian and central reference analysts shared the work, using information available that day. Between April and October, reform leaders made the largest turnover of provincial leaders since early 1983.

Fourteen provincial party heads and ten governors were replaced, the summary reports. The new men mostly back reform and fit Deng's ideal of younger and better educated. About half of the 43 new provincial leaders have engineering backgrounds. The rest split between former Youth League cadres and career local officials. Many had been marked for promotion years before, a sign of growing reform strength and skill.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302340001-2:
China and the Soviet Union maneuver inside a three-way triangle with the United States, in a memorandum dated 20 December 1985. East Asian and Soviet analysis offices shared the work, using information available that day. Over the past year Beijing has moved on its own to widen the frame for normal ties with Moscow.

The steps could open wider political talks and a return of party-to-party contact. They show China's growing confidence, fed by steady gains in ties with Washington and by Soviet signals of interest. Beijing likely expects no quick change in Soviet security policy. Still, it may probe how far Moscow can bend, and gains leverage with Washington either way. Soviet caution and mistrust of China temper the outlook.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000100030002-2:
General Counsel Stanley Sporkin circulates his proposed answers to a Bar Association questionnaire in a memorandum dated 12 March 1984, OGC-84-50139. The memo goes to the Director, his deputy, and the heads of the directorates and key offices. Further comments are asked by 21 March.

The questionnaire covers oversight and accountability in the intelligence community. Sporkin stresses that the answers are his personal views, not those of the Director or the Agency. His cover letter to Frederick Hitz makes the same point. The attached answers then work through the questions one by one. Covert action is among the topics: one answer describes how proposals are weighed for legality by counsel and the Attorney General.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000100040010-2:
The science and technology directorate answers a Bar Association questionnaire in a memorandum dated 2 February 1984, DDS&T-094-84. The Chief of the Management Staff writes to the Associate General Counsel for Intelligence Community Affairs. An office assignment slip for the General Counsel heads the file.

The response was compiled with the help of each office in the directorate, the memo states. Its numbered paragraphs are keyed to the questionnaire, so readers can match each answer to its question. The covering memo offers further help if needed. The questionnaire concerns oversight of the intelligence community, and this file is one directorate's piece of the Agency-wide reply that the General Counsel was assembling that winter.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000100040113-2:
Readings for an Aspen Institute seminar are listed in a table of contents for the 1980 edition. Selections marked with asterisks also appear in the 1978 edition. The first week is mapped day by day, with themes stated before each set of texts.

An overture day pairs Plato's Republic, Book VII, with the Grand Inquisitor chapter from Dostoevsky's Brothers Karamazov. A day on the individual and society draws on Mencius, Hsun Tzu, the Bible, Milton's Paradise Lost, and Ghazali's Counsel for Kings. An afternoon session takes up Dürrenmatt's play The Visit. A later day turns to twentieth-century views of human nature, with T. S. Eliot's Hollow Men among the poems.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000100050004-2:
Two retirement letters between senior officers make up a May 1979 file. General George Blanchard, Commander in Chief of United States Army, Europe, writes to Stansfield Turner on 22 May 1979. Counting down to retirement, he thanks Turner for support to the Army in Europe during his tenure.

Blanchard credits Turner's personal efforts to get intelligence to the levels where it is needed, in the manner required. He expects the same support for his successor, Fritz Kroesen. Turner's reply, dated 24 May 1979, says sorrow is not an adequate word for his feelings. The Army will miss Blanchard's leadership, he writes, and he will miss their direct working relationship. Both men plan to stay in touch.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000100320004-2:
A draft curriculum for professional intelligence officer education moves forward in a memorandum dated 14 May 1980. Robert Gates, writing from the Director's office, sends the draft and a proposed cover memorandum. A handwritten cover note from a secretary named Pat sits on top of the file, flagging one unsure word in a draft.

Gates asks for additions and revisions by phone so final papers can be prepared for the weekend. He proposes no changes to a companion concept paper by George, and suggests the papers be combined as the cover memorandum sets out. Comments on all three papers, cover memo, concept paper, and curriculum, are wanted by close of business Thursday.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200430001-2:
A Director's trip to San Francisco from 4 to 7 August 1977 is laid out in schedules and a covering memorandum dated 3 August 1977. The official party is the Director, Herb Hetu, and security. Flights out of Dulles and a stay at the Stanford Court hotel frame the visit.

Friday 5 August is the working day: breakfast, a news conference at the Commonwealth Club, then lunch at the Sheraton-Palace with a 27 minute address and questions. The afternoon goes to Sunnyvale for tours of Lockheed and ESL. Backup correspondence fills the rest of the file, including an August letter in which the Director regrets a missed meeting in San Francisco.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200480015-2:
Vincent Davis proposes a different way to better ties between scholars and government in a memorandum dated 3 May 1977. It is the fourth and last in a series written over 72 hours, after Turner invited him to serve. This one is written on International Studies Association paper, Davis being its past president.

The memo opens with a history of strained relations between academic people and government people in foreign affairs. One thread runs through the pages: professors pass their view of government on to students. If leaders are indifferent to helping professors grasp the problems of government and the world, Davis argues, those leaders feed public cynicism and misunderstanding. An old talk with an intelligence bureau chief serves as his example.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200490014-2:
A Senate hearing on creating a United States Foreign Service Corps fills a printed volume held in Agency files. The hearing sat before the Subcommittee on Education of the Committee on Labor and Public Welfare on 29 January 1970. The bill was S. 939, amending the Higher Education Act of 1965. The Government Printing Office issued the record in 1970.

Senator Claiborne Pell chaired the subcommittee, with senators from both parties listed on the title pages. Testimony in the body weighs how foreign affairs training should be run. One passage describes an institute that has grown far beyond a mere training school for the Foreign Service. About half its work is done for other agencies, the witness notes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200600093-2:
Arms control after a failed first mission to Moscow is debated in a magazine article headed Strategic Restraint, Mutual and Assured. The piece is marked as forthcoming in a summer 1977 issue. Secretary of State Cyrus Vance's first mission produced mixed results and mixed emotions, it opens.

Public hopes for a breakthrough fed equal disappointment when no movement came. The article runs through the guesses then flying: Brezhnev's health, a Soviet test of the new president, a proposal built for home support, and human rights pressure answered by hardness. Such readings are too pat, it argues. Deep differences in force structures and needs explain the outcome. Its close sets the goal as managing weapons that will not go away.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000300790001-2:
Guidelines on employee conduct, with policy on the media, academia, and the clergy, are sent to the Director in a file dated 18 March 1977. John Blake, Deputy Director for Administration, transmits the material by routing sheet and memorandum, DDA 77-1484. A verbal request from a commander in the Director's office prompted the package.

The core attachment is a Handbook of Required Regulatory Readings. It sums up Agency rules on what employees may do and how they must act, and its own cover letter requires wide circulation. Further background papers deal with Agency ties to parts of American society. A long attachment on public attitudes toward intelligence and defense also sits in the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000300830015-2:
A fourth public hearing on charter legislation is reported in a memorandum for the record dated 25 April 1978. The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence took testimony on S. 2525. Senators Huddleston and Mathias sat for the committee, with staff. Three former deputy directors testified.

The witnesses were a former deputy for operations, Thomas Karamessines, a former deputy for intelligence, and former science chief Herbert Scoville Jr. Each read a prepared statement. Karamessines argued that the bill carries too many reporting procedures. He sought sanctions for unauthorized disclosure of sources and methods. He also held that reporting intelligence liaison deals to Congress by law would damage those relationships, and that cover duties should be stated in the bill.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000501230036-2:
Computer Security Seminar, 15-16 January 1980 gathers an invitation and a program. The seminar dealt with the Department of Defense Computer Security Initiative. It was held at the National Bureau of Standards in Gaithersburg, Maryland. A planning item (79-260) records the request. The request was received 27 September 1979. It asked Director Turner to give the keynote address. His topic was computer security interests in the intelligence community. He was set to speak at 9:30 on Tuesday 15 January.

Stephen T. Walker's invitation letter explains the seminar. It was the second in the series. It aimed to inform industry and the public about trusted computer systems. It also covered progress in defense research. The program lists talks on certification. It lists industry and maker views, and future designs. Speakers came from General Motors, MIT, and Univac. Speakers also came from the System Development Corporation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000501300001-2:
November 1979 press clippings fill a Central Intelligence Agency file led by Iran. A head note in the file names Iran the week's biggest subject. A Los Angeles Times report is dated 13 November 1979. It tells of a United States protest made in two capitals. The protest hit Soviet radio broadcasts beamed into Iran. The broadcasts ran during the siege of the embassy in Tehran.

The broadcasts cast the seized embassy as a spy nest. Other cuttings track a land in upheaval. Jokes told in Iran get space too. They act as a valve for strain, one piece notes. One crisis drove most print about the region that month.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601370003-2:
Correspondence dated 21 September 1977 brings Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, a blunt, long letter. The writer's name is withheld in the release. The writer was at work on a lecture. The course was on deterrence, at the Naval War College. The letter quotes Turner's own May interview at length. Turner had called the Soviets weak in trade and in creed.

From those quotes the letter builds a grim view. It sees Moscow turning arms strength into sway. It ends with a plea for care in giving interviews. The file holds one reader's full reply to public words. Part praise and part warning, it shows how a lecture hall read the director that year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601390001-2:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) schedules for March through June 1979 fill a thick file. Later long-range pages sit with them. One daily sheet is marked secret. It sets out Friday 1 June 1979 by the hour. A White House stop leads the day. Talks on SALT testimony come next. A Senate call covers safe briefing on the Hill.

An address for Vietnam Veterans Week fills the mid-day. Other pages list trips, guests and study time. A memo asks Turner to rule on open pledges. The file is the paper trail of a director's days. It shows who he met and where he went. It shows how staff sequenced his talks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601400045-2:
Staff cuts in the spy arm get a full airing in this note. It is dated 14 December 1977 and numbered 17. The note prints the statement Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, gave Congress. He had been asked for the facts behind the cuts. The cuts hit the Directorate of Operations. Soon after he came in March, he heard the branch held too many people.

Too much oversight was part of it. Too little real work for some was part too. The statement gives the scale and pace of the cuts. Notice will start early, he says. No one must leave before 1 October 1978. He grants the short blow to morale. The long aim, he argues, is the reverse.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601460030-2:
Change of command at Newport, Rhode Island anchors this program dated 22 June 1978. The Naval Education and Training Center held the ceremony. Music came from the Northeastern Navy Band. The order of the day lists an arrival of the official party, the anthem and an invocation.

Remarks by Admiral Stansfield Turner sit in the middle of the program. He was then Director of Central Intelligence, and the program styles him so. Awards and the change of command rite follow, with orders read for the outgoing and incoming captains. A benediction closes the day. The file is the printed program for a naval rite the director attended as guest of honor.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601470020-2:
Fact sheet from the White House explains the new order on grading state papers. It was held for release after the briefing of June 29, 1978. A study team from across the agencies drafted the order. The National Security Council and home policy staffs led that work. Congress panels and public groups were asked for views.

The sheet sets the new order against the old one from 1972. Two tests must now be met before a paper is graded. The facts must fall in a set class, and harm must be shown. Old rules let papers stay secret to age 30 with ease. The sheet, kept in Central Intelligence Agency files, walks through each shift in plain terms.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601480029-2:
Economic Club of Detroit announces a civic development luncheon in this notice. The date is Monday noon, January 16, 1978. Cobo Hall is again the place. Two guests of honor share the bill: James M Roche and Lynn A Townsend. Both had chaired great car firms, General Motors and Chrysler.

Their subject is a new foundation for Detroit's future. Both men co-chaired the city's economic growth bodies. Mayor Coleman A Young would preside. Prices and seat rules match the club's set form. The notice sits in the Central Intelligence Agency file as part of the club's run of luncheon paper for that season.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601480038-2:
Williamson Murray wrote on March 6, 1978 from the history department at Ohio State. He sends Turner several clippings from the student paper, The Lantern. He expects no trouble with the Admiral's visit, he says. But the visit may draw sharp queries at the open meeting and lecture.

The queries would likely deal with Central Intelligence Agency involvement on campus. Morton Halperin had been on campus and stirred things up, Murray notes. One of the better halls had been secured for the talk. The letter is a friendly warning from a host: the spy chief should come ready for hard questions from students that April.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601510007-2:
Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, wrote to Karl G Harr Jr on 23 September 1977 with regret. Harr had invited him to address a fall meeting in Phoenix in November. An overflowing schedule forces Turner to decline once more. He asks instead to be kept in mind for the spring meeting.

Williamsburg is the spring site he names. He will do his best to hold those dates. Events could take over again, he grants, and force a fresh delay. In any case, he closes, let us keep trying. The short letter shows the push and pull on a spy chief's diary: groups sought his name, and his staff had to ration it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601540004-2:
Turner wrote to Morton S Baratz on 10 April 1978 about a panel in New Haven. The panel would treat the intelligence agencies and the academic community. It was set for 10 June 1978. Turner thanks Baratz for a prompt reply to his verbal pledge to take part.

Lunch with Professor Peter Steiner is gladly accepted. One proviso stands: a roughly twenty percent chance that Turner might not make the engagement. He notes that the agency's general counsel would also take part. The letter shows a director willing to face scholars on a sore theme, campus ties, while hedging his diary in plain odds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601560075-2:
Houston Clubber for September 1977 fills this Central Intelligence Agency file as a club magazine. An early advertisement treats paperwork and the flood of information in business. Forms that speed the flow of facts are its pitch. Member news then takes over the issue.

New full resident members get family sketches. One man's six children are listed by name and age. His home in Kingwood is named too. Another new member heads two firms making control systems and rig lights. School and degree facts fill each sketch. The issue shows the club's habit of welcoming new men in print, with home life set beside business standing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100040008-2:
Admiral Stansfield Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, sits for Dan Rather in this long 60 Minutes transcript. A public affairs staff sheet dates the file 3 February 1981. Rather opens by asking for a world tour. He wants the trouble spots a family at home should watch. Moscow and Western Europe head his list.

Turner picks three spots he calls long-range but real. The talk then ranges over the state of the world as he left office. The file is a full broadcast interview in print. It shows a past director, days out of the job, giving his map of risk to a mass audience in plain words.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100090003-2:
Recommendations summary dated 20 June 1977 lists what advisory groups urged on Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence,. The first ask sets up a small office of personnel policy. It would sit under the deputy director. It would set staff policy for the whole house and watch that the policy held. Senior careers would get its special care.

More asks follow in number order. Lower grade promotions should grow more competitive, to ease a bulge at the top grades. Manager posts should shrink to make room for specialists. Time-in-grade rules should relax. The summary is a reform menu from the ranks, put to a new director in his first summer.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200660018-2:
Briefing by the Federal Women's Program Board fills this memo of 7 November 1977. The board thanks the Director for the chance to meet on 9 November. It advises the Director of Central Intelligence and his deputy, it notes. Yet it had never met a DCI since its start in April 1973. Only one deputy meeting had taken place.

That gap was largely of the board's own making, it grants. Fresh thought in the past year changed its course. A two-day conference in September laid out a program for fiscal 1979. Goals from that conference shape the briefing. The file is a board introducing itself, and its plans, to a new director.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200680007-2:
Agenda for a meeting with Admiral Turner and the agency secretarial group fills this routing sheet. The sheet is dated 14 October 1977. It comes from a staff office and moves by the routing form. The meeting was set for Wednesday 19 October 1977. The time was 1:30 to 2:30 in the DCI conference room.

The form carries the standard columns for receipt and forwarding. Officers' comments space sits beside the agenda heads. The file is brief in text but clear in what it shows: the director gave an hour to the secretarial group as a body. Their agenda joined the run of group meetings he held that autumn.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200780015-2:
Central Intelligence Agency is the plain title of this information booklet. Its contents page lists the parts. About the Central Intelligence Agency leads. Excerpts from the National Security Act of 1947 follow. Excerpts from the Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949 come next. Executive Order 11905 excerpts and a list of directors close the book.

A question-and-answer part opens the text. What is intelligence, it asks first. Nations have survived by knowledge as much as by arms, it answers, citing Sun Tzu. What the CIA does, who controls it and who works there all get plain answers. The booklet is the agency explaining itself to the public.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200780024-2:
Director of Central Intelligence media contacts fill this log for 1977 and after. Page 88 of a larger log is marked in the print. A Godfrey Sperling breakfast on 9 March 1977 leads the page. A Time bureau dinner follows on 17 March. Names of Time men fill out that entry.

A New York Times luncheon in Washington comes on 31 March. Hedrick Smith, John Herbers and David Binder are among the names. A Chicago Daily News man and a Post editorial board lunch follow in April. The log shows a new director courting the press in form: meals, names and dates, all entered as part of the job.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000300940016-2:
Second Century 1979 annual meeting program fills this thick American Bar Association book. The meeting ran August 8 to 15, 1979 in Dallas. A welcome note opens it. The annual meeting is the major educational and social event of the association year, it says. This year carried special weight.

The year marked the first of the association's second century. More than one hundred major programs had been devised, the note says. The book lists them with their times and rooms. For the Director of Central Intelligence's file, the program was the guide to a week when the nation's lawyers gathered, and a spy chief came among them as a guest.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000301090019-2:
Pace in the Eighties is the title of this president's report for 1980. Working Partnerships is its theme line. The report calls itself a record of what working partnerships made possible. It is a different kind of report, the opening says. Past accomplishment is only part of its scope.

Friends and colleagues of Pace University are its audience. The book sets out the school's aims for the new decade beside its record. Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, received it in the season of his Pace commencement visit. The file holds a university's self-portrait at a turning point: proud of its partners, and pitching its next ten years to its own people.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000301100017-2:
Judicial Conference of the Tenth Judicial Circuit fills this program. The conference sat from July 30 to August 1, 1980. The Brown Palace Hotel in Denver, Colorado hosted it. Registration opened at 11:00 a.m. on Wednesday, July 30. A meeting of the district judges' association came first that day.

Federal judges only could attend that first session, the program notes. An executive session of the circuit followed in the same room. Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, addressed the conference during his western trip that summer. The program is the printed order for a judges' meeting, kept in the trip file beside his remarks and the background tabs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401130068-2:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) invitation item 79-274 logs a film night at the Kennedy Center. The item was received on 17 October 1979, with a suspense date of 23 October. A letter from Representative Jim Wright brought the invitation. The event was a film presentation of the work of the Genesis Project. It launched a nationwide observance of National Bible Week.

The Laymen's National Bible Committee hosted the evening. The hour was 2020 on Sunday 18 November 1979. The file is the staff sheet for a Congress member's invitation. It shows the range of civic rites that reached the director's desk in a season: film, faith and a national week, all in one form.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401160001-2:
Arif R Sarfraz wrote on June 27, 1980 from the University of Pennsylvania. He wrote for the Wharton Graduate Association at Vance Hall. The Multinational Enterprise Club of the Wharton School would be honored, he says, if Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, would address its students. A date in the fall semester, from September on, would suit. The date could be set to mutual convenience.

Students working for the Master of Business Administration would form the chief audience. The letter is a business school's ask to a spy chief. Its theme fits the club's name: firms that span borders, and the world as a theater of trade, taught by a man who watched that world for a living.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401180018-2:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) scheduling item 80-293 logs a briefing for company chiefs on Tuesday 9 December 1980. A letter from Philip W Klutznick brought the item, received on 26 November. Klutznick was a cabinet officer and a man of business. The DCI would brief the chief executive officers of major American companies.

The day is laid out on the form. Welcoming remarks come at 1000. Lunch follows at 1245. The briefing itself runs from 1330 to 1415. A suspense date of 1 December is marked. The file shows the spy chief summoned, in his last weeks, to tell the heads of great firms what he saw in the world.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501420001-2:
Newspaper clippings for September 1980 make up a thick Agency file released in 2009. Opening pages carry a New York Times report dated 18 September 1980 on a Senate panel vote. The panel sought to narrow a bill that would shield the names of covert agents from disclosure.

Coverage then moves across the month's main stories in no fixed order. Reports on the new Iran and Iraq war weigh how a blocked Gulf route could cut world oil supply. Energy officials and oil firms are quoted on stocks, imports, and tanker risk near the Strait. The file preserves the open press record staff chose to retain that month.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601700027-2:
Crisis duties for the Director form the core of a short memo dated 25 April 1977. Stansfield Turner wrote to the deputy for the intelligence community in his own hand of office. He asks for a walk-through drill of how a crisis would run.

Turner wants the drill to show task groups and contact nets in at least outline form. He states he needs more grounding in his own role when a crisis hits. Added pages dated 5 and 6 April 1977 list wider community topics, from nuclear spread checks to budget control. Those notes range across study load, product reach, and staff tenure concerns.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601740005-2:
Max Frankel of the New York Times writes to Admiral Turner in a letter dated 23 July 1978. Frankel replies to Turner's note on a Times editorial about staff who publish after service. He welcomes the chance to answer and grants shared ground on the core problem.

No checks on government secrets can work, Frankel argues, since courts lack the facts to judge such claims. He cites the Pentagon Papers case and the Marchetti book as proof of weak secrecy claims. He backs a narrow law, along lines linked to Mr. Colby, barring staff from naming secret agents. The letterhead gives the Times office at 229 West 43 Street, New York.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601760003-2:
Views shared by nine members of Congress after a trip to the Soviet Union are summed up in a memo dated 4 May 1979. The Director wrote after a White House meeting with Dr. Brzezinski on 3 May. The group had met Soviet hosts and talked at length on arms talks.

Members report warm welcome, plain talk, and strong Soviet wish to close a SALT deal. Soviet speakers blamed United States shifts for slow progress and feared long talks on a next round. Fear of China runs through the account, as do claims on exit visas and civil defence. Later pages weigh how to act on a suspect treaty breach.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000100090001-2:
Economic data for 1961 fill a handbook dated June 1961, numbered A.ERA 61-3. The Office of Research and Reports issued it as an economic research aid. Its stated aim is to aid study of bloc economies and their match against NATO states. Charts and summary tables carry the most weighty data in visual form.

Tables give years 1950, 1955, 1958 to 1960, and 1965 plan figures. Bloc estimates are stated as of 1 May 1961 and rest mostly on office holdings. Summary tables compare the United States with the USSR and China with India. One table counts sheep in millions of head across those years. The Soviet flock there rises from 93.6 million in 1950 to 144 million in 1960, with a 1965 plan mark of 189 million.
cia-crest-cia-rdp08s01350r000100220001-2:
East European debt to the West is estimated in a research paper dated January 1980. The paper, ER 80-10001, came from the National Foreign Assessment Center. Research closed on 3 December 1979, and new methods use NATO, OECD, and bank data.

Gross debt for six states at the end of 1978 is put at 46.9 billion dollars. Net debt, after Western bank deposits, is put at 42.3 billion. Poland owes most at 17.8 billion gross, then East Germany and Hungary. Country pages then weigh each state's debt service load and due dates. All totals are framed as the paper's own estimates.
cia-crest-cia-rdp09k00541r000700100004-2:
Coordination across the intelligence community is the theme of a course talk dated 2 October 1961. The talk was given for Project USEFUL number 8, a familiarization course. The speaker served as Assistant for Coordination to the Director.

A history opens with the lack of a national system at the start of World War II. The Joint Intelligence Committee, the Coordinator of Information, and the Office of Strategic Services are traced in turn. Later pages sort reform advice under heads such as staff, secret collection, and security. One strand urges a career path for service intelligence officers with better training and rank.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10-01569r000100040005-2:
Policy for winding up the Strategic Services Unit is set in N.I.A. 3, dated 27 March 1946. The report comes from the Director with full board concurrence. It quotes the Executive Order of 20 September 1945 on the old Office of Strategic Services.

A War Department meeting on 8 February 1946 agreed a study was needed at once. The study would judge which unit tasks and sites should be kept for peacetime use. Kept tasks would pass to the Central Intelligence Group or other agencies so their worth is not lost. The rest of the unit must be wound up as fast as can be done, before 1 July 1947.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10m02313r000704040004-2:
PD/NSC-55 and the APEX system are taken up in White House memos dated 29 June 1981. One memo, TS-810236/1, goes to William J. Casey as Director. Richard V. Allen signs it as the President's security adviser.

APEX had stirred sharp dispute among agencies, the memo states. The attached memo ends the setting up of APEX, as Casey had asked. Casey is asked to seek views from the community on changes to PD/NSC-55. He must then send his advice on those changes forward. An Agency routing note dated 30 June 1981 asks the council staff about marking the file down to Secret grade.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100380001-2:
Correspondence from 1941 fills a very large file whose scan is poor from end to end. Only a few letters can be read in full in the copy held here. Letterheads of the Coordinator of Information at 270 Madison Avenue, New York, recur through the pages.

One letter dated 9 December 1941 thanks a Hollywood contact for a wire just sent. Donovan signs it and states there is nothing to be done at that moment. A second letter dated 5 September 1941 comes from an old comrade-in-arms in Southern California. He offers his help in that district and recalls past liaison at St. Mihiel. The rest of the file must be used with care, since most pages resist reading.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100410007-2:
Field reports and a Serbia trip account fill a file catalogued for 1944 with a list of reports by author. A memo dated 20 May 1945 from Jen F. Mowinckel treats showing MO material to military chiefs. Caserta headquarters first balked at taking MO prints, the memo states.

A branch wind-up report tells of the last target gone by the end of April 1945. Staff sailed from Naples on 11 May 1945 and reached Washington on 22 May in good health. The writer holds MO a strong weapon in war or peace after that tour. Later pages praise the Swiss Desk in Italy, set up in mid-1944. Its Berne reports on partisan fights near Cannobia are given as proof of worth.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100030022-2:
Briefing notes for the Director are sent in a working paper memo to OSA deputies. John Parangosky signs as Acting Director of Special Activities. The notes went to the DD/S&T for talks the Director might hold with cabinet and agency chiefs.

Staff may be called to add to the notes within two to three weeks, the memo warns. One note treats Agency contract support for secret aircraft work. It names the U-2, the SR-71, and the YF-12A interceptor as kin of past Agency programs. A further note credits joint work on the Mach 3 A-12 and its engine. A secret industrial security program guards the contract work across the land.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100140002-2:
Detachment C training and flight work are summed up for 14 August 1956 to 8 March 1957. The summary comes from the Air Weather Reconnaissance Squadron Provisional III. A timeline opens the report, from unit activation on 12 July 1956.

First U-2 assigned to the unit is logged in August 1956, with first flight hour close behind. Contract pilots finished set training by 24 October 1956, the timeline states. A unit simulated combat mission was also finished that month. The 1,000th hour flown by unit staff came on 21 February 1957. Later pages weigh wind forecasts against winds met in flight, with flame-out in rough air noted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200010014-2:
Six ways the USSR and Cuba might end Cuba overflights fill a State paper dated 27 May 1963. The paper went to the NSC Standing Group at White House request. William S. Brubeck sent it to Director McCone ahead of the 28 May meeting.

Both sides want the flights stopped but feel no gain in loud protest yet, the paper states. Shooting a plane down would bring counter moves they cannot match, it judges. Court action at The Hague is weighed and found a weak path for Cuba. Counter pressure through Berlin is treated as a bid for allied support. A quiet trade of Soviet troops for an end to flights is also raised.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200190006-2:
Briefing charts for the Air Force U-2 support office fill a chart pack with a table of contents. Cover rules bar wide spread of the charts, tied to the IDEALIST, KEDLOCK, and EARNING programs. Contents run from aircraft and engine data to accident history.

One chart sets out the SPO way of work from January 1956. Five staff run the whole task, with two chief engineers among them. Full system care from cradle to grave is claimed with the least paper flow. Later charts list aims: keep Open Sky capacity and back SAC training flights. Change is to be held to safety gains, mission gains, or clear cost savings.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200210003-2:
Open action items from a weapons system meeting fill a resume dated 26 June 1956. The meeting sat at Offutt Air Force Base with SAC, AMC, and WRAMA staff present. First item: no firm operations plan yet exists for the new aircraft.

Tight security is named as the chief bar to a firm plan. SAC ground rules thus stand in as a working plan for now. The squadron would hold two flights of thirteen aircraft each, the resume states. First spares would come from Colonel Gibbs' stock, then be made good in bulk. Training slots on all main gear are still owed by the contractors. Lockheed will teach airframe work at Bakersfield, it adds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200300049-2:
First in a planned run of bimonthly depot reports covers 9 June to 31 July 1969. The report is dated 5 August 1969 and goes to the Director, OSA. A new Ref chief took full charge on 25 June 1969, it states.

A procedures cable from headquarters was read and found close to depot intent. Section chiefs are now sending their comments to the depot commander. A 24 hour duty officer post is still under study, the report states. The depot runs short of staff against posts just approved by headquarters. New badges will use a rubber stamp trick to cut one colour from the print cost.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300150036-2:
April 1962 turned sour in a commander's report dated 2 May 1962. Fuel and maintenance faults together spoiled a month that had promised much. The fuel fault was aired in full with a visiting staff officer, the report states.

Flying stopped on 17 April when headquarters warned the fuel was off grade. One LOW NOTE mission flew, with five training and four test flights beside it. The T-33 was flown 47 hours 05 minutes in the month. Down time went to leave and to catching up on accrued maintenance work. Morale stayed high, and the troops stand set for a long run, the commander writes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300150054-2:
December 1961 flying is summed up in a commander's report dated 3 January 1962. Training and maintenance work landed close to plan for the month, it states. Two slips are logged: a damaged training flight and a weather held test flight.

Eleven training flights and one ferry flight gave 30 hours 50 minutes. The T-33 added 60 hours 35 minutes of training in the month. A Christmas dinner for staff and a hostel party for project children are recorded. Supply pipeline time runs 13 days on run of the mill requests, the report states. A 100 hour check began 16 December, with nine service bulletins worked.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400050018-2:
Memorandum dated 5 October 1962, in a scan that is rough in places, records a meeting with Secretary McNamara, Director McCone, Deputy Secretary Gilpatric, and the Director of the National Reconnaissance Office. McCone presented his paper on revision of the NRO, proposing the Secretary of Defense as Executive Agent to a National Reconnaissance Planning Group. The memorandum reports the reactions around the table.

McNamara stated reservations about the need for a special reconnaissance organisation at all, and raised placing such work under the Defense Intelligence Agency. McCone resisted any subordination of the activity, while Dr Charyk argued for keeping the NRO at its present level so central direction could continue. McNamara closed as satisfied for the present, promising to review the paper and discuss it later.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400050054-2:
Position paper dated 29 November 1961, numbered OXO-2735, states the CIA view on division of responsibility within the National Reconnaissance Office. The Office had been formed by joining parts of the Air Force and the CIA in secret. The paper argues that changes to who runs which program should come slowly, and at the right time. Flexibility is stressed, so new programs are not forced into a fixed pattern.

The proposed split turns on visibility. The Air Force should take prime charge of white work: very large procurements, open bidding, and anything that cannot be hidden from normal defence security. CIA should take the black procurements, hidden from all but those cleared for a given program. Project OXCART management is reaffirmed as remaining under CIA, with its Air Force variants left to the Air Force.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400350033-2:
Memo for operations records dated 29 April 1958 covers a visit to the Firewel Company of Buffalo, New York, prime contractor for the project's oxygen equipment. Its purpose was to put field problems to the maker, propose changes, and study new gear for possible project use. The talks are set out item by item, with the contractor's answers noted.

Oxygen hose connectors that could part in flight are to be reworked, at small stated costs for the whole project. Face piece hose wiring shorts are traced to nylon insulation that turns brittle, and Teflon is to replace it in all future hoses. An exhalation valve fault is eased by trading latex for silicone in the diaphragm, though a leak free seat stays unsolved. A flight feeding orifice leak closes the list.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500060007-2:
Memorandum recording a conversation about a carrier training exercise for IDEALIST aircraft survives in a scan whose text is heavily garbled, though its thread can still be followed. A May meeting with senior naval officers took up a projected exercise with the carrier USS Kitty Hawk. The concept discussed was U-2 operations from fleet carriers, with the Mediterranean named as the theatre that made the idea worth pursuing.

Arrangements move through the garble in outline: agreement in principle from the naval side, a date to be set, and a wish to brief the ship's captain informally before sailing. Briefing other senior officers in the chain is also planned. Because so much of the page is corrupted, names, dates, and figures beyond the ship and the exercise itself cannot be read with confidence here.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500170014-2:
Attachment IV to a U-2R corollary planning paper, document B-0020-67, covers logistics and facilities for the new aircraft. On logistics, a major assembly spares list from Lockheed has been reviewed: it names units that can be swapped in the field, from tires and wing tips to canopy glass. Recommended quantities were factored on an austere basis against the smallest first buy of aircraft.

Existing assets come first throughout: Lockheed and the project are trading supply data so current stocks serve the U-2R where they can, holding new buying to a minimum. Facilities planning for the flight test program at Edwards Air Force Base, North Base, then lists building changes, added construction, storage, and prefabricated structures. Security fencing, ramp paving, and expanded communications are also counted among the needs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500190012-2:
Signed by Brockway McMillan, Director of the National Reconnaissance Office, a letter to a briefing officer weighs a proposed boost glide vehicle for reconnaissance. No date is printed in the legible text. The writer calls the likely program cost equal to or greater than that of an advanced airplane, and asks for full, honest analysis before any commitment.

Points drawn from the briefing include a need for fast reaction, data return after one pass, and a photo swath fifty miles wide. The letter questions whether a manned vehicle is needed at all. It then asks for paid design studies of an air launched glider, carried by an aircraft no larger than a B-52, from McDonnell, Boeing, and if possible Martin.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600040008-2:
Flight planning work at Detachment H is set out in SOP H-50-18, dated 28 March 1969, which replaces a version from 1 July 1968. Mission prep is shared between the flight planner and the pilot. The senior planner runs the section and keeps watch over its work on each flight.

Once a cleaned route message arrives, planners have five hours to get ready. Tasks include making the pilot's chart, drawing the route in blue pencil, and marking flight lines in red. Mission data goes up in the Command Post, and a planner must be at the launch site twenty minutes before takeoff. Last pages cover fuel curves, kept in a notebook and updated after engine changes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600040035-2:
Morale travel for staff at Detachment H is governed by SOP H-20-7, dated 10 January 1968. The Environmental and Morale Program gives each person one trip per year to one named place. A second place is allowed only when no first time traveler is waiting. The scheme is open on an equal basis across rank and grade, but contract technical staff cannot take part.

All travel is space available and at no cost back to the traveler, mainly by military air lift under joint service rules. Each person must carry enough funds for a paid return trip if military lift falls through. A security briefing before the trip and a debrief on return are both required.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600040116-2:
Command Post work at Detachment H is governed by SOP H-50-20, dated 27 July 1971, which replaces a January 1970 version. The Director of Operations writes the rules for the post and enforces them. Only the Detachment Commander may change those rules on the spot. The stated aim is simple: give the pilot the best help that can be given, in changing conditions, so the mission ends safely.

On operational flights the commander directs and controls the whole mission from the post. Staff track any drift from the agreed flight plan. Steps for emergencies cover faults reported in flight, choices to abort or divert, and an aircraft thought to be down. The last step sends a flash message to headquarters.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600050034-2:
Turning property back to Unit Supply is covered by ATTG Reg 67-4, dated 12 February 1974, signed by Colonel Roger L. Cooper as group commander. The aims are firm control of items that can be repaired or recovered, and clear failure data for depot and contractor staff, so repair turnaround stays short. The Chief of Supply enforces the rules.

Each item turned in must be tagged by state: fit for repair, fit for use, or condemned. Tags carry the stock or part number and serial number where there is one. Items coded R must reach Supply within seventy-two hours of a replacement being issued. Large items that cannot be moved are handled by hand-carried papers instead.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600070041-2:
Emergency recovery of a classified aircraft that has landed away from its home base, called Homeplate, is planned in standing operating procedure 45-3064-1, dated 27 December 1966. Because the aircraft is secret, any unscheduled landing needs fast action by the commander to guard it and bring it home. Named staff and gear are picked in advance so work can start at once.

Recovery teams and equipment fly out in a C-130, an F-27, or the Connie, or by other air lift asked from headquarters. Tasks at the site include guarding the aircraft, removing film and tape records, clearing the inertial system drum, and preparing a slow, low return flight. A staffing table for the recovery task force closes the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000700050015-2:
Bundled papers open with a flight test status chart meant for the Project Headquarters Control Center. Its columns cover test name, priority, start and finish dates, planned and completed sorties, and percent complete. Next comes OXCART directive 50-10-13, dated 18 September 1967, on shipping invoices for project take. It replaces a June 1967 instruction.

Detachments must send an invoice with each shipment of take, giving positive control from landing to final destination. Copies go to the project, the registry, the sender, and each receiver. Later pages set status reporting. Ready pilots on leave or grounded must be named. Aircraft ready state is reported by gear fitted, from tracker and cameras to drop tanks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000700050024-2:
Long bundled file starts with sample message form No. 1 for an IDEALIST mission alert, sent to JSPC with an information copy to DIRNSA. Fields cover the intended track by coordinates, entry into and exit from hostile territory with times, and the mission number. The form is short, but the papers bound after it widen the scope a great deal.

Project Headquarters directive 50-155-1, dated 15 May 1965, sets a single method for preparing operations plans and orders, with a working panel drawn from each staff office. Other sections cover airlift scheduling by the control center and rules for project directives: who may amend them, and how copies are shared among detachments, contractors, and the project depot.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000700050033-2:
Bundle of Office of Special Activities travel directives opens with OSA directive 22-5-2, dated 30 September 1966. Travel by non-CIA staff that OSA arranges and pays for needs written approval from the Director or Deputy Director of OSA before the trip starts. A statement of the travel purpose must support each request made under the rule.

OSA directive 22-5-4, dated 29 June 1967, then assigns all overseas permanent change of station and temporary duty travel action to the OSA Personnel Division. Later pages treat rental cars: one car for a group traveling together, and later approval where a car proved cheaper or safer. A 1963 notice changing OSA work hours to 0800 to 1630 closes the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800020008-2:
IDEALIST report for 1 April to 30 June 1974 is sent 18 July 1974 by Wendell L. Bevan. Its development summary gives program totals since the U-2R entered service: 13,524.8 hours on 4,168 sorties as of 30 June 1974. The quarter's own table lists flights and hours for aircraft 051, 053, 054, and 055, with 054 flying the most time in the period.

An operational summary opens the report, its first item counting ten missions in the quarter, though the scan cuts across that passage. Support sections close the packet. A life support item notes research work moving to Brooks Air Force Base, Texas, and a scientific meeting of the Aerospace Medical Association in Washington, 6 to 9 May 1974, is recorded.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800250003-2:
Memorandum 9141-68, dated 19 July 1968, signed by Colonel Donald H. Ross, sends OXCART and IDEALIST progress reports for 1 April to 30 June 1968. Tab A notes that the SCOPE COTTON decision shapes the OXCART section from its first page. Five copies of each report go to the Director, CIA Reconnaissance Programs, with the usual OSA distribution behind them.

IDEALIST pages give a full fix story for the U-2R ejector tailpipe. Noise trouble was cured by a thirteen inch extension and free floating bypass doors at the engine face. The doors stay shut on the ground and open in flight for cooling air. A ground handling accident is also reported, and a delivery table lists aircraft 3 to 6.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800250012-2:
Two papers are bound in one file, sent 4 April 1968. The first is the research and development quarterly report for January, February, and March 1968, addressed to the Director of Operations, OSA. The second, dated 3 April 1968, is the OXCART monthly operational summary for March 1968, reporting one A-12 operational mission flown during that month.

Camera work fills much of the quarterly text. Twenty-two non-operational missions are reported without a failure. Thirteen Type IV missions had one failure, when a drive motor froze twenty seconds after turn-on from a faulty seal. Low sun tests were finished in late March, with data sent to Perkin Elmer for study. New Type I exposure tables entered operational use, the report states.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800320005-2:
Fact sheet headed OXCART Information gives a short history of the A-12 program in dates and counts. Design and model work began 29 August 1959, fabrication on 8 February 1960, and first flight on 26 April 1962. The first Mach 3.2 flight came on 27 November 1963. Operational dates are listed for Mach 2.8 in November 1964 and Mach 3.2 in December 1965, as printed.

Flight totals as of 29 February 1968 stand at 2,731. Aircraft on hand as of 15 March 1968 total nine: five operationally ready, one test, one trainer, and two in storage. Deployment pages add that the Kadena deployment was directed on 16 May 1967 and completed ten days later, with twenty-eight missions flown by 8 March 1968.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800340021-2:
Memorandum OSA-3054-67, dated 16 August 1967, sends a progress report on the OSA history to the chairman of the DDS&T Historical Board. The executive officer notes a staffing snag: the person who had worked full time on the OSA history now carries extra secretarial duties. A first draft will therefore slip to the end of the year, the memo states.

The attached form puts the main report at fifty-five percent complete as of 15 August 1967, with about 135 annexes planned and about eighty already prepared. The history outline runs from background through test programs, pilot recruiting, and security and cover arrangements. Later chapters reach the satellite program and the U-2 successor program, GUSTO and OXCART, from feasibility study to termination.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800340030-2:
Handbook dated 5 January 1967, prepared by the Historical Staff in the Director's office, tells staff how to write directorate histories for DDI, DDS&T, and DDS. Its contents list five chapters: introduction, organization and procedures, content and treatment, style and format, and sources. Two appendices cover outside interviews and reference material, including a table of directors and deputy directors by date.

The introduction argues that a systematic record is needed for orderly management of the agency's work. Rules follow on security marking, with sensitive material segregated into a separate text where possible so the main paper can circulate more widely. Full and accurate referencing is called fundamental, with source notes for every challengeable point and key fact in the history.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000100130043-2:
Series of monthly progress reports from the Printing and Reproduction Division, opening with a report dated 6 January 1953 to the Chief, General Services. The first month's volume is stated plainly: 2,942 jobs received and 2,795 delivered. Tables break the work down by office and by process, from photostat and ozalid through letterpress, mimeograph, addressograph, ditto, and bindery, with prints and impressions counted.

Later reports in the run repeat the same form for later months, with backlog figures and Government Printing Office production totals. One month's GPO output is given as 2,369,115 letterpress impressions and 229,355 offset impressions, with 139 NIS sections in backlog. The series shows the division's load across the agency's offices, month by month, in the same tabular shape.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000100140006-2:
Memorandum dated 12 August 1953, to the Acting Deputy Director for Administration, comments on a proposal to move General Services functions to other agency components. The writer states the proposal rests on a belief in a more efficient operation. Savings in staff and money are also claimed. No detailed study backs that belief, the memo notes. It cites the proposer's own memorandum of 22 July 1953 for that point.

Three steps are urged before any decision. First, sort out the functions of General Services, Logistics, and the Comptroller. The sorting should be done in conference with the people who hold the functions now. Those who would take them over should also sit in. Second, review General Services performance against past performance elsewhere. Third, weigh other points the text lists. A history of the services office and its many transfers, running to 1952, closes the memo.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030007-2:
Transportation manual in four parts covers how the services office moves people, cargo, and vehicles. Part 1 states the general duty: arrange travel for civilian and military staff on temporary duty and on permanent change of station, with dependents and household effects. The service books hotels, air, rail, and steamship space, issues transportation requests, and prepares itineraries.

Overseas work adds theater clearances, passports and visas, air priorities, and briefings on clothing and local conditions. Later parts treat cargo shipping documents, liaison with dispatch agents and ports of embarkation, and the motor pool. Closing pages set garage rules: trucks run from the garage on the supervisor's dispatch, and any accident must be reported in writing by the driver within three hours.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030179-2:
Flow chart and forms set shows how Forms 36-7 and 36-10 move through the Services Division for supplies and equipment that are not expendable. The requisition is prepared in quadruplicate. The requester signs the deliver to space and sends copies one through three forward, keeping copy four in a suspense file. On receipt of the goods, copy four is destroyed and the delivery ticket copy kept on file.

Approval and posting steps follow in boxes across the chart. Branch officers approve and sign all copies. A requisition number is assigned, and copies route to the warehouse and supply offices. Debit voucher numbers are placed on set copies, which are then posted to stock record accounts. Specimen copies of the September 1946 requisition form, with its preparation instructions, are bound into the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050195-2:
