Second copy in this slice of Public Law 600, 79th Congress, the act authorizing certain administrative expenses in the government service, approved 2 August 1946. Its transfer rules are the heart of the text. An employee moved for permanent duty between official stations, on written authorization in the travel order, is repaid travel costs for himself and his immediate family. The government also pays packing, crating, temporary storage, drayage, and unpacking of his household goods and personal effects.

The weight ceiling in the text is seven thousand pounds uncrated, or eight thousand seven hundred and fifty pounds if crated. Advertising rules for government sales follow, and exemptions in other law for amounts of one hundred dollars or less are repealed. Wholly owned government corporations are covered for their administrative transactions only. Witness fees and travel costs at hearings close the main body.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200100009-2:
February 1953 closes with a report dated 3 March from the Records Management and Distribution Branch. Fourteen Mail Control staff face pending transfer or reassignment, against one at the Records Center and none in Records Management. Four new applicants were interviewed. Leave runs three in Records Management, six in Mail Control, five at the Records Center. The Jackson Commission analyst and the Transportation courier remain on full month detail.

Project news leads the middle pages. The Correspondence Control System and the Subject Numeric System of classification and filing have been installed in four divisions, among them Transportation, Supply, and Purchase. Divisions report the systems save time and cut duplicate copies of correspondence. Two divisions still lack the systems. Work improvement projects stand at eighty-five percent for two items, and ten percent for the card conversion.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00355a000100020038-2:
Course outline for Section IV, Principles of Strategic Intelligence, plans thirteen lectures, each followed by discussion. The section defines intelligence terms and sets current, basic, and staff intelligence side by side, showing how they differ. The parts of strategic intelligence are then taken one by one in detail, and again together, in terms of how they relate to each other and to national security problems.

The opening lecture, by the Director of the CIA Intelligence School, defines national, departmental, current, basic, staff, strategic, operational, and combat intelligence. Later lectures treat single fields: political, sociological, and economic intelligence among them, each by the office that owns it, with the factors abroad that bear on United States security. The closing lecture, by the Office of Training staff, draws the parts together for appraisals of foreign capabilities and vulnerabilities.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00011a000100030037-2:
Weekly activities report dated 8 August 1952, from the Chief, Plans and Policy Staff, covers 31 July to 7 August 1952. No projects were completed in the week. Work in process leads with Project 52-1, revision of a CIA regulation on agency briefing, coordinated and approved through the training chain and sent to the Director of Training. Project 52-8, a staff study on a proposed series of national security presentations, is also in process.

Project 52-17, the Near East language and area program, faces an 8 August deadline for applications for its October session. Six places are open, and the named offices expect to fill them. Project 52-37 will produce a pilot manual on collection and source exploitation for the Basic Intelligence Course, testing a plan for a manual series. Seven projects sit in suspense at the end, from a survey of non-O/TR training to a bill for training federal civilian staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00037a000100030002-2:
Weekly Activity Report number 30, dated 12 August 1952, is a sample report to the Chief, Plans and Programs Staff, covering 5 to 12 August 1952. A guidance head lists what new activities should hold: changes in staff assignments, new teaching material, staff work in other courses, revision of training materials, and allied training work. Personnel changes lead: one instructor moves from the Basic Orientation Course to the Operations Course on 1 September 1952, and a resignation cuts the staff from three instructors to two.

Material work follows. All training materials dealing with cover are under review, to improve handling of cover problems in world areas. Chief instructors in the Advanced Training Division must each prepare a one hour survey of their course for the War Plans Staff Officers Course. Revision of the Communism Week materials in the Basic Orientation Course is also under way.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00037a000100040083-2:
Weekly Activity Report dated 2 July 1953 updates the same project list as the report of 16 July in this slice. The training film library holds fourteen retention prints and thirty-four loan prints out, with six loan films sent in the week. Instructor Training Course number 10 ran with twelve students: five from MTB/TR(S), four from FI, and one each from COMMO, PM, and TAB. The new instructor course for TR(S) staff keeps its 15 September target.

The mobile audio-visual device will be shown to the DD/TR(S) in the coming week. A fresh try will be made to interest the operating divisions in the machine. The tradecraft manual translation stands at three chapters received from FDD. A film strip for BIS was planned out in forty-two frames. Enrollment tables at the end count staff in TRG courses, 381 in regular classes by one line of the table.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00037a000200120001-2:
Staff study on admission of students to training sets the problem in one line. Procedures must secure enrollment in TR(S) courses. They must also secure right choice of courses for each student's projected assignment, and respect for course prerequisites. Two assumptions follow. The operating offices accept that new staff need time for courses tied to their assignments. Field returnees likewise need time for courses tied to their next posts.

A 15 May 1951 paper on training officers is cited as the authority base. Test work is treated: fair tests can judge waiver requests, showing whether a student knows enough to skip a basic course. Recommendations close the study. A post of Senior Registrar should be set up in the Office of Training (Special). Training officers in the covert offices should be bound by regulation to support the system.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100020010-2:
Official report on the Sixth Agency Orientation Course covers the program of 8 to 11 April 1952 in the Department of Agriculture Auditorium. It was the second course under the quarterly regulation. Growth already strains the hall: beyond its 585 fixed seats, about twenty-five extra seats were set up for invitees not registered on the course. Even at four courses a year, the report states, the office cannot catch up with agency growth.

The four parts run Background, Basic Components in the Intelligence Process, the Production Process in Intelligence, and the Impact of Intelligence. Attendance checking is questioned in the body. Credit was given to seven of eighteen named people who attended three quarters of the course, the standing norm. Empty seats on the middle days prompt a proposal: a simple check each day, in place of trust in the first and last registration cards alone. Thanks to the staff close the report.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00166a000100010001-2:
Index to orientation course material, with dates from February 1953 onward. Early entries name Training Bulletins from the eighth orientation course. More entries cover the ninth and tenth courses. Speakers named include the Director of Central Intelligence and his deputy. William H. Jackson and the Vice President also appear. Memos on bulletin costs are indexed too.

Later entries cover the eleventh and twelfth courses. Draft talks by Allen W. Dulles are listed. Drafts by Charles P. Cabell are listed too. Lyman B. Kirkpatrick appears as a speaker as well. Covering memos for bulletins eight through twelve follow. A large body of course text comes after the index. It holds training for set duty assignments. It also holds talk text on the good intelligence officer. Handling security in daily social life is covered there.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100020013-2:
Task Force memorandum dated 8 May 1961 to the Assistant Deputy Director for Administration, on problems in giving administrative support to the Agency's covert work. Support troubles are split into two kinds: basic ideas needing notice and policy rulings at the top, and single pressing tasks that can be handed to groups for study and action.

An attachment argues that American work in the covert field since the Second World War shows much confusion, waste, and insecurity, with fixes that eased signs rather than causes. Points stressed include the weight of action at the point of work overseas, where the agent is usually neither staff nor an American citizen. A second attachment lists tasks. The memo urges senior notice of the basic issues and assignment of the task list.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100040002-2:
Task Force memorandum dated 5 June 1951. It went to the Assistant Deputy Director for Administration. Senior Review Committee action was requested. The subject is taxicabs and private cars. Washington travel posed an acute problem. Staff sat in many buildings across the area. Many staff had to visit other agencies in person. Off-site training places added more travel.

Agency rules on taxis were tighter than government rules. The Confidential Funds Regulations allowed taxis for security needs. CIA rules allowed them for urgent fixed meetings. Bulky or delicate loads also qualified. Both rules predated a 1950 public law. The paper asks how far rules should be eased. It also asks what controls would stop waste. Private car mileage gets close review. The paper doubts mileage for short city trips. Processing such claims could cost more than the claims.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100060019-2:
Discussion piece on contracts for agents and covert buying. It opens with a plain definition of a contract. Two parties agree that each will perform an act. Writing states what the government promises. Writing also states what the person promises. Pay and benefits form the core of the text. Working details of gathering secrets stay out.

Only covert contracts are treated here. Legal limits shape what can be offered. Internal policy adds further limits. The Confidential Funds Regulations set the chief bounds. Case officers hold the working link with most agents. They assure a person that the Agency will pay. Later pages cover guarantees that may be added. Leave and sick leave are not automatic rights. Retirement credit gets detailed treatment. A covert worker may later join a staff post. Service years spent under cover can then count.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100020069-2:
Outlines for the Human Resources Program in supervisor training. Group meeting number one opens the set. Its purpose is stated at the start. Supervisors should use themselves and their people fully. Support comes from the Management Training Division. Each office gets the program on set terms. Those terms are agreed before the program starts.

Meeting one defines management in plain words. Management means getting work done through people. It also means the development of people. Five functions of management are listed. Five key principles follow the functions. Each supervisor then holds a half-hour conference. A card is prepared for every Agency employee beforehand. Time in the unit is noted. Strengths and weaknesses are noted too. Later outlines list common management problems. Communication up and down appears often. Coordination in a growing office appears too.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100020078-2:
Paper on publications for the Office of Training. The office is compared to a university. It has two colleges and many programs. Off-campus links form part of the picture. A budding extension service is growing too. Textbooks are the weak point in this picture. Some departments have a scattering of them. Others have none at all.

Extra readings exist for many courses. For some courses, even those are lacking. Few courses have a true reference book. Teaching must lean on lectures as a result. That reliance carries two clear costs. Course efficiency drops without books. Agency staff who cannot attend gain nothing at all. The paper sets three fronts for the work. Building a working literature is the broad task. Limits, scope, and writers must still be settled. Each text needs a publications number. Spread of each text must weigh use against hazard.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100040003-2:
Organization text dated 20 March 1953. One section states the Office of Training mission. The Director of Training develops Agency training programs. Office training programs are reviewed by him too. He speaks for the Director on training subjects. He helps shape Career Service Board policy. Training facilities in the United States are his concern.

Public Law 110 governs outside training places. Staff may train at public facilities under it. Private facilities abroad also qualify under it. Standards of achievement are set by the Director. A list of functions follows the mission. Policies, plans, and programs are his to frame. Language and area training must be provided. New staff get indoctrination in the Agency. Orientation serves government staff as required. Management training serves executives and supervisors. Its aim is care of human and physical resources.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000030056-2:
Document referring to letter contract number EC-1806. The contract was between the Agency and Eastman Kodak Company. A distribution list names offices to receive copies. Contractor, service, and finance copies are listed. Reading and chrono copies appear as well. An exhibit schedule forms the heart of the file. It was issued under an amendment to the contract.

Exhibit A lists equipment the contractor shall furnish. Stage I items are photographic processing machines. A film processor heads the visible list. Its total price reads as fifty-nine thousand dollars. A continuous film printer follows at eighteen thousand. Other processors carry prices in the tens of thousands. A second schedule lists smaller supply items. Sorters, selectors, and printers appear among them. Quantities are mostly one per item. A total near three hundred ten thousand dollars is shown.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000070106-2:
Amendment number six to contract number A-101. The amendment is dated 13 March 1956. Copy five is the copy shown here. Under its terms, the Agency makes three moves. It deletes certain items from the contract work. It changes payment for certain other work. It extends the period of performance as well.

The contractor must perform added work under the change. Additional facilities and tooling are required for it. That work ties to studies named in the schedule. Development and test work are covered by the terms. Production of items at set facilities is covered too. Results of studies go to the government. Both low and high altitude work fed those studies. Further clauses amend the schedule in detail. Spare parts for a named system are deleted. Other schedule paragraphs are struck or replaced. The scan is partly garbled in these pages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000080178-2:
Follow-up memorandum dated 4 April 1956, sent through the Contracting Officer. Its subject is the suppliers' meeting of 1 March. The writer refers back to a report of 4 April. Thanks are offered for help given on that report. A discussed matter had been taken up with another party. A preliminary showing was described in reply. Little promise for further effort was seen there.

Richard M. Bissell Jr. signed the memorandum. Distribution ran widely across the Agency project. The Deputy Project Director received a copy. Directors of administration and materiel were listed. Security and finance copies appear as well. Attachments in the file list contract items. Contract number SP-1913 is named on one attachment. Names tied to those items are partly redacted. The scan of the body text is partly garbled. Its heads, date, and distribution stay legible throughout.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000130127-2:
Memorandum for the record dated 14 May 1956. A meeting at Westinghouse forms its subject. The APQ-56 radar was the topic of the meeting. It sat on 9 May 1956 at Friendship Airport. Westinghouse Air Arm engineering offices hosted it. Westinghouse and Agency project staff both attended. Names of attendees are redacted in the copy.

Delivery of spares was the first item taken up. Project concurrence went to a proposed procedure. Written concurrence was forwarded after the meeting. The spares list should support two programs for a year. That was the view recorded in the memo. Two-thirds of spares go to AQUATONE. Groups one and two make up that share. Group three goes to the other program. Three AQUATONE flyaway kits come from group two. A test waiver is also recorded. Flame spread in a proof test caused it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000160133-2:
Project Operations SOP number one, dated 15 June 1956. Admittance to the Project Operations Control Center is its subject. Control procedures are set to ensure maximum security. The Control Center area is defined by room numbers. Rooms 522 through 562 are listed in the text. A floor plan inclosure shows the layout. A restricted area sits inside the center.

Rooms 554, 558, and 562 form that inner area. The projection room and its anteroom are included. All assigned Agency personnel bear personal responsibility here. Strict adherence to the SOP is required of them. A special intelligence officer checks the measures. He recommends revisions as circumstances warrant. The senior controller keeps a receptionist at the entrance. Access turns on an official access list. Names not on the list are turned away. Security checks guard against slips in that process.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000170169-2:
Negotiated Agency contract number B-5111A, in a very long file. The contractor was an atomic instrument company in Cambridge. Its address was 33 University Road, Cambridge 39, Massachusetts. The company was incorporated in Massachusetts. The parties executed the contract in June 1956. The schedule controls over general provisions in any clash. That rule is stated on the contract face.

The contractor must furnish facilities under the deal. It must deliver supplies and perform services too. Those duties are set out in the attached schedule. Appendix one forms part of the contract set. A corporate certificate accompanies the signature page. Deep in the provisions, royalties are treated. A threshold of one thousand dollars per year appears. Licensor names and patent numbers must be reported. Filing dates and royalty bases must be given as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000200020061-2:
Course sheet for cryptographic and communications security courses. A staff training course leads the sheet. It runs three weeks, with 120 hours minimum. Eight students form the class size given. Building L is the location named. Small Agency overseas stations must train all their people. Stations of one to three persons are meant. Larger stations train a set trio instead.

That trio is one responsible officer plus two staff. Secretaries or clerks fill those two places. Lectures, study, and practical work form the methods. A final briefing comes just before departure overseas. Cryptography is applied to the single station. A chiefs' course runs one week instead. It carries a forty-hour minimum and two students. Station chiefs and deputies of large stations take it. Its subjects brief the longer course material.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100020005-2:
Memorandum for the Director of Central Intelligence on ceiling. Depletion of the Director's Ceiling Reserve is the subject. The same problem question opens this version. A reservoir of civilian positions is needed on a continuing basis. The reserve supplying that reservoir is diminishing. Facts follow, with figures redacted in the copy. Ceiling as of 31 August 1954 is the base date.

Unused slots are spread among six major components. A tab covers eleven recent months of data. Ceiling increased slightly over that span. Staff on duty declined a little meanwhile. The gap appears fairly constant across the months. Perpetual attrition and hiring problems explain it. The fiscal 1955 operating budget is cited next. Average employment under ceiling is its figure. Options for rebuilding the reserve are listed. Recapture of unused ceiling is one option. Recapture from casuals is another named option. Junior Officer Trainees count among those casuals.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100100006-2:
Report dated 16 April 1952 on the Executive Registry. Its Top Secret control system is the subject. An Organization and Methods examiner wrote the report. The registry is the area control office for several heads. Material for the Director's office flows through it. Deputy directors and the Inspector General are covered. Uniform methods across the Agency were the review aim.

Survey dates ran in late March and April 1952. Departures from the basic system are listed first. Separate logs are kept for each material type. IAC and daily digest materials have their own logs. Project and originated documents have separate logs too. Security hazards get their own section in the report. Hand-carrying of material outside channels is prevalent. The registry fights it by seeking other areas' help. Detached cover sheets break continuity of control.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100100024-2:
Report dated 7 March 1952 on the ORR control office. The research and reports office is the area covered. Its sub-station sits in the Cartographic Branch. An Organization and Methods examiner wrote the report. It went through the CIA Top Secret Control Officer. Survey dates were 6 and 7 March 1952. Incoming and outgoing alternate officers are listed.

Departures from the basic system are listed first. Outside documents are hand-carried from the central office. They go straight to ORR on receipt there. Examination and quantity decisions happen before routine processing. That order gives speed but risks uneven treatment. A guide to ORR requirements is suggested instead. The Liaison Division would use that guide for spread. Extract files get detailed treatment in the report. Pages seven through ten hold extracted material. Analysts sign for extracts they have filed. Bindings of documents are called not secure enough. Pages tear away under frequent handling, it states.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100150001-2:
Bound set of management staff studies on the Agency reports office. The Office of Reports and Estimates is the subject throughout. Regional divisions are studied in the first part. The National Intelligence Survey Division follows in the set. Map Division and Publications Division come next. An administrative staff study closes the bound set.

Findings on the regional divisions open the studies. Their competence rests on a defined production plan. Basic intelligence research duties need that definition. Coordination of national intelligence needs it too. A requirements organization is also called for. It would insure speedy but coordinated action. Support duties between components need clarification as well. Collection support should grow and improve. Requirements staff role gets close attention later. That staff should expedite and troubleshoot requirements. It should not act as a restrictive channel.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200010014-2:
Office memorandum surveying the Agency Services Office. Its procedures and organization are the survey subject. The survey began around 18 January 1949. The Services Officer had requested it himself. Operating office officials were consulted on problems. Faster, better, and cheaper service was one objective. Relief of operating staff from extraneous duties was another. Work inside the office should shrink without harm.

Some authorized positions might then be eliminated. Forms, files, reports, and records should all shrink. Findings call the service rendered adequate overall. Supervisors grasp their responsibilities well, it states. Too many controls exist despite recent simplification. Too many records, forms, and files persist as well. Many forms in use bear no numbers. Property control burdens operating offices unnecessarily. Procurement and contract service is slowed by reviews.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200100014-2:
Analysis of case control and statistical reporting procedures. The Security Division of Inspection and Security is the subject. A special study was made during a wider survey. The Agency Deputy Security Officer requested the study. Punched card methods were the focus of it. Simpler case control was the aim sought. Easier statistical reports were the second aim.

Reporting on security clearances was analyzed alongside. Three offices figure in that wider analysis. The Personnel Office is one of those offices. The Machine Records Branch is the second. Inspection and Security itself is the third. Consistent monthly statistics were wanted from all three. Procedures for requesting clearances were developed from it. A memorandum of 14 August 1951 implemented them. A control record would reconcile count differences. Cases forwarded and cases opened could be matched. Discrepancies between the offices would surface that way.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200120021-2:
Instructions for writing an installation report, Exhibit A. Punch card setups are covered by the exhibit. Bookkeeping machine setups fall in the same reporting. Ordinarily a separate report fits each type. Incidental gear of one type may join another report. Dual-type setups use a single report. Related gear can be included when integral.

Addressing gear and electric typewriters are examples given. Adding machines fall in that same class. Summary reports serve units with several setups. One report per setup is still required beneath them. Department or agency summaries are arranged as needed. Contract services by private bureaus are reported too. Each agency or bureau is named in that section. The amount of each contract is entered there. Functions performed need a brief note attached. Extra material may support that account. Major functions should be clear from the entry.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200200004-2:
Staff policy study on Agency dealings with employees. It is addressed through channels to the Deputy Director. The problem asks what rules should govern. Use of Agency services toward employees is at issue. Selection, training, and handling of employees are named. Placement, relationships, and morale complete that list. Progressive use of each person, or ending service, is the end.

Assumptions frame the study before its facts. Staff administration differs in rule nowhere, it holds. Agency actions touching persons must flow from policy. Set policy cannot be many-sided in nature. Efficiency must be sought throughout the Agency. Needless and duplicating costs must be avoided. Facts then list forces outside staff jurisdiction. Medical and psychiatric forces sit at headquarters. Psychological force is outside that pale too. Security handling forms a third outside force. Unchecked one-sided operating parts add a fourth. Each force bears heavily on the person.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200200040-2:
Memo dated 20 November 1952 on psychological assessment. It went from the Agency Director of Training to Plans. The review function and purpose need fresh study. Some time has passed since their last talk. Recent changes in the chart warrant that new look. Current revision of steps and policies adds reason. Needs of the plans complex frame the study.

Strengths of the Assessment Staff frame it equally. Talk on future needs is hoped for here. Sound planning and staffing depend on it. The Assessment and Evaluation Staff would plan in line. The Assessment Branch staffing is described. Two senior psychologists staff the branch now. One psychologist and one junior psychologist follow. A junior psychologist in training completes the five. Two more senior psychologists serve emergencies. Special reviews can draw on those two. Use of review lacks uniform policy. Some divisions process nearly everyone through it. Promotion fitness is one routine use named.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00259a000100030004-2:
Minutes of an OTR staff meeting on security and training. The chief of training went over a deputy's meeting. General Cabell's concern for security led the summary. A Washington newspaperman anchors the warning case. He was friendly with three plans staff. Social talk at different occasions let him piece things together. The nature of sensitive work emerged. Widely separated parts of the world were involved.

Cabell was set on tightening against such leaks. Unapproved leaks are his target. He pressed the concern on Agency reservists too. His address to them fell on 13 September. Training needs received equal stress there. Staff needing training should take the first step themselves. Supervisors should process them into regular programs. Student grading proposals appear later in the record. Fixed question sets could skew would-be gradings unfairly. Final decision rested with the Training chief. Sending out outside training notices closes the items.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00259a000100030013-2:
Minutes of an OTR staff meeting, 14 April 1954. Opening remarks reported a recent meeting with the Director. Staff should check promptly with the security officer. Congressional Loyalty Hearing requests trigger that check. Security Hearing requests trigger the same duty. Budget Hearing treatment satisfied the Director reasonably. Representative Taber is named in that connection.

Mr. Dulles had gone on record in the hearing. CIA would make further efforts to cut personnel. The Washington area was singled out for cuts. The Hatch Act provisions get attention next. All employees were urged to know them fully. The Benton Petition draws a specific caution. Staff were warned not to sign that petition. It was being circulated throughout the country. A central file inside OTR appears later. Case history work should be tracked centrally there. Who works on what, and why, should be knowable. An instruction on the matter was being issued.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00259a000200040011-2:
Summary report on a Human Resources Program for senior officials. It went to the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence. The Director of Training forwarded the report. A ninety minute initial phase was conducted. Six groups of senior officials took that phase. The period ran 1 December 1953 to 12 March 1954. Three groups drew officials from across the Agency.

Two groups were made up of administration personnel. One group held plans division chiefs and equivalents. A roster of ninety-four senior officials is appended. Earlier participants are noted on that appendix too. Objectives in running the program are threefold. Basic supervisory training reached top operating personnel first. Their reactions and suggestions were secured second. Cooperative action to improve management was third. Later pages sketch a management package idea. An up-to-date organization chart would anchor it. A functional statement for each supervisor follows. Periodic evaluation of managerial competence is included.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100120017-2:
Fragmentary meeting notes on administrative questions, heavily redacted. A working fund for operations is discussed first. One speaker deemed such a fund important. No objection stood if the amount stayed reasonable. The reason would go before the review committee. A figure of five thousand dollars was spoken of. Agent contract terms form the second topic.

One year agent contracts carry a clause at issue. An agent terminating voluntarily must pay his way home. Renewal for a second year should amend that clause. Return transportation would be paid by the Agency instead. A home trip at renewal changes that result. Claims handling surfaces in the later fragments. A disallowed agent claim was protested vigorously. The headquarters desk upheld that claim on review. Similar claims at the same station were disallowed. Such action destroys station authority, the notes hold. Administrative field authority cannot survive that pattern.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100150087-2:
Notes for public utterance on Agency functions, in rough scan. Houston of the General Counsel office heads the copy. Audiences for statements divide into three categories. The general public forms the first of them. Uncleared groups with intelligence interest form the second. Cleared groups with much knowledge form the third. Basic thoughts hold one line in all cases.

Speaker problems differ greatly across those audiences. The public poses purely an information problem. Ordinary persons have barely heard of the Agency. Intelligence groups want techniques and function distribution. Cleared groups want specific problems and operations. Flexibility in any outline is therefore essential. These notes approach the uninformed public mainly. The idea of intelligence gets its own section. No exact definition exists despite expert claims. The process is matter-of-fact and familiar. Court proceedings offer a comparison used there. Departments keep their own intelligence work later.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100170003-2:
Memo dated 12 November 1953 on counsel office staffing. It went to the Agency General Counsel. Flat structure is praised as most fitting there. Pyramid pleas and their evils are avoided. Gradual growth fits merit under it. Conscience and opportunity govern that growth pattern. One block stands against the flat aim though.

Physical spread of serviced offices is that block. The counsel office must service scattered locations. Repeated posting patterns accompany that spread problem. Flexibility and in-theory expansion suffer under it. Building postings illustrate the split in practice. South Building handles routine office work and housekeeping mainly. Staffing, finance, logistics, and security sit there. Covert affairs spill into it only sometimes. Posting variety over two years is looked at later. Short duty and permanent change postings both appear. Matters run from office work to field work. A de facto rotation has benefited the office. Developing it into a program is suggested.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100220007-2:
Dated 9 October 1953, a memorandum to the Director of Central Intelligence asks whether set limits and duties should be placed on CIA career staff, and whether law should name them. The paper comes from a task force study of the career service. It notes that staff already serve on call and may be sent where the service needs them. Yet no rule then bound an employee to make the Agency a life career.

An attached tab lists sample limits and proposed duties for career staff. The study weighs signed statements of intent, the pull of personal choice on postings, and staff hired only for duty in Washington. Its core point is plain: the needs of the service come first, ahead of where an employee would rather serve.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400050003-2:
Departmental Circular Number 653 from the United States Civil Service Commission, dated 23 February 1951, revises the program for reemployment rights. Heads of departments and independent bodies are the audience. Under the revision, permanent staff who leave nondefense agencies for defense work gain rights to their old jobs. A nondefense agency can appeal only where loss of the person would harm a vital activity, and the Commission must back that appeal.

Movement between two defense agencies is treated more strictly, since both sides of such a move must agree. The circular links the change to a tight labor market and the need to shift staff toward defense work. It shows how the government tried to move skilled people without stripping the offices they left.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400050012-2:
Part-time and summer-only hiring of staff dependents is the subject of a memorandum dated May 1953 to the Deputy Director for Administration. It asks what bars stand against hiring dependents of Agency staff, or other suitable people, for clerical work in the lower grades. An urgent need for file clerks and clerk typists sits behind the question. A quick survey had found that nearly all offices would use such help.

The paper notes that the Director of Security would have to clear a special instruction for dependents under set conditions. Tests for part-time staff would match those for full-time staff. Pay, hours, and the risk of hiring family members of serving staff all needed settling before the scheme could start.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400060011-2:
Reassignment and separation of staff who perform poorly are the subject of a Personnel Director memorandum from December 1952. It passes on a policy declared on 21 November 1952 by the Deputy Director for Administration. The policy covers staff whose failure looks like a lack of skill that could repeat in a new post. It sits beside older paths such as guidance, training, and separation for cause.

Strong weight falls on moving such staff to work that fits their skills, since placing people well is a stated aim of Agency staffing. The steps for review inside the personnel office are then set out. The memorandum shows an agency trying to handle weak performance by transfer first, while keeping removal as a later step.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400060165-2:
A letter dated 3 July 1946, sent to the Policy and Regulations Branch of the Civilian Personnel Division in the Office of the Secretary of War, lays out two hard cases. Both men had been restored to civilian posts after duty with the United States Navy. Each held permanent classified civil service standing, and each used reemployment rights under the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940. Both had left for military leave from the Office of Strategic Services.

On 1 October 1945, under Executive Order 9621, the wartime office's people, records, property, and funds passed to the State or War Departments. The men's own activity went to the War Department's Strategic Services Unit, where they were restored. The letter asks how their rights should be treated after that transfer of employer.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400160100-2:
Forms for moving staff overseas fill an untitled instruction covering employees, their families, and their household effects. One named form, Number 36-44, is a request for overseas transportation started by the sponsoring branch chief. It travels with the clearances needed before the movement can be booked. Another, Number 53-27, is a request for movement of family and household effects, started by the employee himself.

Copies of that second form go to the immediate officer, the transportation section, and the fiscal or special funds section. One copy is held as the base for the request itself. The instruction also explains how funds are set aside for the cost. Read as a whole, it turns a family's overseas move into a chain of signed paper.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400180009-2:
Sources of law for territorial post differentials and allowances are gathered in a General Counsel paper dated 19 December 1952. Counsel had been asked to supply extracts from the laws and rules that govern such payments. The lead extract comes from section 207 of Public Law 491 of the 80th Congress, as changed by Public Law 852. Funds for salaries, it provides, may also pay extra compensation to staff stationed outside the continental United States or in Alaska.

That extra pay rests on two grounds: living costs well above those in the District of Columbia, or working conditions that differ sharply from those at home. Further extracts take up rates and the classes of staff covered. The paper is a reference brief for anyone fixing pay at distant posts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400180045-2:
Whether the Agency may pay travel tied to home leave for overseas staff moving for good to the continental United States is posed in a General Counsel opinion of November 1952. Three spring papers frame the file: an Assistant Comptroller note of 13 May, and Finance Division notes of 21 April and 11 April. Those papers dealt with changing dependency reports and with the granting of home leave itself.

Counsel begins by tracing the idea of home leave as written into the governing law. From there the opinion tests how a permanent change of station interacts with a leave trip home. The question mattered in money terms for every returning family. It also mattered for fairness, since leave earned abroad was meant to be spent at home.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500020005-2:
How foreign embassies treat their local staff in Washington is surveyed to help United States agencies set policy for local hires abroad. Findings were gathered on twelve points for each country, from head counts and base pay to leave, pensions, and severance. Holidays, overtime, bonuses, and the tie to United States Social Security are also covered. Eight countries' practices are set out one by one, starting with Brazil.

A summary of major conclusions closes the survey. The mirror logic is plain: what foreign missions pay Americans in Washington hints at fair terms for locals hired by American missions overseas. Local employees, the paper notes at the start, are the aliens each embassy takes on where it sits. The result is a compact guide to practice in the early 1950s.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500050084-2:
Dual compensation limits, applied to hiring a government worker for extra hours, are worked through in an office memorandum dated 10 March 1949. The Agency planned to use a serving employee for work outside his normal hours. No clash between the two jobs was expected or foreseen. Pay might run by salary, per diem, or fee, and each route raised the same legal question.

Present law, the memorandum says, grew from statutes reaching back to 1839, found in sections 58, 62, 69, and 70 of Title 5. Read together, they bar pay for extra services and added allowances to a person already paid, unless law clearly allows it. The rest of the text sorts the planned hiring against each of those bars.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500050093-2:
Notes on the statutes cited in a proposed bill, in the draft of 9 June 1947, are forwarded by a memorandum dated 2 July 1947. The bill is taken section by section. One note gives the rule at 10 U.S.C. 570: an Army officer who accepts a civil office stops being an Army officer, and his commission is vacated. A clear exception must therefore be written into the proposed law, the note warns.

No like blanket bar covers Navy officers, so no statute is cited for them. A further note covers assignment of Foreign Service officers to other agencies under the Foreign Service Act. Hiring any retired officer of the named services is the aim of a later section. The draft is cleaner to read than its twin copy in this file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500070028-2:
Questions on paying consultants reach the Office of General Counsel in a memorandum dated 3 December 1951, sent through the Acting Chief of the Finance Division. Authorised certifying officers signed the request. They state that points on consultants' compensation had lately caused trouble and that the rules need clarifying. A ruling from counsel is sought on each point listed.

Quoted rules give a consultant travel costs between home or business and the place of duty, plus per diem while away. One quoted rule treats a consultant who serves without break as staff for certain purposes. The rest of the paper works through edge cases in those rules. Redaction marks cross the text, but the finance problem at its heart stays clear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500080009-2:
Weak disability benefits for Agency staff hurt on extra-hazardous duties are flagged in a memorandum of 19 August 1953 to the General Counsel. The writer had reviewed one worker's compensation case, with names redacted. The man was injured in this country on 28 July 1952. Doctors found a crushed first lumbar vertebra, with nerve harm in the sacral area and total loss of bladder function.

The Bureau of Employees' Compensation paid medical care and benefits during total disability. The bone had healed enough for doctors to allow desk duties, though a support was still worn. Even so, the case showed how thin standard benefits ran against injuries tied to duties found only in this Agency. Counsel is asked to weigh benefits matched to the assignment's real risk.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500080063-2:
Defining hazardous comes first in a summary statement prepared for the Hazardous Pay Committee. The word, the paper insists, means more than danger to life and limb from violence on duty. Some jobs are risky by nature: guarding and handling explosives, parachute training, and unshielded work near radioactive material are named. Such work is hazardous at home and abroad alike.

Foreign postings widen the picture. Staff abroad carry on work that makes them targets for naming and attack by other nations' intelligence services. A code clerk or clerical secretary, the paper notes, can become a prime target in that setting. The summary pushes the committee to count exposure as well as obvious physical risk when it grades a post.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500090008-2:
A Rating Official's Guide, effective 1 January 1944 and filed as Form Number 3823A in October 1946, speaks straight to supervisors who grade staff. Its first question asks whether the reader uses the uniform system approved by the Civil Service Commission. A quotation from Abraham Lincoln on labour and its fruits heads the text. The guide then argues that fair awards need the whole product of a worker's labour to be known.

From that base it works through how to judge the parts of a job and mark them honestly. Praise, blame, and habit all threaten fair ratings, and the guide warns against each. It was written to be kept for future use, and its tone is that of a coach rather than a rulebook.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500100024-2:
Public Law Number 831 of the 70th Congress, from S. 3936, regulates the practice of the healing art in the District of Columbia. Its stated aim is to protect the public health there. Opening sections define the words the act uses. Disease covers any blemish, defect, deformity, disorder, or injury of the human body or mind, and pregnancy as well.

The healing art is defined just as widely, from detecting disease to preventing, relieving, or curing it. Care of women and infants through pregnancy and birth is named in the definition. Later parts set licensing and the bars on unlicensed practice. The act sits in an Agency legal file as a District statute staff might meet in claims and medical questions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500120004-2:
Preparation of Agency Form 34-42, the Time and Attendance Report and Pay Roll Change Slip, is covered by detailed instructions for time clerks. The form replaces Standard Form 1130, which clerks had been sending to the Payroll Branch. Completed forms go by hand to Room 1710, Quarters Eye. They must arrive by 1600 hours each Monday after a two-week pay period closes. Items 1 through 10 must be filled in evenly and correctly first.

Item 1, the employee name, must be typed or printed last name first, matching the pay list. Forms joined to others are to be separated, carbons left in place, and the set arranged in name order. Later items cover hours, leave, and pay changes. The sheet is payroll routine reduced to numbered steps.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500140011-2:
H.R. 5523, brought in by Mr. Love on 24 February 1948, would amend the Civil Service Retirement Act of 1930 for Treasury investigatory staff. It went to the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service. The bill adds a new paragraph to section 1(h) of the retirement act. A named Treasury officer or employee, aged at least fifty, could retire on his own application after twenty years of service in such posts.

Retirement would need the consent of the Secretary of the Treasury. The annuity is set at two per cent of pay for each year counted, under the formula the bill writes in. Investigatory work was treated as wearing and risky, like the law enforcement classes already given early annuities. The bill extends that same logic to Treasury's own investigators.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000700100013-2:
A check list for the contracting officer opens with security questions that only a covert service would ask. Has clearance been obtained for use of the agent, informant, or cutout named in the deal? Has an acknowledgement of pseudonyms been signed and filed, or is the person precisely named in covert office files? A third question asks whether the person already works for another government agency in any capacity.

The fourth item sorts the services sought: a nominal cutout or letter drop, an active cutout moving funds and reports, expert advice, or direct support of covert work. Later items test whether terms are clear enough for a true meeting of minds. Pay basis and the handling of funds close the list. It is contracting discipline written for people who cannot be named.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000700120020-2:
Effective 15 March 1949, a secret agreement hires an unnamed employee for overseas service under cover. The United States, represented by the Central Intelligence Agency, is the other party. Recitals explain that his work needs an appropriate cover for operations. The government wishes to send him abroad for intelligence operations, and he wishes to serve under the Office of Policy Coordination.

He accepts the duty of providing his own suitable cover. The first article demands a cover occupation logical to his background and attainments. Outward conduct must match that occupation at all times. Later articles cover how orders reach him, what he is paid, and the secrecy that binds him after service. This is the earliest dated of the career agent forms gathered in this file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000700130001-2:
The International Petroleum Cartel, Committee Print Number 6 of the 82nd Congress, is a staff report to the Federal Trade Commission. It went to the Subcommittee on Monopoly of the Senate Select Committee on Small Business. A contents list opens the huge text: world petroleum resources and reserves come first, then refining capacity, consumption, and the pattern of world trade. Concentration of control is the second great theme.

Seven international petroleum companies dominate that account, alongside control by government monopoly in some states. Control of crude reserves, refining, transport, and markets is traced company by company and country by country. Later parts take up joint ventures and the arrangements between the majors. Agency lawyers kept the report because oil control shaped the foreign questions their own work touched.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040007-2:
A Senate report under Report Number 338, ordered printed on 9 May 1949, backs S. 1809 on government property. The Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments presents the bill as a way to simplify buying, using, and disposing of government property. Reorganisation of certain agencies rides with it. The committee recommends passage.

Historical background opens the report, as in its sibling prints. A sound property system had been wanted for years, and a 1943 House bill had tried to supply it. The present bill picks that thread up again after the war. Analysis then follows the organisation title and the supply titles in order. This report pairs with the S. 1809 bill text elsewhere in the file, each covering the same ground from a different side.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040016-2:
Senate Report Number 1302, ordered printed on 17 May 1948, backs S. 2688, the Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1948. Mr. Saltonstall sent it in for the Committee on Armed Services. The bill would provide for the administration of the Central Intelligence Agency. The Agency had been established under section 102 of the National Security Act of 1947. The committee recommends that the bill pass.

Purpose, the report states, is to grant the Agency the powers its proper administration needs. Procurement, travel, allowances, and related expenses are named first. General authorities and methods of spending appropriated funds follow. The bill also guards the confidential character of the Agency's work and money. This report is the Senate's case for the statute that let CIA run its own house.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000070040-2:
A confidential memorandum for the record covers a talk on proposed revisions of the espionage laws. The writer had met that morning with Mr. Elmer Staats, chief of the Legislative Liaison Division of the Bureau of the Budget. The revisions sit inside the so-called omnibus bill on internal security. That bill grew from summer 1946 talks in a joint committee of the War and Navy Departments and the FBI.

Justice passed the proposals to CIA informally at that time. Comments were later sought from State, Treasury, and the Federal Communications Commission. Treasury dissented strongly on several points, the memorandum records. The President himself is described as keenly and personally interested in the bill. The note preserves how the measure moved through government before it reached Congress.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000070095-2:
Authority to create or revive an Office of Censorship is examined in a memorandum dated 30 January 1951 for Mr. Houston. The original office was set up by Executive Order 8985 on 19 December 1941. That order rested on the President's constitutional powers, on statute in general, and in particular on Section 303 of the First War Powers Act of 18 December 1941. That section expressly authorised an Office of Censorship.

Executive Order 9631 ended the office on 28 September 1945. Then, on 25 July 1947, Congress repealed Section 303 itself. The clear statutory base was thus gone twice over. The opinion goes on to weigh what steps a revival would need in the Korean War climate of 1951, when censorship talk had returned.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100020035-2:
A Department of State letter of 29 April 1952 to Senator Moody gives the Department's view of S.J. Res. 130. Moody had asked on 2 April for views on the proposed constitutional amendment about treaties and executive agreements. The Department answers that such an amendment would not serve the best interests of the citizens or the government. It would cut against the division of powers among the judicial, legislative, and executive branches, the letter argues.

Worse, it would so hamper the executive's historic role in foreign affairs as to endanger American influence in the world. Giving Congress, by joint action, the sort of authority the amendment grants is named as a further fault. The letter is the State Department's formal brief against the Bricker proposal, sent while the fight was live.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100030043-2:
Registration of agents of foreign powers is taken up in a memorandum for the record dated 18 October 1950. Acting on the Director's instructions, the writer had talked with Mr. Foley, head of the Alien Registration Section at the Department of Justice. The Internal Security Act of 1950 had amended the Registration Act of 1938. Registration now reached people trained or tasked in espionage, counter-espionage, or sabotage by a foreign country.

Two hopes behind the change are named: a roster of people who know foreign spy methods, and a standing penalty for those who meant to use such knowledge here for harm. Foley agreed the roster hope was weak, since the bill held too many exceptions. Both men expected filings to be few, and mostly from a narrow class of person.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100040006-2:
Appendix B summarises leading cases that touch diplomatic, state, and military secrets. Marbury against Madison opens the set. William Marbury sought an order forcing Secretary of State James Madison to deliver his commission as one of John Adams's midnight judges. The commission had been made out but not issued before Jefferson took office. John Marshall, who had held Madison's post, now sat as Chief Justice over the case.

The Attorney General, called for questioning, refused one answer about the commission's fate, pleading duty to the executive. The Court's words on the President's political powers and his accountability are then quoted. Later cases take up when courts may peer into secrets of state. The appendix pairs with a companion survey of Congress's own demands for papers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100050023-2:
Copyright relations between the United States and Israel are set by an agreement made through an exchange of notes at Washington on 4 May 1950. It entered into force that day, working back to 15 May 1948. The State Department prints it as Publication 4005, sold for five cents. The Israeli Ambassador's note opens the exchange. It points to section 29 of the copyright law in force in Israel.

Under that section, benefits of Israeli law reach a foreign owner only where his own country has made like provision. The notes settle that test between the two states. American authors and publishers thus gained cover in Israel, and Israeli owners gained cover here. A short treaty text, it settled a point left open by Israel's founding two years earlier.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200030105-2:
What a CIA master plan for production should look like is argued in a memorandum for the record from the autumn of 1949. Three earlier memoranda frame it: one on departmental help in preparing CIA reports and estimates, dated 7 October, and two on the master plan itself, dated 14 and 24 October. The writer warns that a staff officer's guesses here are prone to error. Only the producing parts of CIA hold the experience to build the concept in full.

No firm conclusions are reached, by design. The first trait demanded of such a plan is elasticity, above all in its early stages. Detail would grow as experience built up over time. The paper is a rare look at planners thinking about how intelligence output should be programmed, before the habit hardened.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001300050012-2:
Claims for loss of personal property during a forced evacuation fill a memorandum to the Deputy Director for Administration. Five claims come back with the paper, along with the notes on each. Legal authority to pay them exists under paragraph 10.3 of the Confidential Funds Regulations, the writer finds. That holds if the spending counts as confidential, extraordinary, or emergent under paragraph 1.0 of the same rules.

Even so, this office urges holding the five claims back. A rising flow of like claims makes a full review wise first. A CIA Claims Board and a set of claims regulations are floated as the fix. Future claimants, the paper argues, should be treated by one standard, the same as the present five. Names in the file are redacted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001300070010-2:
Transfer of certain military reservations to the Philippines was effected by an exchange of notes signed at Manila on 14 and 16 May 1949. The agreement entered into force on 16 May 1949, working back to 27 March 1949. It appears as Treaties and Other International Acts Series 1063 and State Department Publication 3670, priced at five cents. The American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim writes first, to the Philippine Secretary of Foreign Affairs.

His note cites an act of the United States Congress behind the handover. The reservations named pass from American hands as the young republic takes over its own ground. The reply note completes the bargain in the usual form. Two years after the bases agreement, this exchange returned land the United States no longer held as its own.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200160014-2:
Printed bill H.R. 7054 was introduced in the House on 7 January 1954 by Mr. Dingell and sent to the Committee on Ways and Means. Its title is to amend the Social Security Act to provide unemployment insurance for federal civilian employees, and for other purposes, in the 83rd Congress, second session.

The bill adds a new Title XV to the Social Security Act, headed Unemployment Compensation for Federal Employees. Section 1501 defines federal service as service performed after 1950 in the employ of the United States or a wholly owned instrumentality, with stated exceptions. Excluded groups listed include elective officers, members of the armed forces, and certain foreign service personnel with special separation allowances under the Foreign Service Act of 1946. Later sections cover how claims are handled through state agencies and how accrued annual leave is treated.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200170013-2:
Draft administrative agreement between the Republic of Korea and the Unified Command, dated at Seoul 7 May 1955 and marked unclassified, sets the status of United Nations forces in and about Korea. Its preamble cites Security Council resolutions of 25 June, 27 June, and 7 July 1950, and the Armistice Agreement signed 27 July 1953, after which active fighting had ceased.

The draft states that United Nations forces would remain until the aims of the United Nations in Korea were met. Terms should be fixed by mutual agreement to cut misunderstanding and aid cooperation. Article I begins the definitions. Later articles cover claims, including a waiver for maritime salvage between the parties. They also cover use of a joint committee under Article XVII to settle liability and assess damage to property owned by either party in Korea.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130179-2:
Legal file excerpt titled Loss of Nationality prints statutory text, in a garbled scan, on how a naturalised person may lose United States nationality. The portion shown gives a rule for such a person who then takes up continuous residence in a foreign state of which he was formerly a national, or where he was born.

Later clauses list classes of persons to whom a section does not apply. Among them are a person with twenty five years of residence in the United States after naturalisation who had reached sixty before the foreign residence began. A spouse or child of an American national by birth in stated cases is also listed. So is a person who lost nationality through marriage to an alien and later reacquired it. Further clauses cover nationality held solely by act of Congress or by treaty.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130205-2:
File on the Missing Persons Act, in a partly garbled scan, prints statutory language on pay and status for persons missing in service. It also records talks with Defense and the Bureau of the Budget. The text shown covers persons in the vicinity of their places of employment who are officially carried as missing, captured, or detained by a hostile force.

Categories are listed for civilian officers and employees and for other persons whose absence came from their employment. Discussion notes that Defense had no interest in one clause on allowances, and a General Counsel view is recorded on a special term. Figures and fine wording need care, since parts of the scan cannot be read cleanly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100070004-2:
Combined August and September issue of Task Force, a periodical reprinting a long article by Mr. P. T. Hartley-Blythe of Fleetwood, described by the editors as head of a worldwide news and political intelligence organization, in one of the most important articles they had published.

In the editors' summary, the author claims and purports to document that the Central Intelligence Agency is treasonably inefficient, far from defending the country and in fact a menace to its safety. United States funds meant to aid resistance movements are said to be turned to the advantage of Soviet regimes. Foreign aid is said only to stabilise Red power and drain United States reserves. The editors urge readers to demand a thorough investigation of the Agency by their senators and congressmen. These are the article's charges, set out as its own case.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100070031-2:
Interview with Senator William Benton, dated 28 April 1956, asks the former senator from Connecticut, who served from 1949 to 1953, about free parliaments and free society. The first question notes that a senator's term is six years and asks how he served four; his answer explains staggered terms, vacancies, and appointment.

Each state has two senators, ninety six in all. The states are divided into three groups, one third electing senators every two years. Vacancies arise by death or, rarely, appointment as a federal judge. Two thirds of senators are lawyers, he notes, and none would resign to be a cabinet officer, since a cabinet officer calls on the senator. Later answers discuss foreign policy, with Democrats claiming President Eisenhower had adopted the Truman policy, and disputes turning on spending levels rather than ideology.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100070121-2:
House Document number 157, 83rd Congress, first session, prints a message from the President dated 1 June 1953 transmitting Reorganization Plan number 7 of 1953, sent to the Committee on Government Operations. The plan, prepared under the Reorganization Act of 1949, provides for reorganization of various foreign aid functions and agencies, with reasons stated in a companion message.

The President declares each reorganization in the plan necessary for one or more purposes of section 2(a) of the Reorganization Act of 1949. He likewise declares the provisions for appointment and pay of officers named in the plan. Sections then move functions. One transfers the Institute of Inter-American Affairs, with its functions, to the new Administration. It also moves functions vested in the Secretary of State under the Institute's act to the Director, including rules on staff detailed as employees or board members.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100110009-2:
Notice of Pending Legislation dated 7 May 1956, from the Legislative Counsel, circulates bill H.R. 10989 for information and comment. The bill was introduced in the House on 3 May 1956 by Mr. Broyhill and sent to the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service, in the 84th Congress, second session.

Its title is to provide permanent reemployment priority for persons holding career appointments in the competitive civil service. The comment section, from the Director of Security, states the office's understanding that all Agency employees are in an excepted category and so would not be affected by the bill. The bill applies solely to persons in the competitive civil service. The bill text keeps a separated person on a reemployment roster until he asks in writing to be removed or accepts a non-temporary federal post. Removal also follows if he declines a like post or fails to reply in a reasonable time.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100150087-2:
Minority views of Frank Fellows, a member of the Committee on the Judiciary, dissent in the House inquiry into stolen government documents. During the year, the views state, documents of the State and other departments, some marked top secret, were taken from the files by certain individuals. Several hundred were found in New York City in the office of the publisher of a magazine called Amerasia, whose name was Jaffe.

Resolution 430, providing for a thorough investigation of the disposition of charges of espionage and possession of documents stolen from secret government files, is quoted. Three men, Jaffe, Larsen, and Roth, are noted as indicted for conspiracy to violate sections of Title 18, and section 101 on receiving stolen public property is quoted in full. A later tally lists classified items by the agency that prepared them, by level and by original or copy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100160031-2:
Printed joint resolution H.J. Res. 157 was introduced in the House on 20 January 1955 by Mr. Walter and sent to the Committee on the Judiciary, in the 84th Congress, first session. Its title is to establish a Commission on Government Security, and the text is printed with line numbers.

Section 1, a declaration of policy, states that it is vital to the welfare and safety of the United States that there exist at all times adequate protection of the national security. That protection includes safeguarding national defense secrets and defense installations, against loss or compromise from espionage, sabotage, disloyalty, subversive activities, or unauthorized disclosures. Congress policy is then stated as a sound government program, covering security procedures for hiring and keeping government employees. It covers investigation, evaluation, and adjudication where needed, and security requirements for persons privately employed on work needing access to defense secrets.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100160040-2:
Printed joint resolution S.J. Res. 21 was introduced in the Senate on 18 January 1955 by Mr. Humphrey, for himself and Mr. Stennis, and sent to the Committee on Government Operations, in the 84th Congress, first session. Its title is to establish a Commission on Government Security, 

Section 1 declares it vital to the welfare and safety of the United States that there be adequate protection of national security. That includes safeguarding national defense secrets and defense installations, against espionage, sabotage, disloyalty, subversive activities, and unauthorized disclosures. A sound government program is stated as policy, covering security investigation, evaluation, clearance, and adjudication of government employees, and security requirements for persons privately employed on work needing access to defense secrets. Later sections cover staff, temporary services at up to fifty dollars per day, and FBI investigation of employees.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100190038-2:
Senate Resolution 50, 81st Congress, first session, was submitted on 3 February 1949 by Mr. Johnson of Colorado and sent to the Committee on Interstate and Foreign Commerce, reported with amendments in February and March 1949, and considered, amended, and agreed to on 11 April 1949. The printed text traces that whole course.

The resolution authorises and directs the committee, or a duly authorised subcommittee, to make a full and complete study of problems it deems proper. The problems relate to the financial stability and operational efficiency of the airline industry, all matters on the United States merchant marine, and all domestic land and water transportation. Points to settle include whether conditions conform to the national transportation policy declared in the Interstate Commerce Act and how large spending of public money and private capital affects transport charges. Later clauses reach the licensing work of the Federal Communications Commission for radio stations.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200010018-2:
House Document number 415, 81st Congress, second session, is titled Reports to Be Made to Congress. It is a letter from the Clerk of the House of Representatives dated 3 January 1950. The letter sends a list of reports that any officer or department has a duty to make to Congress. The letter states it is sent under rule III, clause 2, of the House Rules.

The list is arranged in table form: the officer and nature of the report, the authority, and when the report is expected. An opening entry covers the head of each department, citing 5 U.S.C. 106, with annual reports due at the start of the session covering the transactions of the preceding year. Later entries run through departments and agencies in detail. One report describes operations under the Federal Airport Act, with statements of development accomplished, the status of each project, and allocation of funds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200020026-2:
Calendar number 601 prints S.J. Res. 96 as reported in the Senate, Report number 602, with amendments shown by struck through text and italics. The resolution was introduced 30 June 1953 by Mr. Hickenlooper and seven co-sponsors, sent to the Committee on Foreign Relations, and reported 18 July 1953.

Recitals ground the proposal in the weight of the overseas information program. They cite the President's message of 2 February 1953 on making international information work more effective. They also cite a subcommittee finding of 15 June 1953 that linking Atlantic nations and much of the non-Communist world in vast television networks was feasible. The commission to be created would study the status and potential of international use of all forms of telecommunications. Staff and expert pay terms appear in the amended text, with experts capped at seventy five dollars per day for each individual.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200020044-2:
Copy labelled Tab B holds S.J. Res. 96 in the form reported to the Senate, with the part struck through to be omitted and the part in italics to be inserted. The heading gives introduction on 30 June 1953 by Mr. Hickenlooper with seven co-sponsors, reference to the Committee on Foreign Relations, and report on 18 July 1953.

The resolution would establish a Commission on International Telecommunications. Its recitals rest on the overseas information program and the President's State of the Union message of 2 February 1953. They also rest on the special subcommittee report filed 15 June 1953 on the feasibility of vast television networks. Operative sections in the pages shown cover agency help on a reimbursable basis. They also cover experts and consultants at not over seventy five dollars per day for each individual. Reimbursement, without regard to other law, of travel and subsistence for staff, experts, and consultants on commission work is provided.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200020053-2:
Clean copy of S.J. Res. 96 as introduced in the Senate on 30 June 1953, without report markings, in the 83rd Congress, first session. Mr. Hickenlooper introduced it for himself and Mr. Knowland, Mr. Wiley, Mr. Mundt, Mr. Fulbright, Mr. Green, Mr. Gillette, and Mr. Hill, and it was read twice and sent to the Committee on Foreign Relations.

The title is to strengthen the foreign relations of the United States by establishing a Commission on International Telecommunications. Recitals quote the President's State of the Union message of 2 February 1953. They also quote the special subcommittee report filed 15 June 1953 suggesting a commission to study the present status and potentialities of the international use of all forms of telecommunications. Membership terms provide that executive branch members keep their government pay while serving, with travel reimbursed, and private life members receive not over seventy five dollars per day.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200050014-2:
Memorandum for the Director dated 10 December 1954, subject Congressional Lunches, 1955, recommends that the lunch program begun the year before be re-instituted after the 84th Congress convenes in January. A tentative schedule for January and February 1955 follows, with a note on each guest.

First, for 10 January 1955, are Chairman James P. Richards of South Carolina. With him is Congressman John M. Vorys of Ohio, of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, then on a world trip with emphasis on the Far East. Richards had had no Agency briefing and Vorys very little, and a debriefing could follow lunch. The memo notes Richards had introduced a Joint Committee on Central Intelligence bill in the 83rd Congress, largely from friendship for Senator Mansfield. Later dates name Senator Russell, Senator Hayden, Senator Knowland for 21 February, and Senator Walter F. George for 28 February 1955.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200100027-2:
Foreign Service despatch from the Embassy at Manila, dated 27 November 1956, reports the visit of CODEL-IPU on 11 to 12 and 23 to 25 November. The Inter-Parliamentary Union delegation arrived in Manila on two military aircraft at about 5:00 on 11 November, and the party is listed in full, with spouses.

Senators named include Gordon Allott, Frank A. Barrett, Albert Gore, and A. S. Mike Monroney, and congressmen include Henry O. Talle, chairman of the group, Hale Boggs, and W. R. Poage, with Congresswoman Katharine St. George. Staff, a group physician, and escort officers complete the list. Later lines describe a call on the President of the Philippines, then a drive toward Tagaytay to see the countryside and the view of Lake Taal, and a luncheon.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200100045-2:
Despatch from the American Embassy at Taipei reports the visit of Senator Bourke B. Hickenlooper of Iowa to Taiwan. The Senator, accompanied by Mr. Francis R. Valeo of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, arrived at Taipei at 4:45 p.m. on Sunday 5 August 1956 and was met by the Ambassador and mission officers. The visit was part of a study tour on United States relations with Far Eastern countries and overseas Chinese allegiance.

The schedule was kept purposely light under instructions sent 27 July. After an informal dinner at the Grand Hotel, the visitors were briefed Monday morning by chiefs of the principal United States missions in Taiwan on the military and economic aid programs. They then called on the Foreign Minister and the Chairman of the Overseas Affairs Commission. The Senator departed for Tokyo on Wednesday, and a schedule and guest list are enclosed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200100054-2:
Joint ICA and State message, marked unclassified, announces the trip to Europe of Representative A. L. Miller of Nebraska and his wife. Posts addressed include Ankara, Athens, Casablanca, Florence, Genoa, Istanbul, Madrid, Milan, Naples, Nice, Palermo, Tripoli, and Turin, and posts are asked to meet the party, expedite customs, and arrange hotels.

Miller, ranking minority member of the House Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs, would be in Europe and the Near East during November and December. He would study irrigation and reclamation matters, especially works built with United States funds, visiting several power stations. He was authorised to use local currencies in the Congressional Travel Account for official expenses, and hotel confirmations were to reach him before departure. Project descriptions follow, including in Turkey the Sariyar Dam and Power Plant on the Sakarya River, with initial capacity stated and transmission lines to Istanbul and Ankara.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100010002-2:
Printed bill S. 3897, Calendar number 2286, Report number 2265, was introduced in the Senate on 21 May 1956 by Mr. Kennedy for himself and thirty other senators, and reported by him without amendment on 19 June 1956, in the 84th Congress, second session. Its title is to improve governmental budgeting and accounting methods and procedures, and for other purposes.

Section 1 amends section 201 of the Budget and Accounting Act, 1921, by renumbering and adding new matter, and a later passage amends section 216 of that Act. New subsections would require that requests of departments and establishments for appropriations be developed from cost based budgets, in such manner and at such times as the President determines. The bill text is printed in full, with line numbers, amendments shown by the changes to the 1921 Act's structure, and sections running on through the budgeting and accounting scheme.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100560002-2:
