Printed bill H.R. 9429, Report number 1805, Union Calendar number 631, was introduced in the House on 20 February 1956 by Mr. Kilday, sent to the Committee on Armed Services, and reported with an amendment on 22 February 1956. Its title is to provide medical care for dependents of members of the uniformed services, and for other purposes.

Title I, section 101, declares the purpose to be an improved and uniform program of medical care for dependents of members of the uniformed services. Congress calls such a program sound public policy and a factor in high morale throughout the services. A plan section lets the Secretary arrange care under insurance, medical service, or health plans. Covered care includes hospitalization in semiprivate accommodations for up to three hundred sixty five days per admission, with necessary services and supplies, and medical and surgical care.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100560020-2:
Printed bill H.R. 7792 was introduced in the House on 1 August 1955 by Mr. Vinson and sent to the Committee on Armed Services. Section 1 names it the Armed Forces Dependents Medical Care Act of 1955. Its title is to provide medical care for dependents of members of the Armed Forces of the United States.

Section 2 declares the purpose to be a uniform program of medical care for such dependents. Congress states that a uniform program is sound public policy and an important factor in morale. It assures personnel at home and overseas that their dependents' medical care is provided for by the Department of Defense. Section 3 authorizes care for dependents, and later sections address hardship cases. Definitions in section 7 cover a member of the Armed Forces, including reservists on extended active duty over ninety days, but not persons on duty for training only.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200010001-2:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel, dated April 1956 and marked as reviewed by the Office of General Counsel, comments on H.R. 2639, a bill to amend the Classification Act of 1949 so as to authorize longevity step increases for officers and employees in grades above grade 15 of the General Schedule.

The memorandum notes the bill would amend section 703 of the Classification Act, from which the Agency is specifically exempted. It concludes that no further action by the Legislative Counsel's office is required. If the proposal were enacted, however, adoption of the amended provision by the Agency is recommended, so its employees receive at least comparable benefits to those in the classified service. The notice of pending legislation form and the bill print are attached in the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200100001-2:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel, through the Deputy Director (Support), dated 16 May 1958, comments on S. 2948, a bill to provide preference in government employment for persons who incur permanent disabilities while serving as civilian employees of the Government.

The memorandum explains the bill would give preference to former staff with lasting physical disabilities incurred in the line of duty, apparently by granting five points to earned ratings. It notes the bill is not an amendment to an existing act and its coverage is very broad. On the merits, the memorandum argues such a preference would limit the Agency's flexibility and efficiency in using personnel. It would tend to shrink the pool of staff qualified and available for overseas service. The Agency wishes to place its own disabled staff in sedentary work. The bill print, referred to the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service, is attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200290001-2:
Letter dated 8 April 1955 to Mr. Roger W. Jones at the Bureau of the Budget refers back to a letter of 11 January 1955. The letter concerned the Budget Bureau's referral of 10 December 1954 of a draft bill to provide leave of absence for officers and employees stationed outside the United States.

The letter states that the Agency does not wish to include a repeal of its own statutory home leave provisions in the proposed new government leave statute, as first requested. Such a repealer would require amending section 5(a)(1) of the Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949, better placed in a separate Agency bill. Changes in the draft listed in the file include the same leave benefits for persons recruited from Territories or possessions. They also include removal of the forty five day maximum accumulation for overseas staff, giving a uniform thirty day limit.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200470001-2:
A CIA legislative file on H.R. 6277 deals with storage of household goods for military personnel on permanent change of station. The bill, introduced by Mr. Vinson on 16 May 1955, would amend subsection 303(c) of the Career Compensation Act of 1949. The Director of Logistics comments that it applies specifically to the military and so reaches personnel detailed to CIA, not civilians.

The comments compare the bill with existing cover. Public Law 110 allows ninety days' storage tied to a move outside the United States and permanent storage only for people assigned to emergency areas. Public Law 600 allows sixty days for moves within the country. Logistics flags an inequity: staff sent to ordinary overseas posts must pay storage themselves, and it recalls an earlier recommendation to allow permanent storage worldwide.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100010078-2:
Senate Report No. 379, dated 26 June 1947, reports S. 1350 favourably. It comes from the Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments. The bill covers relief for accounting officers and other disbursing staff. Such staff can be liable for loss of government funds, vouchers, records, or papers. The Treasury Secretary had asked for the law.

The report calls the relief fair. It covers only losses clearly beyond the liable person's control. At the time, relief took a special act of Congress. Or the person had to sue in the Court of Claims at his own cost. Both routes were slow and dear. The committee widened the bill to cover secondary as well as primary duty. It also gave the final decision to the Comptroller General, not the Treasury Secretary.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100040011-2:
A report of the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee, kept in CIA files, investigates the episode of the Russian seamen. Five seamen who had sought asylum in the United States redefected and returned to the Soviet Union. The subcommittee, suspecting Soviet activity in the United States had set the return in motion, held a fifteen-day inquiry and reached unanimous findings, conclusions, and recommendations.

The facts begin with the Soviet tanker Tuapse, seized on 23 June 1954 while carrying jet fuel to Red China and taken to Formosa with a crew of 49. Of the crew, 29 went back to the Soviet Union through French diplomatic efforts and 20 stayed. Nine came to the United States in October 1955 on parole; three found work near Washington and six in New York, earning roughly $50 or $60 a week.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100340009-2:
An office memorandum of February 1953 from Lawrence R. Houston gives a legal opinion on Senate Resolution 19 of the 83rd Congress, passed by the Senate on 9 January 1953. The question was what legal force it carries. It was a Senate resolution only, not a joint resolution, with no sign of being sent to the House.

The opinion answers that it has no compulsive legal effect on an agency that refuses to supply the information requested. It rests on the presentment clause and a long line of Attorneys General opinions: a separate resolution of one House, outside its own parliamentary business, cannot constrain the President or department heads. A joint resolution passed by both Houses and approved by the President, by contrast, has the force of a statute. The memo leaves the politics of refusal aside.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200090006-2:
A CIA memorandum takes up relief in personal hardship cases. It went to SSA-DD/S. The Agency's inability to provide some benefits had caused serious hardship to staff and dependents. The memo was asked to outline the reasons and suggest solutions. Five missing benefits head the list. They are travel of dependents for hospital care, and medical care for dependents overseas. They include return home on critical illness or death of parents, and medical checks for dependents before and after overseas posts.

The memo quotes General Counsel opinion 52-3 for the governing rule. Staff are reimbursed only for costs any government employee would be reimbursed for. An exception applies where the Agency's own operational or security needs force the cost. On the first problem, the memo finds no authority to pay for dependents' hospital travel. But military transport is sometimes available where staff are stationed, and it should be used.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200350098-2:
A CIA legal memorandum of 18 August 1954 answers questions on leave for contract personnel. It went to the Chief of the Special Contracting, Allowances and Processing Staff. The questions concern sick and annual leave for contract agents and contract employees. A sample contract clause is quoted. It grants leave equal to that of CIA employees, under the same rules, at approved times and places.

The opinion draws a sharp line. A true independent contractor is not entitled to statutory leave. He is not an officer or employee of the federal government. Leave written into his contract is a contract benefit only. Contract employees, as defined in section 14.8 of the Confidential Funds Regulations, stand differently. They are employees for leave purposes. They get statutory leave whatever their contracts say. A clause excluding leave would have no legal effect for them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300010067-2:
Minutes record the third meeting of the Working Group on Career Benefits. It sat on 1 November 1951 at 3:30 p.m. The group belonged to the CIA Career Service Committee. Members came from the General Counsel's office, Policy Coordination, Special Operations, Communications, and Personnel. Names are redacted. The second meeting's minutes were approved, with one point clarified.

That point concerned hazardous duty benefits. The agenda spoke of higher base salary for service with unusual hardship and hazard. The group agreed the aim was higher base compensation. But it should not rest on a higher civil service grade. The group also settled its scope. It would weigh the tangible side of career benefits first. Some intangible aspects would still need attention. For hazardous duty, members agreed to use the military services' pay system as the base for study. The talk turns to jump pay, flight pay, submarine duty, and demolition work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300230036-2:
A small CIA file of October 1954 handles a complaint forwarded by General William J. Donovan. Donovan wrote on 4 October 1954. He enclosed a letter from a man whose name is redacted. The man was working in Cambodia. His complaint concerned difficulties from his wartime OSS service. He feared he could not get a further clearance for duties with the Department of State in Washington. Donovan asked that the complaint reach Mr. Dulles.

The Acting General Counsel replied the same week. The matter would be looked into at once. It would also be brought to Dulles's attention. A second memorandum, of 12 October, goes to the Director of Security. It passes on the letter and asks for the available information. It also asks for suggestions on handling the matter. Donovan had told the man to see Mr. Houston first.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100140002-2:
A CIA memorandum of 26 September 1955 announces area training development. It went to the Deputy Directors for Intelligence, Plans, and Support. The Language and External Training School is building a series of area training courses. They are meant to sharpen how intelligence personnel understand the foreign areas tied to their missions. Recent reports on intelligence activities had shown the need.

Each office is asked to name liaison officers for an ad hoc advisory committee. Mature area specialists are wanted, men drawn to advanced academic specialization. Working papers are attached for discussion. A course outline follows. It opens with an introduction to the people, their culture, and their environment. It covers the economic structure: manufacturing, agriculture, transportation, trade, and national accounts. Current political, economic, and social conditions follow. The structure of government and its policies close the survey.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030028-2:
A CIA letter of 13 January 1956 reports the Agency's manpower actions to House committee counsel. It went to Frederick C. Belen, Chief Counsel of the Post Office and Civil Service Committee. It follows a letter of 14 October 1955 from Chairman Murray to Mr. Dulles, and Dulles's interim reply of 18 November 1955. The letter sums up steps taken and planned. The aim is the most effective use of manpower, with reductions wherever they cost no efficiency.

The letter sets the problem in the Agency's recent history. U.S. intelligence ran at a reduced pace after World War II. The outbreak of hostilities in Korea forced rapid expansion. Growth was swift in both functions and personnel. The letter then turns to the survey questions put to components. They ask what functions duplicate those of other agencies. They ask what savings would follow if such functions were discontinued.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030055-2:
A letter from the Director of Central Intelligence answers a congressional inquiry on manpower. It went to James C. Davis, chairman of the Sub-Committee on Manpower Utilization. It replies to his letter of 17 May 1956 and follows an earlier letter of 9 February 1956. The Agency's survey covered savings from 23 separate considerations. Five concern internal duplication. Four concern duplication against another agency.

Two items cover services performed for another agency. Four might be transferred to one. Five are of common concern in the intelligence community. Three deal with combining like functions. Each part went back to the office concerned for conclusions. One lengthy study found eliminations operationally impossible, given a project's sensitive nature. Progress elsewhere includes unfilled positions under a curtailment ceiling. One large overseas installation has closed. Another is being cut down.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100040018-2:
A CIA paper sets out the functions of the Office of National Estimates. Its primary mission produces national estimates. Byproducts include post-mortem reviews of intelligence deficiencies in NIEs. Studies of the validity of estimates are also listed. Other functions cover special memoranda for the DCI and staff support to Agency representatives. Those representatives serve on the NSC, the NSC Planning Board, and the OCB.

The office also provides the IAC Secretariat. It gives estimative guidance to other components. On-duty strength on 31 October 1955 mixed professionals, one administrative staffer, and 22 clericals. The total cannot be split by function. Each of the office's three components touches every function. A ten percent cut would be extremely hard to place. The functions interlock, and the primary ones derive from duties to the IAC. They could not be reduced unilaterally.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100040027-2:
A CIA memo of 25 November 1955 reports manpower use in the Office of Central Reference. It went from the Assistant Director, Central Reference, to the Deputy Director, Intelligence. On-duty figures as of 31 October 1955 are heavily redacted. About some persons sit in an uncleared pool. They contribute nothing to OCR's work and are excluded from the counts that follow. The study covers only those actually carrying the load.

OCR's major functions are seven, each run by a separate division. Ranking them by priority is doubtful; all are essential to the Agency's mission. A sharp cut should fall on each division rather than abolish any one. Tab A gives studies of each division's functions. Small savings are itemized. A support operation for the DD/P might have to be given up.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100040036-2:
A CIA survey of manpower use in ORR is dated 25 November 1955. It went to the Deputy Director/Intelligence. ORR's functions fall in three groups. The first is intelligence support answering priority demands of CIA components, the IAC, the NSC, and others. The second is coordination delegated to ORR by direction. The third is research and specialized services held as common concern.

All present functions must continue, the office holds, if it is to meet its basic duties. Curtailment inside activities is the only sign of priority available. Strength figures use on-duty staff as of 31 October 1955, mostly in man-years. Background research and editing are pro-rated to direct support. A table lists activities with curtailment losses. One cut ends the ORR records management program. Duplication with Air Force economic research is noted, much reduced through the EIC.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100010062-2:
A progress report covers the Geographic Area, ORR, for March 1957. It was a relatively quiet month. Effort went to coordination on Arctic-Antarctic IGY work, unconventional warfare, map procurement, and photographic intelligence. Much research done in March will appear as production in April. The Cartography Division completed 37 maps and charts. Thirty-five went to CIA and two to State.

Requests for the month numbered 56. The Map Library Division received 3,338 maps and 703 related publications from foreign sources. It sent out 19,772 map sheets in answer to 1,388 requests. The request count set a new all-time high for the division. The Photo Intelligence Division completed five photographic intelligence memoranda. Two staff members entered on duty during the month. One officer attended the Special Forces School at Fort Bragg on military duty.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100400005-2:
A coordination report of May 1957 surveys intelligence work across the government. Its contents divide into tabs. Tab A covers economic intelligence. Tab C covers geographic intelligence. Tab D covers photographic intelligence. Each tab reviews facilities, accomplishments, and coordination problems. The economic section traces the coordinating mechanism back to NSC Action 202. In May 1951 CIA completed a survey of government needs for foreign economic intelligence.

The report describes continuing review of consumer requirements. It covers the quality of intelligence and the production of coordinated work. Collection guidance and dissemination procedures also come under review. Economic reporting from Bloc posts, the report notes, has roughly doubled in four years. Its quality and pertinence have improved markedly. The Economic Intelligence Committee now joins in systematic guidance of collection.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410013-2:
A Cartography Division project status list is dated 1 February 1957. It is organized by branch. The USSR-Satellites Branch leads. Entries give a map number, title, requester, status, due date, classification, and distribution. Many USSR charts are complete for January. They cover crude steel production, the ferrous metal industry, and the Academy of Sciences. Soviet Arctic sheets cover orientation, physical regions, transportation, and polar stations.

Romania entries serve the NIS program. They cover provinces, vegetation zones, forested areas, soil zones, and sawmills. New Lands sheets appear in first revision. Grain acreage for 1954 and New Lands transportation are also listed. A Europe-Africa Branch section follows with its own numbered projects. Requesters include ORR, OSI, the DD/P, and the NIS program.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410022-2:
A Cartography Division project status list is dated 1 November 1957. The USSR-Satellites Branch leads. A plan of Burgas appears for Bulgaria. A Moscow/Fili airframe plant chart runs to four parts. USSR gold exports and trade balance are charted. Trade with selected countries takes six chart numbers. Time zone changes and copper deposits are also listed.

A USSR religion sheet appears in first revision. Areas closed to foreigners are charted for the USSR and for Moscow. Czech industry sheets continue from the prior month. Later Europe-Africa sections carry proof deadlines into December and January. One item is marked urgent for the OCI. Standard base maps for Rumania and Albania appear in revision.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100460009-2:
A CIA memorandum of 4 December 1957 proposes an outline and schedule for NIS Chapter I Annuals. It went from the Chief, Coordination Staff, through the Geography Division to the Chief, Geographic Area. Background cites NIS Committee meetings 253 and 254 and the first Annuals conference of 27 November 1957. A tentative outline guide and first-year schedule had already been forwarded. A Yugoslavia prototype was not yet available.

The comments open on a premise. The idea that NIS Chapters I should replace the OCI Handbooks is unsound, the memo argues. The NIS holds basic intelligence, not current intelligence. Publication lag alone bars its use as a current source. Chapters I take five months or more to produce. The schedule would grow toward 75 Annuals a year by 1964. That means about three Annuals every two weeks, on top of already overloaded producing units.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100490015-2:
Minutes record NIS Committee Meeting No. 249 of 16 July 1957. The committee reviewed Chapter I on NIS 23, Bulgaria. The draft was approved with certain changes. The Task Group was asked to review agency comments. One point was specific. The name Varna should replace Stalin for the port city, if the Board on Geographic Names has accepted it. Otherwise both names appear, Varna in parenthesis.

Revised NIS Contributor Statements were approved with minor changes. An area name change followed. The British Caribbean Federation had been formalized. NIS 81 becomes British Western Atlantic Possessions. NIS 81A is the British Caribbean Federation, and 81B Bermuda and the Bahama Islands. British Honduras and British Guiana stay outside for now. The Navy member circulated a CINCPAC list of areas wanted early for Pacific planning.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000200050030-2:
A U.S. Geological Survey status map shows topographic mapping of the United States in January 1957. The legend explains the sheet. It displays quadrangle maps made by the Geological Survey and other federal agencies. Scales run from 1:24,000 to 1:250,000. Categories mark modern maps, maps needing revision, maps of limited usefulness, and maps needing resurvey. Planimetric maps and work in progress are also shown.

Insets cover areas outside the continental United States. American Samoa is drawn at 1:1,500,000 and Guam at 1:500,000. The Panama Canal Zone appears as well. Sales indexes for each state list the published map names. Further text in the file turns to geodetic error. It distinguishes random operational errors of a missile from systematic geodetic errors. Those arise in connecting launch and target points on the earth's surface.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000200100007-2:
A short divisional report excerpt covers work in support of other components. The Photo Intelligence Division reports first. A memorandum analyzing a large volume of photography was completed for the DD/P. Work continues on the MM-50 camera evaluation and on a guide project. Three topographic map sheets covering a selected drop zone area were prepared and published.

Support to the Office of Training follows. A lecture went to the Basic Intelligence Course. The division's first Basic Photographic Interpretation Course ended in early August. A special course for geographers began, to end 1 October 1957. The second basic course is set for 8 October. Work also began on periodic inspection of the Langley building site for OSI. Administrative and coordination items close the excerpt.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000200100016-2:
A monthly report covers the Photo Intelligence Division for October 1957. Activity stayed at a high level. Most effort went to top priority projects for the DDI, DDP, and DD/S. The division completed 23 reports, memoranda, and working papers. Eighteen papers are in edit and nine in reproduction. Of thirty requirements processed, twenty came from ORR. Branches are working on 133 requirements.

Much work was joint, with Navy and Army photo intelligence teams. The division keeps testing new instruments for exploiting photographic materials. The third Basic Photographic Interpretation Course began on 8 October. The Special Projects Branch finished a study comparing filter effects and sun angle. The Geographic Branch completed fourteen memoranda and working papers. Mensuration, slotted templet work, and controlled mosaics fill much of its effort.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100190020-2:
A frank internal list, headed The Most Common Management Problems Encountered to Date, names the faults supervisors across the Agency were most often seen to make. The first is poor communication up, down, and across. It is blamed on weak use of staff meetings and on misunderstanding of need-to-know limits. Over-strict use of channels at lower levels is blamed as well.

Further items fault personnel management. Follow-up interviews are not held as a routine. The Career Service Program lacks energy. Supervisors get no guidance on the Agency's basic management policy. Unit and individual responsibilities are not clearly defined. The list also notes confusion between dynamic personal leadership and what effective supervision actually requires. It closes by assigning duties to the deputy directors and other senior officials.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100070007-2:
Notes on a Deputy Director (Support) senior staff meeting held on January 9 report decisions of interest to the Director of Training. The Director of Central Intelligence had decided to invite speakers from various offices to his deputies' meeting one morning each week. Each briefing would run no more than fifteen minutes, about ten for the talk and five for discussion, and would normally be given by the office head.

The Deputy Director had canvassed his offices the day before and held a consolidated list of proposed subjects about five pages long. The notes also record the Director's wish that senior supervisors get out among their people and see what is going on, and a discussion of issuing a general information newsletter.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100090005-2:
A tentative analysis titled Some Lessons of the Hungarian Revolution studies the popular uprising against the Communist government in Hungary. The rising ran through October and November 1956. The paper opens with a line from President Eisenhower's second inaugural address. It calls Budapest a symbol of man's yearning to be free. The paper calls the rising the most dramatic blow yet struck against the world Communist movement.

The Agency analysis rejects the official Communist account of the revolt. That account blamed counterrevolution and foreign meddling. The paper warns that Western information is still incomplete and open to conflicting readings. It reaches for deeper causes, including the Soviet system's own strains. It weighs comparisons with Hitler's dictatorship. That was the one totalitarian system the West had been able to study from its start to its end.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100090014-2:
A program for encouraging voluntary development of the Agency's language resources is sent upward. It goes to the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence through the Deputy Director (Support). The covering memorandum explains that the attached paper answers a recent request. The request asked for a plan to provide incentives. Those incentives would stir personal initiative in language study by Agency staff. The sender asks for approval of the principles on which the program rests.

If those are approved, he will take up the legal questions involved in using Agency funds for the purpose. He will also take up the budgetary cost of supporting the program. The attached plan itself sets out the need. It proposes an announced program, open to staff. The program is meant to grow the Agency's stock of language skill from voluntary effort, rather than assigned training alone.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100100003-2:
Information for the Killian Committee report is supplied by the Director of Training in a memorandum dated May 31, addressed to the Special Planning Assistant to the Deputy Director of Support. The material was requested for the DD/S portion of the report. Its first item concerns foreign language proficiency across the Agency.

A Language Development Program, the memorandum reports, was established on February 4, 1957. It rests on a practical point: the Agency cannot halt important work while staff train, so employees must build much of their language skill alongside their daily duties. An affirmative opinion had been obtained from the Comptroller General on paying awards to those who reach and keep a set level of proficiency. Later items turn to training given to foreign liaison services and the limits of the staff available for it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100140027-2:
A critique form asks members of the Foreign Service Inspection Corps to judge the CIA briefing given to them on January 19, 1955, so that future presentations can be improved. Respondents are invited to comment on any or all of the listed points, or to add observations of their own about the whole briefing or any part of it. Completed comments were to go to Raymond Miller, the Chief Inspector.

The form recalls the lecture titles the visitors heard: the organization of the Agency and its overseas activities, foreign intelligence operations, overseas operations, Agency overseas communications, and Agency inspection problems. It is a feedback instrument rather than a report, and it shows the Agency asking an outside audience to grade a recurring briefing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200030019-2:
A proposal dated March 1, 1957, comes from the Director of Training. It is addressed to the chief of the Junior Officer Trainee program office. It would establish a Special Assignment Program as a pilot operation. The new program, run by the JOT office, would take selected candidates. Those candidates do not meet all the standards for junior officer trainees.

The reasoning is about waste. Many JOT applicants have desirable qualities but lack some qualification. They are rejected and often lost to the Agency. Others look acceptable on application, then come out borderline after security investigation. The benefits claimed are practical. The program would give a pool of basically trained people ready for immediate assignment on a crash basis. It would give a closer look at doubtful candidates in action. It would also give a stimulus to competition among trainees.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200100002-2:
The October report of the Committee on Language Development records a committee at work. Its subject is the machinery of the Agency's new language program. Its October 10 meeting covered several items. They included submittals of Form 444c, the language data record, as of September 30. They included the state of proficiency test development and plans for giving the tests. Applications for foreign language achievement awards were covered too.

At a special meeting on October 31 the first award applications were decided. A sum of 725 dollars went to ten of thirteen applicants. Two were found ineligible. A third payment was deferred pending a better check of the facts. The report's running tally claims proficiency in 95 languages. That is an average of 1.9 languages per person reporting. It counts 802 persons reporting from the field. Proficiency tests were in preparation for dozens of languages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200100011-2:
A letter dated March 21, 1957, comes from Alan T. Waterman, Director of the National Science Foundation. It asks Allen W. Dulles, the Director of Central Intelligence, for advice. The Office of Defense Mobilization had made a proposal. The Foundation should extend its register work to cover area and language experts. Its Register of Scientific and Technical Personnel then listed natural scientists and engineers only. Certain related fields were included as well.

Before widening the register, Waterman writes, the Foundation wants to be sure of one thing. A real need must exist for a register of this character. It also wants to learn something of the problems involved. The letter explains how registers are used. They locate people for consulting, part-time work, or appointments. It notes their limits too. The facts come from the people themselves, through forms they fill out.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030018-2:
Weekly Activities Report number 26, dated July 3, 1958, comes from the Acting Chief of the Agency's Language and Area School. It marks a milestone. June 30 saw the completion of the first phase of the Language Development Program. One officer is given great credit for sound and competent work. Written tests in thirty-six languages had been prepared by him or under his supervision. The testing was carried through, slips and misjudgments notwithstanding.

Experience with special crash courses points the other way on method. In the long run, the report concludes, one course is cheaper. It is cheaper to authorize tutorial training for such individuals. Training them inside the school costs more. A French contract instructor's departure closes the week's personnel notes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030027-2:
Weekly Activities Report number 17, dated May 1, 1958, comes from the Chief of the Agency's Language and Area School. It gives pride of place to the monthly roundtable. That month it met at Syracuse. It was co-hosted by the Air Force and Syracuse University. The chief calls it by far the most outstanding meeting in the roundtable's year or so of life. It was also the most significant.

The secret, he writes, was being captives together for twenty-four hours. The setting of hospitality bred professional talk. Other items are smaller. Lectures drew about as many people as the lecture room will conveniently hold. An hour and a quarter was spent in a downtown safe apartment. A student and tutor were briefed there on modern methods of intensive language teaching. A follow-up visit was planned.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300050043-2:
The Registrar's Weekly Activities Report number 1 covers December 26, 1957, to January 7, 1958. Its significant item is set in capitals. Never before in the history of the Agency's Office of Training had there been so much instructional activity. That was in the week beginning January 5, 1958. Resumption of the big Operations Course after the Christmas holidays came in the same week. New classes starting then brought the total to an unprecedented seventy classes. Once, that resumption alone would have been a major undertaking.

A box score breaks the load down by course type. Personal items follow. The office's candidate at the Air War College in Montgomery, Alabama, visited on December 31. His financial accounts were brought up to date. He carried back greetings from another student there.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300110019-2:
Weekly Report number 19 comes from the Assessment and Evaluation Staff. It covers May 7 to 13, 1958. The chief reports an invitation from the American Psychological Association. He was invited to take part in its conference on Graduate Education in Psychology. The conference would be held in Miami from November 29 to December 7, 1958. He has tentatively accepted, subject to the Director's approval. This kind of professional recognition, he argues, helps attract able people to the Agency.

A recruiting follow-up runs the other way. A man who had turned down an offer to join the staff explained his reasons. He wanted more scope for therapy and teaching than the post seemed to offer. He was, however, interested in the Career Reserve. Contact on that program was arranged for him.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400010034-2:
Weekly Report number 46 comes from the Clerical Training faculty. It covers November 18 to 24, 1958. An Agency survey on the present and potential use of Flexowriters was still running. The office in charge had promised the Office of Training a copy of its report. The week's numbers follow. Forty-eight people were in Clerical Induction Training during the week of November 18. Nine of them were entering for the first time. Thirteen people were in Clerical Orientation.

Results of the official Agency tests given by Clerical Induction are reported as well. The file also carries a reflective piece on shorthand teaching. It asks how short a shorthand course can be. It weighs the college graduates who take the stenographic route. They enter a career they feel their liberal arts degrees should have opened directly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400060020-2:
Weekly Activities Report number 12 comes from the Agency's Instructional Services Branch. It covers March 26 to April 8, 1958, and is devoted to film production. The Logistics Film was nearly done. Extra shooting took place on April 1 and 2. About a page of changed narration remained for Mr. Garrison to record. Completion was hoped for by the end of April.

The Secret Writing Film had hit a snag. The contractor delivered the answer print. It was screened in the branch auditorium. The print was rejected and sent back. Other projects moved on paper. Two personal security films for senior audiences had been approved in draft. Suggestions were given for final scripting. Writing continued on the DDI film about the intelligence process.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000200050004-2:
A memorandum for the record reports a survey of the Assessment and Evaluation Staff of the Agency's Office of Training. The surveyors met the staff's chief and branch heads. They went over functions, tables of organization, manpower, workloads, and overtime. Functional statements for the staff had been written. They carried the chief's concurrence. A proposed table of organization had been submitted on March 26, 1954. It came with full job descriptions and an activities statement.

That proposal called for thirty-eight positions. They ran from the chief and deputy down through staff psychologists and clerks. The survey works out the arithmetic of the assessment load. It uses a planning factor of eighty assessments a year for each senior psychologist. It provides one junior psychologist for every two seniors. The factor is built up from the working weeks in a year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000200060021-2:
A memorandum dated September 20, 1954, summarizes the Army Psychological Warfare Officers Course. It uses course material borrowed from the Office of Training library. The course forms part of the Psychological Warfare School. The Army established that school at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. It is an eight-week, full-time course of 352 hours. The writer works through its syllabus. He judges its value for the Agency's own teaching.

His verdict is striking. As far as the material on hand allows him to tell, the Army course is infinitely more thorough. It beats the Agency's own counterpart course. He notes that it ranges beyond the logical limits of Army psychological warfare operations. It reaches into black propaganda and international political organizations. Army tasks in the field, by contrast, are mostly tactical. They do not involve running foreign agents.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400120007-2:
An organization chart of the Office of Training is paired with the office's mission and functions. They are stated in the Agency regulation of January 18, 1954. The Director of Training is charged with five tasks. He is to develop and direct Agency training programs. He is to review the training programs of the other offices. He is to represent the Director on training subjects. He is to share in making Career Service Board policy. He is to determine the Agency's needs for training facilities in the United States.

The functions that follow run from teaching to housekeeping. They include administrative service to the office's own headquarters. That service covers personnel, budget, transportation, and records. They include review of proposed Agency regulations for the office's concurrence. They include compliance with the Agency's security, records management, and emergency evacuation programs. The Junior Officer Trainee Program's duties are set out in the same detail.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100030002-2:
A Management Staff survey report covers the Agency Finance Division's Special Support Staff. It is dated March 1950. It ends in a memorandum of May 1, 1950. That memorandum resubmits the division's table of organization to the Director. Its purpose was establishing position grades. The covering note describes how such questions were settled. A survey by the Management Office determined workload and procedures. Position requirements and grades were built from that survey.

The division's cash work is described in detail. It covers preparation of vouchers and disbursement from the cashier fund. It covers keeping the account, and helping in its examination. Tentative recommendations would move one function. The cash payment function and its account would go to the Disbursing Officer. That move was proposed in the Finance Division's new organization. The recommendations would otherwise leave the table of organization unchanged.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100040001-2:
A management study of the Finance Division in the Office of the Comptroller is dated August 22, 1955. It states its problem at the top. The team was to examine the division's structure, staffing pattern, functions, and procedures. It was to recommend changes. Those changes would render better financial support to the covert components of the Agency. The facts begin with stability. The structure and table of organization then in force had been approved in October 1953. No major changes had followed since.

The findings are a catalogue of paper failures. Extension contracts on contract employees and agents were not always received. Neither were contract cancellation actions. Many financial reports and dispatches were delayed in the area divisions. They did not reach the Finance Division promptly. Financial documents on their way there repeatedly became separated from their companions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100120002-2:
Overtime in the Agency's Office of Training is taken up in a memorandum. The memo makes fiscal 1957 the base year. The office's overtime costs for that year are stated at 116,695.23 dollars. The paper works forward from that base. The microfilm and related lines provide the extended overtime services. They are costed in detail. Specified savings are estimated for fiscal 1958 and fiscal 1959, as tighter rules take hold. Unit detail follows. It runs down to the first week of a terminal course and a training school's hours.

The scan is heavily garbled. Many of the hour counts cannot be read with confidence. The memorandum's purpose is plain, though. It shows where training overtime was being spent. It shows what could be saved by cutting it back over the two years ahead.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100160008-2:
The Comptroller answers a Management Staff study of his own Agency Program Analysis Staff. He agrees with most of it. He accepts the study's analysis of the staff's mission. He accepts its findings on function, procedure, and staffing needs. He calls the work thorough. It is, he says, a fair presentation of the staff's activity, its difficulties, and its accomplishments to date. Its conclusions match a realistic appraisal of the situation.

His comments then take the recommendations in order. The vacant position on the table of organization has been filled. The discussion underneath is candid about numbers. The staff's ceiling allows six positions. It had been functioning for some time with five people. One of them was on detail from the Audit Staff. The clerk-typist post stood vacant.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100210011-2:
A survey of Agency shipping and procurement procedures follows a shipment's paper from branch to branch. The operating branch receives the requisition and cargo documents. It passes a copy to the Shipping Branch, which sets up a master letter. A letter center supplies the markings for most shipments. It works from its own instructions, without consulting the Shipping Branch. Shipping documents move in colored copies. They are white when material goes from depot to port. They are pink on another leg of the journey.

The survey's chief recommendation is consolidation. Two things would be fused into a single traffic branch. They are the fraction and control functions, and the two sets of files kept for shipping and control purposes. Their duplicate filing labor would disappear. The survey also notes one gap. Future tonnage was not being projected against the shipment sources available.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100220001-2:
A Management Staff study dated June 30, 1954, reviews the organization and staffing of the Agency's Logistics Office for the Deputy Director (Administration). Operating experience since the office's structure and table of organization were set, plus the need to fix the staffing its mission truly requires, drive the review. Its aims are to realign certain staff functions and refine the structure of the operating divisions, and to set a realistic staffing pattern tied to actual workload.

That pattern would test the present personnel ceiling: either prove it adequate or justify changing it. The study's redistribution of the ceiling identifies an increase of nine positions. Three further proposals for added staff are expressly left out, since their workload problems lay outside the Logistics Office's control and arose only after the classification work was done.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100220010-2:
A staff paper on the Supply Division of the Logistics Office lists five changes in the proposed organization. The Facilities Staff changes position and name, becoming the Storage Operations Branch. It holds control over the receipt, storage, issue, and stock checks of supplies, ordnance material excepted. Certain staff elements rise to branch level. Current requirements work moves out of the Coordination and Requirements Staff. A Control Staff is established. The warehouse units in the departmental area are drawn together.

Above the warehouses sits a system-wide duty: watching the Agency supply system itself. The division corrects its faults and improves it. It tests how well the system works through close liaison with the operating elements it serves. Visits render expert help wherever the system runs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300030001-2:
A very large bound set opens with a short House committee letter dated 1 September 1959, sending a friend the committee report on S. 2162 and the hearings on health benefits for federal employees. The writer notes that the House passed the bill that day and that the reader had taken part in the hearings. The letter acts as a cover for the printed volumes that follow, and no personal name is legible in the signature block shown.

The hearings themselves ran before the House Post Office and Civil Service Committee in July and August 1959, over many sitting days. They cover S. 2162 and similar bills to build a health benefit program for government employees. Deep in the volume, plan terms list what is excluded, such as tuberculosis, alcoholism, dental care, and conditions covered by workers' compensation. Polio treatment limits are also spelled out.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300190022-2:
A memorandum dated 30 December 1958, sent to the Director of Central Intelligence for information only, reports groundwork for Senate Foreign Relations Committee briefings. William B. Macomber, Jr., of the State Department told the Agency of an exchange between Senator Theodore Francis Green and President Eisenhower. Green had asked for briefings from Secretary Dulles, the Defense Department, CIA, and executive branch economic experts, and the President agreed.

Secretary Dulles was named to coordinate the round, and appearances were to fall on successive days, with 15 January 1959 as the target, though Macomber thought that early. The memo also flags a possible clash with Senator Hubert Humphrey's request for a CIA appearance before the Senate Subcommittee on Disarmament. State planned to send other officials there, and agency heads would not appear for that panel.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300210001-2:
A roster of the House Appropriations Committee Defense Subcommittee heads a memorandum for the record dated 3 February 1959. George H. Mahon of Texas chairs the subcommittee, and members from both parties are listed, including Harry R. Sheppard, Robert L. F. Sikes, Daniel J. Flood, and Gerald R. Ford, Jr. The memo then records a briefing by the Director of Central Intelligence before that subcommittee on 2 and 3 February 1959.

The Director, with Mr. Amory and Mr. Warner, sat for two hours in the morning and two in the afternoon on the second day, after a shorter first session. One note says a copy of material would be kept in the Agency without the subcommittee's knowledge. Follow-up requests include a briefing for Mr. Sikes comparing Russian and American defense values, and information Mr. Flood wanted on arms seizures and caches in Panama.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100020079-2:
A report on war planning was sent to the Deputy Assistant Director for Geographic Research after a planning meeting on 25 August 1958. It states that the Geographic Research Area's war tasks were already set. Planners had fixed key wartime duties, the methods and equipment needed, the agencies and parts the area would work with, and a mobilization plan. The relocation center had been stocked with geographic reference material and cartographic equipment for emergency operations.

A list of planning papers follows, including an intelligence annex to a global war plan dated October 1955 and later wartime service memos. Gaps remain, the report warns. Office plans differ from each other in scope, policy, and content. Area plans do not fully match those of the plans directorate on agreed roles. The writer also lacked firm word on outside agency plans.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100090009-2:
General background information on the iron and steel industry explains what the ferrous metals field covers. Beyond iron and steel output itself, the field includes mining and preparing the raw and alloying materials used in production. Chief raw materials are iron ore, manganese ore, metallurgical coke, and limestone. Alloying materials include ores of chromium, cobalt, molybdenum, nickel, tungsten, titanium, and vanadium, among others named.

A table matches products to facility types. It lists open pit and underground mines for ores, crushing and enriching plants for concentrates, and smelters and furnaces for ferroalloys. Coke ovens for coke complete the table. Later pages turn to investment shares, noting a planned shift toward electric power at the expense of engineering and steel industries. Heavy industry takes about ninety percent of industrial investment under a three year plan.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100180009-2:
A memorandum dated 29 September 1958 sends in the Fourth Semi-Annual Report of the Ad Hoc Committee on Exchanges, signed by its chairman on 26 September. The committee was set up by Intelligence Advisory Committee action on 28 February 1956 to gain the most intelligence value from East-West delegation exchanges. A later expansion added release of materiel to its field, and paper IAC-D-103 served as its guide and terms of reference.

The report describes the committee's organization and its work across the half year. One duty was helping carry out exchanges, a long and tangled process where plant visits were involved, with proposals and counter-proposals to juggle. Another passage notes that agencies had let contractors or consultants make private proposals to the Soviets, usually through the State Department, and that better coordination was still needed on that front.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100180018-2:
A partial listing of exchange programs between the United States and the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe forms an appendix. It was prepared for a meeting of an advisory committee of college and university presidents on 24 March 1958. Programs are sorted into academic year and short-term grants, summer projects apart. Sponsors are grouped as United States and international organizations and agencies, universities and colleges, and foreign governments. Entries pair each sponsor with its program or grant.

The American Council of Learned Societies, a refugee service commission, the Carnegie Corporation, and the Ford Foundation appear on the opening page. Farther in, proposed exchanges grow concrete. One passage outlines matching delegations of ten persons each, visiting for three to four weeks. They would be made up of specialists in designing and building pipe-rolling mills and in producing pipe, with Soviet visits to named American plants.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100180036-2:
Minutes of the Intelligence Advisory Committee's Ad Hoc Committee on Exchanges record a meeting on 25 March 1958, with a new chairman presiding in place of the retiring one. Members listed come from State, the Army, the Air Force side, the Joint Staff side, the information agency, and the Atomic Energy Commission. Extra guests were present for talks on an oil-shale exchange and on census observers. CIA also sat at the table.

The chairman reported State's thanks for committee support on exchange matters. He also passed on a point from the Director: the intelligence community had a great stake in the exchange program and must stay close to it. Later business returns to an agricultural exchange, where Soviet reluctance to give meaningful statistics had not changed the first assessment. Continued refusal, though, might force a fresh look at the whole matter.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000200020005-2:
Paper CFEP 568, in the version marked 568/2, sets foreign economic policy recommendations for Africa south of the Sahara. Agriculture opens the paper. Most Africans live by farming, small-scale subsistence farming is the rule, and many economies rest on one crop for most foreign exchange earnings. Land tenure that does not recognize individual ownership is named as a brake on growth.

Recommendations follow each heading in direct form. For farming, the United States should expand technical help as a priority, aimed at higher output and more varied crops, and should not withhold help over crop choices. Later sections argue that, as colonies move toward independence, free world states should add economic and technical help, best given in a coordinated way. The paper is a policy brief for aid as an instrument in a changing region.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00423a000100020007-2:
Tab A, dated 18 August 1954, sets an Inspection and Review analysis beside the plans directorate administration's own statement on a manpower survey of the Far East Division. The two columns argue point by point. The administration side held that, with one major exception, the survey's statements were generally statements of fact. The exception was a claim that the division had passed its total personnel ceiling. On that point, the analysis agrees the claim was wrong.

As of 30 June 1954, filled civilian positions sat within the ceiling, and extra staff on projects were not chargeable to it. Those project staff had apparently been counted in reaching the survey's figure. A second dispute concerns inferences drawn without a detailed basis. Later items defend reported assignment practices, including the constant need for temporary duty details of many kinds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00423a000100080001-2:
A survey report with names and places removed by sanitization gives findings on travel paperwork in an unnamed division. One finding urges that the division be told it must give essential, accurate information before cases go to the travel side, and that staff be kept informed of their clearance standing. Where a division asked for an unwarranted number of travel orders, administrative action should follow to cut the number down.

Payroll checks are also covered. Action had been taken to sweep a division payroll to test whether staff employees were charged properly. Shipment requests raised hard problems in estimating and settling obligations, a point the Logistics transportation side also confirmed. A workload finding says one hundred sixty-nine hours a month went to preparing travel vouchers in one section, work the report says should stop and move to the Central Processing Branch.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00442a000100060039-2:
Weekly Activities Report No. 15 from the Chief, Field Training, dated 20 April 1959, covers 13 to 17 April 1959. The first item is personal. After a call on 16 April, the chief reassured a named instructor of the high professional esteem in which the Director of Training and his own chief, Colonel Edwards, held him. Faults found, the instructor was told, may have reflected the choice of students and the choices made above him rather than any failing of his own.

The man was grateful, and a settled future improved his morale. Later items cover talks on a possible reorientation of a presentation, with a plan judged the most logical and profitable way to present the material. A staff change is also noted: one man took over physical training and unarmed combat instruction from another who had handled it before enrolling in a course himself.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00463a000100010013-2:
Public Law 85-468 prints H.R. 10589, an appropriations act dated 25 June 1958 for the Executive Office of the President and sundry general government agencies. The money covers the fiscal year ending 30 June 1959 and comes out of Treasury funds not otherwise appropriated. Title I opens with the President's compensation, set at 150,000 dollars including a 50,000 dollar yearly expense allowance under a 1949 act. The White House Office follows, with salaries and expenses and a capped sum for outside services under a 1946 act.

Pages run on through the small boards and funds of general government. One late passage covers a War Claims Act fund, not available for obligation after June 1959. It also covers the Subversive Activities Control Board, with citizenship requirements, affidavit, and penalty notes beside its salaries and expenses line. Statute citations fill the margins throughout.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000100240025-2:
A memorandum dated 18 June 1954, numbered EIC-D-71(a), reports an Economic Intelligence Committee review of Joint Intelligence Committee paper JIC 635/1, on the capabilities of Chinese Communist railroads, roads, and inland waterways. The parent committee had ordered the review at a meeting on 26 May 1953. The JIC paper was finished that August and sent over for review the same month.

After long discussion, the committee's Transportation Subcommittee finished its review in January 1954 and restudied the subject. Its conclusions, approved by member agency representatives, agreed in general with the JIC figures for roads and inland waterways. Railroad capability, the largest part of the paper, remained in dispute. The memo calls for further joint study as a priority once enough new information arrives to settle the facts under the main points of difference, and for greater collection effort.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200030045-2:
Attachment B to a Top Secret paper sets coordinated intelligence assumptions for a Net Evaluation Subcommittee exercise covering 1958-1959. The problem is narrow: to give that subcommittee agreed assumptions on certain Soviet military capabilities and American warning capability in mid-1962, following an outline the subcommittee itself supplied. The subcommittee needs quite specific numerical projections for its special-purpose work.

The authors warn that agency views were in places compromised to meet that need. Numbers were also projected in fields where present knowledge might not justify their use in an estimate for general circulation. Later assumptions deal with bomber readiness: about eighty-five percent of the long-range bomber and tanker force could be serviceable for operations after a five-day stand-down if Soviet planners chose maximum-scale attacks. Jet medium bombers of tactical and naval aviation are covered by the same factors.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200040008-2:
Public Law 703 of the Eighty-third Congress prints H.R. 9757, the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, which rewrites the Atomic Energy Act of 1946 in full. A long table of contents opens the volume, chapter by chapter. It covers declaration, findings, and purpose, then definitions. Organization of the Atomic Energy Commission follows, with its members, office, general manager, divisions, and advisory and military liaison committees. Research, production, and further subjects come after.

The body runs to well over one hundred pages of statute. A mid-volume chapter on control of information states the Commission's policy: to control the spread and declassification of Restricted Data so as to protect the common defense and security. Chapters on research assistance, Commission research, and research for others appear early. The file holds the whole act as enacted, a reference text rather than a summary or a report.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200050025-2:
An Army memorandum from the Office of the Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, dated 15 December 1954, proposes amendments to a draft special budget analysis for fiscal 1956. The memo goes to the Chairman of the Intelligence Advisory Committee and refers to paper IAC-D-77. Each amendment is given by page and paragraph, in delete-and-substitute form, so the draft could be changed without a fresh draft.

One substitute sentence covers joint arrangements for effective use of a wide range of publications and materials. Another states that agency requests meet only minimum essential needs, and that staff shortages still hamper overt collection, above all in publications procurement, agricultural reporting, and Foreign Service peripheral reporting. A third faults Washington coordination of economic intelligence requirements and of the collection action taken to meet them, calling it still insufficient.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200080004-2:
A memorandum dated 15 March 1957 sets out dangers in the Egyptian-Israeli situation for the Director. Prospects for fresh violence had risen, it argues, because of the provocative manner of the return to Gaza. Egypt, in its judgment, felt strong in diplomacy though not in military terms. It had stressed that Gaza lay under Cairo's jurisdiction under the armistice agreement, with the United Nations present only on Egyptian sufferance. That position had apparently been accepted by senior United Nations officials named in the memo.

Egypt's president could assume, it continues, that the United Nations would be very slow to use its emergency force to impose new restraints Egypt had not accepted. The force included detachments from states such as India and Yugoslavia. A closing warning holds that tighter Egyptian control of Gaza would lead Israel toward military action, and that Israel might choose force even if Egypt offered some compromise.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200080013-2:
A memorandum dated 19 February 1957 estimates the probable effects of a United Nations General Assembly resolution, backed by the United States, recommending sanctions against Israel. The sanctions would run until Israel complied with the call to withdraw from Sinai and the Gaza Strip. The memo does not judge whether such a resolution would pass. It assumes the United States would halt all government help to Israel, block Israeli funds, and block private transfers of goods and dollars.

Participation is forecast first. Arab states and the USSR, which had already halted oil shipments to Israel, would support the program. Most Arab-Asian states and, under American lead, many Latin American ones would also join. Economic weight is then measured. Israel depended heavily on outside money: forty-five million dollars a year in American help and over one hundred fifty million raised privately, mainly in the United States, beside German reparations.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300050015-2:
Paper IAC-D-101, dated 24 January 1956, circulates a Joint Staff memorandum on intelligence requirements covering United States citizens held in Sino-Soviet Bloc countries. The attached memorandum, numbered DDIM-6-56 and dated 11 January 1956, goes from the Joint Staff's intelligence side to the committee chairman. It is sent as a preliminary to early committee consideration of action.

The Joint Staff memo traces the matter to a November 1955 request from the Assistant to the Secretary of Defense for Special Operations. The request asked the Joint Intelligence Committee to study the intelligence requirements for an effective program in this field. A present requirement is stated plainly: a coordinated, continuing effort to collect all available information and produce reporting on missing persons. That effort is called mandatory, forming the basis for recovery work and for final disposition of each case.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000200050060-2:
General provisions written for technical services contracts open with the stock definitions used across this band. Secretary, contracting officer, and related terms are defined in the standard pattern, with one addition. The commander of the Air Force activity is brought into the contracting officer definition for this contract type. That detail marks the set as an Air Force facing version of the provisions. A subcontract passage in the middle draws lines by size and kind.

Subcontract, for that clause, excludes purchase orders not over one thousand dollars. It also excludes subcontracts or purchase orders for public utility services at rates set for uniform use by the general public. The paragraphs are stated to add to any other contract terms on the same subject, not to replace them. The file runs past fifty pages of such clauses.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300020071-2: A balance forward listing repeats account rows in the 10016, 13016, 26016, and 30016 series, each with coded reference numbers and small running figures. Words visible in later sections include a Director's Project heading and the name Aquatone beside balance rows. Column heads cover date, description, requisition, allotment, and current and prior year totals. The sheet is a raw machine print with no narrative, and its digits are partly garbled in the scan.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300050041-2: A listing titled Current Month Only gives date, voucher, description, and cost current 57 columns for Aquatone account entries. The account shown is 100410001 in a 6002 group, and rows are keyed by voucher numbers in a 20076 and 10076 series with small costs. Unlike the cumulative prints in this band, the title limits the sheet to one month's entries. It is a raw accounting print with no narrative text and partly garbled digits.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080048-2: A July reconciliation worksheet for fiscal 1957 survives as handwritten figures in ruled columns. A few words near the foot of the page suggest totals and posting notes, but no account heading, figure, or remark can be read with confidence from the scan's text. The sheet can be grounded only as the July entry in the monthly reconciliation series for the project accounts; its workings cannot be recovered from this copy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080066-2: A fiscal 1957 worksheet for account 7-1004-10-001, named in its catalog title, survives as handwritten figures in dense columns. A few amounts can be seen as shapes, including a five-figure sum near the head, but no heading, figure, or remark can be read with confidence from the scan's text. The sheet can be grounded only as a handwritten working page for that account; its content cannot be recovered from this copy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080084-2:
Large set of allotment ledger pages, dated through 1957 in the entries, lists payroll and related charges against accounts in the 7-1004 series. Rows name main roll and staff agents pay periods, with voucher numbers, allotment numbers, and amounts for each charge. Balance forward lines open many of the account sections in the file.

The scan is rough, and many figures are hard to read, but the structure stays clear across the pages. A summary account is broken into dated charges, pay period by pay period, so spending can be traced charge by charge. The file shows the volume of routine posting needed to keep one set of Agency accounts current.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00900a000100130014-2:
Recommendation No. 1 in this Agency management set proposes ending the FE Division IBM system and releasing its card punch and sorter equipment. Work handled by the TS and R unit would move to the DD/S RCA-501 system, with a target date of 1 October 1960. The paper says the new system would supply the needed data, on a better schedule, for Area Divisions.

Savings are put at 130 dollars a month in equipment cost, plus staff hours freed for other work. Later recommendations limit interim changes to the present system, assign document control duties, and call for IBM card files to be held for a three month trial after conversion and then destroyed. Standard personnel records for the chiefs are also proposed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00900a000100170001-2:
Memorandum dated 3 February 1961 to the Assistant Executive Officer, DD/P, reports an Agency study of document preparation for WALNUT photography. It follows a request of 31 October 1960 and test work by the Technical Services Division. Typewriter type came first: Elite type was to be avoided, Pica was acceptable, and better types existed but were not in common field use.

The paper recommends Pica type and paper carbon ribbon feeds as standard on electric typewriters bought for field stations. Other findings cover ribbons, carbon paper, paper stocks, and pens. Letterex one-time carbon and medium black carbon paper gave good results, while coloured tissues and light carbon papers reproduced poorly after early copies.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00901a000200030031-2:
United States Atomic Energy Commission bulletin GM-SEC-5, dated 7 January 1951 in the scan, gives rules at section 17 for destruction of classified documents. Top Secret papers were normally destroyed by the authenticating official whose symbol they bore, or by that official's successor or a higher authority. A record copy had to be kept by the authenticating official. The copy in this file sits in the Agency's records.

A custodian could destroy a Top Secret document only with written authority from that official or a higher one. A stated destroy-by period on the document was binding unless extended in writing. Certificates of destruction had to record that the document was intact and complete when checked, and they were signed only after that check, then sent to the authenticating official.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00137a000100130004-2:
Draft memo dated 23 December 1957 records a meeting held on 11 December 1957 at NSA, Fort Meade. The subject was the status of work under Agency Requirement 6E-236. The same task is cited as PROD RQT 87-57. Names of those present are redacted in the scan. The first part of the meeting traced the past of the requirement. It also traced the effort to build a table of the data the requirement called for.

Machine handling caused the main trouble in the work. A machine run had come in, but proofing found so many errors that a fresh run had to be asked for. That fresh run was then delayed. A move into a new building also slowed the work. Background from a 17 May 1957 meeting of NSA and CIA staff was set out again for members new to the case.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100020102-2:
Untitled Agency paper seeks detailed facts for economic work on the telecom and postal systems of North Korea. The services in scope are telephone, telegraph, facsimile, radio and wired broadcasting, and postal service. They are carried by wire lines, by cable, by fixed radio, and by line-of-sight radio relay. The first section covers the setup and control of the system as a whole.

Questions ask for the structure of the Ministry of Communications. They ask the chains of command for policy, control, security, planning, operation, building, and upkeep. They ask the role of the military in the basic system. Telephone items go down to small points of fact. One asks where receivers were got, whether from the USSR, Communist China, or the Satellites. Others ask the cost of a telephone, and the share of North Korea that phones can reach.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100030101-2:
General needs paper backs the Agency's whole transport intelligence mission. Rail transport comes first in it. Sound figures are the chief need it names. Figures for a span should be flat totals. They may also be given as a share rise or fall against a planned or true base. Data are wanted for a whole country, single lines, an area, or a city. A note adds that one named system hauled as much in a year as the British railroads, a fact called of value in itself.

Rail traffic and working figures are listed in detail. They run from tons carried and ton-kilometres to car loadings and passenger counts. Later sections cover water transport. They ask sea and shore staff numbers, pay, output, and morale, and shipping agreements. Air transport closes the paper, from two-way agreements and ICAO and IATA ties to airport readiness for jet work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100030156-2:
Covering note dated 26 March 1957 puts forward needs for the Agency's OCI Periodic Requirements List. The list runs from 1 May to 31 August 1957. It covers the USSR and Eastern Europe. Items to keep are listed by page and item number. New items are added to the list as well. One new item on the USSR follows civil defence. Civil defence is named there as a high aim for 1957, perhaps in the text of the Sixth Five-Year Plan. The item asks what protection was needed in 1956, and what effect that need had on building work.

Bulgaria gains a housing item in the same note. The country was said to have much rural housing built, most of it private. Yet it seemed short of cement, brick, and lumber for a program of that size. Collectors are asked what such houses on state and cooperative farms were in fact built from.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180024-2:
Minutes ED/EC M-226 in the Agency's files record a meeting of the Executive Committee of the Economic Defense Advisory Committee at 10:30 a.m. on Monday, 18 February 1957, in Room 1213, Maiatico. Mr. Hale of MDAC chaired, with members from Defense, ICA, State, and Commerce listed. Agenda notes cover a contemplated change in Public Law 480 and the work program on general policy.

On the law, the chairman reported word from the General Counsel that the Bureau of the Budget had asked agencies for views on legislative changes. A Senate draft proviso would allow barter with countries other than the USSR, Communist China, and North Korea, which drew State comment. Draft outlines for the policy statement were due to reach the committee before 1 March.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180042-2:
Minutes ED/EC M-255 record a meeting at 2:00 p.m. on 15 July 1957, in Room 1213, Maiatico. They were issued on 22 July 1957. A note covers List II quotas for China. Numbered items take up a Commerce action proposal. The proposal calls for a review of the joint security control program. The items take up the NSC and CFEP policy review task as well. The quota note records agreement on the substance of a reply cable to Paris.

Defense put in a paper on package quotas for International List II items. The items were for Communist China. Talk then turned to the Commerce proposal. The chairman asked the Agency a direct question on it. The paper called for an intelligence review. Could the intelligence community take that task on? Could it answer with data and studies of use in a fair time? Commerce had put forward 15 September for the work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180051-2:
Minutes ED/EC M-265 record a meeting at 2:00 p.m. on 13 August 1957, in Room 1213, Maiatico. They were issued on 20 August 1957. Mr. Hale chaired the meeting. The Agency, Commerce, Defense, ICA, State, and Treasury members attended. The single agenda head is fitness for aid. The country names under that head are redacted in the scan.

Two actions were set at the meeting. An opinion would be sought from the ICA General Counsel. The question was whether the Battle Act chief could in law find Finland fit for aid. Future shipments of Title I Category B items to the Bloc were already known to be coming. State would also draw up a paper for the committee's review. It would give facts on all exports of strategic goods to the Bloc in 1956. The chairman would draft a memo to EDAC from the talk.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180105-2:
Addendum pages in the Agency's files list trade agreements and other trade accords of the Soviet Bloc with countries of the Near East and Africa, entry by entry. Each entry gives the countries, the kind of agreement, its duration, principal commodities each way, estimated values, and payments and renewal provisions, plus the sources the entry rests on and their classification. Texts of the agreements were often not available, the entries note.

A Morocco and Hungary entry covers a first trade and payments agreement of December 1957, running 1 October 1957 to 30 September 1958. Hungarian exports listed include rubber goods, tyres, chemicals, paints, radios, textiles, electric motors, motorcycles, bicycles, farm machines, and canned foods. Moroccan exports include tropical fruits, sardines, seaweed, seeds, fodders, fish meal, phosphates, and wine.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200010067-2:
Monitoring compilation in the Agency's files, dated 8 September 1954, is headed China: Communist. It mixes translated press items. One item quotes a Japanese paper's commentary on a Northeast Asian bloc. The paper warns Japan against joining such a bloc. It calls the move unwise for Japan's own interests. It says the move would make Japan a sacrifice for United States policy. It urges better ties with Asian countries instead. The item notes Secretary of State Dulles's moves in Manila and a planned Japan visit.

Other material in the file turns to factory rules. A passage explains one term in Chinese shop floor proposal rules: improvement in the procedure of technical production. It means a change in the shape, size, nature, or quality of the thing worked on. Cases given are multi-blade and high-speed metal cutting methods. One more is the merging of many labour processes into one.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200120010-2:
Agency Current Support Memorandum No. 614, dated 14 October 1958, reports plans to move Szechwan oil on the Yangtze. It is marked as containing code word material. Refining figures in the paper speak of plant able to handle around 1,000,000 tons of crude oil a year, with a 3,000,000-ton refinery scheduled to be built at Nanking.
