Communist China had already begun work on moving Szechwan crude down the Yangtze.

Plans called for 100,000 tons to move in the current year and 1,000,000 tons in the next. Current efforts ran two ways: dredging the channel of the Chialing River to a minimum depth of 1.3 metres, and converting large numbers of existing vessels to carry oil. The paper treats river depth and boat supply as the limits on a major new crude flow.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100050075-2:
Untitled agenda paper in the Agency's files lists the questions for a psychological strategy working session. Early items cover the defection of Communists from their movement. They cover the strategy to be followed on the death of Stalin in national policy. They cover measures to increase desired defections while keeping a general appeal for peace. They weigh a disarmament proposal for countering a Soviet peace campaign. The year in that item is garbled in the scan.

Later items name psychological strategy in the Cold War as a heading in itself. They call for a study of policymaking machinery in psychological operations. They call for a survey of work in that field. They call for a review of how effective psychological operations had been. Questions put to the group include what measures could restrain Soviet aggression, strengthen allies and potential allies, and define Cold War aims.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400050018-2:
Special National Intelligence Estimate SNIE 100-2-57 is titled Soviet Capabilities for Deception. It is dated 28 May 1957 and marked Top Secret. It was submitted by the Director of Central Intelligence. It was prepared by the Agency with the intelligence organisations of State, the Army, the Navy, the Air Force, the Joint Staff, and the Atomic Energy Commission. The Intelligence Advisory Committee concurred in it the same day. The FBI Assistant Director abstained, the subject lying outside his jurisdiction.

The estimate holds that Soviet deception does not rest on one or two pieces of false information, but on a substantial body of supporting data. In a major crisis, the danger would be considerably greater. An agent's report might provide the last straw for a United States decision, with no time to test its credibility. Or deception might delay a valid judgment, or render it so tentative as to be of little use.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400100030-2:
Untitled Agency photo report on Lebanon and Syria lists airfields and military sites in numbered order. Lebanon entries are short: Estabel, Kleiat, and Metulla airfields each showed no aircraft or activity, and Tripoli harbour showed 2 coastal freighters. Syria takes most of the report. Aleppo Airfield showed 2 Meteor and 4 derelict aircraft. Bab el Haoua Airfield was reported unserviceable and would no longer be reported unless reactivated.

Damascus Airfield showed 9 Fresco, 1 Fagot, 6 Meteor, 2 C-47 type, 3 C-54 type, 1 C-131 type, and 32 liaison type aircraft with 1 Crate. Deir ez Zor and Djerah airfields showed no aircraft, while Dumier Airfield's southwest half of runway was being prepared for surfacing, with construction equipment evident. Ground items include a Damascus military depot with 35 probable field artillery pieces, 75 vehicles, and 12 possible tanks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600010001-2:
A daily office diary, headed RDD Diary, runs to well over a hundred pages. Early entries cover the first days of June 1953. They record calls and meetings about a study laid on the Economic Intelligence Committee, work tied to NSC-29, and handling of a report marked EIC-R1-S2. One entry notes an Indochina report heard by the Intelligence Advisory Committee on tape. Another settles how Air Force officers in Washington could see material tied to work in Vienna, with 190 reels involved.

Entries proceed day by day in short numbered form. Later ones take up release questions and a long meeting that sorted files by office interest. The diary gives a close, routine view of coordination work inside the Agency in the early nineteen fifties.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600080004-2:
A tentative list of items for panel discussion fills the file, organised by panel. Panel I, on policy, opens with broad working concepts for Special Forces. It then takes up ties with other agencies, the place of Special Forces inside an unconventional warfare task force, and command of guerrilla forces. Recruiting closes the panel, with a focus on which nationalities should be sought under global plans.

Panel II turns to planning. Items cover the state of guerrilla warfare planning, the makeup of guerrilla units, and how many guerrillas each target area should raise. Stay-behinds, deserters, and defecting units appear, as do mission priorities such as communications, personnel, and sabotage. Delivery of teams, weapons for guerrilla forces, and plan annex formats round it out. A further panel covers intelligence and research, citing the survey program, Army G-2 projects, and work at Georgetown University. Training items follow later.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600140016-2:
A Navy paper lists the offices and units tied to a sensitive materials program. Section A maps the structure in two parts. Departmental offices in Washington come first: the Secretary's research aide, naval intelligence, research and ships bureaus, and the photographic interpretation centre. Marine Corps headquarters also appears.

Operational units follow by fleet. Atlantic, European, and Pacific commands each list numbered fleets and fleet intelligence centres. One Atlantic centre is noted as due to open in January 1961. Unified commands served through the Navy close the list, among them the Pacific command and the Taiwan Defense Command. Section B then states what these offices do with Mission 9009 material. They use it to plan theater operations and force structure, and to feed wider Navy planning. A chart spells the links out in detail.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600150006-2:
A draft dated 19 May 1960, marked G-2, tests a set of propaganda propositions against photo selections. Each claim gets a short comment and a verdict. The first claim casts the Russians as a menace. The reviewer finds that the selections do not prove an urgent danger of attack, so the claim fails.

A second claim, that Moscow hides a devilish new weapon for blackmail or surprise attack, is judged not proven. A third claim fares better: Soviet war preparation in the open can be shown, if each print has a like United States print already released. Even then, the point would be short lived, since secret work sits outside any photos. Later claims turn to open skies. The reviewer argues that planned display could prove inspection workable more strongly than scattered prints could.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600150024-2:
A memorandum dated 27 January 1960 warns the Director of Central Intelligence about a plain gap: no one knew where a single working Soviet ICBM site stood. Mr Khrushchev claimed missiles that could hit any target on earth with nuclear warheads. United States estimates granted Moscow an early ability to fire such missiles at America. Yet no launch site ready for use had been found.

The unknowns run deeper than location. Staff could not say how many missiles stood ready, how fast more were added, or whether sites were hard, soft, or mobile. The Strategic Air Command thus lacked target facts for those weapons. The President and Secretary of State also lacked hard facts before a tense round of talks. The memo backs a board call, backed by the intelligence board, to use the Chalice program hard in hunting launch sites.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700010028-2:
An Intelligence Advisory Committee paper dated 9 September 1953 proposes stronger support for some collection work. It opens with a State Department letter to the Acting Director of Central Intelligence. That letter, held at Tab A, sets a frame: the Director could fund collection past the lowest level the Department's own budget could carry. Deep cuts frame the plea.

The Foreign Service budget for 1954 had been cut hard, State warned. The cut landed as demands for collection work, many of them from CIA, were rising. Worse, the lower level looked set to last for years, weakening a key collection arm. A study at Tab B, drafted by the Office of Intelligence Coordination, holds advice for committee action. The paper calls the choice basic to the future of the whole federal intelligence system, not just a short term fix for one department.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700020018-2:
Notes prepared for a speech by Mr Reber gather the early law on services of common concern. One main duty of the Director, the notes stress, is running such shared services for the whole community. Shared services are those the Security Council judges better done at the centre. Its rulings usually rest on the Director's advice, with committee agreement.

The notes quote a letter of 22 January 1946 from President Truman to the Secretaries of State, War, and the Navy. Weeks later the National Intelligence Authority set up a Central Intelligence Services office inside the Central Intelligence Group. Early shared tasks listed are secret collection abroad, tapping home sources for foreign facts, and some foreign economic research. Handling foreign language publications may join them. Later notes cite directives on home source work and on foreign economic intelligence, each assigning CIA a central role.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700060005-2:
An Intelligence Advisory Committee copy of the DCID 4/5 review, dated 11 June 1956, circulates the 25 May text. The review was made with agency staff, at the Director's request. It asks how information needs and collection tasks are built and joined up, measured against the priority national objectives. Those objectives, cleared by the committee and noted by the Council, set the community's broad course.

Yet they never act as the sole guide, the review repeats. Offices also serve their own departments, whose needs often match the national list. Gaps found in research become the raw stock of collection requests. Field committees lend order in set areas: atomic energy, science and technology, guided missiles, economics, and basic intelligence. Tasks so backed turn into formal requests to the agency charged with collection. A closing pass notes that task building leads back to how research offices are run and directed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700060014-2:
A draft memorandum dated 29 March 1955, from the Special Assistant to the Director for Planning and Coordination, seeks office views on requirements coordination. Staff had met on 18 February. Agency representatives had talked on 4 and 5 February, and more informal talks had followed. The writer now plans a report to the Director, drafted along the lines of an attached text. He asks offices whether the draft states their views fairly.

Replies are asked by 8 April. Offices may suggest changes, or file opposed views as a separate annex. Once the Agency settles its line, the draft would go to member agencies, minus two paragraphs sent apart. The attached draft cites the January review paper, IAC-D-50/5. It records that agencies weighed current arrangements jointly. No new device was urged, save one current intelligence office idea: a subcommittee to list needs flowing from DCID 4/4.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700070211-2:
A memorandum dated 2 December 1953 sends round a draft rewrite of CIA Regulation 50-17. James Reber signed it. Copies went to every assistant director, plus the comptroller, general counsel, and chiefs of logistics, security, and training. Views were due by Friday 11 December. The rule would then go to the deputy director with a plea for issue.

The rule itself covers coordination of external research. It sets out how the Agency orders studies from outside hands. Sections lay down general policy, who owns each step, and the steps to follow. The Security Office must clear people before secret material reaches outside contractors. Money and legal checks sit with the comptroller and general counsel. A note covers cases where Agency interest in a study may be shown to a would-be contractor.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100110011-2:
Papers for study EDIC/IR-27 set out how a report on Sino-Soviet bloc merchant shipping will be built. The subject runs from 1956 to 1960. A January 1957 meeting agreed the shape of the work, though parts of the scan read poorly. The plan opens with background on export control talks. COCOM and CHINCOM shipping rules, and controls now in force, come first.

Later parts sort the task by theme. One part lists bloc fleets, with naval auxiliaries, by ship type, speed, and age. Another weighs bloc needs for tonnage. A third asks how far the bloc can supply its own shipping, and what Western yards might add. Current trade deals and tonnage under build or repair both enter the count. A closing part weighs Western power to curb shipping for the bloc in a tight case, and the odds of finding extra tonnage beyond what is already in hand.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470003-2:
Approved terms of reference for the Economic Defense Subcommittee go out under a memo dated 11 December 1958. The subcommittee sits under the Economic Intelligence Committee. Its executive secretary sent the terms. The mission is stated first: to give a working frame for economic defence intelligence. That work must serve two policy bodies, the Economic Defense Advisory Committee and the Advisory Committee on Export Policy.

Membership mixes full and associate seats. Member agencies name their own people, subject to approval from above. Associate seats go to staff from the mutual defence office, Commerce, State, the Treasury, and the aid agency. Any other office with skill or stake in the field may be called in. Set duties follow. Chief among them: find real gaps in research and collection tied to the two policy bodies' needs. Then build and report ways those gaps are being, or could be, closed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470012-2:
Minutes of the fifteenth meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee cover a session held on 5 April 1956. The minutes are dated 17 April. February minutes won approval first. Next came a paper on bloc buying of mercury in 1955. State would use it as background when weighing a fresh Italian mercury exception for 1956. Shipments from Italy to the bloc in 1955 had been sizable, the paper showed.

A companion paper on bloc nickel buying in 1955 was noted, though one point could not be pinned down. Aluminium and its sources, bauxite among them, filled a further item. Members then asked for a survey of recent studies on bloc merchant shipbuilding. The acting secretary was told to build a reading list first. That list would show whether deeper study was needed. A draft paper on a borax find in Tibet, drawn from a Battelle study, also came before the group.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470021-2:
Minutes of the sixth meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee are dated 21 February 1955. The group met on 11 February. Copper controls head the record. The acting chairman reviewed talks in the joint operating arm on curbing copper trade. A negotiating paper was being built for COCOM use. CIA was also drafting a separate study of secret copper trade, as ground for talks on bloc copper imports.

State and CIA staff would meet soon to draft a paper on those imports. That session, he stressed, was an intelligence exercise, not a negotiation. Next came method for a paper on tests for the China list. State and CIA had agreed to write it jointly. Two advisers urged that intelligence staff ignore political snags and propose the tests that would work best for United States aims.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100490001-2:
A numbered inventory of papers fills the file, listing memos and records tied to economic defence work. Early items date from the start of 1955. They include views on a draft estimate on controls on trade with Communist China. One memo covers how current economic defence facts reach action agencies. Another weighs rules on spreading and using intelligence material.

Later items track a downgrading project for COCOM and CHINCOM papers. Progress notes, a survey of the files, and a draft Agency stance all appear. Other entries log committee minutes, a desk report for January 1955, and a list of strategic goods sent round. Monthly activity summaries for a defence aid newsletter recur. A stock list of economic defence projects also appears. The inventory reads as a file clerk's map of one busy office's paper flow across the first months of 1955.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100490038-2:
A balance sheet of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee's wins and gaps is dated 21 April 1955. Its executive secretary wrote it. At the March meeting the acting chairman had floated a rewrite of the committee's terms. April talks took the idea further. This paper gives background for that debate. It claims no full study, only the basic points shown by nearly three years of work.

Source papers are listed first. They run from the group's founding terms of July 1952, revised in February 1953, through its working rules and two yearly reports. Staffing plans and memos on channelling agency requests join the list. On the debit side, one charge is delay in backing action desks. The paper grants it some truth, then answers back. Like delays hit staff support sent direct from intelligence to action agencies too. It cites backing for yearly talks and for the China list review as cases in point.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100510062-2:
A draft of the fourth yearly progress report of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee goes out on 25 September 1956. The vice chairman sent it for review before the next meeting. The report covers the year to 30 June 1956. Its program section has five heads. Support for goods controls comes second, after a general survey of the year.

Other heads track backing for studies of Soviet bloc trade tricks. Trade in freed goods and exception shipments gets its own part. Work to sharpen collection closes the program. Tabs list finished reports and cases, cases still open, and papers sent to members. Gains named in the text include a marked lift in allied control trade figures. CIA's own channels for gathering and spreading economic defence facts grew stronger. A reporting guide for the field was also prepared. The draft thus reads as both a score card and a pitch for the year ahead.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200050044-2:
A letter dated 25 June 1958 from the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base encloses a seminar talk. The talk, by a Mr Kent, was given on 14 June 1956. Its title is Some Aspects of Soviet Solid Propellant Technology. The centre offers the copy for a bound set of seminar papers, and asks for copies of that set in return.

The talk opens with a blunt limit. What is known of Soviet solid propellant work is fragmentary, and much of it is guesswork. Liquid propellant knowledge stands far firmer by contrast. Known items are then laid out: propellant grains tied to the MIG-15, and work on two types, one the old nitrocellulose and nitroglycerin mix. A German type pairs with it. On composite propellants, the talk admits, almost no data exists.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200050062-2:
Minutes of an Economic Intelligence Committee meeting held on 12 April 1956 are dated 26 April. Dr Otto Guthe of CIA chaired, in Room 2125 of the M Building. First, March minutes stood approved by silence: no member had objected by the set date. Next, the chairman flagged a fresh report, the 1955 half-year survey of research projects on the Sino-Soviet bloc.

That report's cost drew a warning. The heavy work behind it might force a move to yearly issue only. An eight months progress report on the committee's work also went round the table. The chairman then read from letters swapped with the guided missiles committee chair. That chair held his body must cover the same ground an older missiles group had held. So, he argued, this committee need not push further on joining up that field.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200160024-2:
A draft report on the Diversion Control Network covers its first three months, January to March 1954. The net began work about 1 January. It rests on a parent body ruling of 20 October 1953. Its birth came from a shared verdict: backing and blocking moves on diverted goods were too loose and unsure. Closer ties between action and intelligence desks were the cure sought.

Membership is stated with care. Officers from State, the aid office, and CIA form the core. Commerce, Treasury, and Defense name liaison officers. They join only where a case touches their own stake. No agency's broad duties changed, the draft stresses. The net exists to speed the swap of facts and join up Washington moves against incoming diversions. Later pages sort what a case can win. A block may fail yet still yield facts enough to press an allied land into sealing the gap in its own enforcement net.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200170010-2:
A legal memo dated 3 December 1957 answers a planning question on Mobilization Plan C. The emergency planning officer had asked for counsel's view. Must CIA now draft any presidential action papers the plan needs? A letter of 15 October 1957 from the acting head of the Office of Defense Mobilization set a deadline. Such papers were due from all agencies by 15 December.

Counsel's answer is short: no papers are called for from this Agency under the plan. The planning officer, by phone, shares that view. The mobilization office's own call letter rides in the file. It notes the plan, dated 1 June 1957, went out on 10 June. Classification guidance follows: a summary sheet is graded by its own contents alone. No weight need be given to the plan it serves, nor to its ties to other papers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300060011-2:
A memo dated 24 July 1957 sends the Director of Training a guide to death cases. It forwards extracts from state code titles that govern deaths not from natural causes with a doctor present. Three titles are mined: one on boundaries and jurisdiction, one on criminal procedure, and one on health. The duties of the medical examiner sit in the criminal title, the memo notes.

The extracts get concrete fast. One section covers land ceded to the United States. The state keeps the right to serve civil and criminal process on such land. If the land is sold or leased for private business, the ceded jurisdiction ends at once. Death record rules follow in fine detail. Certificates must carry the place and date of burial, and a witness name and address. Personal facts, items one to thirteen, must name the informant and where he can be found.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300070001-2:
A memo weighs a plan to send picked college graduates through full-time graduate study in economics, at Agency cost. The research office built the plan. Counsel was asked for its view by the deputy director for support. Then doubts crowd in, each given a letter. 

If economics graduates grow in step, sharp hiring might fill most needs without such a scheme. A second doubt is fairness. Staff now serving, with no chance to compete for the prize, may resent it. A third is the draft. Picked students still owe military service unless deferred. They would be called away before turning truly productive. An alternate path is floated later in the memo. It would build skill in serving staff, with study credit that could count toward degrees. The core plea is care: buying economists this way may cost more, in coin and morale, than it gains.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400050020-2:
A memo dated 16 September 1957 clears a joint copying plan in law. Counsel had read the plan in the light of Order 10501. The sum of it is safe, the memo holds. Shops may copy, for their own use or each other's, just the stock that all of them have already had. No breach of the third agency rule lurks in that.

That rule bars on-passing a shop's facts to a third shop sans its leave. A hard read of two texts might clear a wider path, the memo grants. Section 7 of the order, read with section 102 of the 1947 act, could be said to let CIA pass the rule by. In fact the Agency holds the strict line: no such facts move without the source shop's leave first. The Minicard kit gets its own fence. It will never touch rule-bound stock.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400060001-2:
A memo dated 23 November 1959 takes up leaks of state facts. Lawrence Houston writes to the head of the USIB security panel. The board had sent round a draft White House note on facts let loose that touch the nation's safety. Its stock forms the theme of this file.

The Agency's stance is firm. Guard rules in Order 10501 set who may stamp a fact and who may free it. That last call rests with the head of the shop that holds the fact. No blanket White House text should blur that line, Houston argues. One point is the Agency's alone. Its sources and methods sit in no other shop's hands. A loose fact from its files can burn a source or a craft in a way no twin fact from a plain shop could. A draft note and a close study of the board's text ride with the memo.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100080006-2:
Notes from a conference of senior support officers held on 14 to 16 October 1959 fill this declassified Central Intelligence Agency record. The gathering brought together senior officers in the support career service, support chiefs, deputy support chiefs, and smaller numbers of staff from other directorates. Talks covered broad questions and future trends rather than routine procedure.

Summaries record a talk by Sherman Kent on intelligence problems in the world today and one by Lyman Kirkpatrick on future trends and what they mean for support work. Later pages turn to career service, promotion slowdowns, and a selection-out plan for staff whose skills are no longer needed. Readers get a candid look at how Agency support leaders weighed morale, staffing, and world events in 1959.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000100160012-2:
French proposals for changes in Lists I and IV of the allied export-control system are submitted in a Coordinating Committee memorandum dated October 1959, numbered 5700. The French delegation reserves the right to send later proposals on the munitions and atomic energy lists. Requests to move some items from the munitions list into List I are also flagged for later.

An annex sets out the List I changes, starting with metal-working machinery. A gear-making item is redrawn around a module limit, with remarks explaining that very fine gear machines serve watchmaking and precision work rather than heavy industry. Other entries treat special cables that lack the capacity of normal telecommunications cable, and steels with set limits on cobalt and chromium content.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200010062-2:
Renewal of the trade agreement between Canada and the Soviet Union is submitted to the Coordinating Committee by the Canadian delegation in document 4039, dated 22 June 1960. Three annexes carry the substance. The first is a statement to the Canadian House of Commons by Gordon Churchill, Minister of Trade and Commerce, made on 25 April 1960.

Churchill tables the protocol signed in Moscow on 18 April 1960, which renewed the agreement for three years. His remarks note that both sides wanted more varied trade, not just larger trade, and that the Soviet Union had become a regular wheat exporter. The remaining annexes carry the protocol text itself and letters exchanged between the two parties, giving allied export-control officials the full terms to study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200020016-2:
Discussion inside the Coordinating Committee on 29 April 1960 is recorded in document 3984 B, issued on 16 May 1960. Delegates from Canada, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and the United States heard an oral report from the chairman of the Sub-Committee on Export Controls. The sub-committee had met over the three days just before, from 26 to 28 April.

The report follows the sub-committee's draft agenda in order, with a Netherlands question on the import certificate system added along the way. Pages record how member states handled cases where a resident acted in a deal shipping goods to the Soviet bloc from a country outside the scheme. Statements from the United States and United Kingdom on their own systems were noted for the record.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200050004-2:
A draft reorganisation of the China Special List is sent out by the China Committee on 7 July 1953 as document CH/139. The aim was to bring the list's form closer to that of the international lists. The committee had agreed the idea in principle on 29 June 1953, after which a sub-committee on lists worked out the changes proposed here.

After debate on 2 July, the committee chose to send the draft to national capitals for study before adopting it. In the meantime the list as issued in document CH/125 would stand, subject to later reorganisation. The draft itself defines items in English and French side by side, from watercraft and motor vehicles onward, each tied to its source document.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200070011-2:
Widening the China embargo is the goal of a program paper on major list extension for the China Committee. Progress so far, the paper says, had been slow, moving through position-by-position exchanges between governments. Much of the work grew from a British supplementary list first raised in the Coordinating Committee, and part of it had already produced a China Special List.

Four British proposals had been added outright, among them gas carburising furnaces, cement guns, fork-lift trucks, and metal spraying equipment. Other proposals sat before the committee awaiting decision. Before the United States moved, the paper insists on three things: a settled view of the coverage wanted, agreed tactical steps, and enough technical preparation on each item proposed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200110007-2:
United States policy on Japanese export controls is stated in full in a summary marked secret security information. The aim is plain at the start: win effective controls in Japan that serve the free world's shared security interests. That aim had to sit alongside other policies, and the summary lists them so officials could see the tensions.

Helping Japan become economically self-supporting and raise its output of strategic materials for the free world stands near the top. Other stated policies press friendly countries to apply controls that cut Communist China's war potential, and seek alternate sources for basic materials then drawn from the Soviet bloc. Later analysis weighs China's need for capital goods and Japan's need for export markets, and warns that growing Chinese dependence on Soviet supply could strain both economies.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000100220002-2:
Committees of the United States Intelligence Board are listed in a revised roster dated 1 October 1959, document USIB-D-27.1/7. Both standing committees and ad hoc committees and working groups are included. The roster was sent out for information, with changes to be reported to the board's secretariat.

Each entry names a chairman and secretary, their agency, building, and telephone extension. Early entries cover communications intelligence, critical communications, documentation, and exchanges, with officers drawn from the State Department and the Central Intelligence Agency. Later entries reach the Guided Missile and Astronautics Intelligence Committee, chaired from the Pentagon, and an interagency defector committee. The roster maps how the intelligence community divided its shared business in 1959.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000100250009-2:
Missile accuracy depends on knowing exactly where both launcher and target sit on the earth, and an article on geodetic control explains why. Long-range missiles may fly several thousand miles, yet each type carries a built-in error of its own. That error, called circular error probability, mixes human error, machine error, and weather into one measure of likely miss distance.

Cutting the built-in error still leaves a missile astray if the position data behind its trajectory is faulty. Survey tools named in the article include transits, steel tapes, geodimeters, theodolites, tellurometers, and gravimeters, used to measure distance, angles, and gravity. For wide areas survey parties cannot reach, electronic systems such as Hiran take over. A world geodetic system developed by the Air Force tied launch sites and targets into one frame of reference.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000200210011-2:
Gravity meters, long a tool for oil prospectors, gained a wider strategic role once exact positioning between continents mattered, argues a 1959 geographic memorandum. Recent gains in the instrument matter here. A modern gravity meter was light, easily carried, and able to give highly accurate readings, though its use was still limited to the land surface of the earth.

West German work had adapted the meter for use on surface vessels, and efforts were under way in the United States to use it in aircraft. Airborne gravity data from far-off regions would sharpen knowledge of the earth's shape. The memorandum also reports Soviet interest in buying Western gravity gear, and reads continued Soviet buying efforts as a sign of the true state of their own instrument building.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000200260016-2:
Research finished and under way in April 1959 is covered in a progress report of the Geography Division. A contribution to a national estimate on Soviet science and technology was completed in expanded form. Another study, requested by the Director, estimated flood loss if a single nuclear blast breached the High Aswan Dam while it stood full of water.

That estimate rests on stated assumptions printed in the report, among them a dam not filled before 1970, an Egyptian population of about thirty-two million, and no warning to the public. Briefing material on land, people, economy, and transport for Tibet and China was also prepared. Antarctic work located useful intelligence on Soviet gravimetry and on the urgency the Soviets gave to airborne gravity surveying.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000100030021-2:
Comments on an Inspector General survey of the Foreign Documents Division are sent to the Director of Central Intelligence in this memorandum. The writer, whose office ran the division, states general agreement with the survey's findings. Recommendations marked A through D win full concurrence, though carrying them out fully would need the extra manpower named in a further recommendation.

One recommendation, marked E, is rejected. Its procedures had been in force in the division until recently, and experience showed they loaded too little duty onto section chiefs while clogging the branch chief's office. A later point takes up grading of proofreading posts. Repeated bids to raise those grades had failed, with personnel officials holding that proofreading was low-grade clerical work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000500040017-2:
A tentative February schedule for an Office of Personnel survey lists which offices the survey team would visit, week by week. The first week, from 9 to 13 February, is given to the Contract Personnel Division. The week after turns to the chief of the Benefits and Casualty Division, its casualty affairs branch, and then the insurance branch.

The last week of the month opens work on the Personnel Operations Division. Staffing tables follow, setting out organisation titles, position titles, and grades for the offices under survey. Contract personnel, military personnel, liaison, manning, and reserve affairs posts appear, with grades running from junior clerical levels up to GS-18. Names of the post holders are blacked out in the released copy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200020036-2:
Far East deployment of AQUATONE is taken up in a 28 November 1958 memorandum to the Director of Central Intelligence. The Air Force chief of staff, General Twining, had replied that the Air Force could not support both AQUATONE and BLACK KNIGHT in the Far East. He proposed holding Detachment C in reserve, to reinforce wherever world events required.

Against that stands a meeting with the President on 18 November, where the Japan plan was explained. The President agreed the unit should be based in Japan unless the State Department objected on further thought, and he noted the Agency aircraft's edge over the BLACK KNIGHT planes. The memo warns against leaving a hard-won reconnaissance capability idle in the United States while East-West tension sharpened.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200030008-2:
Project AQUATONE's birth and early build-up are recounted in a draft paper dated 19 November 1955. On 23 November 1954 the Intelligence Advisory Committee had warned of serious gaps in coverage of the Soviet bloc and named aerial reconnaissance as the most practical remedy. The project was approved and set in motion on 1 December that year.

Speed marked everything that followed. Lockheed began work on a high-altitude, long-range reconnaissance aircraft on oral assurance alone, and a leading optical specialist set to work on lenses and cameras beyond any existing design. Letter contracts came first, with final contracts close behind. By mid-February, specialised equipment was in development at six companies. Early technical troubles, such as a fuel control fit for jet engines at extreme altitude, are noted as on their way to solution.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200040061-2:
Slow progress on AQUATONE is charted in a 24 January 1957 memorandum to the Director of Central Intelligence. The writer walks the record step by step. A firm request for Far East facilities was made on 25 October, at a meeting with Generals Cabell, Radford. Twining, and a survey group was sent out at once and warmly received in the region.

A written request went to Twining on 13 November. Two days later the President accepted the Far East deployment and implied AQUATONE should take priority over Black Knight. By December the approach had shifted to asking Admiral Burke for facilities at Atsugi, still without an Air Force reply. The delay is called deeply discouraging, above all for pilots who knew the Soviets were working hard on means to intercept the aircraft.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200080049-2:
Section reports from an overseas project unit cover administration, materiel and maintenance, and communications. The administration section reports a settled period: new staff had arrived, more office space had been gained. Staff had returned from leave after months of heavy processing of people in and out. No outstanding problems are claimed, and the present staff is judged fully able to handle daily work.

One warning is entered. Rumours of new posts under a fresh table of organisation should not trigger hiring unless new tasks come with them, since the balance of jobs to workers looked right as it stood. Communications staff concerns appear later, over wording in an operations order annex about support aircraft. The writer explains was a wording change only, not a complaint or a bid for more gear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100080040-2:
Trends in the engineering industries of Communist China are the subject of a requirements paper sent to the Industrial Division in April. Earlier collection summaries from 1957 and 1958 are cited as background. The paper asks for fresh information across the engineering sector, with a view to judging whether present capacity and output match the claims made for them.

Shortages of raw materials are flagged as a recurring brake on a number of engineering plants. Agricultural machinery gets special attention, with questions on production levels, the spread of plants, and whether output is economically sound. The paper's aim is not a catalogue of factories but a judgment on direction: where Chinese engineering is growing, where it stalls, and what limits bind it most tightly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100110154-2:
December 1958 closes the Industrial Division's year in a monthly report dated 7 January 1959. Security matters open it. The Aircraft Branch was contacted by the Office of Security for help in investigating a possible disclosure of classified material about the Soviet Bounder aircraft to unauthorised persons. Several division staff were interviewed about their dealings with representatives of the Convair Division of General Dynamics.

Research support fills the rest. Staff spoke on Soviet guided missile production and deployment at a guided missile forum run by the scientific intelligence office that month. The Aircraft Branch also worked with another staff on a paper about Badger aircraft. A deputy chief briefed the Agency's planning group on the range and variety of the economic research product, using sample report types to show what the office produced.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100130062-2:
The cost of building planes is worked through in a letter dated 9 April. The name of the person addressed is blacked out. The writer takes up a point from an earlier letter. The airframe serves so many types of plane. Its cost thus tends to grow much larger in cost terms. Items grouped as 'other items' make up most of the airframe cost. That holds for the first unit built.

Learning curve sums follow. The 'other items' share may hold as output grows. If so, total cost can be worked out across a whole run. Tables give the sums for named bomber and fighter types. Some type names are blurred in the scan. The tables give mean costs at the fiftieth and hundredth units. They also give totals for the first fifty and first hundred units.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100130071-2:
A gaps statement on the aircraft industry of Communist China is forwarded for review on 27 March 1959 by the Aircraft Branch. Growth of an indigenous aircraft industry is named one of the most important recent developments in Communist China. Yet information on the description, numerical designation, production, and in some cases even the location of the producing facilities is almost totally lacking.

Knowledge of the industry's scope, progress, present production, and future intentions is of increasing strategic importance to the United States, the statement argues. The industry sits mainly in three geographic centres: Mukden, Nanchang, and Sian. Much less is known about plant activity around Sian, and the amount of Soviet fabricated components used in Chinese aircraft is unknown, so the largest gaps cluster there.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100170022-2: A declassified CIA file with comments on a draft project about long-term supply trends. The draft, critiqued. The document holds the comments. The file remains. Declassified files like this open a window on the past.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100040073-2:
Two covering letters dated 9 December 1959 send out the same enclosure. The enclosure is the Director's statement to the Joint Economic Committee of Congress. It was given on 13 November 1959. Its topic was United States and Soviet growth rates, side by side. The writer notes the press accounts of the statement. He offers the full text to readers who saw only the press form.

The talk is said to hold the Agency's latest thinking. Its theme is Soviet economic growth. It also shows, the letter adds, the close tie between spy work and policy. Copies went to those addressed, with the enclosure. File copies stayed with the economic research offices. Those offices had drafted the talk. The pair of letters shows how a director's public talk was passed round as a reference paper. It went both inside and outside the Agency.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090005-2:
Soviet economic growth is the subject of an address by Allen W. Dulles to the Subcommittee on Economic Statistics of the Joint Economic Committee, delivered 13 November 1959 as part of the subcommittee's study comparing the United States and Soviet economies. He opens by praising the papers submitted by experts from the academic world, government, and research groups. Warns that the deliberations bear directly on the response the country must make to the growing challenge of Soviet power.

Since his recent visit to the United States, Khrushchev has been preaching peaceful coexistence, raising hopes of a genuine relaxation of tensions. Against those hopes the address sets the measurement problem: widely divergent views are aired in academic circles, the press, and Congress, and the crucial question is who can forecast the future. Earlier American long-term growth is weighed as one benchmark for judging Soviet claims.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090023-2:
'The Challenge of Soviet Power' is an address by Allen W. Dulles to the Edison Electric Institute at New Orleans on 8 April 1959. The audience makes the topic apt, he begins. Lenin defined Communism as the Soviet system plus electrification. The first Soviet economic plan of the early 1920s set a modern electric power system among its chief aims.

In effect, the Soviets propose to electrify Marxism. They may shock their backward political order into key with their modern technical skills. Or they may electrocute the archaic Marxist system itself. The measuring chapters follow. Soviet primary energy output is set as a share of American output in 1958. By 1965 it will come close to sixty percent. The absolute gap has narrowed since 1950. The gap in steel output has likewise shrunk for five years. The widest gap in steel capacity was apparently reached in 1958.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090041-2:
The Soviet economic challenge is taken up by William Benton in an address to the Economic Club of Chicago, 8 April 1959, preserved in Central Intelligence Agency files. Benton praises the club's talks on the gravest economic problem of the time. He has not read the papers of his three predecessors on the program, he says, so as not to steal their material or be accused of stealing it.

He expects to be their Cassandra. His friend Philip Reed had predicted the Soviet Union would take a century to catch up with the United States in electric power output. Benton sets his own darker view against that comfort. Chicago, where his career began in 1928 at Lord and Thomas, breeds optimism, he concedes. The speech dwells on harder matters. One is the unsolved problem of succession in a dictatorship, where power must pass without terror and bloodshed: Khrushchev is already sixty-five.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090050-2:
Speaking notes on Soviet economic penetration were prepared for a Department of Commerce committee meeting. The committee deals with Soviet activity and world trade. The notes open with a caution: cold war issues cannot be expressed solely in economic terms, since the Soviet challenge also embraces military, political, and subversive arenas. Military force and its threat, used often postwar to take over the European satellites, were Stalin's principal weapon.

Iran, Greece, Berlin, and Korea are named as places where military action or its threat was used. Yet the notes judge that the Soviet Union does not now intend to use military power in a way that risks general war. Economic penetration gets its own case. Yemen is called a prime example of investment in disorder. Soviet arms and aid stir incidents in its disputes near the Aden Protectorate. The spot controls one entrance to the Suez Canal.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090104-2:
Notes on Soviet Economic Penetration is a short declassified Agency note built from figures rather than prose. It puts Soviet gross national product in 1957 at about 170 billion dollars. At the stated growth rate, that sum would reach 225 to 235 billion dollars.

The note weighs how light the aid burden sat on Moscow. Bloc credits and grants to free world nations came to about 1.5 billion dollars over four years. That cost ran under one tenth of one percent of Soviet output per year. Tables at the end set Bloc and United States aid side by side for nations such as Burma, Egypt, and Greece.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100021-2:
ERA/RR Orientation is a declassified Agency recruiting talk given at a university in the fall of 1959. The speaker lays out the pros and cons of Agency work and invites students to personal interviews. The Agency is described as eleven years old, set up under the National Security Act of 1947.

The talk explains where the speaker's own part of the Agency fits. It held the major national duty for economic intelligence on the Bloc. Work there differs from university research, the audience hears, because the National Security Council is the customer for all of it. A new permanent building, funded at over fifty million dollars, is cited as proof of support in Congress.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100049-2:
A portion of a declassified Agency address on Soviet power, in rough scanned type, opens in mid-argument on radio and electric power. It states that no nation, not even Hitler's Germany, used radio for subversion on the Soviet scale. Millions of words for Communism were beamed to the free world each day.

The text adds that the Bloc spent heavily to jam broadcasts aimed at its own people. Soviet electronics output had grown eight times between 1950 and 1958, to roughly half the United States level. Military electronics output reached 150 percent of the United States figure. Later pages weigh the energy gap, which a cited study expected to widen somewhat.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s01099r000100010010-2:
Summary of Survey Report of FI Staff, DD/P is a declassified Agency survey summary on how a staff in the Clandestine Services was working. It finds the staff's own mission statement imprecise. The statement did a poor job of defining the staff's role in guiding area divisions that collect foreign intelligence.

Two units, the Operations Division and RQM, spent much of their time reviewing single projects one by one. The summary judges the gain too small for the effort spent. New authority letting Division Chiefs approve projects up to 10,000 dollars freed the staff to shift its effort. A deeper flaw is also named: no long-range plan could form while senior staffs competed for the same area division resources.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100120001-2:
Economic Penetration of Underdeveloped Areas by the Communist Bloc is Staff Study No. 12 of the CFEP Drafting Group, held here with revised and new pages laid over the draft of May 20, 1955. Substituted pages include page 1, page 3 with its long footnote, and pages 6 and 7. The study asks what stance the United States should take toward Bloc aid offers.

Its argument keeps room for judgment case by case. In some places, the study grants, Bloc aid might add to growth and calm in the nation that took it. Such an outcome could even serve United States aims by chance. Each offer is thus to be weighed on its own facts and setting. The study survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100160007-2:
Staff Study #16, U.S. Policies on Enforcement of Controls, is summed up here in a declassified analysis of its problems and deficiencies section, pages 10 to 16. Joint flaws lead the list. Talks dragged, and partner nations showed little zeal for an enforcement program.

That coolness is traced chiefly to the political climate in Europe. Rising hopes for coexistence made controls harder to sell, and fears of uneven sacrifice played a part too. Understaffed enforcement offices and weak legal bases are also named. The China differential is called the most active and troublesome enforcement problem. United States checks on non-list goods close the summary. The summary survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100170006-2:
Illegal and Clandestine Trade is section IV of a declassified Agency study of unrecorded trade with the Sino-Soviet Bloc. Intelligence work in this field, the section states, had rested mainly on single transactions. Some effort had also gone into estimates of Communist China's unrecorded imports and of Bloc exchange available to pay for them.

Banned goods leave no statistical trail, so estimates stay rough. Smaller volume goods named for China include precision instruments, petroleum products, and transport equipment. Recent signs pointed to a shift in Chinese wants toward more advanced industrial goods. The section is candid that no firm total value for such imports can be given.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100190004-2:
A declassified Agency office memorandum dated 20 June 1955 sends two CFEP staff studies out for fast coordination. The studies are No. 8, on differentials between United States and joint controls, and No. 19, on the balance of payments of the European Soviet Bloc. Copies had arrived on June 30, and the drafting group was set to meet in near continuous session.

Attached comments take up Study No. 19 in detail. Soviet gold sales draw the sharpest scrutiny: 150 million dollars in 1953 and about 125 million in 1954. Those figures, the comments note, carried the largest margin of error of any in the study's main table.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100200011-2:
Political Impact of Free World Controls on Trade with the Sino-Soviet Bloc is Staff Study No. 20 of the CFEP Drafting Group in revised form, draft of June 27, 1955. It was contributed by the Defense Department. Like its earlier form, it weighs what joint trade controls cost the Sino-Soviet Bloc against what they cost the free world.

New material takes up Yugoslavia and the reach of Titoism. The study quotes the June 1955 Belgrade and Brioni declaration by the Yugoslav and Soviet governments. That text praised wider economic cooperation and the removal of blocks to it. Such moves, the study implies, test how flexible the Western control system can be. The Agency's CREST files preserve the study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000200060124-2:
Information Relating to Names Listed in Paris Tel. 1212, 23 September 1953 is a declassified Agency name file on firms tied to East-West trade. Its first entry covers P.S.A.L. of Antwerp, whose initials stand for Polish Steamship Agency. The firm had sat on the Commerce Watch List since 3 May 1951.

A Commerce report quoted here calls P.S.A.L. the most active East-West forwarder in Antwerp. It handled shipments to Polish and other East Baltic ports as broker, insurer, and transit agent. A second entry covers Hoveco of Brussels, listed as an import-export firm. Later notes tie an Antwerp branch to a planned diversion of Belgian copper wire to Poland that a Geneva firm's refusal helped stop.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000200100002-2:
Diversion Control Panel Case Inventory Supplement No. 12 is a declassified list of suspected trade diversion cases, each with file references. Case 459 covers borax: a Zurich firm, Oleine SA, shipped 23 tons to DIA Chemie in East Berlin by way of Austria. Swiss officials told inquirers the case would be checked against Swiss controls.

Case 460 turns to wide band oscilloscopes routed from Germany toward China by way of Belgium. Four cases holding one such scope were reported aboard a ship. A third case weighs a businessman's claim about vast amounts of Venezuelan Bunker C oil. Each entry stays brief: goods, route, source cables, and what action had followed. The list survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000100040055-2:
Report on Operation of Audio Surveillance Equipment Course is a monitoring report by an observer who sat through the course from 9 to 15 May 1960. Its stated aims were threefold. Students were to run certain audio gear, handle minor first level upkeep, and use selected gear under cover.

Four students were booked, but only three attended, at grades GS-12 to GS-14. Most were bound for overseas posts within months. The observer questions the course's place in the catalog. A field technician who installs the gear could check out local staff on its use, he argues. Still, he stops short of calling the course needless, and weighs that fix instead. The report survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000100040091-2:
Intelligence Orientation Course #37 is the subject of a monitoring memorandum dated 18 January 1960. The observer followed the course from 4 to 15 January 1960 at the request of the Chief of the Intelligence School. Its first block, Introduction to Intelligence, carries the weight of the course.

That block aims to teach the basic concepts of intelligence and its place in national security. The roles of the several intelligence agencies, and their links, come next. The functions of the Agency itself, from collection to the sharing of finished work, close the list. About ninety percent of the block's time serves those aims. Fixes urged include more time on questioning and discussion skills.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200020083-2:
Comments on Part-Time Training is an office memorandum dated 29 July 1960 from the Chief of the Intelligence School. It names the courses that suit part-time training best. They are courses in skills tied closely to the student's own job, where practice between classes can be watched and applied.

Writing, speaking, management, and research techniques head that list. Courses that prepare students for jobs they have not yet begun are ruled out by the same logic. A practical gain is also claimed. In full-time courses, teachers must steal their own preparation and paper reading time from class hours. Part-time pacing, the memo argues, eases that squeeze. The memo survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cicero-letters-shuckburgh-vol-2:
Caesar's rise darkens the second volume of Cicero's letters, in Shuckburgh's 1899 version. The Republic slides toward its death throes year by year. Cicero endures exile, wins return, and watches old freedoms fail around him.

He writes to friends in hope one week and despair the next. Power gathers into fewer and fewer hands in his reports. The greatest letter writer of antiquity records his world's end in real time. Readers gain both fine drama and rich fact here, since no source shows the texture of late republican life, its fears and favors, half so well.
cinq-mars-volume-2:
Alfred de Vigny builds court tension in Cinq-Mars, Volume 2 of the English edition. Young Cinq-Mars now shines as favorite of Louis XIII, while Richelieu's agents watch every step he takes. A crowded trial scene fills key pages, with judges filing back as a packed hall holds its breath. Political agents, De Vigny shows, had primed the crowd with mysterious tales beforehand.

Simple people in the hall cling to first judgments even after clear evidence speaks against them. De Vigny pauses over that stubbornness, since courts and crowds decide real fates in his story. Favor at court proves just as fragile as a verdict in such an air. Marie de Gonzague still draws the hero's heart upward, beyond his station. Readers in this second volume watch the machine of Richelieu's France at work, grinding slowly, while the favorite dances on its edge and calls the danger glory.
comte-positive-philosophy-martineau-1853:
Volume 2 of The Positive Philosophy of Auguste Comte appeared in Harriet Martineau's English version in 1853. Comte, the French founder of positivism, ranked the sciences and traced how human thought moves from theology to science. Martineau condensed his six French volumes into two clear English ones.

Volume 2 reaches the higher sciences and Comte's new science of society, which he helped name sociology. He argued that social life, like nature, follows laws that study can find. Martineau's version, praised by Comte himself, completed the English Positive Philosophy. Through it, British and American readers met positivism in a form they could actually finish, and debates on science and society changed.
conscience-volume-2:
Hector Malot follows a murder being planned in Conscience, Volume 2 of the English edition. Saniel, the poor Paris medical student, has settled the day and weapon for Caffie's death. A butcher's knife, he notes, will point police toward the wrong trade. Morning weakness angers him; he calls himself lamb at dawn and tiger by night.

Malot turns the planning into a study of a divided mind. Saniel rehearses philosophy to avoid rehearsing the act, and knows it. The francs his future needs wait behind an old man's door. Glady and the Wednesday circle move on, ignorant of the design. Conscience here is still a voice Saniel argues with, not yet its master. Readers midway through the novel watch a starved man reason himself across a line other villains cross in rage.
coralie-everyday-life-library-no-2:
Coralie, by Charlotte M. Brame, issued as Everyday Life Library No. 2, is a first-person tale told by Edgar Trevelyan. Passing rich on eighty pounds a year, he begins, though he went without a good dinner far oftener than he had one. His father, Captain Trevelyan, died in his childhood; his mother, a meek invalid, never recovered the loss.

She contrived three years of college for him out of slender means, believing in his dreams of fame. A summons home ends them. His mother is dying, and his sister Clare, once a blooming girl of eighteen, lies on a couch with a spinal complaint from which she is not likely to recover. At twenty he is alone with her, his mother's income gone. A lady with a spray of heliotrope enters later, fastening it in Sir Edgar's coat.
corinne-or-italy-volume-1-of-2:
A novel in two volumes by Mme de Staël, printed here in English as Corinne, or Italy, fills this first volume. The London edition from J. M. Dent and Company is dated MDCCCXCIV and carries an introduction by George Saintsbury. Its story joins Oswald, a young English lord, with Corinne, a famed poet and guide to Italy.

Early books bring the pair through Rome and the rites and sights that shape their bond. Corinne shows Oswald her pictures, speaks on art and letters, and wins fame at the Capitol. The talk ranges over Italian manners, faith, and the place of women. Readers get both a love story and a close look at Italy as the heroine reads it.
correspondence-of-wagner-and-liszt-volum:
Volume 2 of the Correspondence of Wagner and Liszt, in Francis Hueffer's English translation, carries the two composers' letters from the mid-1850s to 1861. Wagner writes from Zurich, London, and Paris: exiled, indebted, and composing the Ring and Tristan between appeals. Liszt answers from Weimar, where his court theater premieres the works Germany will not touch. The letters mix money, casting, publishers, and doctrine. Each man is the other's only full audience, and both know it, which gives the friendship its voltage and its quarrels.

Inside, the Tannhäuser catastrophe in Paris closes the volume's arc. Liszt's generosity (loans, performances, and praise in print) meets Wagner's genius for needing more. Hueffer, the Wagnerite critic, lets the letters speak without varnish. Readers get the central friendship of nineteenth-century music in its working years, the decade when the music of the future was financed by letters like these.
cosmopolis-volume-2:
Paul Bourget poisons his Roman salons with anonymous letters in Cosmopolis, Volume 2 of the English edition. Novelist Julien Dorsenne, a guest in the Steno and Gorka circle, turns detective against his will. Twelve letters, someone claims, have warned Count Boleslas Gorka about his wife. Julien has lied once already to shield the set, and his conscience will not pardon the lie.

Countess Steno, a Venetian beauty of the old stamp, has told her lover everything herself, Julien reasons. Madame Gorka seems too truthful to deceive, and too easily deceived by others. Spiteful Lydia Maitland, the American wife, watches every crack in the circle widen. An Italian proverb guides the hunt: who cannot feign friendship cannot play the enemy well. Bourget slows the plot into pure motive study here. Readers in the second volume learn how gossip works as a weapon among people too polished to strike openly.
critical-and-historical-essays-volume-2:
Thomas Babington Macaulay's second volume of Critical and Historical Essays sorts its pieces under foreign history, political controversy, and literary criticism. Macaulay opens with Machiavelli, defending the Florentine's name against centuries of abuse, and continues through Ranke's History of the Popes, the War of the Spanish Succession, and Frederic the Great. Political essays take up Southey's Colloquies, the civil disabilities of the Jews, and Gladstone on church and state.

The literary half judges Bacon, Bunyan, the Restoration dramatists, Addison, Samuel Johnson, Madame d'Arblay, and Byron. Every essay argues a verdict with parade-ground confidence and a memory stocked with quotation. Readers may quarrel with the sentences Macaulay passes, but few essayists have ever made judgment itself this entertaining.
curiosities-of-literature-vol-2:
Short pieces of literary lore by Isaac Disraeli fill this second volume of Curiosities of Literature. Frederick Warne and Company of London issued this new edition, edited with memoir and notes by the author's son, the Earl of Beaconsfield. The contents run to near a hundred heads.

Charles the First, the Duke of Buckingham, and the death of Charles the Ninth open the set. Later pieces treat fireworks, writing stuffs, the early drama, and the Jews of York. Richardson, usurers of the 1600s, and the trade in tea, coffee, and chocolate all find a place. Disraeli mixes anecdote with short inquiry. The volume is a storehouse for readers who like odd facts about books and men.
curtius-history-greece-vol-2:
Tyrants and lawgivers rule the second volume of Curtius's History of Greece, in Ward's 1868 version. The archaic age sees Greek cities test one form of rule after another. From these trials the polis, the self-governing city-state, is born.

Solon, Sparta's stern order, and thriving colonies fill the account. Curtius traces how Greece hit on its most original gift to politics. Trade, verse, and law grow together in his broad picture. The volume shows a world of rival cities learning freedom the hard way, long before Athens rose to the height that later volumes celebrate in full.
darwin-descent-of-man-vol-2:
The second volume of Charles Darwin's The Descent of Man appeared with the first in 1871. Darwin gives most of it to his theory of sexual selection, first sketched in volume one. The volume closes his full case for the evolution of man.

Bird by bird and beast by beast, Darwin shows how mates choose by song, color, horns, and display. He argues such choices shaped the peacock's tail and much of human variety too. The book's closing chapters turn to mankind itself. Together, the two volumes caused a storm that has never fully settled.
darwin-life-and-letters-vol-2:
Volume Two of Darwin's Life and Letters, edited by his son Francis in 1887, covers fame and its costs. The Origin of Species appeared in 1859, and Darwin's quiet home at Down became the center of a scientific revolution. His letters carry the fight.

Friends like Huxley, Hooker, and Gray defend evolution in public while Darwin works at home. The Descent of Man and his books on plants and worms follow in turn. Ill health, family sorrow, and steady kindness mark the private record. The volume closes with his death and burial in Westminster Abbey in 1882. His working habits, down to his daily walks, come out in the letters.
davis-rise-and-fall-vol-2:
Volume Two of Davis's Rise and Fall, also from 1881, turns from argument to the war itself. Davis narrates the campaigns, his quarrels with generals, and the collapse of the Confederacy. He writes from the Confederate White House point of view.

He defends his choices on strategy, appointments, and the defense of Richmond. The fall of the capital, his flight, and his capture close the narrative. Davis shows little doubt and less regret, which shapes how historians use the book. Read beside the memoirs of Grant and Sherman, it completes the war's great triangle of command accounts.
demosthenes-public-orations-pickard-vol-:
Demosthenes was Athens' greatest public speaker in the fourth century BCE. Arthur Wallace Pickard-Cambridge translated his public orations, and volume two completes the set. On the Crown, his most famous speech, anchors the volume.

Demosthenes spent years warning Athens about Philip of Macedon's growing power. The Philippics urged resistance, while the Olynthiacs pleaded for aid to allies. On the Crown defends his whole career against a rival's prosecution. His sentences build like waves, mixing law, history, and patriotism. Pickard-Cambridge keeps the argumentative fire readable. Together with volume one, the set preserves Greek oratory at its peak.
dialogues-of-the-buddha-vol-2:
Volume two of the Dialogues of the Buddha, translated by T. W. and Caroline Rhys Davids in 1910, continues the Digha Nikaya's long discourses. The middle suttas of the collection stand here. The talks range over courts, groves, and debating halls of the Buddha's India.

The great discourse on the origin of things retells creation as a slow fall from light into craving and kingship. Other talks weigh sacrifice, self-mortification, and the bliss of meditation in careful steps. The Buddha often teaches by parable and by questions that turn the hearer around. The Rhys Davids version keeps the Pali's dignity in plain English.
dialstone-lane-part-2:
Chapters five to eight of W. W. Jacobs's novel fill this second part of Dialstone Lane. Mr Chalk's planned trip to the Southern Seas has become a standing joke with the Captain. The Captain waylays him to ask after his progress and to advise him on every sea emergency, known and unknown.

Tired of the sport, Chalk stays away from Dialstone Lane for a spell. The Captain takes instead to Edward Tredgold, whose sharp word on Binchester folk pleases him. His niece, Miss Drewitt, professes not to have noticed the young man's gifts. Mrs Chalk presides in gloomy silence at the coffee pot in a breakfast scene. This file holds part two only, and breaks off mid-tale.
diana-of-the-crossways-volume-2:
Volume two of George Meredith's Diana of the Crossways spans chapters nine to seventeen. Diana Warwick, a brilliant Irishwoman separated from her husband, holds a delicate position in London society. A night of conflict opens the portion, as friends press her to defend herself. She chooses dignity and flight instead.

A journey in a chariot carries Diana and her talk across England. Her friend Emma, an invalid of deep loyalty, anchors the emotional story. A midnight bell and an early morning scene raise the tension. Diana earns the name Princess Egeria, the advising nymph, for her counsel to a rising statesman. Meredith fills these chapters with dialogue of unusual sparkle. Reputation, friendship, and a woman's right to her own life are the stakes throughout.
diderot-and-the-encyclop-dists-vol-1-of-:
The first volume of John Morley's study of Diderot and the Encyclopaedists fills this file. Macmillan of London and New York issued it in 1905, in a line first published in 1886 and reprinted since. Morley says in his preface that the book closes his studies on the literary road to the French Revolution.

Unlike his Voltaire and Rousseau volumes, this one stays close to transcript and analysis. Diderot's circle, Morley holds, cannot be taken as known. Faults of the great Encyclopaedia's plan get fair play: printing is set under logic beside heraldry, and naval architecture falls under social jurisprudence. Taine's bright, one-sided attacks are noted and weighed. The volume is a full map of a movement, in volume one of two.
die-alchemie-das-ist-die-lehre-von-den-g:
A plea for the lost secret medicines of the old doctors fills Dr Gottlieb Latz's book, printed at Bonn in 1869 at his own cost. Its title calls alchemy the teaching of the great secret means of the alchemists, and of the speculations tied to them. Latz writes first for doctors, he says, and then for every educated thinker.

His preface sets two scales side by side. In pathology, modern exact research crushes the vague guessing of old times. In therapy, he argues, the old doctors stand higher, for thousands of years ago they knew the arcana, and that knowledge is lost but for himself. The emerald tablet and its philosophy of the whole world get close study. The book is one man's bid to restore a lost art of healing.
dio-cassius-roman-history-cary-vol-2:
Books twelve through thirty-five of the Roman History of Dio Cassius survive, like the first books, only in fragments. Earnest Cary's Loeb translation carries them in this second volume. Dio wrote around 230 CE, and Byzantine excerptors saved these pieces after the full text of the early books was lost.

The fragments track the takeover of the Mediterranean world by Rome. They cover the defeat of Macedon, the ruin of Carthage and Corinth, and wars in Spain and the east. The full history ran to eighty books and is the broadest Roman narrative that survives. This volume bridges the lost early books and the whole books that follow.
diodorus-library-booth-vol-2:
Volume Two of Booth's Diodorus holds Books Eleven through Twenty of the Library of History. The Sicilian's survey now reaches firmer historical ground. Greek wars and the rise of Macedon fill these books.

Persian invasions, the Peloponnesian War, and Alexander pass in review. Later books cover the heirs who split Alexander's empire. Diodorus often copies good sources that else are lost. That habit makes him vital despite a plain style. The volume is a big, useful store of ancient history, much of it found nowhere else in full. Scale and survival give the set its worth.
dionysius-halicarnassus-roman-antiquitie:
Books three through five of the Roman Antiquities of Dionysius of Halicarnassus appear in this second volume of Edward Spelman's 1758 English version. Dionysius wrote around 7 BCE. His tale now moves from the later kings to the birth of the republic.

Tullus Hostilius and the Tarquins rule, fall, and give way to consuls. The young republic fights its neighbors and strains between rich and poor at home. Dionysius tells these years at great length, with speeches he composed for the actors. His account is the fullest that survives for the last kings and the first decades of free Rome.
doe-osti-17198160-analysis-report-for-pr:
Mahawa-Essa Akara of Sandia documents how the 2025 groundwater surface map was built for the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant in New Mexico, in report SAND2026-27313R. The plant buries defense nuclear waste deep in salt beds. Above it, the Culebra layer of the Rustler Formation carries groundwater, and its water level surface is mapped every year under a 2009 state order.

Well water levels feed an averaged MODFLOW6 groundwater model. Calibration used an ensemble of 100 parameter sets for transmissivity and related values. Output gives contour lines of equivalent freshwater head across the site for 2025. Particle tracking then traces where a drop of water would travel. Measured and modeled heads are compared, and an appendix tracks yearly water level trends.
doe-osti-2999083-sierra-sd-its2sierra-us:
Dagny Beale, Gregory Bunting, David Day and fellow members of Sandia's Sierra Structural Dynamics team wrote this user's manual, SAND2025-12459, printed 2 October 2025. It covers Its2Sierra version 5.26, a small tool with one bridging job. Radiation codes in the Integrated TIGER Series compute where energy lands inside a part. Their output grids rarely match the grids a Sierra strength analysis wants to use.

Its2Sierra maps energy deposition and volume values from the radiation code's zones onto the Sierra mesh, stored in the shared Exodus file format. The manual gives release notes for each version, then the input and running instructions. Recent versions added smarter placement of values, including weighting by inverse distance to the nearest Gauss point on the output mesh. The handoff matters because a sloppy transfer quietly corrupts every stress result downstream. The tool stays under active development by the Sierra/SD team.
doe-osti-3001898-refining-peakdecoder-ve:
Aivett Bilbao, Ashfiqur Rahman and Andrea Harrison of PNNL report a software rebuild in September 2025: PeakDecoder version 2. Metabolomics tools stack separations, liquid chromatography plus ion mobility plus fragment spectra, into data cubes too dense for manual reading. PeakDecoder is an AI tool that interprets such mass spectrometry data, finding and counting single metabolites in complex mixtures.

Version 2 re implements the software in C#, chosen to suit commercialisation. The training set grew, the model was fine tuned on it and benchmarked, and a prototype inference module with a graphical interface was built. That lets biologists, not just programmers, run it. Support for an additional ion mobility instrument vendor's format widens the market. Funded through the lab's LDRD strategic investment, the short report records a translation step. Research code was hardened into a product shaped tool, with checks to show nothing was lost in the move.
doe-osti-3008976-science-amp-technology-:
The December 2025 issue of Science and Technology Review, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's magazine, leads with optimizing future design. Writers Noah Pflueger-Peters, Elliot Jaffe, and Lilly Ackerman are among the issue's contributors, and the magazine appears eight times a year for a broad audience.

The cover feature describes Livermore's pairing of additive manufacturing with high-performance computing design codes to move from concept to prototype quickly, including parts built for extreme environments. Research highlights cover low-temperature radiation detectors that resolve atomic-scale physics and new tools against wildfires. A commentary by Anup Singh opens the issue, and laboratory news items fill the back pages.
doe-osti-3010168-final-scientific-report:
Final report for SPIRAL, DOE award DE-SC0022305, led by Lara Estroff of Cornell with co-investigators at Johns Hopkins, Michigan, and elsewhere, covers September 2021 to August 2025. SPIRAL pairs artificial intelligence with laboratory experiments to find better solar cell materials than silicon.

The test material is metal halide perovskite, as efficient as silicon but fragile against water and ultraviolet light. New AI codes embed more of the underlying chemistry of how atoms interact, and experiments tracked how ingredients cluster in solution before heat forms the crystal. Cesium proved a key player in forming the lead-iodide species that seed perovskite nuclei. Three codes and their datasets were released publicly.
doe-osti-3014949-national-laboratory-of-:
The United States geothermal market is surveyed in the National Laboratory of the Rockies 2025 market report, written with Geothermal Rising. Coverage spans power generation, direct use, and heat pumps, with cost trends, drilling economics, and the project pipeline tracked since 2020. Dayo Akindipe led the author team.

Sections follow power purchase and offtake activity, federal incentive updates, and development on public land, including wells on Bureau of Land Management acreage and projects at Defense Department installations. One thread tracks enhanced geothermal systems as they move toward commercial use, with capital cost broken down by activity and drivers of drilling cost reduction examined in detail. The levelized cost and power sales price analysis ties the market numbers back to what buyers actually pay for geothermal power.
