doe-osti-3017994-project-1-collects-proj:
Guangdong Zhu of the National Laboratory of the Rockies was technical contact, with John King also named on the record, for this February 2026 cooperative research final report, NLR/TP-5700-93777. It bundles two projects under agreement CRD-16-00625. Project 1, COLLECTS, worked with Combined Power's Hyperlight Energy on concentrating solar collectors. Project 2 handled measurement and verification for a Saputo Cheese solar project.

COLLECTS chased disruptive collector designs meant to push concentrating solar power past the SunShot vision targets and toward cost parity with conventional generation. The laboratory gave technical consulting through the project. One thread guarded the design against a real risk: failing the SRCC OG-600 solar collector standard, which the lab helped the team design to pass. The second project verified performance at the cheese plant installation. Together the two halves show the laboratory's solar role in miniature: push new designs, then measure what actually got built.
doe-osti-3365792-maccs-user-guide-versio: MACCS got guide-5.2'd, and this DOE user guide covers version 5.2. The pages detail the findings. The engineers get their data. The guide was user. The data were engineer. The 5.2 were version. The engineers were data. The guide were user.
doe-osti-3408141-software-verification-o: VARPOW got software-verified, and this DOE text covers Rev.2 verification. The pages detail the software findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The version was 2. The data were nuclear. The Rev.2 were software. The VARPOW were verification. The 2 were version.
donovan-pasha-and-some-people-of-egypt-v:
Donovan Pasha and Some People of Egypt, Volume 2, by Gilbert Parker, opens with Fielding Had an Orderly. Parker describes Ibrahim the orderly without kindness. His legs were like pipe stems. His face seemed made of brown putty. His eyes had the dull, sullen look of a mongrel dog. When he was excited, they turned brownish red. Everyone could read trouble in that glare.

Selamlik Pasha blamed hashish. Fielding blamed Ibrahim's mixed blood. Little Dicky Donovan blamed something else, and kept his eye on the man. Fielding believed in people who served him. Parker calls that habit bad in the Orient. The Eye of the Needle, A Treaty of Peace, At the Mercy of Tiberius, and All the World's Mad complete the volume. Five tales circle one question. How does an Englishman know whom to trust in a country that is not his?
droll-stories-volume-2:
Honoré de Balzac wrote his Droll Stories as tales supposedly collected from the abbeys of Touraine, and volume two holds the second ten. Balzac dresses the tales in mock-old French dress and sets them among kings, nuns, clerks, and courtesans of an earlier France. Titles promise the merry tattle of the nuns of Poissy, the continence of King Francis the First, and a succubus, a demon who visits sleepers.

His prologue scolds critics who attacked the old-fashioned language and vows to finish a hundred such tales. The stories are bawdy, brief, and built for a punch line, with adultery, trickery, and clerical mischief as steady fuel. Balzac the tireless realist began as Balzac the gleeful storyteller, and this volume proves it.
dynevor-terrace-or-the-clue-of-life-volu: Dynevor Terrace, or The Clue of Life, volume two, by Charlotte Yonge. The tale concludes. This book preserves that Victorian novel. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
embers-volume-2: Gilbert Parker's Embers, volume two, is a book of verse opening with Dolly, a spring ballad of King Rufus hunting deer. Granada, epitaphs, the sea-reapers, the watcher and the waking follow, with poems of love, the lily flower, an ancient pledge and a tribute of kings. The collection moves between ballad, lyric and epitaph, closing in twilight, waiting and a last dream.
ethics-part-2:
Benedict de Spinoza devotes part two of his Ethics, in Elwes's translation, to the nature and origin of the mind. His preface says he will treat only what can guide readers toward understanding the mind and its greatest happiness. Body, he defines, is a mode expressing God's essence under extension.

Spinoza argues that the mind is the idea of the body. Ideas, he says, follow the same order as things. Our knowledge of outside bodies comes through our own body's changes, so it stays partial. Memory, imagination, and the kinds of knowledge are sorted in the propositions. The part ends by opening his theory of the emotions, developed next, and of human freedom beyond.
euclid-elements-heath-vol-2:
Volume two of Heath's Euclid covers Books Five through Nine of the Elements. The 1908 translation moves from shapes toward numbers in these books. Proportion theory opens the volume with Book Five's masterly treatment.

Eudoxus's theory of proportion handles ratios of any magnitudes, even irrational ones. Books Seven through Nine then build arithmetic from definitions of number. Primes, even and odd numbers, and perfect numbers receive proofs. Euclid shows that the primes never run out in Book Nine. The bedrock of arithmetic was set down twenty-three centuries ago here. Heath's commentary connects each proposition to later mathematics with care.
euripides-plays-way-loeb-1912-vol-2:
Volume two of Way's Loeb Euripides, first printed in 1912, holds Electra, Orestes, Iphigenia in Taurica, Andromache, and Cyclops. The scan staged here is a 1929 reprint. Electra and Orestes work out the price of avenging their father in blood.

Orestes, half mad after the deed, faces trial by his own city. Iphigenia in Taurica turns a priestess of human sacrifice toward rescue and escape. Andromache shows Hector's widow crushed between a new mistress and old grief. Cyclops, the lone surviving satyr play, plays the Polyphemus tale for rough laughs. Way's verse keeps all five in one English voice across the volume.
evan-harrington-volume-2:
Volume two of George Meredith's Evan Harrington carries the tale from chapter eight to chapter thirteen. Evan, the tailor's son passing as a gentleman, travels among people who must not learn his trade. His sister the Countess de Saldar directs the campaign from afar. An eccentric old diner at the Aurora tavern opens this portion.

The Countess descends into low society to manage her brother's chances. Doings at an inn mix comedy with risk of exposure. A cricket match, Fallow Field against Beckley, gives the volume its sporting centrepiece. Evan's love for Rose Jocelyn grows while his secret grows heavier. Meredith keeps the tone bright, but every laugh turns on the English terror of being found out as a tradesman.
eve-s-diary-part-2:
Twain's Eve's Diary, Part 2 continues Eve's daily record in Eden. Mark Twain keeps the frame of a translated original diary. This part moves through Sunday and Monday entries. Eve's mood lifts after heavy days she prefers not to recall.

She tells how she tried to fetch Adam some forbidden apples. Poor throwing foiled her, though she thinks her intent pleased him. On Monday she tells Adam her name and is hurt by his indifference. She reflects that a loving heart is true riches. Adam's rare, well-chosen word that morning gives her hope for him. Her longing for companionship shapes this part of the diary.
evliya-travels-hammer-vol-2:
Deeper into Asia goes the second volume of von Hammer's Evliya selections, from 1834. Anatolia, the Caucasus, and lands beyond pass before the traveler's eye. Cities, shrines, trades, and wonders are cataloged with the same delight as before.

Evliya is half Marco Polo and half gossip columnist in these pages. He loves a good story and rarely lets doubt spoil one. Yet his detail on daily Ottoman life is rich and rare. Readers who finish this volume will grasp why his Seyahatname, the book of travels, stands unmatched as a portrait of an empire at ease with itself.
falkland-book-2:
Lytton's Falkland, Book 2 turns to Emily Mandeville and her dangerous awakening. Edward Bulwer-Lytton's early tale here reflects on a married woman's inner life. Emily wed young, before she knew herself, to a man she could not love. Her son's birth gave her feelings one safe channel.

Falkland's arrival breaks that dormancy of feeling. The narrator warns that stillness and self-communing suit Emily ill. To fly the world's follies proved less safe than to pursue them, he argues. Her tenderness spreads over all around her by nature. Meeting Falkland ends her separate, selfish existence, the text declares. Book 2 dwells in motive and mood more than event. It sets the moral stakes for the books ahead.
following-the-equator-a-journey-around-t:
Following the Equator, Part 2, by Mark Twain, brings his round the world steamer close to Australia. Twain opens Chapter IX with a calendar maxim about climate and human surroundings. Then he gives a night scene fifty miles from Sydney. Passengers are called up in the darkness to watch the sea catch fire. Splashes of phosphorescence, the cold light made by tiny living organisms, stretch into corkscrew shapes. They look like sea serpents, fifty feet long and clothed in living fire, racing past the ship.

Twain writes the display as pure wonder before settling back into diary and conversation. Part 2 carries the voyage through Australian waters and colonial ports. His usual cargo comes aboard: character sketches, statistics argued over, and local people quoted at length. The lecture tour that paid his debts is the engine underneath the narrative. The book hides that labor under magnificent scenery like this.
frederick-chopin-as-a-man-and-musician-v:
Frederick Niecks's second volume of Frederick Chopin, as a Man and Musician continues the biography into the Paris years. The first volume ended with the young Pole's arrival in the west. Here the mature career unfolds: fame as pianist and teacher, and the long liaison with George Sand. Niecks gathers letters and testimony with his declared method, facts before conclusions.

The rupture with Sand, the English and Scottish tour, and Chopin's early death close the life. Later chapters judge the music itself, work by work, with a scholar's patience. Niecks corrects Liszt's rhapsodies from documents wherever he can. This volume carries the heavier half of his evidence, including the recollections of pupils and friends. Together the two volumes made the foundation on which all later Chopin biography stands. Dry in manner, it remains indispensable in matter.
freeman-norman-conquest-vol-2:
The year 1066 itself fills the second volume of Freeman's Norman Conquest, from 1867. Stamford Bridge and Hastings decide England's fate within three weeks. Harold falls, William triumphs, and nothing in the island's life stays the same.

Freeman narrates the most famous year in English history at unmatched length. Marches, omens, shield walls, and the fatal arrow all get their due. He writes as scholar and as Saxon partisan at once. No fuller telling of the two battles exists, and readers who want the Conquest in depth, day by day and source by source, start their study here.
freytag-soll-und-haben-bd-2:
Anton Wohlfart's trials deepen in the second German volume of Freytag's Soll und Haben, in the 1874 printing. The firm's fortunes sway with debt, speculation, and war's shadow. Anton must hold to honest work while others chase quick gain.

Love, loyalty, and loss test the young merchant to his core. Freytag closes his epic of commerce with the triumph of steady character. The ledger's two heads, debit and credit, frame a whole ethic of life. In its own tongue, the book shows the style that taught a rising class to see itself as worthy of serious fiction.
friends-in-need-ship-s-company-part-2:
Jacobs tells a comic tale of three thirsty friends in a waterside pub. Joe Gibbs is out of work and out of money. His mates Brown and Kidd hatch a scheme. They will report that Gibbs drowned while helping on a lighter. Then they will pass the hat for his widow. Gibbs only has to stay out of sight.

The fraud works better than planned. Sympathy raises a solid sum at the local pubs. But Gibbs chafes at hiding while others hold the cash. The friends must break the news that he lives before his wife spends it. Jacobs builds the joke from pub talk and sharp timing. The dialect carries much of the humor.
froissart-chronicles-johnes-vol-2:
The second volume of Froissart's Chronicles, in Thomas Johnes's translation from the 1844 Smith edition, completes the work. The story runs from the war's middle years to the deposition of Richard II in 1399. Froissart himself visited Richard's court in 1395 and presented the king a book of his poems.

Revolts shake both kingdoms here: the peasants of England and the towns of Flanders rise and are crushed. The volume ends with Richard's fall to Henry Bolingbroke, told with an eye for ceremony and doom. Froissart's index closes the set. His chronicle remains the fullest narrative of the fourteenth century's wars and courts.
fromont-and-risler-volume-2:
Alphonse Daudet shifts his gaze to the wives in Fromont and Risler, Volume 2 of the English edition. Claire Fromont, the partner's wife, reflects on her childhood playmate Sidonie, now Madame Risler. Their friendship is falling away bit by bit. Claire, busy with a child and a mother in dotage after a tragic death, has little time to dwell on it.

She refuses jealousy of Sidonie's rise from the Chebe shop to near equality. Claire tries to teach the younger woman society's ways, like a provincial pupil. Sidonie accepts advice badly, gratitude nowhere. Risler, too old for his bride, adores her past warning. Daudet shows the factory household through its kindest eyes here. The effect is damning: even Claire's charity cannot make Sidonie honest, and the marriage shows its cracks to everyone except the husband.
froude-english-ireland-vol-2:
Secret societies stalk the second volume of Froude's Irish history, from 1872. The Whiteboys swear oaths and strike by night in the countryside. The Volunteers arm in the towns, and government loses its grip year by year.

Froude traces the long slide toward the rising of 1798. Grievance piles on grievance as reform fails again and again. His vivid style carries readers through a century of trouble. All his strong opinions stand on display, for friend and foe to judge. The volume forms the tense middle of his Irish tale, where patience runs out and violence gathers its forces.
froude-history-england-vol-2:
Henry the Eighth breaks with Rome in the second volume of Froude's History, from 1856. The divorce from Catherine of Aragon drives the quarrel with the pope. The Act of Supremacy then makes the king head of England's church.

Froude's bold defense of Henry begins in earnest in these pages. He casts the king as the rough tool of a needed national change. Monasteries fall, old loyalties tear, and a new order takes shape. The account stirred fierce dispute among clergy and scholars alike. It remains a gripping, partisan telling of the birth of the English Reformation.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1004a-2: Editors of the Foreign Relations volume placed this note right after document 1004, as a signpost to a new subject. It tells readers where papers on the allocation of shipping are printed in the volume. Those papers cover the employment of captured German vessels, among other questions. They appear later, at page 1191, under the heading United Kingdom — Allocation of Shipping. The note is a finding aid only. It records no decision and adds no facts about the Potsdam talks themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-2:
An editorial note in volume two covers a meeting for which no official record has been found. It follows document 710 among the unnumbered items of the Potsdam papers. The meeting was President Truman's first with Prime Minister Churchill at the conference.

The editors quote Truman's own later account of the visit, which he calls social. No business of the conference was discussed, Truman writes in his memoirs. He did tell Churchill he had an agenda he would like to present at the meeting. Asked if he had one, Churchill answered that he did not need one. The two men then talked briefly about the latest news from the Pacific war. The note is a small lesson in the limits of the archive. One of the summit's first encounters survives only in a participant's memory.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d750a-2: A second editorial note follows document 750 in the second Potsdam volume. Two notes at one point signal a knot in the record the editors wanted untied. The Foreign Relations series uses these brief guides to cite files and mark links. Readers crossing this part of the volume get extra bearings here.
gao-gaoreports-b-290452-2:
The matter of VSE Corporation is decided in GAO decision B-290452.2, dated April 11, 2005. VSE protested the cancellation of a solicitation for storage, upkeep, and disposal services for personal property seized by federal agencies. The buyer was the Bureau of Customs and Border Protection, in the Department of Homeland Security. The request for proposals bore the number CS-00-007. GAO denied the protest. This copy is a redacted version cleared for public release.

The digest gives the core ground: the solicitation no longer matched the agency's needs. Funding for it was also unsettled. Nearly five years had passed since proposals first came in. New sources might now compete, the agency held.
gao-gaoreports-b-293134-2:
Blue Rock Structures, Inc., sought its protest costs in GAO file B-293134.2, decided October 26, 2005. Blue Rock had won a protest over construction contracts at Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, North Carolina. The Navy was the buyer. GAO recommended reimbursement, with sums that included $19,728. The decision works through the rules on legal fees. Fees need not be split between won and lost issues where the issues share one set of facts.

A rate above the cap in the Federal Acquisition Regulation could still stand if it matched going rates for like work. Time spent on settlement talks and on a debriefing, though, could not be charged.
gao-gaoreports-b-294266-2:
SWR, Inc., brought both a protest and a cost claim in companion GAO files B-294266.2 through B-294266.4, decided April 22, 2005. The Marine Corps had awarded Starlight Corporation a contract to wash aircraft at three air stations in the Carolinas. GAO denied the protest and the cost request. The board's finding that SWR's technical plan was unacceptable rested on real flaws. They included weak plans for managing work across sites and for tracking tools.

Recent poor work at one of the same sites fairly outweighed older, better records elsewhere. The cost claim failed on timing: it reached the agency more than 60 days after counsel got the protected decision.
gao-gaoreports-b-295399-2:
On July 25, 2005, GAO issued its ruling in file B-295399.2, the protest of B.H. Aircraft Company, Inc., a small business. The Defense Logistics Agency had bundled spare parts for the F404 aircraft engine into one logistics contract. The deal covered more than two thousand national stock numbers. The firm held a current parts contract that the new deal would absorb. It claimed the bundling broke the Small Business Act and the Competition in Contracting Act of 1984. GAO denied the protest.

The agency had shown a measurably substantial benefit from buying the parts under one contract. It had also shown that the single contract was needed to meet its needs. Both showings, made as the law requires, carried the day.
gao-gaoreports-b-295402-2:
Lockheed Martin Corporation sought proposal preparation costs in GAO file B-295402.2, dated November 1, 2005. The costs arose from its bid for a design and development contract under the Air Force's small diameter bomb program. GAO had sustained a Lockheed protest in that purchase in February 2005. Here, though, GAO declined to recommend reimbursement. The digest states the outcome in one line: on the record as a whole, the costs would not be repaid.

Proposal costs are repaid only in narrow settings, tied to agency fault that forced the spend. The decision weighs the full record and finds that test unmet. No sum is granted.
gao-gaoreports-b-295529-2:
Dated June 27, 2005, GAO files B-295529.2 and B-295529.3 record Johnson Controls World Services, Inc., as the protester. The Army had judged it cheaper to run base operations at Walter Reed Medical Center with its own staff. The judgment came from an A-76 cost study. The firm said the in-house cost figure left out required costs. While the case ran, the Army's Independent Review Official withdrew certification of the in-house plan. That step, the digest holds, rendered the protest academic.

With the certification gone, the cost comparison it backed could not stand as issued. There was nothing left for GAO to undo.
gao-gaoreports-b-295530-2:
CW Government Travel returns, with five fellow travel firms, in companion GAO files B-295530.2 through B-295530.4, dated July 25, 2005. The target this time was the price scheme of the Army travel solicitation. GAO sustained the protest on that point. Offerors need not propose binding fees for the services sought. Without binding fees, the agency could not judge what offers would cost the government. It had not explained why it could not ask for such pricing.

A second point denies CW Government Travel's bid to reopen the earlier minimum-amount ruling. The new material gave no basis to disturb it.
gao-gaoreports-b-295533-2:
GAO ruled in files B-295533.2 and B-295533.3 on July 1, 2005, in the protest brought by SOS International, Ltd. The Drug Enforcement Administration had awarded McNeil Technologies a contract for linguistic services at its San Diego Field Division. SOS said the winning bid should have been thrown out as nonresponsive. GAO denied the protest. The winner's tiered pricing did not condition its bid in any way. Its bid was low at any of the tiered prices.

A second point covers quantity. The winner offered more than the stated maximum. Its bid did not limit the government's right to buy only up to that maximum, so the offer stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-296090-2:
Kola Nut Travel protested Army awards for travel services in GAO decision B-296090.2, dated June 17, 2005. The winners were Ravenel Brothers and AirTrak Travel. The work was travel help for Defense staff. The firm said the winners were not true small firms. It also hit a fee deal and its own marks.

GAO denied the protest. Firm size is a call for the Small Business Administration, not GAO. The fee deal paid a share of gains from the work. GAO saw no proof of undue sway over officials. The marks on the firm's plan were backed by clear notes. No strong reply was made.
gao-gaoreports-b-296135-2:
City Chemical protested Army awards for two dyes in GAO decision B-296135.2, dated June 17, 2005. The winner on both calls was Nation Ford Chemical. One call sought solvent yellow dye 33. The other sought solvent green dye 3. The firm said its dye was wrongly tagged as a foreign good.

GAO denied the protests. The raw dye from abroad made up more than 50 percent of the cost of all parts in the dye. That share made the end good foreign under the Buy American Act. A price mark-up tied to that rule was thus proper. The ruling is a neat guide on how cost share sets origin.
gao-gaoreports-b-296136-2:
Advanced Environmental Solutions sought its protest costs in GAO decision B-296136.2, dated June 20, 2005. The first fight was over an Air Force award to Eason Enterprises. The work was to move and dispose of hazardous waste. The firm had hit how past work was scored.

GAO denied the request for costs. The fight had gone moot on its own track. The Small Business Administration found the winner not fit for the award. The Air Force then cut the deal and set a fresh pick. GAO said that chain broke the link to the protest. Costs need a protest that drove the fix. That link was not shown here.
gao-gaoreports-b-296176-2:
Clean Harbors protested a National Institutes of Health award for waste work in GAO decision B-296176.2, dated December 9, 2005. The winner was Clean Venture. The work was full chemical and low-level radioactive waste care on the main campus. The firm said past work marks were flawed.

GAO sustained the protest. The call told the agency to weigh how close past jobs were to this one. GAO found no try at all to weigh that fit. That miss went to the heart of the marks. The ruling shows a stated test must be used. Skipping it can undo an award, even when the rest looks sound.
gao-gaoreports-b-296231-2:
Med Optical protested a Veterans Affairs award for eyeglasses and eye exams in GAO decision B-296231.2, dated September 7, 2005. The winner was Vision MarketPlace. The work served veterans in Broward County, Florida. The firm said the winner lacked a site within 5 miles of a VA site, as the rules required. It also hit past work marks.

GAO denied the protest. The record backed the past work marks for the winner. Claims about the firm's own marks also failed. Any slips there did not harm its chance to win. The ruling turns on harm. A mark error that did not change the result will not undo an award.
gao-gaoreports-b-296246-2:
The Sandi-Sterling Consortium sought its protest costs in GAO decision B-296246.2, dated September 20, 2005. The first fight was over an Army award in Iraq. The winner was Meridian International Center. The work set up a health care partnership. It aimed to help Iraq staff, train, and run its health system.

GAO denied the request. The Army moved to fix the buy before it filed its main report. That early move cut the claim for costs. The grounds were also not shown to be clearly strong. Costs need a strong claim or a slow agency. Neither was shown on this record.
gao-gaoreports-b-296371-2:
Metro Business Systems protested a copier purchase order in GAO decision B-296371.2, dated July 13, 2005. The seller was Ameritel, a Canon dealer. The buyer was the Corporation for National and Community Service. The order was for 16 copiers. It used federal supply schedule rules.

GAO denied the protest. The agency did not have to state needs for network fit and safe use in advance. It had not left the pick of goods to the vendors. It could weigh traits shown in product books. Traits that can be seen in the books are fair game. The pick thus stood on a sound base.
gao-gaoreports-b-296435-2:
Incident Catering Services protested its loss in a Forest Service food contest in GAO decision B-296435.2, dated September 7, 2005. The work was mobile meals at fire sites. Firms would feed crews in the field. The firm hit its tech marks. It also said facts near at hand were missed, and that talks were due.

GAO denied the protest. Marks fit the stated tests and were sound. Facts not in the bid need not be hunted down. Gear facts can shift from call to call, so the bid must state them. Talks were a choice call for the buyer. No abuse of that choice was shown.
gao-gaoreports-b-296516-2:
Optical Systems Technology protested the loss of a night sights contest in GAO decision B-296516.2, dated March 17, 2006. The winner was Knight's Armament Company. The buyer was Special Operations Command. The sights clip onto rifles for night use. The firm said its test sights were tried in a flawed way.

GAO denied the protest. The agency took sound steps to mount and set the sights well. There was no base to find those steps failed. Even if the set-up was not perfect, the sights broke down and lost strength in tests. That trait made them not fit. A good that fails in fair tests can be shut out.
gao-gaoreports-b-296697-2:
Intercon Associates sought its protest costs in GAO decision B-296697.2, dated June 14, 2006. The first fight hit the terms of a General Services call for e-forms tools. The firm had won on one point and lost on one. It sought 76,014.06 dollars in costs. The agency backed a far lower sum.

GAO denied the full claim and backed the lower sum. The sum backed was 25,328.03 dollars. Costs for the lost point could be cut out. That point stood on its own facts. A page count of the briefs was a sound way to split the costs. The method split won and lost work by the space each took.
gao-gaoreports-b-296855-2:
Odyssey International protested a Labor Department bar to fixing a bid slip in GAO decision B-296855.2, dated November 16, 2005. The work was a new dorm at the Red Rock Job Corps Center. The site held 178 beds. The firm's low bid held a slip it sought to fix. The bid stayed low after the fix.

GAO sustained the protest. The firm proved its slip and its true bid with clear proof. Sheets and sworn words backed the claim. The agency barred the fix due to other slips it feared. Those fears were not shown and were not raised with the firm. A proved slip in a still-low bid can be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-b-296948-2:
YORK Building Services protested an Agriculture award for cleaning work in GAO decision B-296948.2, dated November 3, 2005. The sites were three office blocks in Washington. A fourth site was for reuse work only. The buy was set aside for small firms. The firm said marks broke the call terms.

GAO sustained the protest. The pick note did not match the call. The call gave more weight to tech points and stressed tech edge. The pick note gave no clear cause that fit that weight. A pick must be writ in a way that shows the stated weights were used. A bare note that skips the weights cannot stand.
gao-gaoreports-b-297178-2:
TECHi2 protested a General Services task order for Marine Corps work in GAO decision B-297178.2, dated November 28, 2005. The winner was Anteon Corporation. The work backed command and control plans. It served the Corps force growth center. The firm hit past work marks for the bids.

GAO denied the protest. Past work marks fit the scheme in the call. They were also sound on the facts. The order was on a time and goods base. Past work fights need a flaw in scheme or facts. No such flaw was shown here. The order thus stood. The case is a brief past work ruling with a clean scheme check.
gao-gaoreports-b-297234-2:
Wiltex protested a Veterans Affairs award for a medical air unit in GAO decision B-297234.2, dated December 27, 2005. The winner was Medical Gas Technology. The site was the VA Medical Center in Syracuse, New York. The work was to set a scroll medical air compressor unit. The firm said the winner's bid missed key terms.

GAO sustained the protest. The winner's bid did miss key terms in the call. The agency still gave it the deal. At the same time it cut the firm's bid for like gaps. That split was unfair. Like gaps must face like calls. A firm cannot be cut for a gap that the winner was let to keep.
gao-gaoreports-b-297240-2:
OMNI Government Services protested an Army and Small Business choice in GAO decision B-297240.2, dated March 22, 2006. The work was media and visual help for a missile command. The need was put in the 8(a) plan. It was set for Alutiiq Global Solutions. The firm held the old deal and sought to bid.

GAO denied the protest. The new need would cost far more than the old deal. The gap topped 25 percent of the old cost. That gap made it a new need in the rules. A new need can go in the 8(a) plan. The old holder has no right to block that step. The choice thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-297261-2:
MadahCom sought a fresh look at a cut of its protest in GAO decision B-297261.2, dated November 21, 2005. The Army Corps sought alarm systems for sites in Germany. The buy was held to holders of set task deals. The firm said that bar was wrong. It also said the orders would top the scope of those deals.

GAO granted the fresh look. The cut as late was wrong. A claim that a call bars fair play is on time when filed before the close for task bids. The 10 day rule used for the cut did not fit this claim. The cut was thus undone. The merits would be heard on the right clock.
gao-gaoreports-b-297276-2:
Information Ventures protested a Centers for Disease Control award in GAO decision B-297276.2, dated March 1, 2006. The winner was BRI Consulting Group. The work was help for a cancer control unit. It held facts growth and spread work. The firm hit cost and tech marks on staff counts.

GAO sustained the protest. Cost and tech marks clashed on staff counts. The agency did not square that clash. It also leveled work hours in its cost check in a flawed way. Leveling hours can hide true cost gaps. When cost and tech views clash and hours are leveled with no cause, the pick cannot stand.
gao-gaoreports-b-297320-2:
Spectrum Security protested a Homeland Security award for guard work in GAO decision B-297320.2, dated December 29, 2005. The winner was Ahuska Security. The work was hold and move services for detainees. The buy was set aside for small firms. The Small Business office later found the winner was not small. Size was the lead claim.

GAO sustained the protest in part and denied it in part. No pre-award note of the winner's name was given. A size claim thus came after award. The winner was found not small on time. The deal should end and go to a small firm. Other claims failed. Sub work share and sub past work use were both fit under the call.
gao-gaoreports-b-297391-2:
East-West Industries protested an Air Force award for aircraft cranes in GAO decision B-297391.2, dated July 19, 2006. The winner was Regent Manufacturing. The cranes lift canopies, seats, wings, and more from planes. The firm hit past work and risk marks for both bids. It named flaws in the winner's past jobs.

GAO denied the protest. Of four past jobs, just one matched this work in size and depth. Two were part match and one was no match at all. Those calls were sound. On the winner, most named flaws were not known to the buyer in person. Known flaws were weighed and did not cut its mark. The award thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-297425-2:
KIC Development protested a Housing award for lead checks in GAO decision B-297425.2, dated January 26, 2006. The winner was Legin Group. The region was the Atlanta region. The same lead test call was at stake. The firm's bid was cut as not fit. The call set a skill test the firm met through its sub firm.

GAO sustained the protest. The scheme let firms meet skill tests through key staff or sub firms with a firm pledge. The sub firm clearly met the test. To bar the bid for the lead firm's own gap broke that scheme. Sub skill counts when the call says it counts and the pledge is firm.
gao-gaoreports-b-297444-2:
Low and Associates protested a National Science Foundation award in GAO decision B-297444.2, dated April 13, 2006. The winner was Dynamic Research Corporation. The work was visual facts support services. The firm held part of the old work. It said the agency eased key call terms for the winner with no new call.

GAO sustained the protest. An agency must score and pick by the tests and terms in its call. It cannot ease or shift those terms in the dark. To shift them, it must amend the call. All firms must then get a fair chance on the new terms. Easing terms for one firm alone breaks fair play.
gao-gaoreports-b-297447-2:
Gemmo-CCC protested a Navy award for power work in Italy in GAO decision B-297447.2, dated July 13, 2006. The winner was Consortium Montservis-DeFranceschi. The site was Aviano Air Base. The work was to upgrade the power grid. The firm hit marks. It also sought a chance to cure gaps in its bid. One gap was missed vendor data for switch gear.

GAO denied the protest. Marks and the pick fit the call tests and were sound. The cure sought would have been talks, not a mere clear-up. Talks were not due here. The call had warned award could rest on first bids. Gaps left in a first bid thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-297535-2:
SAP Public Services protested an Air Force award for combat support software in GAO decision B-297535.2, dated February 10, 2006. The winner was Oracle Corporation. The pack held software, rights, support, and training. It backed a new field support system. The firm said the winner's quote broke call terms on market sale of the goods.

GAO denied the protest. The record showed the winner's quote met the terms. The firm in plain words had no proof for its claim. Dissent with scored views on non-price points is not a base to win. Risk marks on cost growth were part of the call. The trade-off used costs as the call set them.
gao-gaoreports-b-297687-2:
Magnum Medical Personnel protested an Air Force award for clinical staff in GAO decision B-297687.2, dated June 20, 2006. The winner was Luke and Associates. The work puts health staff in Air Force clinics in the United States. The buy was set aside for small firms. Up to five deals could be made. The firm was the low price bidder.

GAO sustained the protest. Marks for the firm and the winner broke the terms of the multi-award call. The firm was hurt by those flaws as the low price bidder. In a multi-award call, marks must track the set plan for each deal. Flawed marks that cost the low bidder a deal cannot stand.
gao-gaoreports-b-297791-2:
Ideamatics protested a Marine Corps award for tech support in GAO decision B-297791.2, dated May 26, 2006. The winner was Kadix Systems. The system tracks manpower moves for active, reserve, and retired staff. Work held study of the system and upgrades to its tools. The winner was higher rated and higher priced.

GAO denied the protest. Marks and the pick fit the call and were sound. The firm's claims were mere dissent with the end calls. Dissent alone does not show a review was wrong. A firm must point to a flaw in facts or method. No such flaw was shown here. The award thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-297807-2:
Al Long Ford sought bid and protest costs in GAO decision B-297807.2, dated October 18, 2007. The sum sought was 477,051.31 dollars. GAO had backed the firm in the truck case. The Army fought the claim. Proof and timing were the flaws it named. Talks with the agency were also at stake.

GAO denied the request. The claim was not well proved and was not on time. The firm also made no fair try to reach a deal with the agency first. Cost claims need full proof, on time, after a fair try to settle. All three steps failed here. A win on the protest does not cure a weak cost claim.
gao-gaoreports-b-297815-2:
Information Ventures protested the axing of a Health call in GAO decision B-297815.2, dated February 13, 2006. The user was the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry. The work backed peer review work. It held plans for review meets and picks of expert panels. Funds for the buy were pulled. The firm said the axe dodged its past protest.

GAO denied the protest. Lack of funds is a sound cause to axe a call. That cause holds even when a protest spurred the axe. Bad faith in the fund pull must be shown to beat it. No such proof was made. The axe thus stood on the fund gap.
gao-gaoreports-b-297879-2:
Metro Machine protested the same Navy ship award in GAO decision B-297879.2, dated May 3, 2006. The winner was again Earl Industries. The work was ship fix and refit work in Norfolk. The firm hit the cost check on the winner's bid. The winner would use team firms for most hands-on work. Those firms charged more.

GAO sustained the protest. The cost check missed the team firms' higher rates. That miss skewed the true cost of the winner's plan. When team firms do most of the work, their rates drive true cost. A cost check that skips those rates is not sound. The pick thus fell on cost grounds.
gao-gaoreports-b-297904-2:
Starlight Corporation protested the axing of an Air Force call for plane services in GAO decision B-297904.2, dated April 14, 2006. The site was McChord Air Force Base in Washington. Work held plane wash, de-ice work, and alert help. The firm had won the deal. A rival protest then hit how skill terms were read. The call was axed.

GAO denied the protest. The skill term in the call was vague. Two fair reads of it stood in clash. One read asked for more skill than the true need. That clash could harm fair play. An agency may axe a vague call that could skew the field. The axe had a sound base here.
gao-gaoreports-b-297910-2:
Foresight Science protested a National Science Foundation pick in GAO decision B-297910.2, dated November 30, 2006. The winners were Dawnbreaker and Development Capital Networks. The work was tech help for small firm grant teams. Those teams held phase I awards for new tech growth. The firm held the old work. It hit marks and the pick.

GAO denied the protest. Marks and the pick fit the call and were sound. The record backed the scores for the quotes. An old holder has no edge in a fresh contest. It must win on its quote as drawn. Dissent with scores, sans a flaw in facts or method, will not undo a pick. The choice thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-297915-2:
CIGNA Government Services protested a twin Medicare claims award in GAO decision B-297915.2, dated May 4, 2006. The winner was Palmetto GBA. The same claims call was at stake. After last bids were in, the agency spoke with the winner. The winner then shifted its bid. Work hours it would give were part of the shift.

GAO sustained the protest. Talks that let a firm shift its last bid are true talks. True talks must be held with all firms in the field. The firm got no such talks. That gap broke fair play. A post-final shift in hours is a key shift, not a mere clear-up. The award thus fell.
gao-gaoreports-b-297986-2:
Boersma Travel Services protested a Veterans Affairs travel award in GAO decision B-297986.2, dated November 17, 2006. The winner was Duluth Travel. The same travel center call was at stake. The buy was set aside for firms owned by disabled veterans. The firm hit marks on its bid. Two marks were cut in error.

GAO denied the protest. Marks and the best value pick were sound in the main. Two slips did cut the firm's bid in two spots. Those slips were not large. They did not sway the pick on this record. Harm is the test. Slips that do not change the win do not undo an award.
gao-gaoreports-b-298076-2:
Morgan-Keller protested an Air Force award for a new commissary in GAO decision B-298076.2, dated August 1, 2006. The winner was Nelson Refrigeration. The site was Fort Detrick, Maryland. The user was the Defense Commissary Agency. Past work far outweighed price in this call. The firm hit skill and past work marks and the pick.

GAO denied the protest. Skill and past work marks fit the call tests. The pick flowed from those marks in a sound way. When past work is top weight, a firm must win that test to win the deal. No flaw in those marks was shown. The award thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-298156-2:
Alaska Structures sought protest costs in GAO decision B-298156.2, dated July 17, 2006. The call was for a portable hospital system. The buyer was an Army medical unit. The agency fixed the first call fast, before its report was due. It then set a new call. The firm filed a fresh protest on the new call and sought costs for both.

GAO denied the request on both rounds. Fast fix before a report is due bars costs for round one. That rule spurs fast fixes. Round two costs failed as well. The flaw the fix left was not shown to be clearly strong. Costs need clear strength or a slow fix. Neither was shown.
gao-gaoreports-b-298164-2:
Alfa Consult protested an Army Corps fix plan in Iraq in GAO decision B-298164.2, dated August 3, 2006. The firm held a deal for build and refit work. A rival protest had hit that award. The agency chose to end the firm's deal, hone the call, and take fresh bids. The firm said that fix was needless and wrong.

GAO denied the protest. The call was vague on how the win would be set. It mixed best value words with a low cost path. That clash could have swayed the first win. A fix that ends a deal won on a vague call can be sound. Clear pick rules must come first.
gao-gaoreports-b-298201-2:
Veteran Enterprise Technology Services protested an Army choice in GAO decision B-298201.2, dated July 13, 2006. The holder was Wexford Group International. The work backed the Rapid Equipping Force. The deal was set aside for firms owned by disabled veterans. The Small Business office found the holder was not such a firm. The firm said the deal must end.

GAO denied the protest. The Army had made a sound call of urgent need at award. The rules let work go on in that case, despite the size find. An urgent need call, when sound, can keep a deal live. The plea to force an end thus failed.
gao-gaoreports-b-298216-2:
SDA sought protest costs in GAO decision B-298216.2, dated September 11, 2006. The call was for a lease to build a federal courthouse. The site was Bakersfield, California. The lease would run for 10 years. The holder was Castle and Cooke California. The agency ended that lease and axed the call. The protest was then cut as moot.

GAO denied the request. The firm did not show the lease end was a fix for a clearly strong protest. Costs need that show. An agency act that ends a fight is not proof the fight was strong. With no proof of strength, costs fail.
gao-gaoreports-b-298232-2:
Waltron sought protest costs in GAO decision B-298232.2, dated August 18, 2006. The calls were for a liquid cooling system corrosion inhibitor. The pack sizes were 55 gallon drums and 5 gallon drums. The buyer was a Defense Logistics Agency center in Richmond. The sole backed good was Nalcool 2000. The agency had pledged a fix.

GAO denied the request. The agency did not drag its feet on the fix. It moved in a fair time. Costs for a slow fix need proof of undue delay. No such delay was shown here. A prompt fix, even after a pledge, does not earn costs on delay grounds.
gao-gaoreports-b-298233-2:
Dellew Corporation protested an Air Force award for logistics readiness work in GAO decision B-298233.2, dated September 13, 2006. The winner was Defense Contract Services. The site was Hurlburt Field in Florida. The buy was set aside for small firms. The work held a broad set of readiness tasks. The firm hit past work marks and the pick.

GAO denied the protest. Past work marks fit the tests stated in the call. They were also sound on the record. A firm must show a flaw in scheme or facts to win a past work fight. No such flaw was shown. The award thus stood on clean marks.
gao-gaoreports-b-298237-2:
Doug Boyd Enterprises protested a FEMA choice on home upkeep in GAO decision B-298237.2, dated August 6, 2007. The work was care and shut-down of made homes and trailers in Mississippi. Ten small firms held wide deals for the work. Each deal ran for 5 years. Low and high caps were set for each deal. The firm was passed by for a task order.

GAO dismissed the protest. Task orders under such wide deals sit outside GAO protest power. This order was no down-pick that would change that rule. A firm in the pool has no GAO path to fight a missed order. The choice thus stood with no review.
gao-gaoreports-b-298240-2:
Kolob Canyons Air Service protested its cut from a Forest Service contest in GAO decision B-298240.2, dated July 11, 2006. The winner was Courtney Aviation. The work was planes for air attack on wild fires. Planes serve as posts for air bosses. They guide the air space over a fire. Gear rules for the planes were key.

GAO denied the protest. The firm's planes missed the gear rules in the call. Its plans to fix that gap were too thin. A bid must show it meets gear rules or give a full fix plan. Thin plans leave the agency unsure the planes can fly the task. The cut from the field was thus sound.
gao-gaoreports-b-298281-2:
Bannum protested a Bureau of Prisons award for halfway house work in GAO decision B-298281.2, dated October 16, 2006. The winner was Dismas Charities. The zone was Orlando, Florida. The work was community corrections center services for federal offenders. The call set award on first bids to the bid in the best interests of the state. The firm hit award with no talks.

GAO denied the protest. No talks were due on this record. The bids let the agency tell which bid was best value with no more facts. Talks are due when they are needed to pick a win. When first bids are clear, an agency may pick with no talks.
gao-gaoreports-b-298313-2:
Aviation Technology protested a Marine Corps award for pump test stands in GAO decision B-298313.2, dated September 21, 2006. The winner was Dayton T. Brown. The goods were two hydraulic pump test stands. The winner was higher priced and higher rated. Points were set for plan, past skill, and past work. Plan held half the points in all.

GAO denied the protest. The buy was a best value buy, not low price wins. The price and tech trade was sound on the record. A higher rated firm can win at a higher price when tech points weigh that much. The firm did not show the trade broke the call terms.
gao-gaoreports-b-298421-2:
Metcalf & Eddy Services, Inc. protested a U.S. Agency for International Development source selection in Egypt. The agency picked CDM International, Inc. for talks on engineering services. The work covered small-scale infrastructure projects. GAO decided B-298421.2 and B-298421.3 on November 29, 2006.

The firm said the agency scored the firms' presentations in a flawed way. It also claimed talks with the agency were too thin. GAO read the record against the solicitation terms. It found the scoring tracked those terms and the briefs given to rivals. No flaw in the process was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298436-2:
Kearney & Company protested the rejection of its quotation under a General Services Administration request. The buy sought financial management services for the Department of Homeland Security. Awards would take the form of blanket purchase agreements. GAO ruled in B-298436.2 on October 4, 2006.

The agency found the quotation technically unacceptable. GAO agreed with that call. The quotation lacked facts on a team member in the planned teaming plan. Without those facts, the agency could not fully judge the offer. A gap that blocks review can sink a quotation. The rejection was fair on this record. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298494-2:
Four firms joined in protesting the Defense Information Systems Agency's Encore II awards. The protesters were Computer Sciences Corporation, Unisys Corporation, Northrop Grumman Information Technology, Inc., and IBM Business Consulting Services--Federal. The contracts cover information technology services for defense and other federal users. GAO ruled in the B-298494.2 series on May 10, 2007.

The firms faulted the scoring of technical merit, past record, and price. They also attacked the agency's talks with offerors. GAO focused on talks about subcontracting plans. Plans were scored, many were first found unfit, and firms rewrote them after agency input. Such talks count as discussions, with the duties that follow. GAO sustained the protests.
gao-gaoreports-b-298543-2:
Maden Technologies protested the same Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency award at issue in a linked case. The contract went to Beta Analytics, Incorporated for support services. The work serves the agency's Security and Intelligence Directorate. GAO ruled in B-298543.2 on October 30, 2006.

Maden raised a conflict-of-interest claim about a subcontractor. That person had once served as an agency evaluator. GAO found the risk eased by a signed non-disclosure pact. The record showed no aid in drafting the winning proposal. Maden also alleged a bait and switch on nine swapped staff. No proof of a false promise was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298582-2:
Aeronautical Instrument & Radio Company protested a Navy award to Tel Instrument Electronics Corporation. The contract covered aircraft navigation test sets. The gear serves tactical aircraft at the mid-level of upkeep. GAO decided B-298582.2 and B-298582.3 on January 10, 2007.

The firm raised three lines of attack. It said the agency slighted a stated taste for off-the-shelf goods. It faulted praise for the rival's program manager pick. It also sought leave to fix a claimed price error. GAO found each claim weak on the record. The rivals used shelf goods to a like degree. The price claim lacked proof. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298626-2:
Raytheon Company, Space and Airborne Systems, protested an Army award for the joint cargo aircraft. The contract went to L-3 Communications Integrated Systems. The plane's tasks span supply runs, troop movement, and relief flights. GAO decided B-298626.2 and B-298626.3 on September 27, 2007.

Raytheon attacked the scoring of both its offer and the winner's. A key point was the aircraft service ceiling test. GAO found the terms gave fair notice that ceiling skill would count. Raytheon's plan rested on a new flight mode with thin proof. The agency could fairly mark it as a high risk. Its own score of marginal stood. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298682-2:
Global Solutions Network, Inc. filed a fresh protest on the same Army HRsolutions buy. The contract again covered task order management and financial support. The set-aside was for HUBZone small firms. GAO ruled in B-298682.2 on December 10, 2007.

This round, the firm said agency needs had shifted since bids went in. On that view, the terms and offers no longer fit the true work. The Army granted some growth in workload. It said staff hires and more machine aid would absorb the change. GAO found that account fair. The terms still matched the agency's needs. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298772-2:
Freedom Lift Corporation protested Veterans Affairs awards of lift line items to Bruno Independent Living Aids, Inc. The buy covered wheelchair and scooter lifts for vehicles. The users are veterans with limited mobility. GAO decided B-298772.2 on January 25, 2007.

The firm saw mixed picks across items as a flaw. GAO held that each item had its own price-merit trade-off. Distinct calls on distinct items can stand side by side. The firm also read a 350 pound lift rule loosely. The terms set that bar with no share-of-vehicles qualifier. Its narrow reading found no base. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298810-2:
Hernandez Consulting LLC protested the rejection of its proposal as technically unfit. The Federal Emergency Management Agency ran the buy. The work covered site operations and upkeep at FEMA housing sites in Louisiana. The set-aside was for veteran-owned small firms. GAO ruled in B-298810.2 on December 21, 2006.

The agency found key facts missing from the proposal. Those facts were needed to judge the offer in full. GAO agreed that the gaps were real. A firm must supply the facts its bid is judged on. Thin bids cannot shift that load to the agency. The rejection was fair. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298840-2:
Global Analytic Information Technology Services, Inc. protested an Agriculture Department award to Information Technology Experts, Inc. The contract covered end-user information technology support services. The protester was the prior holder of the work. GAO decided B-298840.2 on February 6, 2007.

Two flaws drove the result. The agency marked the firm's offer down for thin cost-saving facts. Yet savings were not a stated test for scoring. A hidden test cannot shape a score. The agency also let the winner file a required price rate late. Rivals had to file that rate at the set time. Unequal talks broke fair play. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298935-2:
M.Braun, Inc. protested an Environmental Protection Agency purchase order to Premier Technology, Inc. The buy covered a glovebox for the agency's lab in Denver, Colorado. The box lets staff probe risky substances in a sealed space. GAO ruled in B-298935.2 on May 21, 2007.

The winner's bid, GAO found, had come in late. The terms held a late-bid rule with set exceptions. None of those exceptions fit this bid. An agency may not weigh a late bid when its own rule bars it. The order thus rested on a bid that should have been set aside. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298949-2:
Caddell Construction Company, Inc. renewed its protest after the State Department stood by the same embassy award. The work again covered a new compound in Djibouti. The winner was American International Contractors (Special Projects), Inc. GAO decided B-298949.2 on June 15, 2007.

This round turned on business volume. The 1986 security law asks for volume at least equal to the project value. That mark must be met in 3 years of the 5-year span before the buy. GAO found the agency's read of the law strained. Its read cut words out of the statute. It also clashed with the law's past. The winner was not fit for award. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298953-2:
GPA-Buffer, LP sought payment of costs from a protest over a sole-source lease deal. The General Services Administration had struck the deal with the state of Florida. The land would host a U.S. Army Southern Command headquarters. GAO acted in B-298953.2, a costs ruling, on March 21, 2007.

Cost payment needs a strong protest plus slow agency action. GAO found the record short on both counts. It did not show the agency sat idle in the face of a clearly sound claim. The land deal gave the state a 40-acre site role at no cost. Such facts blurred any claim of clear merit. The plea failed. GAO denied the request.
gao-gaoreports-b-299042-2:
Southwest Research Institute protested an Air Force call to cancel and reissue a request for quotations. The buy covered boom operator and trainer simulation systems. The gear trains crews to run the refueling boom on KC-135 aircraft. GAO ruled in B-299042.2 on March 23, 2007.

The firm said its bid met all terms and earned an order. The agency saw the case in a distinct light. It found the scoring scheme did not match its true needs. A new scheme would also spur wider rivalry. An agency may cancel when its terms miss the mark. That call was fair here. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299046-2:
Para Scientific Company protested a National Institutes of Health award to Fisher Scientific Company LLC. The buy covered laboratory supplies for a diabetes and kidney diseases institute. The request listed 22 items with set counts. GAO ruled in B-299046.2 on February 13, 2007.

The agency made one award for the whole list. It picked the bid with the lowest total price. GAO found a cheaper path in the record. A split award for 6 items to the protester would have cut the total bill. Nothing showed a split would hurt the agency. The single-award call was not in the government's best interest. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299091-2:
AdaRose Inc. asked GAO to revive an earlier protest over Army armaments software support. The Army Joint Armaments Contracting Center ran the buy. The plea also sought payment of protest costs. GAO acted in B-299091.2 on January 14, 2008.

The first protest had been set aside as moot. The agency pledged a fix and dropped its pick. That pledge made the old fight moot in full. GAO then weighed the delay claim. It found no undue delay in the agency's fix work. A revival plea fails when the old pick is gone. A cost plea fails without shown delay. GAO dismissed the revival plea and denied the costs.
gao-gaoreports-b-299241-2:
Shirlington Limousine & Transportation, Inc. protested the rejection of its proposal as late. The Homeland Security buy again covered agency-wide transportation services. The firm held a slice of the work as prior contractor. GAO decided B-299241.2 on March 30, 2007.

The firm blamed the agency for the late arrival. It also said the government held the bid before the deadline. GAO found no such facts. The late receipt was not caused by agency acts. The bid had not reached the named site, in hand and under control, in time. Late bids sent by a firm's own path stay late. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299310-2:
Chenega Federal Systems, LLC protested an Army award to Calnet, Inc. The contract covered translation and interpretation services in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba. The work would run on an as-needed basis for years. GAO decided B-299310.2 on September 28, 2007.

One claim said cost talks misled the firm. The record showed the agency shared deep cost facts. The firm weighed those facts and made its own calls in reply. A second claim revived a conflict charge. The agency had probed that charge in depth and found no clash. Mere doubt, with no fresh proof, cannot undo such a probe. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299340-2:
OfficeMax, Inc. protested an Internal Revenue Service award to Corporate Express. The buy covered delivery of office supplies. The contest ran through a request for quotations. GAO ruled in B-299340.2 on July 19, 2007.

One rule sat at the heart of the case. The agency's fill-or-kill policy was a firm must-meet term. A vendor must fill each order line in full or reject that line. The firm's ordering systems did not meet that rule. Nor did the firm plan to come into line. GAO found the unfit call sound. Talks could not cure a gap the firm would not close. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299369-2:
M&M Investigations protested its removal from a Homeland Security competition. The buy again covered guard services at the Plum Island Animal Disease Center. The planned award went to Eagle Technologies, Inc. GAO decided B-299369.2 and B-299369.3 on October 24, 2007.

The firm's bid scored lower on technical merit. It also cost far more than the rival bid. GAO found the scoring fair and in line with the terms. The firm said its flaws could be cured in talks. The gap in score and price was too wide for that hope. A range of one fit bid can stand on such facts. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299546-2:
Control Systems Research protested an Army award to Atmospheric Technology Services Company. The contract covered weather support services at the Kwajalein Atoll test site. That remote site sits in the Marshall Islands. GAO ruled in B-299546.2 on August 31, 2007.

The firm attacked the technical and past-record reviews. GAO tested both against the stated terms. It found the agency scored the bid as the terms directed. The site's harsh, far-flung setting shaped the needs at stake. A score that tracks the terms for such work can stand. No breach of the scheme was shown. The pick that followed rested on that sound review. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299548-2:
Paragon Systems protested a Homeland Security task order to NCLN20. The order covered armed security guard services at federal sites across Arizona. The Federal Protective Service ran the buy. GAO ruled in B-299548.2 on September 10, 2007.

The fight turned on past-record checks. The agency spoke with a person who knew the winner's work. That person was not the contact the firm had named. GAO found that step fair, since the person knew the work first-hand. The firm also asked for fine grades of relevance. No rule forces such fine splits among past deals. The review tracked the stated tests. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299600-2:
Takota Corporation sought payment of protest costs from the Coast Guard. The plea grew from a bid buy for replacement pier services in Norfolk, Virginia. The agency had canceled the first buy and made a linked award. GAO acted in B-299600.2, a costs ruling, on September 18, 2007.

Cost payment needs a link to the agency's fix. The firm's protest had fought the cancel call and a side award. GAO found no such link on this record. The fix did not grow out of the points the firm raised. A cost plea fails when the fix has other roots. The long gap in the case did not change that test. GAO denied the request.
gao-gaoreports-b-299605-2:
Financial & Realty Services protested an Environmental Protection Agency award to Apex Logistics. The contract covered warehouse operations and labor services. The buy was set aside for small firms. GAO ruled in B-299605.2 on August 9, 2007.

The firm held the lower price in the contest. It said its technical score should have run higher. On that view, it should have won the award. GAO read the scoring against the stated terms. It found the marks fair and the pick well grounded. A lower price does not win by itself in a best-value buy. The score gap was backed by the record. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299660-2:
Operational Support & Services protested a sole-source Army award to Shee Atika Languages. The U.S. Special Operations Command ran the deal. The work covers foreign language interpretation, transcription, and translation. GAO ruled in B-299660.2 on September 24, 2007.

The award ran through the section 8(a) business development program. The firm claimed bad faith and rule breaches in that path. GAO found the program path clean. Meeting a need through the 8(a) program broke no statute or rule. A claim about the winner's status class went to the Small Business Administration. That office, not GAO, settles such status points. The core plea failed. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299675-2:
General Dynamics C4 Systems protested an Army award to Northrop Grumman Mission Systems. The contract covered trailer mounted support systems for tactical operations centers. The Aviation and Missile Command ran the buy. GAO ruled in the B-299675.2 series on May 30, 2008.

The firm attacked the scoring and the best-value call. GAO found the marks fair and in line with the stated tests. The pick memo showed a clear grasp of the results. It weighed the strengths and flaws of each bid with care. Such a memo is what a sound trade-off needs. A pick backed by that depth of review can stand. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299705-2:
Metson Marine Services protested a second Navy award to Seaward Services on the same day. This deal covered port operations and vessel services in Panama City, Florida. The sites serve a diving and salvage training center. GAO decided B-299705.2 on July 20, 2007.

The firm attacked past-record scoring and the talks held. It also faulted the award call that followed. GAO found the agency's calls fair. They tracked the terms of the buy. The firm's points came down to mere dispute with those calls. Mere dispute does not prove a flawed review. The record backed the pick of the rival firm. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299744-2:
XTec protested the same General Services Administration task order to Electronic Data Systems. The order again covered an end-to-end fix for federal identification cards. The firm raised the same Approved Products List point. GAO decided B-299744.2 and B-299744.3 on August 6, 2007.

GAO took the firm's read at its best for the sake of the plea. Even then, the claim failed on harm. The firm's bid scored lower and cost more than the winner's. It said it could have swapped goods and cut price. That claim stayed broad and thin. Speculation of that kind does not prove lost ground. No prejudice was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299758-2:
Business Consulting Associates protested a Housing and Urban Development award to MBI Consulting. The contract covered post-closing portfolio management support services. The loans at issue come from a mark-to-market housing program. The buy was an 8(a) set-aside. GAO ruled in B-299758.2 on August 1, 2007.

The agency judged the two bids technically equivalent. On that call, price broke the tie. GAO found the equal call fair. The firm also faulted a conflict fix plan. One subcontractor held a possible clash on a small work slice. The plan moved that slice to the prime firm. That firm could do the work alone. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299798-2:
The Council for Adult & Experiential Learning protested the same Army GoArmyEd award to IBM Global Business Services. Its claims spanned the terms, a claimed conflict, and the scoring. GAO ruled in B-299798.2 on August 28, 2007, with a split result.

Claims against the terms came after award. Such claims must be raised before the bid date. Those pleas were set aside as late. The scoring claims fell for a second flaw. They rested on the same late points. They also failed to name a clear flaw in the review. Broad claims cannot undo a scored award. GAO dismissed in part and denied in part.
gao-gaoreports-b-299856-2:
RKR Joint Venture sought payment of protest costs from the Air Force. The plea grew from an A-76 case over base operating services at Keesler Air Force Base, Mississippi. The agency had chosen in-house work over a contract award. GAO acted in B-299856.2, a costs ruling, on December 7, 2007.

The agency later canceled the buy in that case. It said time had made the terms stale. GAO found that call fair on the record. A cancel driven by stale terms is not a fix for a protest. It is a fresh call on changed facts. With no fix tied to the plea, no cost award could rest on it. GAO denied the request.
gao-gaoreports-b-299870-2:
Barnes Aerospace Group sought payment of costs from a second protest over F100 engine part repairs. The Air Force had made an interim sole-source award to Ferrotherm Corporation. The plea said a prior fix was slow to land. GAO acted in B-299870.2, a costs ruling, on September 17, 2007.

GAO refused the cost claim. The agency moved fast to propose a fix in the second case. Delay in the first fix had mixed roots. The firm's own acts fed part of that delay. A firm that helps cause a lag cannot bill for its costs. The plea failed on that shared-cause ground. GAO denied the request.
gao-gaoreports-b-299901-2:
Safety Storage protested a Defense Logistics Agency award to Ideal Environmental Products. The contract covered a modular pest control building. The terms set floor bars for the building's design. GAO ruled in B-299901.2 on December 3, 2007.

The firm said the winner's building missed must-meet technical bars. One bar asked for a factory mutual clearance as a hazardous stores unit. GAO read the review the agency made. The panel had judged the building fit on those bars. That judgment rested on the bid as sent in. A rival's claim that the goods fall short needs more than doubt. No flaw in the review was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299904-2:
Zolon Tech protested the same Agriculture Department blanket purchase agreement with Vistronix. The work again covers information systems for the Natural Resources Conservation Service. GAO ruled in B-299904.2 on September 18, 2007.

The agency marked flaws in the firm's depth on core technology. The firm leaned on a consultant, not its own staff, for that depth. Its bid also barely touched the management system point. On price, GAO backed the review. The firm's rates ran far below the estimate and prior firms' rates. That gap marked its price as not realistic and high risk. A best-value pick of the stronger bid stood. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299936-2:
Gonzales-McCaulley Investment Group protested a Health and Human Services call to cancel a training buy. The courses covered grants management for agency staff. They ran under the Government Employees Training Act. GAO ruled in B-299936.2 on November 5, 2007.

The agency first picked the firm, then pulled that pick back. It claimed the firm had copied course text from a rival. GAO found that probe too thin. Proof showed the firm got the text from the agency itself. Its bid also held fresh facts on the course field. The later cancel plea rested on a claimed lack of buying power. No like buys were canceled on that ground. The plea looked like a pretext. The firm's claims held up.
gao-gaoreports-b-299981-2:
Legacy Management Solutions protested the same Department of Energy support award to The S.M. Stoller Co. The work again serves the legacy program for closed nuclear sites. GAO decided B-299981.2 and B-299981.4 on October 10, 2007.

The plea again hit the price realism review. The agency matched bids against its estimate and each other. It checked labor types and hours as the terms set them. GAO found that work sound. A second claim alleged lopsided pricing among the winner's labor rates. Those rates sat inside the full range of bids sent in. Rates in that range show no wild over- or under-pricing. No flaw was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-303495-2:
A House member asked GAO to withdraw a prior legal opinion in the B-303495 line. That opinion hit the Office of National Drug Control Policy. It found fault with prepackaged news stories in video news releases. GAO sent its reply letter in 2005, with no fresh date line in the text.

The member raised three points in the plea. He cited the office's power to run a media campaign. He stressed the free choice of news outlets to air the clips. He also split hidden source by the agency from hidden source by outlets. GAO weighed each point with care. It stood by its first opinion in full. The ban on propaganda use of funds still governed the office's acts.
gao-gaoreports-b-305835-2:
Overtime rules for the rest of the Capitol Police force fill this GAO opinion, B-305835.2, dated August 29, 2005. An earlier opinion covered the three chiefs whose pay is set by law. This one covers sworn members and civilian staff. It also covers a 2006 law that waived repayment of some past overtime.

Staff covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act may earn overtime pay. But base pay plus overtime may not top $156,848 a year. Staff exempt from that act get no overtime pay. They may earn time off if the Chief finds special need. Time off has no yearly pay cap. But staff may carry over at most 240 hours a year.
gao-gaoreports-b-309930-2:
Klinge Corporation lost its protest in GAO decision B-309930.2, dated February 13, 2008. The Marine Corps sought large field refrigeration systems. The award went to Sea Box, Ltd. under a call for offers. Klinge said the winner's system broke the Trade Agreements Act. The claim turned on where the parts were made.

GAO denied the protest. The agency asked the winner for more facts on its parts. It then found the parts would be changed in substance in the United States. That change makes the system a U.S.-made end product. The review was fair on the facts the agency had.
gao-gaoreports-b-309989-2:
Qualicon Corporation lost its protest; the GAO decision is B-309989.2, dated December 3, 2007. The Coast Guard sought pier work at its Little Creek Station in Norfolk, Virginia. The award went to Jessico Inc. under a call for bids. Qualicon said it bid the low total price. It said the agency strayed from its own scoring plan in the pick.

GAO denied the protest. A stray step alone does not void a pick. The loser must show a real chance it was harmed by the stray. Qualicon showed no such chance here. Lack of shown harm sank the claim, fair price plea or not.
gao-gaoreports-b-310123-2:
Optimal Solutions & Technologies lost its protest (GAO decision B-310123.2, dated September 21, 2007). The Internal Revenue Service sought tech support for its systems. The call asked for a skills grade report with each bid. The report had to be dated in the 12 months before the close date. The firm sent a report near 24 months old.

GAO denied the protest. The cast-out of the bid was fair on the call's terms. A stale report does not meet a fresh-report rule. Firms must heed date rules in a call as strict terms. A near miss on a date is still a miss.
gao-gaoreports-b-310273-2:
Protest costs are granted in part in this GAO decision, B-310273.2, dated March 27, 2008. Sysorex Federal, Inc. had fought an award for license plate reader systems. The buy ran through GovWorks for Customs and Border Protection. The readers were hand-held units for field use. Sysorex asked to be paid back for its protest costs.

GAO backed pay-back for one slice of the fight. A fair agency check of the first claims would have shown the win lacked a sound legal base. The gear did not meet the call's specs. Yet the agency stalled its fix past its own report date. Costs tied to that claim merit repayment.
gao-gaoreports-b-310303-2:
Veterans Technology, LLC lost its protest — GAO decision B-310303.2, dated January 7, 2008. The Army sought tech and design aid for its space and missile defense arms. The call was set aside in full for small firms. It set up a set of deals with a base year and four option years. VetTech's bid was judged unfit for award.

GAO denied the protest. The unfit call was fair on the file. A bid that fails the call's terms may be shut out at the first stage. It has no claim to win on first offers. Sample task replies had to show clear depth, and this bid fell short.
gao-gaoreports-b-310311-2:
Engineering Construction Services, Inc. lost its protest (GAO decision B-310311.2, dated December 12, 2007). The firm raised four claims in its fight. It said the winner rewrote its bid in a big way past a key stage. It said the agency then skipped those rewrites in fresh scoring. It said parts of the set review were never done. It said talks were thin.

GAO denied each claim. The file held no proof of a big rewrite. The file showed the reviews were in fact done. Talks flagged each big flaw in the firm's bid. A sub's thin past work was fair to count as a weak point.
gao-gaoreports-b-310340-2:
Angel Menendez Environmental Services, Inc. lost its protest. That ruling is B-310340.2, dated April 11, 2008. The Veterans Affairs office sought build and cleanup work at its San Antonio hospital. The work ran from plain build jobs to asbestos and lead removal. The award went to a firm with a low price and a low score. Tech points as a whole weighed the same as cost.

GAO denied the protest. The loser read one clause of the call in a strained way. That clause set a tie rule for bids found much the same. It did not bar a low-price pick when scores gap. A clause read must fit its plain sense.
gao-gaoreports-b-310359-2:
Sherrick Aerospace lost its protest under GAO decision B-310359.2, dated January 10, 2008. The Army sought test plan and review help for missile systems. The award went to Sierra Lobo, Inc. Sherrick fought the scoring of both tech plans and past work. It said past work crept into a score slot where it did not belong.

GAO denied the protest. The file backed the scores and the pick as fair. The past-work point did no harm in any case. The rest of the pick logic still tipped to the winner. Past work of a winner's sub was fair to weigh as well.
gao-gaoreports-b-310372-2:
A plea to rethink a KC-135 ruling is refused in this GAO decision, B-310372.2, dated February 1, 2008. The Air Force sought a fresh look at a December ruling. That ruling upheld Pemco Aeroplex's protest of a depot care award. The award had gone to Boeing Aerospace Operations. The work keeps KC-135 aircraft fit at a depot.

GAO denied the plea. The plea showed no flaw of fact or law in the first ruling. It raised one new point that should have come up in the fight. Fresh points raised too late earn no fresh look. The first ruling stands as issued by GAO.
gao-gaoreports-b-310551-2:
American Cybernetic Corporation lost its protest; the GAO decision is B-310551.2, dated February 1, 2008. The Bureau of the Public Debt sought a web redo and host work. The client was the Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board. The award went to Svanaco, Inc., at the top tech score and the low price. The loser bid a much higher price.

GAO denied the protest. Some claims held no merit at all. The rest showed no harm to the loser in the race. A top score at a low price is a hard pick to upset. Claims must show both a flaw and harm from it.
gao-gaoreports-b-310742-2:
Para Scientific Company lost its protests; the GAO decision is B-310742.2, dated February 14, 2008. The Navy supply center in San Diego bought lab goods in two buys. One buy was for microscope slides and slide cabinets. One was for tissue cassettes, cover slips, and pens. The Navy killed one call for quotes and fixed the other.
