GAO denied the protests. The Navy found its call had claimed far more than it needs. A fresh call would draw a wider race for the work. Killing a call that claims too much is a fair step. Wide claims chill the race a truer call would draw.
gao-gaoreports-b-310803-2:
Domain Name Alliance Registry lost its protest; the GAO decision is B-310803.2, dated August 18, 2008. The Commerce Department sought net domain name services. The award went to NeuStar, Inc. A past fix had led to a fresh look at quotes. The firm said the fresh look needed talks and new bids. It waited till the new pick to press that point.

GAO threw out that claim as too late. The agency's acts made plain no talks were planned. The firm sat on its claim while the fix ran its course. The rest of the claims failed too. The scores of the quotes held up as fair.
gao-gaoreports-b-310822-2:
Goel Services, Inc. lost its protest — GAO decision B-310822.2, dated May 23, 2008. The General Services Administration sought build work at a State Department site in Washington. The job tore down and built a guard check zone. The award went to Grunley Construction Company. Goel said a zone-based price boost was owed to it. The boost aids firms from poor trade zones.

GAO denied the protest. The call for bids held no such boost clause. A boost not in the call can not be forced on the race. The claim that it should have been in the call came too late. Terms must be fought before bids close.
gao-gaoreports-b-310828-2:
Protest costs are backed in full in this GAO decision, B-310828.2, dated April 28, 2008. Burns and Roe Services Corporation had fought an award for plant aid work. The Interior Department sought aid for the Yuma Desalting Plant. The award went to CH2M Hill Constructors. A GAO-led peace talk showed the protest had real force. The firm then asked for its costs back.

GAO backed pay-back for all claims raised. The claims shared one set of core facts. They wove through each part of the fight. GAO will not split wins from losses in such a case. Shared facts mean shared costs for the whole protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-310927-2:
Protest costs are refused in this GAO decision, B-310927.2, dated April 21, 2008. Tremco Incorporated had fought a roof award at a Boston-area veterans site. The Veterans Affairs office gave in on the due date of its report. It cut the award and planned a fresh call. The flaw was a late bond by the winner. Tremco then asked for its protest costs back.

GAO denied the cost claim. The file shows no stall by the agency. The fix came the day the report was due. That is not a lag in the face of a clear win. Costs flow when an agency drags its feet, not when it acts on time.
gao-gaoreports-b-310966-2:
Alanna Orr lost her protest — GAO decision B-310966.2, dated May 14, 2008. The Forest Service sought cleaning work at its Big Valley Ranger District office. The order went to Jan Breakfield. Orr said the win quote lacked a sound tech plan. She said the agency gave the winner a sample quality plan. She said the winner's tech pages were cribbed from a peer's work.

GAO denied the protest. The call scored just price and past work. Tech plans were not a scored point in this race. Claims on a point not scored can not shake the pick. The race turned on the two points the call named.
gao-gaoreports-b-311234-2:
Clark E. Myatt saw his protest thrown out. GAO ruled in B-311234.2 on April 15, 2008. Myatt spoke for the in-house team in a Navy race. The race pitted state crews against firms for guard aid work. It ran under the A-76 rules for such tests. He fought terms of the call as skewed. The Navy said no firm bid in the race was fit to take.

GAO dismissed the protest. The terms at stake could do him no harm now. With no fit firm bid, the A-76 path is plain. The Navy must fix and rerun the call, or give the work to its own team. A flaw that can not bite is no base for a fight.
gao-gaoreports-b-311245-2:
MCT JV won its protest under GAO decision B-311245.2, dated May 16, 2008. The call warned firms not to bid costs too low to be real. The winner capped its side rates at marks well past its true costs, on the low side. The agency scored the bid with no eye to the risk in that cap. Low caps can choke the work once the job starts.

GAO sustained the protest. The agency missed the risk the cap posed. Talks with MCT had a flaw as well. They did not flag the clash in how work hours split in its two bids. Talks that miss the point are not frank talks.
gao-gaoreports-b-311254-2:
Canon USA, Inc. lost its protest (GAO decision B-311254.2, dated June 10, 2008). The Army held blanket deals for copier services with eight firms. Canon was one of the eight. Its base schedule deal ran out in the fall of 2007. Talks to renew that deal fell through. The Army then cut an order it had made to Canon.

GAO denied the protest. The order came once Canon's base deal was dead. A blanket deal rests on the base deal that backs it. When the base deal dies, new orders lose their base. The cut of the order was a fair act on those facts.
gao-gaoreports-b-311314-2:
Trammell Crow Company won its protest. GAO decided B-311314.2 on June 20, 2008. The General Services Administration sought office space for the Justice Department in Washington. The lease went to CS Master V, LLC. The winner's block got marks for perks to come by move-in day. The call asked for third-party proof those perks would be there. The winner gave its own word and no more.

GAO sustained the protest. A firm's own word is not the proof the call asked for. Talks held a flaw as well. Big weak points on key staff were not raised with Trammell Crow. Talks that skip big flaws are not frank.
gao-gaoreports-b-400109-2:
Savantage Financial Services, Incorporated lost its protest. GAO decided B-400109.2 on July 28, 2008. The same tech shop sought aid for its trade systems arm. The order went to The MIL Corporation as in a twin case. Savantage fought the scores of its tech and cost bids. The tech score found thin facts on its lead tool. It found thin facts on its named chief as well.

GAO denied the protest. The file backs each flaw the judges found. A long hire path posed a risk to the start of work. Past work with made-to-fit help desk ware was thin. Thin facts earn low marks in a fair race.
gao-gaoreports-b-400145-2:
Ahntech-Korea Company, Ltd. lost its protest in GAO decision B-400145.2, dated August 18, 2008. The Army sought civil build services at its bases in Korea. The award went to Kyungil Industrial Development Co., Ltd. The call asked for 3 years of like past work. Ahntech's bid was judged unfit on that point. It pled the past work of its parent firm in its place.

GAO denied the protest. The firm lacked 3 years of like work of its own. The bid did not pledge the parent's tools and crews to the job. Past work of a parent counts when its wealth is pledged. No pledge was shown in this bid.
gao-gaoreports-b-400224-2:
Hendry Corporation lost a Coast Guard dry-dock repair award to RiverHawk Marine, LLC and then attacked the winner's fitness to do the job. Hendry raised the claim in B-400224.2. GAO issued its ruling on August 25, 2008. The work came under request for quotes No. HSCG80-08-Q-3FAD73.

Hendry said three RiverHawk founders had a poor past record at a prior firm. It cited a firm failure and two lost repair jobs there. GAO held that such claims do not meet its bar for review of a fitness call. The facts pled would not strongly bear on fitness. The protest was dismissed.
gargantua-and-pantagruel-illustrated-boo:
Book 2 of Rabelais's five-book tale of giants turns to Pantagruel, son of Gargantua, in the English version by Sir Thomas Urquhart and Peter Antony Motteux. Pantagruel grows to vast size and goes out to study, fight, and see the world. His friend Panurge joins him, a sly fellow who loves tricks, talk, and wine.

The book mixes school satire with wild pranks. Panurge fools crowds, plays jokes on proud folk, and argues in signs when words will not do. Wars and feasts fill the gaps between the jokes. Rabelais piles up wordplay, lists, and learned spoof in a rich old style. It is the liveliest portrait of Pantagruel as a young prince among rogues.
gellius-attic-nights-rolfe-loeb-vol-2:
Books six through thirteen of the Attic Nights of Aulus Gellius fill this second Loeb volume, in John C. Rolfe's translation. Gellius wrote in the second century, gathering notes from his reading in Rome and Athens. The middle books keep the same free, curious range as the first.

Questions of grammar sit beside court cases, ghost tales, old Roman rites, and lines from poets whose works are lost. Gellius loves a puzzle: why a word means what it does, or how an old law read. His quotes save fragments of early Latin plays and speeches found nowhere else. The volume is a storehouse for anyone who loves the byways of Roman life.
gerfaut-volume-2:
Gerfaut, Volume 2 continues Charles de Bernard's Academy-crowned French novel of 1838 in English dress. Octave de Gerfaut, the young Paris writer whose books and salon talk have made his name, travels toward the Bergenheim estate in the provinces. The dismissed workman Lambernier and his curses hang over the road like weather. Bernard pauses over Octave's ambitions and the ease with which fame opens country doors.

Inside the volume, the guest studies the chateau, its master, and its mistress with a novelist's trained eye. The Baron's hearty welcome and the baroness's guarded kindness give Octave two puzzles at once. Country visits and long evenings let acquaintance ripen toward the attachment the story promises. Bernard writes desire as observation: every glance is noted, weighed, and stored. Readers in the second volume watch Octave's curiosity turn into a feeling he must hide from his host.
godolphin-volume-2:
Volume 2 of Godolphin opens at chapter fifteen, with the feelings of Constance and Godolphin toward each other. Its chapter head speaks of the contrast in their characters and of the effect the world works on Godolphin. The pair walk and ride together, and in the evening he hangs over her chair to hear her sing, her voice rich and soft past common singers.

Lady Erpingham watches with secret delight, sure of a growing attachment. She loves Constance for herself and Godolphin for his father's sake. Omens and rural scenes fill the chapters, up to a first indistinct confession. The volume is the courtship heart of Lytton's novel of society, where hope is still bright and the costs not yet counted.
godwin-political-justice-1793-vol-2:
Volume two of Godwin's Political Justice, also from 1793, completes his enquiry. The first volume laid down the rule of private judgment against government. This volume turns to property, the root of much rule in his view. Great wealth, he argues, breeds dependence and warps both rich and poor.

He sketches a society held together by reason and voluntary fairness. Human perfectibility, the slow growth of minds toward truth, anchors his hope. The two volumes together complete the work as issued. Later anarchists drew deeply on Godwin's pages. His vision of a stateless order starts here. The style is cool where the claims are hot.
goethe-wilhelm-meister-carlyle-1824-vol-:
Volume 2 of Carlyle's Wilhelm Meister appeared in 1824, continuing Goethe's novel of Wilhelm's apprenticeship and travels. Thomas Carlyle's translation carried the second half of Wilhelm's theater years and beyond. Wilhelm moves among actors, estates, and a secret society that watches his growth.

Encounters with the strange Mignon and the Harper deepen the book's mix of song, sorrow, and mystery. Wilhelm's mistakes in love and art slowly teach him the limits of the stage life he craved. Goethe used the tale to ask how a person forms a self in a changing world. Carlyle's English made that question part of British literary debate.
govdocs-archive_org-kalevala-the-land-of:
The Kalevala is Finland's national epic, built by Elias Lönnrot from rune-songs he collected from singers in Finland and Karelia. Volume 2, in the Berserker Books edition, holds the second half of the poem, carrying the long story that volume 1 began to its close.

Here the heroes Väinämöinen, Ilmarinen, and Lemminkäinen move through quests, weddings, feuds, and the forging and loss of the Sampo, the magic mill that brings wealth. The verse keeps the driving rhythm of the original sung runes, in English dress. For Finns the Kalevala is a founding book; this volume finishes it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CBSPart2_CBS_Pa: Harold Weisberg wrote to George Herman of CBS News on March 30, 1974, one of hundreds of letters the assassination author sent to the journalists who covered the case. Weisberg spent decades arguing that the press had failed on the Kennedy story, and he argued it directly, by mail, to the men and women on the air. The letter is filed with material on CBS's coverage of the assassination. It is kept as part of his media correspondence in the archive.
gregory-tours-history-franks-dalton-vol-:
Volume two of Dalton's 1927 translation completes Gregory of Tours' History of the Franks, the ten books of Merovingian history finished in 594. The later books are Gregory's own times, the richest and darkest of the set. He writes as bishop of Tours from 573, in the middle of the events.

Kings Chilperic and Guntram, and the queens Fredegund and Brunhild, drive a story of assassinations, civil wars, and church councils. Gregory records his own trials: accused before kings, sheltering fugitives in his church, and defying royal tax men. Saints' miracles thread through the politics. The volume ends with his survey of his own episcopate. It is the best single source on the Frankish kingdoms.
grihya-sutras-oldenberg-vol-2:
Hermann Oldenberg translated the second volume of the Grihya Sutras in 1892. It appeared as volume thirty of the Sacred Books of the East. The Grihya Sutras give rules for Vedic domestic ceremonies in the home.

Birth, naming, first feeding, and the child's first haircut receive rites. Marriage ceremonies and funeral customs occupy large sections of the texts. Grand public sacrifices fill other books, but these sutras show religion at the family hearth. Oldenberg was a leading German scholar of early Indian religion. His volume preserves the texture of ordinary ancient Indian life. Intimate antiquity, rather than royal splendor, defines these pages throughout.
haeckel-evolution-of-man-vol-2:
The second volume of Haeckel's Evolution of Man, from 1874, turns from the embryo to the family tree. Where volume one traced man's growth before birth, this one traces the descent of mankind itself. Haeckel, Darwin's German bulldog, writes with total confidence.

He builds the genealogical tree of the human race, linking man through the apes and lower mammals to the earliest vertebrates. He even names a missing ancestor, Pithecanthropus alalus, the speechless ape-man, decades before Dubois found Java Man and made the guess look prophetic. The volume completes his popular account of human origins, dated in detail but huge in influence.
haeckel-history-of-creation-vol-2:
Volume two of Haeckel's History of Creation completes his 1868 survey of evolution. Volume one laid down the general doctrine; this one works through the special morphology and family history of organisms. Man's place among the primates is its destination.

Haeckel classifies life form by form, drawing the famous genealogical trees that branch from simple monera to mankind. He assigns each group its ancestors and its age in Earth history. The certainty outruns the evidence, as critics noted even then. Even so, the book's trees taught two generations to picture descent. It remains the boldest family album of nineteenth-century Darwinism.
hafez-divan-clarke-1891-vol-2:
The second volume of H. Wilberforce Clarke's Divan of Hafez, from 1891, completes the first full English rendering of Persia's beloved poet. Hafez sang in Shiraz in the fourteenth century, and his lyrics are still quoted daily across the Persian world. Clarke's prose keeps his copious commentary running beside the poems.

More ghazals follow here, with the odes, fragments, and longer pieces that close the Divan in its set order. Wine and the beloved carry the double sense Clarke labors to unfold: earthly joy and the soul's thirst for God. His two volumes are a library in themselves. With this one, the English reader holds the whole Hafez of the Victorian scholars.
haft-paikar-wilson-1924-vol-2:
Volume II of Wilson's Haft Paikar, from 1924, holds the commentary that partners his translation. Notes unpack Nizami's allusions, names, customs, and verses line by line for the English reader. The companion assumes the translation in hand and works as its guide through a dense Persian classic.

Scholars use the commentary to trace sources and untangle the poem's rich wordplay. Without it, much of the Seven Beauties' art would pass unseen by a foreign reader. The two Wilson volumes together, text and notes, form the first complete English presentation of Nizami's romance, issued in Probsthain's Oriental Series.
hallam-constitutional-history-vol-2:
Civil war and republic fill the second volume of Hallam's Constitutional History, from 1827. Parliament defies the king, war follows, and Cromwell rules in the Interregnum. Hallam finds the roots of modern liberty amid the chaos of the sixteen forties.

He treats both royalists and parliament men with cool fairness. Charters, trials, and ordinances pass under his lawyer's eye in turn. His liberal passion burns beneath a surface of strict calm. The volume shows a constitution tested by the sword and remade by law, a key chapter in the long tale of how England learned self-rule.
hallam-middle-ages-vol-2:
Spain, the Eastern Empire, and the Crusades fill the second volume of Hallam's View of the Middle Ages, in the 1863 printing. His gaze moves beyond France and England to the whole medieval world. Kingdoms, caliphates, and crusading hosts interact across three continents in his account.

Hallam's method was bold for its day: Europe read as one system. He compares laws, faiths, and governments across wide borders. Constantinople and Cordoba stand beside Paris in his broad canvas. The volume shows a historian thinking in civilizations, long before that habit grew common, and it widens his survey into a true portrait of an age.
handy-andy-a-tale-of-irish-life-volume-2:
The second volume of Samuel Lover's Handy Andy, a tale of Irish life, continues the blundering hero's adventures. The volume opens on a pitch-dark night, as Dick's whistle is answered by approaching wheels and a horse's rapid footfalls, and a smart gig draws up.

Illustrations show Tom Organ Loftus's Coldairian system, Tom Connor's cat, Andy's cooking extraordinary, the abduction, a crack shot, the challenge, and the party at Killarney. Lover, who drew his own illustrations, keeps Andy's mishaps rolling through Ireland's lanes and big houses. Readers who enjoy Irish comic fiction will find Handy Andy's second volume as cheerful as the first.
hawkesworth-account-voyages-southern-hem:
Volume two of John Hawkesworth's Account of the Voyages, the official 1773 record of Britain's Pacific expeditions, turns from Cook to the captains before him. It holds the circumnavigations of Commodore Byron, Captain Wallis, and Captain Carteret in the 1760s. Hawkesworth shaped their journals into one narrative.

Byron's Dolphin, Wallis's voyage in the same ship, and Carteret's battered Swallow each circle the globe in turn. Wallis's landfall at Tahiti in 1767, the island's first European contact, is the volume's famous scene. The accounts mix hard seamanship with first meetings between peoples who had never heard of each other. Cook's greater voyages frame the set.
heath-history-greek-mathematics-vol-2:
Volume two of Heath's History of Greek Mathematics appeared in 1921 with the first. It carries the story from Aristarchus to Diophantus, the later flowering. Astronomy, conic sections, and algebra dominate these later centuries.

Archimedes receives the attention his genius demands in these chapters. Apollonius's conics and Hipparchus's astronomy show Greek science at full stretch. Ptolemy's system and Diophantus's algebra close the ancient story. Heath tells the tale with a translator's closeness to his sources. He had personally Englished most of the major texts he discusses. The golden age and its brilliant aftermath fill the volume. Together, Heath's two volumes remain unmatched as a single-author survey. It is clear, full, and fair to all sides.
herodotus-histories-macaulay-vol-2:
Volume Two of Macaulay's Herodotus holds Books Five through Nine of the Histories. The Greek writer brings his great subject to its climax here. Persia invades Greece with a vast host by land and sea.

Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, and Plataea anchor the tale. Herodotus honors brave stands and questions easy glory alike. He records speeches, omens, and the views of both sides. The result is the base account of the Persian Wars. Every later telling leans on his pages, and his eye for human motive keeps them fresh. Macaulay's prose keeps the pace swift throughout.
hinduism-and-buddhism-an-historical-sket:
Charles Eliot wrote this second volume of his historical sketch of Hinduism and Buddhism. Eliot sets out his spelling rules for many eastern tongues in a preface note. The volume carries the story past the faiths' early age in India. It tracks deep change across the centuries.

Eliot treats the span from about 400 before Christ to 400 after. In those years, he argues, Buddhism waned in India while Brahman faith reshaped itself. The great epics grow in the same span, though their dates stay hard to fix. Volume Two gives readers a calm, learned map of a complex shift.
hippocrates-genuine-works-adams-vol-2:
Volume two of Adams's Hippocrates turns to the surgeon's art in ancient Greece. Fractures, dislocations, and wounds receive the detailed treatment here. The Hippocratic writings in this volume date from around 400 BCE.

Doctors learn to set bones with traction, splints, and bandaging. The famous Hippocratic bench for reducing dislocations gets full description. Head wounds and their trepanning dangers occupy careful chapters. Method feels practical, exact, and startlingly modern in many passages. Adams's surgical experience made him an ideal translator for this material. Ancient doctors setting bones show a skill that impresses modern surgeons. Volume one holds the theory; this volume holds the hands.
histoire-de-la-philosophie-hermetique-ac:
Nicolas Lenglet Dufresnoy compiled this French catalogue of hermetic writers, issued in 1742. It forms part of his history of the hermetic philosophy. Entry follows entry in strict order, each with its facts. Printers, towns, dates, and formats are all set down for the reader.

The hosted copy runs deep into the numbered entries. Names such as Libavius appear with lists of their works and editions. Some entries add notes on the worth of the books. The text is in French, in the old spelling of its day. Scholars can trace who wrote what on alchemy, and where each book was printed.
historia-augusta-magie-vol-2:
David Magie's second Loeb volume of the Historia Augusta, from 1924, plunges into the worst years of the third century. The lives here cover the two Maximini, the three Gordians, and the joint emperors Maximus and Balbinus. The work itself dates to about 400 CE and pretends to have six authors.

Short reigns follow one another: soldier emperors raised by armies and cut down in months. The tales mix real campaign reports with court gossip and invented papers. Even so, for these dark decades the Historia Augusta is often the only connected source. Magie's notes help readers sort the fact from the fun.
history-of-dogma-volume-2:
Adolf von Harnack wrote this second volume of his History of Dogma. Neil Buchanan translated it from the third German edition, for a Boston issue of 1901. The volume studies how the Catholic Church took form. Its first survey sets old and new elements side by side.

Chapters treat the fixing of the rule of faith and the canon. Irenaeus, Tertullian, Hippolytus, Clement, and Origen each get weighed. Harnack shows rites, offices, and books settling into one system. The apologists' view of the world, made by God through his Word, gets close reading. Scholars get a rich, argued map of the early church.
history-of-english-humour-vol-2:
The Reverend A G L'Estrange closes his history of English humour with this second volume, issued in 1878. A printer's slip in the original skips a chapter number, the transcriber notes, though no chapter is lost. Burlesque and parody open the volume. Prior, Pope, and Gay lead the mock-heroic parade.

Defoe's irony and his Ode to the Pillory get their own study. Parodies of Gray's Elegy show how a famed poem invites jest. Later pages gather odd extracts from rare books, in Southey's miscellany and beyond. Readers finish a learned, genial survey of how England learned to laugh in print.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r:
Edward Gibbon's second volume, with Milman's notes, opens at chapter sixteen, his famous survey of the Roman government's conduct toward the Christians from Nero to Constantine. He counts martyrs skeptically, questions Eusebius's numbers, and asks how a small sect conquered an empire. The chapters on Constantine follow his conversion and favor toward the church.

Later chapters treat Julian's pagan revival, the empire's division, and the growing pressure of Gothic peoples on the Danube. Gibbon's footnotes argue with Dodwell, Ruinart, and the church historians in small print. The volume's cool treatment of early Christianity made it the most controversial part of the whole history, and still the most argued over.
hobhouse-morals-evolution-1906-vol-2:
Part two of Morals in Evolution, also from 1906, completes Hobhouse's comparative ethics. The first part traced moral ideas from primitive groups toward civilized society. This part treats the higher morality and its place in the modern state. Hobhouse asks what ethics becomes when reason tests custom directly.

He weighs the claims of duty, the good, and rational self direction. The modern state appears as both a moral agent and a moral problem. His survey closes with ethics as a guide for social reform. The two parts together complete the work as planned. Readers gain a full map of his moral evolution scheme. It stands as a major Edwardian synthesis.
homeward-bound-sailor-s-knots-part-2:
W W Jacobs placed this tale in his Sailor's Knots set of 1909. Mr Hatchard wages a war of grunts against his wife's spending. The treatment worked before, for short spells. Now a pair of huge pink vases on the mantelpiece shows it failing.

Mrs Hatchard admits she bought them, nod by nod. Later talk turns to lodgings, rent, and evenings out. Mr Hatchard peeps at the sitting-room and weighs the place like a buyer. Jacobs draws dry comedy from a marriage of sulk and spend. The dialogue does nearly all the work, in his usual shore-side manner.
hortulus-hermeticus-flosculis-philosopho:
Daniel Stolcius of Stolcenberg issued this hermetic emblem book at Frankfurt in 1627. Lucas Jennis printed it, the title page records. Stolcius greets the philo-chymical reader with an open little garden. In it, he promises, are flowers and a perennial spring for eye and mouth.

Each emblem pairs a copper plate with brief Latin verses. Johannes Austri speaks on the four elements that hold all things. Valerandus de Bosco sings of Venus reddening in the fire. Dedications to counselors of Württemberg and Pomerania front the work. The hosted copy preserves the Frankfurt original. It is a picture book for alchemists, grave and ornamental together.
human-science-or-phrenology-its-principl:
Professor O S Fowler, former editor of the American Phrenological Journal, wrote this vast work of 1873. He lists his earlier books on the title page: phrenology, physiology, self-culture, memory, matrimony, and more. Human Science binds them into one system, he claims, from health to heaven.

Home cures sit beside theology in its pages. Powdered chalk on sores is praised as a perfect healing coat. Dressings, he warns, irritate and must be avoided where possible. Suppuration needs an outlet, which he shows how to make. The copy is the same great compendium as its mate, in another scan: part medical adviser, part moral system.
humboldt-cosmos-otte-vol-2:
Volume two of Humboldt's Cosmos, in Otté's 1849 English translation, turns from nature itself to the human mind facing nature. Humboldt calls it the history of the contemplation of the physical world. Few science books have a second volume like it.

He traces how poetry, landscape painting, and gardens have carried the feeling for nature through the ages. Then he follows the growth of physical knowledge: Egyptians, Greeks, Arabs, the age of Columbus, and the telescope and microscope. The volume is a history of science and art in one. It shows Humboldt the humanist, as learned in verse and paint as in rocks and stars.
humboldt-personal-narrative-williams-vol:
Volume two of Humboldt's Personal Narrative, in Helen Maria Williams's translation, continues the 1799 to 1804 expedition through Venezuela. Humboldt and Bonpland push inland from the coast toward the great plains and the Orinoco. The seven-volume English set began in 1814.

The travelers cross the llanos, the vast grass plains, in crushing heat, studying electric eels and the life of the rivers. Humboldt tests the eel's shock on himself and records it in cool detail. He gathers plants, fixes positions by the stars, and questions missionaries on the peoples of the interior. Science and adventure run in one stream, as always with Humboldt.
huxley-life-and-letters-vol-2:
Volume Two of Huxley's life and letters, edited by his son Leonard in 1900, covers the later career. Thomas Henry Huxley was now a public figure, shaping schools, museums, and debate. The letters run to his death in 1895.

Later battles over science teaching and religious doubt fill many pages. Huxley's work with the Metaphysical Society and his essays on faith appear here too. A full index closes the two-volume set. Together they record how one man helped make science a central voice in British public life. Family letters soften the public image of the fierce debater.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-2:
Vikings and rival kings fill the second volume of William Archer's 1908 English Ibsen. The Vikings at Helgeland and The Pretenders dramatize Norway's medieval past with saga-like force. Sea kings, proud women, and contested crowns drive both plays toward blood and fate.

Ibsen soaked himself in the Icelandic sagas and made their world speak on stage. The Pretenders, his longest historical drama, follows Haakon's rise against the brooding Earl Skule. Passion for Norway's past made Ibsen his country's national poet of the stage. These plays hold the raw material from which the later realist forged his art. English readers meet them in the translation that introduced Ibsen abroad.
idrisi-geographie-jaubert-vol-2:
Africa and Asia fill the second tome of Jaubert's 1836 French version of al-Idrisi's geography. The survey, made in 1154 for Roger of Sicily, moves through seas and islands to the far East. Muslim knowledge of the earth here reaches its medieval height.

Al-Idrisi records routes, ports, peoples, and wonders with a clerk's care. His world stretches from Atlantic isles to the coasts of China. Kings and scholars across faiths prized the work for centuries. The volume completes a monument of medieval learning, one that shows how wide the horizons of the twelfth century could be in learned hands.
ihne-history-rome-vol-2:
Italy falls to Rome sword by sword in the second volume of Ihne's History, from 1871. The Samnite wars test the young republic to its limits. Pyrrhus crosses from Greece with his elephants and wins battles, yet loses the war for Italy's mastery.

Ihne shows Rome's rise step by step, campaign by campaign. Alliances, colonies, and roads bind the peninsula into one system. The republic learns to absorb beaten foes as partners in power. His systematic narrative pleased a generation of serious readers. The volume forms the solid middle base of a history long taken as the standard Roman account in English.
irving-knickerbocker-history-1809-vol-2:
Washington Irving's second volume of Knickerbocker's History of New York, published with the first in 1809, carries the mock-chronicle through the colony's great days and its fall. Diedrich Knickerbocker, Irving's invented Dutch historian, grows more partisan as the English threat nears. His solemn voice makes the absurdities funnier.

The volume's glory is Peter Stuyvesant, the peg-legged governor who storms about defending New Amsterdam against Swedes, Yankees, and finally the English fleet. Battles, councils, and feasts fill the closing chapters, all treated with epic gravity and comic deflation. When the Dutch surrender, Knickerbocker's world ends with them. The two volumes together founded American comic literature and gave New York its founding mythology.
isbe-1915-vol-2:
The second volume of the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia appeared in 1915, edited by the Scottish theologian James Orr. The set was the great conservative Bible reference of its generation, built by scholars who held traditional faith and modern learning together. Volume 2 carries the work through the middle reaches of the alphabet.

History, biography, geography, and doctrine continue in full measure, with signed articles and the same high standard as the first volume. Entries draw on the archaeology and language study of the day to fill in the world behind the text. Pastors and students used the set as their trusted companion for sermon and study alike. Read today, the volume also shows what mainline scholarship of 1915 believed about the Bible's world, stated by its own leading voices.
j-s-le-fanu-s-ghostly-tales-volume-2:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu's Ghostly Tales, volume two, holds a haunted house narrative of 1862 and Ultor De Lacy of 1861. The first piece is presented by a magazine editor as authentic. Many living witnesses, he says, would swear to its incidents in court. It is in no way tied to spiritualism, he stresses.

Ultor De Lacy opens in a large room with a turf and wood fire. An old woman stirs a pot amid piles of faded hangings and trunks. Two ladies in red drugget cloaks fix a boy's fearful gaze. Legend and testimony make the volume's two modes of terror.
jacqueline-volume-2:
Th. Bentzon, pen name of writer Marie Therese Blanc, continues her novel in Jacqueline, Volume 2. Jacqueline de Nailles entertains friends at home while her mother holds receptions. Cousin Giselle de Monredon arrives from her convent, shy and badly dressed among the glittering circle. Jacqueline kisses her kindly and draws her toward the tea table.

Giselle, an orphan raised by a strict grandmother, sees the gay world only on great occasions. Jacqueline watches another arrival more keenly: Hubert Marien, a family friend of forty with a rare, transforming smile. Marien teased Jacqueline as a child, calling her his little wife in family joke. The joke has stopped, and something less simple has taken its place in her heart. Bentzon writes girlhood from inside, with its cruelties, loyalties, and first serious feelings. Readers in the second volume watch a heroine learning that kindness and love may point toward different duties.
james-bostonians-1886-vol-2:
Henry James's second volume of The Bostonians, published in 1886, brings the struggle over Verena Tarrant to its climax. Olive Chancellor wants Verena for the feminist cause and for herself. Basil Ransom wants her for a wife, and for the quiet home he thinks women belong in.

Verena's fame as a speaker grows while her two claimants tighten their hold. A summer at Cape Cod, concerts, and a final great meeting in a Boston music hall raise the stakes. Ransom's courtship turns into a siege, and Verena's own wishes are the last thing anyone consults. The ending, often read as grim beneath its surface, closes one of James's most argued-about novels.
james-portrait-of-a-lady-1881-vol-2:
Henry James's second volume of The Portrait of a Lady, published with the first in 1881, carries Isabel Archer into the marriage she chose so freely. The novel's first half gave her money, travel, and suitors. This half tests what her freedom was worth.

Isabel marries Gilbert Osmond, the refined expatriate collector, and slowly sees the trap: he values her as an object in his collection. His former lover, Madame Merle, helped arrange the match for her own reasons. A deathbed revelation and a final interview in Rome expose the whole design. Isabel's choice in the last pages, to return to Rome, remains one of fiction's most debated endings.
james-wings-of-the-dove-1902-vol-2:
Henry James's second volume of The Wings of the Dove moves the story to Venice. There Milly Theale rents a palace for her last season. Kate Croy's design, built in the London chapters of the first volume, now closes around its victim. The reckoning James prepares is quiet and devastating.

Densher stays in Venice after Kate leaves, and his conscience turns against the plot he serves. Milly learns the truth from a rejected suitor and, in James's famous phrase, turns her face to the wall. Her death, and the letter she leaves behind, change the meaning of her fortune entirely. The novel ends with two people who can never go back. Milly's strange posthumous victory completes the design.
jataka-cowell-vol-2:
Volume two of Cowell's Jataka, issued in 1895 alongside the first, continues the tales of the Buddha's former births. Cowell edited the six-volume Cambridge set, with W. H. D. Rouse and others translating from the Pali. The numbering of the 547 tales runs on from volume one.

The Bodhisatta, the being who will become the Buddha, now lives as birds, beasts, ascetics, and kings. Each birth turns on a choice: greed punished, mercy rewarded, a promise kept at cost. Frame verses give the point, and the Buddha's closing words name who each figure became. The volume deepens the great story cycle of Buddhist Asia.
john-lothrop-motley-a-memoir-volume-2:
Volume two of Oliver Wendell Holmes's memoir of John Lothrop Motley opens in 1860. Its sixteenth chapter finds Motley in England as the American Civil War breaks out. He had just published the first two volumes of his History of the Netherlands. The crisis at home pulled him back from past centuries to his own country's fight.

Motley wrote two long letters to the London Times explaining the Union cause to Europe. Holmes, backed by William Everett's testimony, calls their effect great and timely. In 1861 Motley returned to America and was appointed minister to Austria by Lincoln. Holmes draws on letters from Motley's daughter, Lady Harcourt, for the Vienna years that follow.
joseph-andrews-vol-2:
Volume two of Joseph Andrews continues Henry Fielding's comic novel within his collected works, edited by George Saintsbury. The contents pick up Book Two at chapter fourteen. Parson Adams meets Parson Trulliber, in an interview readers long remember. Adams's forgetfulness then lands him in a fresh adventure.

Book Three opens with praise of biography, then a night scene of wonderful adventures. A gentleman relates the history of his life, filling a full chapter. Another chapter stages a dialogue between Adams and his host that nearly ends badly. The return of the lovers prevents the catastrophe. Fielding mixes road adventure, talk, and moral comedy around his simple, good-hearted parson.
joshua-volume-2:
Volume two of Georg Ebers's Joshua opens at chapter nine, inside Pharaoh's palace. A chamberlain ushers Hosea, the Hebrew warrior, into the audience chamber. The palace lies hushed in deep mourning, its gay crowds fled from pestilence. Priests glide through infected rooms swinging silver censers of resin and juniper.

Bai, second prophet of Amon, greets Hosea cheerfully amid the drooping heads. He assures the warrior that no one blames him for his people's misdeeds. But Hosea confesses he came to beg release from military service. The priest interrupts to remind him of a debt. This volume sets Hosea's divided duty, to Pharaoh and to his own people, at its center.
journeys-through-bookland-vol-2:
Journeys Through Bookland, volume two, is Charles H. Sylvester's plan of reading in the world's best literature for children. The new edition of 1922 gathers tales, fables, and poems from many lands. Aesop opens the volume, followed by tales from the Arabian Nights. The Falcon and the Partridge and The Sparrow and the Eagle appear there.

Blake's Infant Joy and a poem by George MacDonald stand among the stories. Readers also meet Grimm's Discreet Hans, Rumpelstiltzkin, and the tale of Bluebeard. Japanese stories, including The Discontented Stonecutter and The Mirror of Matsuyama, widen the range. Sylvester aimed to lead children, step by step, into great books. This volume mixes fairy tale, fable, and verse for young readers at home.
keeping-watch-night-watches-part-2:
Keeping Watch is a set of stories by W. W. Jacobs, the second part of his Night Watches. The night-watchman narrator opens by reading character in a couple resting in their skiff below his wharf. He tells them he is a student of human nature. Then he begins the title tale, about a girl kept aboard the schooner Belle.

Her father, Captain Butt, a widower, watched over the girl too closely for her happiness. Jacobs's watchman tells such tales to pass his slow nights. Each story turns on small deceptions, courtship, and village cunning. The cozy frame, a yarn begun at the wharf, is classic Jacobs. His humor stays gentle even when his characters scheme.
king-henry-iv-part-2:
William Shakespeare wrote King Henry IV, Part 2 as the second part of Henry the Fourth. Its title page adds two key facts about its scope. It contains the death of the king, it says. It also contains the coronation of King Henry the Fifth.

Part 2 opens with an Induction spoken by Rumour alone. Rumour begs the crowd to open their ears to loud speech. Rumour says the wind serves as a post-horse from east to west. False reports and slanders ride on Rumour's tongue in every language. Rumour claims to speak of peace while hidden enmity wounds the world. That warning frames a play built from talk, report, and distrust.
king-henry-vi-part-2:
Duke Gloucester fights fierce charges at court in the passage sampled from Shakespeare's King Henry VI, Part 2. Gloucester says Beauford's red eyes reveal the malice in his heart. Suffolk's cloudy brow shows stormy hate, he claims. Buckingham, too, unburdens an envious load through his tongue, Gloucester adds.

Gloucester accuses York, the Queen, and others of plotting against his guiltless life. False witness and more treason charges will condemn him, he warns. The Cardinal calls his railing intolerable and orders him taken away. Gloucester warns that Henry casts away his crutch too soon. He says the shepherd is beaten from the king's side here.
kitto-cyclopaedia-1845-vol-2:
Volume 2 of Kitto's Cyclopaedia of Biblical Literature appeared in 1845 and completed the work. Kitto had planned the dictionary as the labor of his life, and deafness and poverty had not stopped him. The closing volume brought the Bible's world, from first article to last, into one finished design.

The entries run through the second half of the alphabet, covering places, rites, natural history, and the daily life behind the text. Kitto's rule holds throughout: explain Scripture by the real customs of the East, not by guesswork. Contributors added the results of new travel and excavation as the volumes grew. The great scholar's life work stands finished here, a monument of Victorian learning. For half a century, few ministers in the English-speaking world prepared a sermon far from Kitto's side.
kropotkin-memoirs-revolutionist-1899-vol:
Volume two of Kropotkin's Memoirs of a Revolutionist, also from 1899, completes his autobiography. The first volume carried him from princely childhood to Siberian service. This volume follows the exile years in Western Europe. Kropotkin joins the anarchist movement and becomes one of its leading writers.

He recalls comrades, congresses, trials, and the slow building of a movement. His science continues beside the politics, in geography and biology. The two volumes together finish the life story he chose to tell. Memoirs by revolutionaries rarely match its grace and candor. It remains the standard life of Kropotkin in his own words. Readers close it knowing the man.
l-abbe-constantin-volume-2:
Volume Two continues Ludovic Halévy's French novel The Abbé Constantin, in English. Project Gutenberg issued it as number forty-two in its French Immortals series. The series honored works crowned by the French Academy.

The story centers on a gentle village priest, the Abbé Constantin. New money and new people press against his quiet world of old faith. Kindness, rather than force, shapes how hearts change around him. Readers who finished the first volume will find the tale's warmth deepening here. The volume stands as the middle part of the complete English issue. Its priest remains the calm center while fortunes shift around him.
layamon-brut-madden-vol-2:
Volume two of Layamon's Brut, in Frederic Madden's 1847 edition with his literal English translation, continues the verse chronicle of Britain's kings. Layamon wrote around 1200, in early Middle English alliterative verse. The story now enters its richest ground: the age of Arthur.

Arthur's birth, his wars against the Saxons, his Roman campaign, and the treason of Mordred fill these pages. Layamon expands his sources with dreams, elves at Arthur's birth, and the king borne away to Avalon. His Arthur is grander and stranger than in any earlier English telling. The volume is the heart of the Brut and of early Arthurian literature.
le-morte-d-arthur-volume-2:
Volume Two of Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur continues the Round Table epic. Its contents open with Book Ten and Sir Tristram. Tristram jousts and strikes down King Arthur himself in one chapter.

Tristram also saves his rival Palomides in another chapter. The two promise to fight together within a fortnight. Sagramore and other knights cross Tristram's path in turn. Love, loyalty, and rivalry tangle as the volume proceeds. Readers reach the richer, sadder half of Arthur's world here. Tristram's love for Isolde shadows his many victories. The volume's tournaments grow darker as old loyalties strain.
lecky-england-18th-vol-2:
Walpole's long peace shapes the second volume of Lecky's History of England in the Eighteenth Century, in the 1892 printing. Jacobite risings flare and fail in Scotland and the north. Meanwhile Britain's trade and empire grow year by steady year under a calm, corrupt, stable order.

Lecky weaves politics, society, and ideas into one broad narrative. He shows how a nation grows rich while its public life sinks into jobbery. Ministers, merchants, and mobs each get their measured share of blame and praise. The volume keeps his panoramic method at full stretch, humane in judgment and vast in learning throughout.
legends-and-lyrics-part-2:
The Second Series of Adelaide Anne Procter's Legends and Lyrics continues her popular verse. This text also comes from the 1890 George Bell edition. A Legend of Provence opens the contents list.

Poems include A Lost Chord, her most famous piece of all. Others treat envy, warnings, golden days, and dreams of life. A New Mother and The Tyrant and the Captive show her range. Procter's simple music carries deep feeling about death and hope. Victorian readers kept her books beside their family Bibles. A Lost Chord alone kept her name alive for decades. Its organ music and lost faith still move modern readers.
lesage-gil-blas-smollett-1749-vol-2:
Volume 2 of Smollett's Gil Blas appeared in 1749, continuing Lesage's picaresque novel in Tobias Smollett's English. Gil Blas, the servant hero, has learned the ways of inns, stages, and sickrooms. In this volume his fortunes rise and fall in new households.

Service with quack doctors, proud nobles, and churchmen gives Gil fresh lessons in human folly. He gains money and polish, then loses ground through trust and vanity, as the form demands. Lesage used the rogue's path to satirize every rank of society. Smollett's lively translation kept the French tale an English favorite, and Volume 2 deepens both the comedy and the bite.
li-chi-legge-1885-vol-2:
Volume two of Legge's Li Chi, published in 1885 as Sacred Books of the East twenty-eight, completes the Book of Rites. The second half of the classic turns to education, music's moral power, and the conduct of rulers in detail. The famous chapter on the Great Learning's roots sits within this classic's wider family of texts.

Legge sustains his method: close translation, full notes, and respect for the commentators. Readers meet a civilization that treated manners as a branch of government. Weddings, funerals, audiences, and archery all carry rules meant to school the heart. Together the two volumes give English its complete Li Chi. Legge's Confucian translations, taken as a whole, were a life's work of rare scale.
li-ki-legge-vol-2:
Legge's second Li Ki volume completed the Book of Rites in 1885. It formed volume twenty-eight of the Sacred Books of the East. The remaining ritual classics of ancient China fill its pages.

Two short treatises in this volume became famous far beyond the whole. The Great Learning teaches self-cultivation as the root of good government. The Doctrine of the Mean praises harmony, sincerity, and the balanced life. Later Chinese education made both texts central for students. Together the volumes state ancient China's vision of social order. That order runs from the family altar to the throne itself.
life-and-letters-of-charles-darwin-volum:
Volume Two of Darwin's life and letters opens in October 1859. Its first chapters cover the publication of the Origin of Species. Letters then trace how evolution spread through 1861 and 1862. Later chapters follow the Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication.

Work on man leads to the Descent of Man in 1871. Botanical letters cover flower fertilisation across forty years. Earthworms, coral reefs, and a life of Erasmus Darwin fill later pages. The volume ends with miscellaneous letters running to 1882. Second editions of Coral Reefs and the Descent also appear here. Cross and self fertilisation experiments occupy the final botanical chapter.
life-and-letters-of-thomas-henry-huxley-:
Volume Two of Huxley's life and letters runs year by year. Its chapters march from 1870 through 1884 in sequence. Leonard Huxley arranged his father's correspondence within that frame. A signed 1857 photograph of the young scientist serves as frontispiece.

These were Huxley's years of public eminence in science and education. The annual chapters let readers watch controversies rise and settle. Letters show the working scientist behind the famous public voice. Paired with its companions, the volume completes a full Victorian life. A Walker and Cockerill photograph of 1857 supplies the frontispiece portrait. Chapters for 1875 and 1876 split across two entries each.
life-of-her-most-gracious-majesty-the-qu:
Volume Two of Tytler's Queen Victoria life continues the reign. Royal progresses to Burghley, Stowe, and Strathfieldsaye open the contents. A powder ball and the Queen's first visit to Germany follow. Railway speculation and the failing potato crop mark the 1840s.

Princess Helena's birth and Ibrahim Pasha's visit enter the record. Prince Albert's installation as Cambridge chancellor receives a chapter. The Queen's western Scottish isles tour closes this portion. Tytler keeps close to court movements and public events throughout. Autumn yachting excursions and the Spanish marriages fill chapter five. The western islands stay at Ardverikie closes the listed contents.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-2:
Part Two begins with Chapter 6, a cub-pilot's experience. The Paul Jones took two weeks from Cincinnati to New Orleans. Rocks at Louisville and other delays slowed the voyage. A pilot befriended young Twain and taught him to steer.

A deck passenger borrowed six dollars and never repaid them. Twain jokes the youth probably died, since he never returned. His Amazon exploration scheme collapses for lack of money and ships. So he plans a siege against his pilot for a new career. Deck passage meant steerage, Twain explains in a footnote. The Paul Jones now bound for St. Louis offered his next chance.
little-lucy-s-wonderful-globe-2:
Charlotte Yonge narrates this picture geography of Lucy's wonderful globe. L. Frölich pictured the new edition for young readers. Macmillan published it in New York and London in 1906. Lucy looks at the great globe Uncle Joe lets her touch.

A Keble verse about young fingers tracing the mimic earth opens it. Yonge had written The Heir of Redclyffe before this children's book. The 1871 work teaches countries through an imagined dream journey. Frontispiece and pictures guide children across the pictured world. Macmillan's new edition reached readers in September 1906. Keble's verse about circling orbs ornaments the title page.
littre-dictionary-1863-vol-2:
The second volume of Littré's great French dictionary continued the work begun in 1863. Littré built the dictionary as his life's monument, gathering quotations and tracing forms with a small army of notebooks. The French Academy's own dictionary gave meanings; Littré gave biographies.

Volume 2 moves through the next stretch of the alphabet, each word followed from its Latin or older roots to its living senses. The historical method is applied with scientific care, and the quotations run from medieval epics to the newspapers of Littré's day. The positivist philosopher's monument to his mother tongue grows volume by volume. Readers meet the life story of every word told in full. The volume kept the standard of the first, and France watched its language receive the fullest record any tongue had yet been given.
lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-volume-2:
Volume 2 of George Meredith's Lord Ormont and His Aminta continues Book 2 of the novel. It opens in Aminta's dressing room, where her aunt, Mrs. Pagnell, presses her for plain news. Aminta is now Lord Ormont's wife, yet her place is far from settled.

Chapters here bring in Mrs. Lawrence Finchley and show a bruised warrior's flash of temper. A game played by two runs through these pages, of love held back and pride held high. Meredith lets talk and gesture carry the tension. Readers see a marriage strained by secrecy and by Ormont's cold pride. Aminta's patience and spirit hold the center of the story.
lost-sir-massingberd-a-romance-of-real-l:
Lost Sir Massingberd is a novel by James Payn, printed in London in 1864. It calls itself a romance of real life. Volume 1 first ran in a popular periodical to uncommon favour, says Payn. The tale turns on a baronet who is lost, and on the mystery around him.

Early chapters bring a dream by the brook, a dumb witness, and a state bedroom. A Mr. Harvey Gerard enters the story, and love plays its part too. Payn builds his plot from secrets, searches, and sudden turns. The style is that of the Victorian sensation novel. This first volume sets the loss and leaves the answer for the second.

Volume 2 completes James Payn's Lost Sir Massingberd, the 1864 romance of real life. The missing baronet is still lost as the volume opens. Chapters promise a search, a stone garden, and a covered cart with something inside. A detective of half a century ago joins the hunt.

Bank-notes, a benevolent stranger, and a procession carry the plot toward its answer. Payn keeps the mystery tight until the search pays off. The volume shows how Victorian readers loved a puzzle of rank and disappearance. Old friends gather as the truth comes out at last. It ends the two-volume tale of the lost baronet.
lucian-works-fowler-vol-2:
Volume two of the Fowler brothers' complete Lucian appeared in 1905. Lucian of Samosata aimed his satire at every target his world offered. Pompous philosophers, greedy rich men, and gullible believers all take their turns.

Dialogues and essays in this volume mock hired intellectuals and social climbers. Lucian stages conversations in the underworld where the mighty learn humility. His dialogue form stays quick, theatrical, and merciless throughout. The Fowlers' translation keeps the jokes and jabs accessible in English. Lucian wrote in Greek for Roman-era readers who recognized every type. Modern readers will recognize the same types without difficulty at all.
luther-works-holman-vol-2:
Volume Two of the Holman Philadelphia Luther, published in 1916, follows the reformer as his movement takes hold across Germany. Sermons, treatises, and polemics trace his battles on several fronts at once. Rome, radical reformers, and his own doubts all receive his attention in these pages.

The English text carries Luther's earthy, fiery German into the language of his modern readers, as far as translation allows. Church order, the sacraments, and Christian freedom in daily life fill out the agenda. Readers see a revolution becoming an institution, with all the strain that change involves. The volume rewards anyone tracking how protest turned into churches, schools, and hymnals across northern Europe.
lyell-principles-of-geology-vol-2:
Volume two of Charles Lyell's Principles of Geology followed the first volume of 1830. Lyell turned here from rocks and forces to living things and their place in earth history. He asked how species appear, spread, and vanish over long ages.

Readers find his account of what later writers called the economy of nature. He weighs extinction, climate change, and the slow succession of life. The volume deepens the case that small causes, repeated endlessly, remake whole worlds. It gave Darwin a framework for thinking about species themselves. It also set up the questions his third volume would answer from the rocks.
lyra-graeca-edmonds-loeb-vol-2:
The second Loeb volume of Lyra Graeca, edited and translated by J. M. Edmonds, turns to Anacreon and the choral lyric poets. Anacreon sang at the courts of tyrants in the sixth century BCE. His true fragments are few, but the gay songs written in his name, the Anacreontea, charmed readers for two thousand years.

Wine, love, old age, and the grasshopper fill his light verse. The choral fragments beside him were made for public feasts, sung and danced by trained bands. Edmonds gathers the scraps from quotes, stones, and papyrus. The volume shows Greek lyric in its public and private moods at once.
lyrical-ballads-with-other-poems-1800-vo:
Volume 2 of the 1800 Lyrical Ballads continues Wordsworth's great experiment. Its poems turn again to rural life and simple feeling. 'Hart-leap Well' opens the book with a tale of a hunted stag. 'The Brothers' tells a pastoral story of loss at sea.

Here are 'Lucy Gray' and the strange fits of passion poems. 'Poor Susan' hears a thrush and dreams of her country home. 'Ruth' tells of a girl betrayed by a wild American youth. 'The Pet-Lamb' and 'The Two April Mornings' keep the tender tone. Wordsworth finds deep feeling in the smallest country scenes. The volume completes a landmark of English Romantic poetry.
maccurdy-human-origins-1924-vol-2:
Volume two of George Grant MacCurdy's Human Origins appeared in 1924. The Yale scholar picks up where his geological first volume left off. Here the later Stone Age and its makers fill the pages.

MacCurdy treats the upper Palaeolithic, the Neolithic turn to farming, and fossil peoples. Neanderthals and Cro-Magnons stand at the center of his account. He writes a careful textbook summary of the evidence then available. Readers can watch a whole science mid-stride, before later African finds rewrote the story. Together the two volumes formed the standard American manual of their moment.
madame-chrysantheme-volume-2:
Volume 2 continues Pierre Loti's Madame Chrysanthème, issued as Gutenberg etext 79. The series presents the book among the French Immortals. Loti, a naval officer, kept this diary during a Japanese summer. His pen name hides his real name, Louis-Marie-Julien Viaud.

The summer at Nagasaki moves forward in these pages. His contract marriage to Chrysanthème runs its odd, tender course. Visits, festivals, and small household scenes fill the diary entries. Loti watches Japan with an artist's eye and a sailor's restlessness. The charm of the place never quite becomes understanding. This middle volume deepens both the beauty and the distance.
mahavastu-senart-vol-2:
Senart's second volume of Le Mahavastu appeared in 1890 and carries the Great Story onward. The Sanskrit narrative of the Buddha's past lives runs through its long central stretch here. The work belongs to the Lokottaravada school, which held the Buddha to be more than a man.

Miracles, former births, and the slow road to waking fill these chapters. The text shifts between prose and verse as the old tellers left it. Senart's notes and care keep the hard passages within reach of study. With volume one, this book forms the core of his life's work on the text.
maqrizi-sultans-mamlouks-quatremere-vol-:
Later Mamluk sultans rule in the second volume of Quatremere's 1845 French version of al-Maqrizi. Plague strikes Cairo again and again as the sultanate's power slowly declines. Pageantry and ceremony mask the rot within the palace walls and the treasury's emptying coffers.

Al-Maqrizi watches his beloved city in splendor and in suffering alike. He records prices, processions, factions, and fires with a native's eye. Few medieval cities are documented so richly by one historian. The volume completes the French rendering of a classic Arabic chronicle, giving readers medieval Cairo through the eyes of its greatest and most devoted historian.
mardi-and-a-voyage-thither-vol-1-of-2:
Mardi, and a Voyage Thither is Herman Melville's third book, here volume one of two. This edition dates from 1864 and is dedicated to his brother Allan. It opens with canvas spread and a ship running out to sea. The narrator sails from Ravavai, an island near Pitcairn's.

He has shipped on a cruise for the whale, whose brain enlightens the world. The course runs toward the Galapagos, the Enchanted Islands of wild currents. Sea life, desertion, and an open-boat voyage follow in the tale. Beyond the horizon waits the island world called Mardi. Melville begins in fact and sails steadily into dream. The volume starts one of literature's strangest voyages.
mardi-and-a-voyage-thither-vol-2-of-2:
Volume two of Mardi carries Melville's voyagers into the archipelago itself. Chapters land them on Maramma, among woods, temples, and a great morai. Pilgrims gather at the Temple of Oro to discourse of gods. Braid-Beard tells of Foni, and all debate the god Alma.

The company includes King Media, the historian Mohi, and the poet Yoomy. Babbalanja, the philosopher, endeavors to explain the mystery of things. The narrator Taji presses on in his search through the isles. Talk of gods, kings, and souls fills island after island. Melville turns a sea tale into a vast philosophical quest. The volume is dense, wild, and unlike any other voyage.
marius-the-epicurean-volume-2:
Volume two of Marius the Epicurean brings its hero to the imperial court. 'Stoicism at Court' opens the third part of Pater's tale. Marius serves in the Rome of Marcus Aurelius and watches its triumphs. 'Second Thoughts' and 'The Ceremony of the Dart' deepen his questioning.

Part four enters two curious houses, one of them a Christian home. In Cecilia's house, Marius sees the early church at prayer. The minor peace of the church, then martyrs, pass before him. His soul is, in the last Latin phrase, naturally Christian. Pater ends his hero's long search among Rome's dying gods. The volume is a classic of English aesthetic prose.
marse-henry-an-autobiography-volume-2:
Volume two of Marse Henry takes up Henry Watterson's tale at chapter thirteen. Watterson writes of Congress, of Charles Sumner, and of Schurz and Lamar. Music enters too, through Stephen Foster and his songs.

Paris fills much of the later part of this volume. He writes of Thackeray, of Monte Carlo, and of Leopold of Belgium. The book closes in the years of Grover Cleveland, with Blaine and President Arthur in view. Hay, Henry Adams, and Frank Mason appear among his friends in these pages. The mix of courts, camps, and news rooms gives the volume wide range.
martial-epigrams-ker-loeb-vol-2:
Books eight through fourteen of Martial's epigrams fill this second Loeb volume, in Walter C. A. Ker's English version. Together with the first volume, the set holds more than fifteen hundred poems. Martial wrote them in Rome across the last decades of the first century.

The later books mix praise of Domitian with gifts poems for the Saturnalia, tags meant to travel with presents of food, books, and gear. The wit stays sharp, and the targets stay human: misers, climbers, quacks, and bores. Martial fixed the epigram's shape for two thousand years. These closing books show him at his most varied and grand.
martineau-autobiography-vol-2:
Harriet Martineau wrote her autobiography in 1855, believing she was dying, and it appeared after her death. Volume Two, edited by Maria Weston Chapman in 1877, covers her mature career. Martineau, deaf from youth, had become a leading voice on reform.

She writes of her American travels and her bold book against slavery, which cost her many readers. Political economy, the Irish question, and the literary world of London fill her pages. Martineau judges herself and others with cool honesty. The second volume completes one of the most striking self-portraits by a Victorian woman of letters.
matthew-paris-english-history-giles-vol-:
The second volume of J. A. Giles's Matthew Paris covers 1250 to 1259, the years when England slid toward civil war. Matthew, writing at Saint Albans, had friends at court and in the barons' camp, and he used both. His chronicle is the fullest English record of the age.

Henry III bleeds the realm for foreign plans, and the barons force the Provisions of Oxford on him in 1258. Simon de Montfort rises as the voice of reform. Matthew tells of councils, quarrels, and the mood of the shires year by year. His pages show a kingdom learning to bind its king with law. The story runs on to open war in the next volume.
melbourne-house-volume-2:
Volume two of Melbourne House came out in New York in 1865. Robert Carter and Brothers printed it, as they did volume one. A picture of Silver Lake fronts this part of the tale.

Daisy rides out late on a warm day in chapter one. Her father and Dr. Sandford sit across from her in the carriage. Mr. Randolph lifts her in and sets her on the front seat. A copy note warns that the source lacks chapters eight and eighteen. The ride sets up the home scenes that fill this volume. Daisy's frail health keeps her kin close and watchful.
memoirs-of-aaron-burr-volume-2:
Volume two of the Memoirs of Aaron Burr opens on his law years. A front picture shows Theodosia, his famed daughter. The contents list his study of law and his odd short training.

Davis treats Burr's own definition of law and his way with causes. He loved to surprise a foe, and chose his agents with care. A tale from the contested election of 1800 shows that cool head. Practice at the close of the Revolution gave him a strong start. Coolness in civil life matched his coolness in war, Davis says. Brevity in all he wrote was a marked trait of his mind.
memoirs-of-extraordinary-popular-delusio:
Volume two of Mackay's Popular Delusions turns to faith and fear. Its contents list just four long studies in this part. The Crusades lead, and the Witch Mania comes second.

The Slow Poisoners and Haunted Houses close the volume's list. Mackay opens the Crusades with a long quote from Paradise Lost. Each age, he says, has its own folly, scheme, or craze. Gain, thrill, or mere imitation can spur it, as can church or state. Love of wonder and scorn of truth get no chapter here. That theme still runs under the four studies in this volume.
memoirs-of-general-william-t-sherman-vol:
Volume two of Sherman's memoirs opens in March 1864. Chapter sixteen treats the Atlanta campaign, from Nashville and Chattanooga. On March 18, Sherman relieved Grant in command of the West.

Grant went East to lead all the armies of the United States. Sherman rode with him as far as Cincinnati to talk through plans. They weighed posts for McClellan, Burnside, and Fremont in the East. Buell, McCook, and Crittenden, cleared by a court on Perryville, awaited fresh posts. Nothing was to be done till Grant wrote back on those posts. War plans and staffing fill the opening of this volume.
memoirs-of-henry-hunt-esq-volume-2:
Volume two of Henry Hunt's memoirs picks up his tale of high life. Hunt writes of hunting, shooting, and fishing by day. Nights went to gay crowds, feasts, and a christening ball.

Upwards of forty friends sat down to dinner at that feast. Yet Hunt says he never forgot the poor at such times. Toast and ale went to neighbors, and servants feasted as well. His birthday, November 6, kept his father's old custom of open house. Servants got a junketing they would never forget, he recalls. Open house at birthdays marked the Hunt family's old style.
memoirs-of-james-robert-hope-scott-volum:
Robert Ornsby wrote volume two of the Memoirs of James Robert Hope-Scott. Hope-Scott was a fellow of Merton College, Oxford, and a Queen's Counsel. Ornsby picks passages from his letters to fill the life.

Chapter eighteen treats the years 1841 and 1842 in this volume. Hope's pamphlet on the Jerusalem bishopric stands at its head. Letters pass between Hope and Newman on that plan and on a monastery. Pusey, Manning, and Palmer write in on church strife of the day. Lady G. Fullerton's memories of Hope add a warm close note. Church law, friendship, and doubt meet in his busy Oxford years.
memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-montesp:
Book two of Madame de Montespan's memoirs opens at chapter seventeen. Monsieur's jealousy and the Chevalier de Lorraine's revenge head the chapter. The King's doubts and his wrath stand in the heads as well.

Henrietta of England had grown more fair in six months of marriage. The King marked the change, though she was his brother's wife. A Dutch war loomed, and England's help was worth much then. Henrietta crossed the Channel on a visit that hid talks of great weight. Her husband learned of her trip and pressed her for its secrets. She kept faith, and his silence turned to sulks and cold words.
memoirs-of-marguerite-de-valois-queen-of:
Book two of Marguerite de Valois's memoirs opens at letter thirteen. The League stands at the head of that letter. War is declared against the Huguenots in its first lines.

Marguerite sets out for Spa as the court turns to war. Her brother comes back to court with the Catholic nobles in train. Le Guast, the King's tool, is dead by his doctor's regimen. The King seeks to turn her brother, and her, against her husband's cause. She begs leave to join her husband, and the King stalls her. Fine words mask a plan to keep her as a court ornament.
memorials-and-other-papers-volume-2:
Volume two of De Quincey's Memorials holds three long pieces. Klosterheim leads, then The Sphinx's Riddle, then The Templars' Dialogues. Klosterheim is a tale, dated 1832 in the contents list.

The tale opens in the winter of 1633 in Suabia and Bavaria. Cold set in hard by the first week of November that year. Winter campaigns had become a fixed part of the war in Germany. Swedish troops, bred to cold, pressed that change on softer southern foes. Whole tracts had become a field of graves by that war's path. That grim ground sets the tale's first mood at once.
merivale-romans-empire-vol-2:
Mad emperors reign in the second volume of Merivale's History, in the 1865 printing. Caligula, Claudius, and Nero form the notorious Julio-Claudian line in full. Court intrigue, madness, and murder fill the palace, a glittering snake pit at the heart of the Roman world.

Merivale tells the lurid age with a master hand for telling detail. He neither gloats nor excuses, keeping a steady moral gaze throughout. Wives, freedmen, and guards make and unmake emperors in his pages. The volume shows imperial Rome at its most dramatic and diseased, a warning on what unchecked power does to rulers and ruled alike.
michel-and-angele-a-ladder-of-swords-vol:
Volume Two of Gilbert Parker's romance brings its Jersey characters to Queen Elizabeth's court. The sample chapter shows Lempriere of Rozel serving, bewildered, as the Queen's butler at Greenwich Palace. Gentlemen kneel to lay the table like an altar. A duke's daughter tastes each dish against poison and feeds the carriers.

Lempriere later retold the scene before the Royal Court of Jersey as the island's great honor. Around such pageantry, the Huguenot lovers Michel and Angele face court dangers. Parker mixes exact ceremonial detail with romantic suspense. The volume shows Elizabethan power as both splendid theater and real peril.
mill-principles-political-economy-1848-v:
Volume two of Mill's Principles of Political Economy completes the 1848 first edition. The first volume treated production and the growth of wealth. This volume takes up distribution, exchange, and the role of government. Distribution, Mill argues, rests on human institutions, not on nature alone.

That claim opened room for reform within classical economics itself. Money, credit, trade between nations, and taxes all receive full chapters. Mill weighs free markets against public action with unusual fairness. The completed work ruled English economics teaching for a generation. Later economists from Marshall onward built on its frame. The second volume holds much of its social thought.
milman-history-jews-vol-2:
Kingdoms rise and fall in the second volume of Milman's History of the Jews, from 1829. Israel and Judah split, prophets thunder, and exile carries the people to Babylon. Return under Persia then rebuilds the Temple and the nation's hope in its own land once more.

Milman applies his humane rationalism to the Bible's most dramatic centuries. Kings are judged as men, and miracles as reports to be weighed. His sympathy for the Jewish people marks every chapter he writes. The volume carries his pioneering history through its richest stretch of story, where faith and politics collide on nearly every page of the record.
miscellaneous-writings-and-speeches-volu:
Volume Two of Lord Macaulay's miscellaneous writings collects his contributions to the Edinburgh Review. The essays begin with John Dryden, from January 1828, and an essay on History from that May. Macaulay then attacks Mill on government in three pieces across 1829. Sadler's law of population draws two more essays in 1830 and 1831.

Later reviews treat Mirabeau, in 1832, and Barère, in 1844. The Dryden essay grants him first place in the second rank of English poets. It credits Dryden with lasting influence on national habits of thought. These reviews made Macaulay's name as the great Whig essayist of his generation.
monsieur-de-camors-volume-2: Volume Two continues Octave Feuillet's Monsieur de Camors in English translation. Its Project Gutenberg header ranks it thirty-first in the French Immortals series. The novel's cynical hero carries his career into this middle volume. The hosted sample, however, preserves no readable content from the volume itself. It holds only the Gutenberg header, naming title, author, and release data. Readers get the volume's identity and series place, but none of its pages.
monsieur-lecoq-v-2:
Volume Two of Monsieur Lecoq appears here in Pearson's Library Edition, translated from Émile Gaboriau's French. The contents run from chapter nine through chapter forty, plus an epilogue. The publisher's list advertises Gaboriau's other cases: The Gilded Clique, The Lerouge Case, In Peril of His Life, and File 113.

Lecoq, the young Paris detective, pursues the mystery begun in the first volume's snowy murder scene. Gaboriau built the modern detective novel on such foundations: clues, disguises, and family secrets reaching back years. This volume carries the inquiry to its epilogue. Pearson's illustrated edition brought French crime fiction to American readers in uniform volumes.
motley-barneveld-vol-2:
Barneveld falls in the second volume of Motley's Life and Death, from 1880. The old statesman clashes fatally with Maurice of Nassau over church and power. A rigged trial follows, and the founder is beheaded in 1619 at the age of seventy-one, before the state he made.

Motley tells the tragedy as his most moving piece of work. The state devours its own maker in the tale's bitter core. Crowds, judges, and a calm old man facing death fill his pages. The volume closes Dutch history's saddest story, told by the Republic's greatest foreign friend, whose sympathy for Barneveld burns through every chapter he writes.
motley-united-netherlands-vol-2:
Antwerp besieged and Sea Beggars triumphant fill the second volume of Motley's History of the United Netherlands, from 1861. The Dutch war of independence against Spain grinds on in siege and flood. A small nation's fight for freedom forms the American historian's grand theme throughout the volume.

Motley writes the revolt as an epic of liberty against tyranny. Dikes are cut, cities starve, and sailors raid in his vivid scenes. His research in Dutch archives gave the tale unusual depth of fact. English readers learned the Dutch struggle from Motley above all, and this volume shows his method at full power: heroic, learned, and partisan for freedom.
mr-crewe-s-career-volume-2:
Volume Two of Mr. Crewe's Career contains Book Two, opening at chapter eleven, The Hopper. Humphrey Crewe's reform bills now sit before legislative committees. Churchill mocks the state-house as a dark and bloody ground of selfish interests. Crewe, far from awaiting fate calmly, demands hearings and floods members with copies and appeals.

Foresters, road builders, and farmers are imported, at paid expenses, to testify. Committee rooms overflow into the legislative hall itself. Yet the bills stall under chairmen Bascom and Botcher, who agree with Crewe at dinner and deliberate forever afterward. Churchill shows exactly how railroad-era legislatures buried reform without ever voting it down.
mr-midshipman-easy-2:
Frederick Marryat published this sea novel in 1836, drawn from his own naval life. It opens with Mr. Nicodemus Easy of Hampshire, a rich man with no children. After ten years he gives up hope and turns philosopher. His pet theme is the rights of man and equality for all.

His son Jack carries those fine ideas into the Royal Navy. As a midshipman he meets storms, fights, prisons, and strict rank. The gap between talk at home and life at sea drives the humor. Marryat was praised for wit and true naval detail. This edition is a second copy of the same classic tale.
mrs-falchion-volume-2:
Gilbert Parker's second volume opens as Book Two, The Slope of the Pacific. The narrator is a young man at Prince's College in Toronto. Exams have ended, and he must choose where to spend his break. Letters from home and friends crowd his desk.
