One welcome letter comes from Galt Roscoe in a new western district. Talk of Miss Treherne shows a love plot already in play. A rival named Clovelly has lost with good grace. The scene mixes Canada, the Pacific slope, and young ambition. Parker moves his first novel from college rooms toward wide new country and hard choices.
muqaddimah-prolegomenes-slane-1865-tome-:
Tome two of de Slane's French Muqaddimah appeared in 1865, continuing his translation of Ibn Khaldun's Prolegomena of 1377. The text here follows the French Wikisource presentation of that edition. Ibn Khaldun turns in this tome to the forms of rule: caliphate, kingship, and the ranks and offices of Islamic states.

He weighs how dynasties age, how taxes first lighten and then crush, and how cities flower and fail. His examples range across Arabia, Persia, and the Maghreb he knew at first hand. De Slane's notes keep the Arabic terms precise for French readers. The middle tome holds much of the political science that made the Muqaddimah famous. Modern readers still mine its chapters on power's life cycle.
my-life-volume-2:
Richard Wagner's second volume covers the years 1850 to 1861 first. It opens in exile near Zurich, in a parish called Enge. His wife Minna had found rooms in an old inn, Zum Abendstern. The flat overlooked the lake and cost a modest rent.

Wagner arrives early and finds Minna still in bed. Old quarrels are put aside by a quick promise. Pets named Peps and Papo cheer the small household. Life abroad was growing more comfortable, he admits. Yet he felt a restless pull against all convention. The volume shows the composer building works and a new life far from Dresden.
narrative-and-miscellaneous-papers-volum:
Thomas De Quincey's second volume gathers essays on wide-ranging themes. It opens with the system of the heavens as Lord Rosse's telescopes showed it. Modern superstition and the temperance movement follow. A paper on Coleridge and opium-eating draws on De Quincey's own fame.

An essay on war and Kant's last days close the set. The heavens paper cites J. P. Nichol of Glasgow from 1846. Kant's old essay on the Earth's age starts its argument. De Quincey ranges from stars to drink with one restless mind. His ornate, intense prose makes even reviews feel like voyages through vast, linked ideas.
nex-pelle-the-conqueror-vol-2:
Pelle leaves the farm for town life in the second English volume of Nexo's epic, the part called Apprenticeship. He learns a trade with his own hands in a small workshop. He also learns how workers live, meet, and begin to talk of rights.

Workshop talk and town poverty shape the young man's mind as much as any book. Old habits of obedience wear thin under new ideas. Nexo follows his hero from rural innocence toward urban struggle step by step. The volume shows a whole class slowly waking up, seen through one alert and hopeful young worker.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-2:
Volume two of Schaff's Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, holds Augustine's City of God together with his Christian Doctrine. The set began in 1886 under Philip Schaff's editorship. Augustine wrote the City of God across thirteen years after Rome's sack in 410.

Pagan critics blamed Christians for the fall of Rome; Augustine answers by retelling all history as two cities, built by two loves. The earthly city loves self to the scorn of God; the heavenly city loves God to the scorn of self. Christian Doctrine then teaches how to read scripture and preach it. Together they are Augustine's most public works.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-2:
Socrates and Sozomen, two lay historians of the fifth century, share volume two of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890. Both were lawyers of Constantinople, and both took up church history where Eusebius left off. Schaff and Wace edited the series.

Socrates covers the years 305 to 439: councils, emperors, and the Arian wars of doctrine, in a cool, fair-minded tone. Sozomen covers much the same ground with more color, adding monks, missions, and the finding of relics. Read together, they continue the story of the church inside a Christian empire. Their double account lets readers check one historian against the other.
niebuhr-history-rome-vol-2:
Barthold Niebuhr rebuilds early Rome in the second volume of his History, in Hare and Thirlwall's 1838 English version. Legend is sifted from fact by a stern new method. Niebuhr, founder of modern critical history writing, questions every tale that earlier ages swallowed whole without a doubt.

He shows how ballads and family pride warped the record of kings and consuls. Source criticism, his new science, remakes the early republic chapter by chapter. German learning found eager English translators in Hare and Thirlwall. The volume marks a turning point in how all ancient history would be written, with doubt itself turned into a tool of truth.
night-and-morning-volume-2:
Volume two of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Night and Morning holds Book the Second of the novel. Chapter heads in this part give no titles, so the tale runs on in numbered steps. Verses from Beaumont and Fletcher head the first chapter here. One speaks of a brother as a last hope.

Mr Beaufort walks home haunted by gloomy, confused terrors. He fears Philip's denunciations will fall less on himself than on his son Arthur. Arthur might meet the wild stranger soon, at the height of his passion. Beaufort also doubts his hold over his son after their last scene. He turns to his wife for comfort or sense.
no-defense-volume-2:
Volume two of Gilbert Parker's No Defense holds Book the Second of the novel. Dyck Calhoun enters the world again in its first chapter. Friends wait in front of the prison on a dour November day. Seven minutes, one says, and Dyck will be out, God bless him.

Dyck has served four years of an eight year sentence, the talk explains. Grey has gathered at his temples in that time. Word of his father's death, and of creditors swallowing Playmore, met him inside. Release may tie to what he told the government about the French navy. Later chapters turn to a mutiny's eve and the West Indies.
normandy-the-scenery-romance-of-its-anci:
Part two of Gordon Home's Normandy opens at chapter four, on the cathedral city of Evreux and the road to Bernay. The deep toned bourdon of the cathedral tower tolls over the old town. A yellow evening light glows on painted stucco walls and cobbled streets. Laurels in the Hotel du Grand Cerf courtyard still hold the golden flood.

Evreux, Home says, needs no fine evening to attract a visitor. Its cathedral nave, he claims, is the finest and best proportioned in Normandy. The belfry, the Norman church of St Taurin, and the museum add their draws. The much divided river Iton gives quaint peeps through the town.
north-america-volume-2:
Volume two of Anthony Trollope's North America continues his account of the United States in war time. He had travelled there from August 1861 to May 1862. Chapman and Hall issued the two volumes in 1862. This volume opens at Washington, with a chapter on Congress itself.

The causes of the war get a full chapter early on. Trollope then rides from Washington to St Louis, through Missouri, Cairo, and Camp Wood. The Army of the North and a return to Boston follow. Later chapters treat the Constitution, the government, law courts, and finances. The post office, American hotels, and literature close the survey. The Declaration of Independence sits in an appendix.
northern-lights-volume-2:
Volume two of Gilbert Parker's Northern Lights holds three tales: To-Morrow, Qu'Appelle, and The Stake and the Plumb-Line. To-Morrow opens with a woman ironing a white petticoat. She lifts her head and cries that nothing is the matter with the world today. It is so good, she says, it almost hurts.

Outside her door a valley runs down from snow tipped mountains. Fir covered foothills and maple and ash woods glow in autumn tints. A stream roars down the ravine from the heights. The bracing air seems part of her own passion for life. Parker sets his western tales in country that shapes the folk who live there.
nsa-crises-alerts-defcons-part-2:
The National Security Archive's 2021 briefing book, part two of a series edited by William Burr, gathers declassified records of American military alerts from 1961 to 1976. The subject is the DEFCON system, the ladder of readiness the United States climbs in a crisis. The records are public government documents.

The alerts run from the Berlin crisis and the Cuban Missile Crisis to the worldwide alert of October 1973, during the Middle East war. Memos and logs show how presidents and generals raised and lowered the nation's guard, and how Moscow read the signals. The set is a history of nuclear brinkmanship told in its own paperwork.
nsa-stopping-korea-going-nuclear-part-2:
The National Security Archive's Nuclear Vault published this briefing book in 2017, the second part of its study of South Korea's secret nuclear weapons program. William Burr edited the collection of declassified United States documents. In the 1970s, President Park Chung-hee quietly set out to build the bomb.

The documents trace Seoul's deal for a French reprocessing plant and its bargain for Canadian CANDU reactors. They then show Washington's pressure campaign: threats over loans, aid, and the alliance itself, until Park backed down. The file is a case study in how the United States policed its own allies' nuclear ambitions. The records are declassified and public.
nsa-us-nuclear-presence-western-europe-p:
The National Security Archive published this Nuclear Vault briefing book in 2020, edited by William Burr. It is the second part of a study of United States nuclear weapons in Western Europe from 1954 to 1962. The documents are declassified records from the height of the Cold War.

They cover where the weapons were based, who held the keys, and how allied sharing was arranged under NATO. Custody fights, safety fears, and secret agreements with host nations fill the cables. The file shows an atomic alliance being built piece by piece, much of it hidden from publics at the time. Many of these deployments still shape NATO's nuclear posture today.
old-mortality-volume-2:
Sir Walter Scott continued his Covenanter novel in volume two. The volume opens near a fresh field of battle. Burley guides Morton to a shepherd's hut for council. Presbyterian leaders meet in smoke, noise, and confusion there. Crowds of countrymen press at the open door.

Burley forces the intruders out with threats and force. Morton then watches the council debate its next moves. Scott shows zeal, fear, and pity in the camp. The second volume deepens the tragedies of the war. It carries Henry Morton's story toward its close. Furze blazes on the hearth while tallow dips light the room. Smoke hangs thick above the heads of the whole council.
one-of-our-conquerors-volume-2:
George Meredith continued his novel in this second volume. It opens with book two, chapter twelve. A loving household can still keep deep silence, he writes. Victor and Nataly each hold the key to the other. A cloud over their daughter's name strikes them dumb.

Both shrink from a crisis they feel drawing near. Subjects that darken toward it are shunned in talk. A mere gesture signals the forbidden topic between them. Later chapters treat Nesta's suitors and Skepsey's misconduct. Meredith writes in dense, flashing, ironic prose. The volume deepens the family's hidden wound and pride.
orderic-vitalis-ecclesiastical-history-f:
The second volume of Thomas Forester's Orderic Vitalis, from 1854, carries the Ecclesiastical History deeper into the Norman world. Orderic, a monk of Saint Evroul, wrote of the men and houses he knew at first hand. His chronicle is the fullest Norman record of the twelfth century.

Wars of the Conqueror's sons, the founding of abbeys, and the deeds of knights and bishops fill these books. Orderic loves a life story and gives scores of them, with deaths, dreams, and judgments. He reports the White Ship's sinking and the sorrow that followed in the wider tale. Forester's English keeps the monk's warmth. The volume is rich ore for the age of Henry I.
oscar-wilde-his-life-and-confessions-vol: Frank Harris's biography Oscar Wilde: His Life and Confessions appeared in 1916. He published it himself in New York in 1918. This volume carries Wilde from his parents' Dublin household to fame and marriage. The hosted sample shows the title page and contents only. The contents promise his parents on trial, and the schoolboy. Trinity Dublin and Magdalen Oxford follow. So do the poems and the quarrel with Whistler. No page of Harris's narrative appears, so this note follows the contents alone.

The second volume of Frank Harris's life of Oscar Wilde opens at the catastrophe. Book two begins with chapter seventeen, on prison: an English prison with its insufficient bad food and soul-degrading routine, inflicted on that amiable, joyous, eloquent man. Above the chapter stands an epigraph from Wilde's own Ballad of Reading Gaol, about the sinner who wakes a dead soul to pain.

Harris published the biography himself in New York in 1918, having known Wilde personally. This volume covers the trials' aftermath, the prison years, and the broken exile that followed, told by a partisan friend who made no secret of his admiration. However later scholars have corrected it, Harris's book fixed the popular image of Wilde's fall for a generation of readers.
pahlavi-texts-west-vol-2:
E. W. West translated the second volume of Pahlavi Texts in 1882. It appeared as volume eighteen of the Sacred Books of the East. Middle Persian Zoroastrian writings form the volume's contents.

The Dadistan-i Dinik gives a priest's answers to ninety-two religious questions. The Mainyo-i Khard, or Spirit of Wisdom, proceeds in dialogue form. Questions cover theology, ethics, cosmology, and the fate of the soul. These texts come from medieval Persia under Islamic rule. Priests wrote them to keep the Zoroastrian faith instructed and alive. West's translations rescued Middle Persian literature for English readers across five volumes. This second installment deepened the rescue considerably.
palfrey-history-new-england-vol-2:
Hard testing fills the second volume of Palfrey's History of New England, from 1858. King Philip's War nearly wipes out the young colonies in fire and ambush. Governor Andros then rules as a tyrant from Boston, until the Glorious Revolution sends shock waves across the Atlantic to free them.

Palfrey shows the Puritan experiment tried by fire in earnest. The second generation learns that the wilderness gives nothing for free. Faith, fear, and stubborn town pride carry the colonies through. The volume deepens his classic account of colonial New England, a work that fixed the region's story of itself for the century that followed him.
pappus-collection-hultsch-vol-2:
The second volume of Friedrich Hultsch's edition of Pappus of Alexandria appeared in 1877, with the Greek text and a Latin version. It holds books six and seven of the Mathematical Collection, and book seven ends with its true closing word intact. Pappus wrote around 320 CE, the last great geometer of the ancient world.

Book seven is the famous treasury of analysis, a guide to the lost works that taught geometers how to find proofs. Descartes and Newton both drew on this spring of ancient method. The volume covers conics, curves, and the working tools of the old masters. No English version exists in the public domain, so the Greek and Latin carry the text.
pareto-cours-economie-politique-1897-fr-:
Tome two of Pareto's Cours d'economie politique came out in 1897, completing his Lausanne lectures. The first tome had laid out general equilibrium and a first form of his optimality idea. This volume carries the course through its remaining ground. Applications and further theory fill out the system he taught at Lausanne.

Pareto presses his mathematical treatment of markets, production, and exchange. The French text remains the only period version, since no public domain English translation exists. The two tomes together form the founding text of the Lausanne school. Students of economic theory still consult them in French. The closing volume shows the system whole. Its reach shaped a century of theory.
pareto-systemes-socialistes-1902-fr-vol-:
Tome two of Les Systemes socialistes, also from 1902, completes Pareto's survey of socialist systems. The first tome moved from utopian schemes toward Marx and his school. This closing volume finishes the Lausanne lecture course. Pareto weighs the later systems and draws his general lessons.

He doubts that any scheme can repeal the rule of elites in society. New orders, he argues, swap one elite for another under fresh slogans. The French text stands alone, with no public domain English translation. The two tomes together form the complete work. Readers meet Pareto's social thought before the great Trattato. Its skepticism set the key for his later fame.
pareto-trattato-sociologia-generale-1916:
Volume two of Pareto's Trattato di sociologia generale, also from 1916, completes his sociology masterwork. The first volume set out residues, derivations, and the circulation of elites. This volume carries the vast argument to its close. Social balance, elites in decline, and the forms of society fill its pages.

Pareto keeps his stance of the cold observer of human self deception. Reasons people give, he holds, mask drives they rarely admit. The Italian original stands alone, as no public domain English translation exists. The two volumes together form the complete Trattato. Sociologists still mine its terms and its data. Few treatises match its scale.
parkman-half-century-conflict-vol-2:
Volume 2 of the Half-Century of Conflict appeared in 1892 under Parkman's hand. King George's War and the road to the Seven Years' War fill it. The taking of Louisbourg marks a high point of the fighting.

Battles shift to the Ohio country as the great storm gathers pace. Parkman builds toward the French and Indian War with full force. Frontier forts fall, armies march, and whole regions change hands fast. The fate of a continent hangs on fights in deep woods. His narrative power drives the long tragedy toward its terrible climax in war. The stakes rise with each campaign he recounts here.
passages-from-the-american-notebooks-vol:
Volume 2 of Passages from the American Notebooks opens with extracts from Hawthorne's private letters. The first letters come from Brook Farm in April 1841, where he had joined the farming commune. Snow still covers the ground, and he jokes that he has wandered into the Arctic Circle.

He describes learning farm work, breaking a hay machine, and sitting at meals with his fellows. Margaret Fuller's fractious heifer gets a mention. These pages show Hawthorne outside his gloomy fiction, laughing at himself while testing a communal way of life that many American writers tried.
passages-from-the-english-notebooks-volu:
Volume 2 of Passages from the English Notebooks continues Hawthorne's English journals into the year 1856. One entry, from that year, describes a dinner at London's Milton Club, a club lately founded for dissenters and nonconformists. Hawthorne sizes up the sixteen guests, most of them authors or men of the press.

He notes the food, the fast-flowing wine, and writers such as Tom Taylor and Herbert Ingram. The entries are social portraits as much as diary notes. They show Hawthorne, the reclusive romancer, moving through London's literary world and quietly judging everyone at the table.
passages-from-the-french-and-italian-not:
Volume 2 of Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks finds Hawthorne in Florence, deep in his Italian travels. A June entry describes a morning at the Uffizi gallery. He walks its long rooms slowly, taking in sculpture and pictures arranged from Giotto and Cimabue onward.

He studies busts of Roman emperors and weighs which likenesses can be trusted. A dark picture of Christ carrying the cross moves him unexpectedly. These pages show an American Protestant writer learning to look at Catholic art, and recording his honest, shifting responses to Italy's treasures.
pausanias-description-greece-frazer-vol-:
Volume two of Frazer's Pausanias, published in 1898, turns to commentary on Attica. Frazer unpacks the traveler's tour of Athens and its countryside in detail. The great sanctuaries receive the same close treatment here.

Eleusis and its mysteries get extended discussion from inscriptions and remains. Frazer compares Pausanias against every other ancient source he can find. Maps, measurements, and excavation reports support his arguments throughout. Victorian scholarship works at full stretch in these notes. Readers learn not only what Pausanias saw but what stood there. The commentary turned a guidebook into a research library for Greek religion and topography.
paying-off-deep-waters-part-2:
"Paying Off" is one of W. W. Jacobs's Deep Waters tales, told by his famous night-watchman. The watchman begins by confessing his faults, which he calls good nature and sharpness. He has spent his life giving free help and advice on the wharf, and nobody thanks him for either.

His story concerns Captain Mellun of the little schooner Firefly, a soft-headed skipper trading between the wharf and Bristol. The watchman kept steering him out of folly, pint by pint at the Bear's Head. Jacobs builds the comedy from dockside talk, gullible sailors, and the watchman's wounded pride.
pentagon-papers-vol-2:
Volume 2 of the Senator Gravel edition of the Pentagon Papers came out in 1971, months after newspapers began printing the leaked study. The Pentagon Papers were a secret Defense Department history of American involvement in Vietnam from 1945 to 1968. Senator Mike Gravel read parts into the record of Congress, and a publisher issued the set in book form.

The second volume follows the war's deepening through the early 1960s, as advisers, money, and covert action piled up. Internal memos show officials doubting the effort in private while pledging success in public. Daniel Ellsberg's leak of the full study shook trust in government and fed the movement to end the war. The Supreme Court protected its publication as a landmark of press freedom.
personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-volume-:
Part 2 of volume 1 of Sheridan's memoirs opens at chapter nine, with the expedition to Booneville in May 1862. Sheridan rides with the Second Michigan and Second Iowa cavalry under Colonel Elliott. Their orders are to cut the Mobile and Ohio Railroad and destroy Confederate supplies below Corinth, Mississippi.

Men and horses suffer in the heat, with guides unobtainable and roads unknown. Local people, mistaking the column for Confederates, give up their reserve stores. Sheridan describes forcing the enemy from the station and riding out to burn a bridge. The success of the raid brought his recommendation as brigadier-general.
personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-2:
Part 2 of Grant's memoirs opens at chapter fourteen, with the army returning from Mexico. Grant reflects that the Mexican War taught him the characters of the officers he would later face. At West Point and in Mexico he had known Lee, the Johnstons, and Kearney personally, and knew them to be mortal, not superhuman.

The chapter follows the evacuation of Mexico, the fever at Vera Cruz, and his marriage at St. Louis in August 1848. Orders for the Pacific Coast follow. Grant's plain hindsight, measuring old comrades who became his enemies, gives these pages their quiet power.
personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-volume-2: The hosted sample stops at the front matter of volume 2 of Grant's Personal Memoirs, the contents pages, with no chapter text visible. The contents begin with Grant's arrival at Chattanooga and the battles around it, then his commission as lieutenant-general and first interview with Lincoln. Sherman's campaign in Georgia, the grand movement of the Army of the Potomac, the crossing of the Rapidan, and the battle of the Wilderness carry the list forward.
personal-recollections-of-joan-of-arc-vo: The sample hosted for this entry shows only the front matter of volume 2 of Mark Twain's Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc, the title page and contents. No narrative text is visible. The title presents the book as the work of the Sieur Louis de Conte, Joan's page and secretary, translated from an unpublished manuscript in the National Archives of France. The contents continue court and camp: the red field of Patay, the crowning of the heir of France, and Joan foretelling her doom.
peter-simple-and-the-three-cutters-vol-1: The hosted sample shows only the front matter of Peter Simple and The Three Cutters, volumes 1 and 2, the title page and the start of the contents. No chapter text is visible. The title page names Captain Marryat, with J. M. Dent of London and Little, Brown of Boston as publishers, in an edition dated 1895. The contents promise a list of Marryat's works, a biographical introduction, and a prefatory note before Peter Simple begins.
pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-far-n:
Gilbert Parker's second volume of Pierre and His People holds three tales: A Prairie Vagabond, She of the Triple Chevron, and Three Outlaws. The set tells stories of the Canadian far north, where Hudson's Bay posts, Mounted Police, and half-breed communities shaped daily life.

A Prairie Vagabond opens on Little Hammer, a vagabond Indian whom missionaries called a disappointment and company officials called no good. The Crees and Blackfeet would have nothing to do with him, yet he loved the post at Yellow Quill, paid back borrowed tobacco, and kept his word to women. Starving and driven from place to place one winter, he still asked for food and shelter as a right, not as a beggar.
plato-dialogues-jowett-vol-2:
The second volume of Plato's dialogues in Benjamin Jowett's translation holds nine works centered on Socrates' last days and his method. Meno asks whether virtue can be taught, and Euthyphro wrestles with the meaning of piety. The Apology gives Socrates' defense speech at his trial.

Crito shows him refusing to escape prison, holding that a citizen must obey the laws even when they kill him. Phaedo then narrates his final day and death, with his arguments that the soul is immortal. The volume also holds the Gorgias, on rhetoric and power, and the two Hippias dialogues and Menexenus. It is the heart of the Socratic story.
plautus-comedies-riley-1852-vol-2:
Riley's second Plautus volume, published in 1852, holds Amphitryon, Mercator, Cistellaria, Truculentus, Persa, Casina, Poenulus, Epidicus, and Mostellaria, plus the fragments. With it, the surviving comedies of Plautus stand complete in his Bohn prose translation. Amphitryon, where Jupiter impersonates a general to reach his wife, opens the volume in high style.

Mostellaria gives Rome's best haunted-house farce, as a slave invents ghosts to hide his young master's spending. Casina turns a household's lust for one girl into a wedding-day trap. Riley's notes explain Roman customs that the jokes depend on. Together the two volumes replaced the library's small earlier selection. Plautus in full shows how much of later comedy starts here.
poems-in-two-volumes-volume-2:
William Wordsworth's Poems in Two Volumes closes with this second volume, which opens with poems written during a tour in Scotland. Rob Roy's Grave leads, followed by the Solitary Reaper, Stepping Westward, Glen-Almain, and an address to the sons of Burns written after visiting their father's grave. Travel in Scotland gave Wordsworth some of his purest lyrics, where a heard song or a highland girl becomes an occasion for meditation.

A second group, Moods of My Own Mind, collects the intimate lyrics: To a Butterfly, Written in March, the Small Celandine, the Sparrow's Nest, and To the Cuckoo. The Blind Highland Boy, a longer tale, follows. The volume's short pieces, many only a page long, are the ones readers have loved most. Proof that Wordsworth's revolution in poetry worked at the scale of a single flower noticed on a walk.
poems-volume-2:
George Meredith's Poems continue in the second volume of the Surrey Edition. Published by the Times Book Club in London in 1912, with his chalet at Box Hill pictured at the front. Meredith spent his last decades at Box Hill in Surrey, walking its downs and writing the nature philosophy that fills these pages. The volume gathers lyrics and meditations in his knotty, brilliant style.

Lucifer in Starlight, his famous sonnet of the prince of air rising on a starred night and sinking before the army of unalterable law, stands near the front. Lines to a friend visiting America, a poem to J. M., Time and Sentiment, and the Star Sirius surround it with his themes of earth, spirit, and acceptance. Readers who work through Meredith's compressed music find one of the Victorian age's most original minds thinking in verse about how to live with nature's laws.
polybius-histories-shuckburgh-vol-2:
Volume two of Shuckburgh's Polybius covers Books 10 through 39, mostly in fragments. Rome's wars move east into Greece and Asia during these books. The fall of Carthage and Corinth in 146 BCE ends the story.

Polybius witnessed some of these events and knew leading Roman generals personally. The surviving excerpts treat embassies, sieges, constitutions, and geography in his probing style. Byzantine excerptors preserved much of what we have here. Gaps are frequent because the full text was lost in transmission. Even fragmented, Polybius explains Rome's world conquest better than any other ancient writer we possess.
poor-jack-2:
Frederick Marryat's Poor Jack opens in the hero's own voice, and Jack begins, as he says most storytellers do, with other people's histories. He believes he was born in 1786, because his father reckoned all dates by naval events. Jack was launched a few months before the Druids were turned over to the Melpomene, an event of January 1787. Anno Domini meant nothing to the old sailor, who dated his own service from before Bunker's Hill.

The father comes alive in a page: picked up unconscious by a press gang, raised through the tops of men-of-war in three oceans. Made captain's coxswain under the preposterous Sir Hercules Hawkingtrefylyan, a poor, proud baronet ruled by his even prouder lady. Marryat's comedy and his exact naval memory are inseparable here. This telling of the 1840 novel starts from the text itself, father first before the son's own Greenwich boyhood begins.
prince-zilah-volume-2:
Jules Claretie's Prince Zilah concludes in this second volume, number fifteen in the French Immortals series and the second of his works in it. The prince's marriage to Marsa, shadowed from the first volume by the secret of her earlier seduction and the villain who holds the proof. Moves toward its crisis: honor, as the Paris of the novel understands it. Demands that a husband answer such a stain with blood or with ruin.

Claretie's melodrama plays out among gypsies, journalists, and duelists, with the prince's magnanimity against society's code as the real contest. The two-volume form was the era's standard dress for a translated French novel of society. The Academy's series branding certified the author an immortal while he still lived. Readers finishing the pair get the complete arc: love, blackmail, and the question whether a great lord can forgive what his world cannot.
proclus-commentary-timaeus-taylor-vol-2:
Volume Two of Taylor's Proclus continues the notes on Plato's Timaeus. Proclus writes as head of the Athenian school in its last age. His subject is how the world soul and nature were made.

He parses Plato line by line with myth and math together. Gods, daemons, and numbers each get their ranked place. Taylor's English stays formal and dense throughout. The volume completes a monument of late pagan thought. Readers who finish it gain a rare view: Plato read by a believer who staked his faith on every word.
queen-victoria-2: Queen Victoria, by Lytton Strachey, appears here in the London edition of Chatto and Windus, 1921. Front matter only is shown. A frontispiece shows Victoria, Prince Albert, and the royal family after Winterhalter. A dedication to Virginia Woolf follows. Then come the first contents entries. Antecedents stands at page 1. Childhood stands at page 18. Lord Melbourne is at page 51, Marriage at page 97, and Lord Palmerston at page 149.
quintilian-institutio-butler-loeb-vol-2:
Books three through five of Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria fill this second Loeb volume, in H. E. Butler's translation. Quintilian wrote the work late in the first century as the master guide to Roman speaking. The student now leaves school drills and learns how a real case is built.

Here Quintilian treats the kinds of oratory, the finding of arguments, and the proof and refutation of charges. He sorts the issues a court speech can turn on and shows how to frame them. The tone stays practical: this is a teacher who tried cases himself. These books give the working core of Roman rhetoric.
ragged-lady-volume-2:
Ragged Lady, volume two, by William Dean Howells, opens its Part Two at chapter fifteen, in a New York hotel where Mrs. Lander arrives with Clementina Claxon. The staff all remember her from journeys north and south with her husband: the clerk shakes her hand across the register, the bell-boy recalls himself, and the elevator-boy smiles in welcome.

At breakfast the foreign accents of the waiters and a touch of strangeness in the cooking shelter the girl, until Mrs. Milray sweeps down on them, kissing Clementina before the whole room and marveling at how grown and pretty she is. Mr. Milray, unwell since his mother's death, takes breakfast in his room while his wife plans to take him abroad.
ranke-history-england-vol-2:
Henry VIII and the break with Rome fill Ranke's Volume 2. Oxenford's English version of the History of England appeared in 1875. The German master brings his calm eye to the English Reformation's politics.

Ranke traces how king, pope, and parliament pulled against each other. Divorce, supremacy, and the fall of great ministers drive his narrative. He judges none of them with heat, yet none escapes his probe. State papers and envoy letters ground each turn of the tale. The cool tone hides a sharp sense of power and its costs. Few accounts of Henry's reign feel so steady or so deep.
ranke-reformation-germany-vol-2:
Volume 2 of Ranke's Reformation history, in Austin's 1845 English, spreads the fire. The new faith sweeps across Germany town by town and court by court. The Peasants' War and the Confession of Augsburg mark its path.

Princes turn Protestant for faith, for land, and for power alike. Ranke sorts their mixed motives with his cool, probing judgment throughout. Cities adopt reform, armies form, and Rome strikes back with bans. A whole land is remade by an idea in one lifetime. The narrative sweeps wide yet never loses the thread of proof. Modern Europe's deepest split takes shape in these pages.
repertory-of-the-comedie-humaine-part-2: Part II of the Repertory of the Comedie Humaine opens, in the pages at hand, with a publisher's header and nothing more. Its title line gives the span of this second part: L through Z, completing the alphabet. The header assigns the item a place in a series by or about Honoré de Balzac. No entry, preface, or contents page is printed after the header here. The part's own listings, from L onward, must therefore be sought past these front pages.
reymont-the-peasants-vol-2:
Winter settles on the village in the second English volume of Reymont's The Peasants. Snow seals the fields, and life turns inward to hearth, church, and inn. Weddings bring feasting and dance, while old conflicts simmer under the frost.

The Boryna household faces strain as desire and land disputes grow sharper. Reymont renders cold, hunger, and rare joy with the same strong hand. Custom rules the season, from holy days to village gossip. The epic's slow cycle gains force here, showing how winter tests both the land and the bonds that hold a village together.
rhoda-fleming-volume-2: Volume two of George Meredith's Rhoda Fleming opens here with a publisher's header and nothing else. That header records the title, names Meredith as author, and marks the text as English. It also assigns the volume a place in a series of Meredith's works, as the twenty-eighth item. After the header comes no page of the novel itself: no chapter heading, no contents list, and no note of where the story resumes. The second volume's own ground in Rhoda Fleming's tale is not shown in these pages.
roger-hoveden-annals-riley-vol-2:
Henry Riley's second volume of Roger of Hoveden, from 1853, runs from 1192 to 1201 and completes the chronicle. Roger served Henry II and wrote on into the reigns of Richard and John. These last years are among the best reported of the medieval English past.

Richard the Lionheart returns from captivity, wars in France, and dies of a crossbow wound at Chalus. John takes the throne and begins the slide toward the loss of Normandy. Roger keeps his clerk's habit of copying state papers into the annals. The volume closes with the author's own age still in turmoil. Riley's version made this dry, rich source a standard tool.
roger-wendover-flowers-history-giles-vol:
The second volume of J. A. Giles's Roger of Wendover, from 1849, completes the Flowers of History. Roger wrote at Saint Albans down to his death in 1236. In this volume the chronicle reaches the reigns he knew at first hand, above all the stormy years of King John.

Roger tells of John's loss of Normandy, his quarrel with the church, the barons' revolt, and Magna Carta. His account of John is harsh and became the standard picture of that king for centuries. French invasion and the young Henry III close the tale. Matthew Paris built his greater chronicle on this base. The two volumes together found the Saint Albans tradition.
romance-three-kingdoms-brewitt-taylor-19:
Volume two of Brewitt-Taylor's Romance of the Three Kingdoms, published in English in 1925, holds chapters sixty-one through one hundred twenty. The scan here follows the 1929 Kelly and Walsh popular edition, a reprint of the first printing. The three kingdoms grind toward their long foreordained reunion under one rule.

Zhuge Liang's northern campaigns, fought with unmatched craft against a stronger foe, dominate these chapters. Deaths of the great founders clear the stage for lesser heirs and final conquest. Brewitt-Taylor sustains the chronicle pace across hundreds of named officers and battles. The novel ends where Chinese history resumes: division, long endured, must end in unity. Together the two volumes give English the complete San Kuo.
roughing-it-part-2:
Part 2 of Mark Twain's Roughing It, in an 1880 printing, opens at Chapter XI with news of Slade, heard again two or three years later. Word reached the Pacific coast that the Vigilance Committee in Montana had hanged him. Twain quotes at length from The Vigilantes of Montana by Prof. Thos. J. Dimsdale, a book he calls thrilling and well worth reading. Dimsdale, he says, shows how frontier people dealt with criminals when the courts of law proved weak.

Two remarks by Dimsdale frame Slade for Twain. Men who saw Slade calm called him a kind husband, a warm host, and a polite gentleman. Men who met him wild with drink, ringed by armed roughs, called him a fiend in human form. The quoted account then tells how the Vigilantes, after hanging five men on January 14, set up a People's Court.
rousseau-volume-1-and-2:
John Morley wrote Rousseau in two volumes, issued by Macmillan in London and New York in a 1905 reprinting. The work was first printed in this form in 1886 and reprinted in 1888, 1891, 1896, and 1900. In a note to the first edition, dated February 1873, Morley says the book offers more of a steady personal history than his companion volume on Voltaire needed. Voltaire's life, he notes, could already be found in more than one sound English book. For Rousseau, he believes, no full life story existed in English.

Morley is blunt about the French lives he had to use. Musset-Pathay's history of Rousseau's life and works, from 1821, is hard work, he grants, but crude and shapeless in plan, with dull readings of the man. Morley bases his references on the Auguis edition of Rousseau's works, in twenty-seven volumes from 1825.
sacred-books-east-vol-17-vinaya-texts-2:
The Vinaya Texts continue in volume seventeen of the Sacred Books of the East, translated by T. W. Rhys Davids and Hermann Oldenberg in 1885. Part two carries the Mahavagga, the Great Series of monastic rules, further along. Volume thirteen held its opening; the story of the order's growth resumes here.

The rules now cover robes, food, medicines, and the settling of disputes among monks. As before, each rule arrives with its origin story: some lapse or quarrel that made the Buddha lay it down. The Buddha appears as a practical founder, shaping a community that could hold thousands. The volume completes the Mahavagga in this series.
sacred-books-east-vol-36-milinda-2:
Volume thirty-six of the Sacred Books of the East, from 1894, holds the second part of The Questions of King Milinda in T. W. Rhys Davids' translation. Part one stands in volume thirty-five. The book records talks between King Milinda, a Greek ruler in India, and the monk Nagasena.

From dilemma 41 onward, the king presses harder puzzles: if there is no soul, who is reborn, and who bears the fruit of deeds? Nagasena answers with famous images, above all the chariot, which is no one part yet works as a whole. The dialogue is the liveliest door into Buddhist thought on self and rebirth. Rhys Davids judged it a masterpiece of Indian prose.
sacred-laws-aryas-buhler-vol-2:
Buhler's second volume of the Sacred Laws of the Aryas appeared in 1882. It formed volume fourteen of the Sacred Books of the East. The Dharma Sutras of Vasishtha and Baudhayana fill its pages.

More ancient codes govern priests, kings, and householders in these texts. Ritual purity, inheritance, marriage, and penance receive detailed rules. The sutras show law and religion fully intertwined in ancient India. Joined with volume one, they preserve Hinduism's oldest legal literature. Buhler's two volumes gave scholars a firm base for studying dharma. Customs described here echo in later Indian law for millennia. The translations remain standard references for the period.
samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-2:
Part 2 of Marietta Holley's Samantha Among the Brethren, written as Josiah Allen's Wife, opens at Chapter IV with a threshing machine arriving without warning. Samantha knew nothing of its coming until about half an hour before. Josiah Allen was not to blame, since it came as unexpectedly onto him as onto her. Solomon Gowdey was to have had the crew first, which would have left her ample time to cook for them. Gowdey was taken down bed sick, so the crew had to come right onto the Allens with no warning beforehand.

The rig had to pass by the side of the house, right by the parlor windows, to reach the side of the barn where the threshing was to be done.
sammlung-von-mehr-als-hundert-wahrhaften: Siegmund Heinrich Guldenfalk, named as a princely Hesse-Darmstadt chief land commissioner, collected and issued a German work printed at Frankfurt and Leipzig in 1784 by Joh. Georg Fleischer. The title, in old German spelling, promises a collection of more than a hundred true transmutation histories. It calls them wholly extraordinary and noteworthy examples of the changing of metals into gold or silver. The title also promises the art and way in which the work was carried out in each case.
sandra-belloni-volume-2: Header matter alone identifies Volume 2 of George Meredith's Sandra Belloni, marked v2 in its title line, with Meredith named as author. Its release date is given as September 2003, and the file was first posted on January 4, 2002, as Etext number 4414, in Edition 10, in English and ASCII. A general note adds that such electronic texts are often made from several printed editions, all confirmed as public domain in the United States unless a copyright notice is included.
satapatha-brahmana-eggeling-vol-2:
Volume two of Eggeling's Satapatha Brahmana appeared in 1885 in the Sacred Books of the East. The translation continues the vast Sanskrit manual of Vedic ritual. Eggeling devoted much of his career to completing this enormous text.

The exposition covers building altars, tending sacred fires, and the sacrificial words. Each gesture of the rite receives an explanation and a mythic reason. Beneath the detail lies a complete ancient worldview of cosmic order. Ritual action mirrors the structure of the universe in this system. Scholars call the Satapatha the foundational Brahmana for good reason. Eggeling's patient volumes remain the standard English route into it.
scott-last-expedition-vol-2:
The second volume of Scott's Last Expedition, from 1913, holds the working record of the Terra Nova expedition. Alongside the story of the search for the lost polar party, it prints the science the expedition brought home. The lost men's diaries and effects were found by the searchers in November 1912.

Reports cover the geology of the polar regions, the weather and ice, and the animals of the south. Other chapters tell how the search party found the tent, the bodies, and Scott's last letters. The volume shows the expedition was far more than the race: it was a full survey of a continent.
seneca-tragedies-miller-loeb-1917-vol-2:
Miller's second Loeb volume of Seneca, first printed in 1917, holds Agamemnon, Thyestes, Hercules Oetaeus, the Phoenissae, and Octavia. The scan staged here is a 1929 reprint. Thyestes, the grimmest of the set, serves a father the flesh of his own sons at a feast of false peace.

Agamemnon brings the Greek king home to his murder, retold in Seneca's hotter style. Octavia, likely not Seneca's own work, dramatizes Nero's court from inside his reign. The Phoenissae survives unfinished, a fragment on Oedipus's cursed house. With this volume Miller's Loeb Seneca stands complete. Its influence on revenge tragedy runs from Kyd and Shakespeare forward through English drama.
sheridan-memoirs-vol-2:
Volume Two of Sheridan's memoirs, also from 1888, carries the Civil War to its end and beyond. Sheridan's cavalry sealed Lee's fate in the spring of 1865. The general then spent years in the West and in high command.

He tells of Five Forks, the pursuit to Appomattox, and the final surrender. Postwar chapters cover Reconstruction duty in the South and the frontier wars against Native nations. Sheridan also served as an observer in the Franco-Prussian War and rose to command the whole army. His brisk second volume completes one of the fullest Union cavalry records.
sherman-memoirs-vol-1-part-2:
Part Two of the first volume of Sherman's memoirs takes the Civil War to the gates of Atlanta. Sherman had risen from early disgrace at Shiloh's shock to high command in the West. The 1875 text keeps his blunt voice.

He recounts Shiloh, the long siege of Vicksburg, and the battles around Chattanooga. Then comes the push into Georgia, mile by mile against Joseph Johnston. Sherman explains his choices as he made them, praising and blaming freely. The part ends with Atlanta in reach and the March to the Sea about to begin. Grant's trust in Sherman runs through the whole campaign story.
short-story-classics-american-vol-2:
William Patten edited this second volume of American short story classics for P. F. Collier and Son in New York, under a 1905 copyright. Patten adds an opening essay and notes. Each tale appears by leave of its author or the author's heirs, the title page states.

Contents open with J. W. DeForest's Brigade Commander and Bayard Taylor's Who Was She. Bret Harte's Idyl of Red Gulch, Harold Frederic, Thomas Bailey Aldrich, and Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen all appear. Students get a guided shelf of American tales from the decades after the Civil War, chosen to show the form at its best.
sketches-new-and-old-part-2:
Mark Twain's sketches new and old continue in this second part, opening with Answers to Correspondents, written about 1865. A writer signed Moral Statistician draws Twain's full scorn. Twain states that he lit his pipe with the man's whole batch of figures on smoking, coffee, and billiards.

Such counters see one side only, Twain charges. Old men smoke and drink coffee across America and live long anyway, he notes, while hearty Englishmen survive wine and fat Dutchmen grow older on both. The solid comfort a habit gives counts for more, Twain argues, than the pitiful savings of giving it up.
soldiers-three-part-2:
Part II of Kipling's Soldiers Three leads with Love-o'-Women. The tale comes from Many Inventions. A sad headnote calls it a tale of things done long ago, and ill done. The narrator arrives after the deed. The horror and the mix-up are all over. Only a dead man's blood calls from the barrack-square. The hot sun has dried it to a cracked gold film. The wind lifts that film as dust.

A quiet, well-kept sergeant stands at the tale's heart. He shot one of his own corporals in broad daylight. The shooting came just after early parade. He then sat on a cot and waited for the guard. Trial by the High Court lies ahead. The narrator must report that trial. He dreads its heat and its sworn proof. More army tales fill the contents around it.
st-george-and-st-michael-volume-2: George MacDonald wrote St. George and St. Michael in three volumes. This is Volume II, printed at London in 1876. The contents run from Chapter XVII to Chapter XXXIII. Heads name the fire-engine, moonlight and apple-blossoms, and the enchanted chair. Molly and the white horse, the damsel who fell sick, and the cataract follow. Amanda, Dorothy, and Lord Herbert share a head, and the witch's cottage and the moat of the keep close the run.
stanley-through-dark-continent-vol-2:
The second volume of Stanley's Through the Dark Continent, in the 1899 Newnes edition, completes the 1874 to 1877 crossing of Africa. Stanley's party follows the Congo from the interior to the Atlantic, a river road no European had traveled. Appendices close the work.

The descent runs through rapids, hostile banks, and starvation, with the boat Lady Alice carried around falls. Of the 356 who started, about a third reached the sea with him in August 1877. The journey proved the Congo a single great river and redrew central Africa's map. It also opened the region to the scramble of empire that followed, a shadow the book cannot shake.
statistics-of-phrenology-being-a-sketch-: Statistics of Phrenology bears the sub-title: Being a Sketch of the Progress and Present State of That Science in the British Islands. The name on the title page reads Hewett C. Watson, amid broken scan letters. Longman, Rees, Orme, Brown, Green, and Longman of Paternoster Row printed the London book in 1836. Stray garbled lines around the title name heads for historical and medical matter, with no clean body text to read.
statius-mozley-loeb-vol-2:
J. H. Mozley's second Loeb volume of Statius completes the Thebaid with books eight through twelve. It then adds the Achilleid, the poet's unfinished epic on the youth of Achilles, and the Silvae, his poems for patrons and friends. The whole surviving Statius stands in the two volumes.

The Thebaid ends in the duel of the brothers, the burning of the dead, and Theseus marching on Thebes. The Achilleid shows Achilles hidden among girls on Scyros, a lighter touch cut off by the poet's death. The Silvae sing of villas, statues, weddings, and grief. Together they show the range of the last great Latin epic poet.
stories-by-foreign-authors-german-volume:
Four longer tales fill Volume 2 of the German set. They are Auerbach's Christian Gellert's Last Christmas and Kompert's A Ghetto Violet. Hauff's Severed Hand and Chamisso's Peter Schlemihl complete the volume.

Auerbach begins at Leipzig on December 22, 1768. The poet Gellert leaves the university at three o'clock. Students and passers-by greet him with deep respect. Yet he wears his fame with a shy, almost sorry air. A note from the publishers explains that some versions were taken over from earlier printings by leave of the owners, while others were made fresh for the series.
strabo-geography-hamilton-falconer-vol-2:
Volume Two of Hamilton and Falconer's Strabo holds Books Eight through Thirteen. The focus turns to Greece, the heart of Strabo's world. He knew its towns, shrines, and battle sites in deep detail.

Town by town, he records myths, products, and famous sons. The Aegean islands and Asia Minor fill the later books. Homer serves as his guide and proof at many points. Scholars mine these pages for lost local history. The tour is long and dense, yet no other ancient source gives Greece at street level quite like this.
strange-stories-chinese-studio-giles-188:
Volume two of Giles's Strange Stories from a Chinese Studio, published in 1880, completes his selection from Pu Songling. The Liaozhai tales continue here with more fox spirits, haunted houses, and journeys among the dead. Pu Songling salted his ghost lore with satire on greedy officials and vain scholars.

Giles kept the tales short and strange, as Pu wrote them, rather than padding them into novellas. His footnotes carry much lore on Chinese religion and daily life. Together the two volumes made a Qing dynasty classic into an English one. Later translators have added more tales, but Giles opened the door. His selection remains the classic first taste of the studio's wonders.
stubbs-constitutional-history-vol-2:
William Stubbs, bishop and historian, issued Volume 2 of his Constitutional History in 1875. The later Middle Ages of England fill this part of his vast work. Parliament rises while kings test the bounds of their power.

Stubbs traces shire courts, great councils, and the Commons step by step. The Lancastrian kings try a kind of limited, law-bound rule. Then the Wars of the Roses tear the realm's order apart. His deep learning finds England's liberties rooted in medieval soil. Later study of the English constitution builds on his base. The volume's calm authority still commands respect from scholars today.
sunny-memories-of-foreign-lands-volume-2:
Volume II of Mrs. Harriet Beecher Stowe's Sunny Memories of Foreign Lands, dated 1854, continues her tour letters from Britain, numbered here from Letter XIX onward. The contents read like a roll of the famous people who received the author of Uncle Tom's Cabin.

One letter reports breakfast with Macaulay and dinner at Sir E. Buxton's; others take her to Lord Shaftesbury's table, an antislavery meeting at Exeter Hall, Windsor and Eton, and dinner at Lord John Russell's. She visits the aged abolitionist Clarkson at Playford Hall, hears the Archbishop of Canterbury preach to ragged scholars, and meets Lady Byron and Mr. Gladstone. The volume is a record of literary fame meeting reform society.
sylvia-s-lovers-volume-2:
Volume II of Elizabeth Gaskell's Sylvia's Lovers, printed at London in M.DCCC.LXIII, or 1863, carries the novel's chapters from XV to XXIX in the complete numbering. It opens with A Difficult Question and Philip alone with his thoughts, deep in humble, penitent gratitude.

The contents show the middle of the story tightening: the engagement, rejected warnings, an eddy in love's current, and an important mission. Loved and lost, a rejected suitor, and deepening shadows follow, then retaliation, brief rejoicing, and coming troubles. A dreary vigil, gloomy days, and an ordeal lead to the last chapter, Wedding Raiment, in which Sylvia marries without knowing the truth that would have freed her heart. Gaskell keeps the whaling town and its press-gang dangers close around the private sorrow.
symonds-renaissance-italy-vol-2:
Volume 2 of Symonds's Renaissance in Italy, from 1875, treats learning's revival. Humanists bring the ancient world back to life in these pages. Petrarch crowns the movement that reshaped schools across Europe.

Greek scholars flee west and find patrons in Italian courts and towns. Old texts are copied, corrected, and taught with fresh zeal each year. The classical course of study is born and spreads from Italy outward. Symonds tells the tale as the age's most warm English guide. His love for the scholars warms even dry points of grammar. The mind's rebirth, as much as art's, defines his Renaissance here.
tabqat-i-nasiri-raverty-vol-2:
Volume 2 of Raverty's Tabakat-i Nasiri, from 1881, continues the Persian chronicle. Later Delhi sultans rule, raid, and fall across its dense pages. The Mongol invasions strike with full fury in this second half.

Minhaj writes of courts he served and camps he saw himself. Intrigue, famine, and war mark the sultanate's hard middle years. His lists of kings and nobles anchor dates that scholars still use. The tone is grave, formal, and rich in names and places. Together the two volumes give an insider's history of thirteenth-century India. Raverty's notes add maps, names, and dates that guide modern readers through it.
tales-from-the-arabic-payne-1884-vol-2:
Volume II of Payne's Tales from the Arabic, from 1884, continues the companion set to his Thousand Nights. Stories drawn from the Breslau and Calcutta editions fill the volume, each a small world of wonder and reversal. Payne's English keeps the plain strength that made his name as the Nights' first complete translator.

These tales never rode in Shahrazad's frame, yet they breathe the same air of jinn, treasure, and sudden fate. Gathering them saved Arabic stories that a narrower canon would have lost. Volume II holds the middle of the supplement, carrying Payne's wider harvest of Arabic fiction forward.
talleyrand-memoirs-vol-2:
Volume Two of Talleyrand's memoirs follows the French Empire at its height. Talleyrand, Napoleon's foreign minister for a decade, saw the great campaigns from inside. Beaufort's 1891 English version carries the story forward.

The narrative covers the years of victory, the making and breaking of alliances, and Talleyrand's slow split with Napoleon. His account of the road toward the Congress of Vienna begins here. He presents himself as the steady hand amid Napoleon's ambition. Historians read him with care, but his seat at the center makes the volume hard to skip. His portraits of Napoleon shift between respect and quiet resentment.
tamburlaine-the-great-part-2: Marlowe's sequel to his Scythian shepherd's conquests: Tamburlaine burns cities, defies gods, and is finally stopped only by death. "Infinite riches in a little room" gives way to cosmic defiance. Elizabethan drama at its most thunderous.
targums-etheridge-vol-2:
J. W. Etheridge published the second volume of his English Targums in 1865, finishing the Pentateuch begun in volume one. It covers Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy in the paraphrases of Onkelos and Jonathan ben Uzziel. These Aramaic versions were the people's Bible in the ancient synagogue.

Through the laws of sacrifice, the desert wanderings, and Moses' farewell speeches, the targums keep clarifying as they go. They explain hard commands, fill gaps in the story, and weave in teaching the rabbis prized. Etheridge's two volumes together made the whole Aramaic Torah open to English readers for the first time.
terence-comedies-sargeaunt-loeb-1912-vol:
Sargeaunt's second Loeb volume of Terence, published in 1912, holds Phormio, The Mother-in-Law, and The Brothers, with facing Latin text. Phormio, named for its quick-witted parasite, untangles two young men's love affairs against their fathers' plans. It is often counted Terence's most deftly built comedy.

The Mother-in-Law, which failed twice in Rome before it pleased, treats a young wife's secret with unusual delicacy. The Brothers debates two ways of raising sons, strict and easy, through two households. Terence's famous line that nothing human is alien to him sums up his manner. Sargeaunt's two volumes give the whole surviving Terence in the standard edition. His smooth Latin shaped European ideas of good style.
terence-comedies-sargeaunt-loeb-vol-2:
Terence, a former slave from North Africa, became Rome's most polished comic poet in the second century BCE. John Sargeaunt translated his plays for the Loeb series. This second volume holds the last three comedies: Phormio, Hecyra, and Adelphoe. With them, the six-play corpus of Terence is complete.

Phormio turns on a sly parasite who outwits two old men for a pair of young lovers. Hecyra, the Mother-in-Law, failed twice on stage before crowds took to its gentle plot. Adelphoe, the Brothers, weighs strict and soft ways of raising sons. Terence writes clean, humane Latin, and his lines were quoted in schools for two thousand years.
the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-volume-: Volume two of The Adventures of Harry Richmond is by George Meredith. Only a Project Gutenberg wrapper is present here. No novel text stands with it. The wrapper marks the part as number 51 in a Meredith set. It gives file 4445. It was first posted on January 31, 2002. It stands in edition 10 and plain ASCII. David Widger made the file.
the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-2:
Part two of Mark Twain's The Adventures of Tom Sawyer opens at chapter four, on a calm Sunday in the village of St. Petersburg. The sun rises on a tranquil world, and breakfast gives way to family worship at Aunt Polly's house.

Her prayer is built, Twain says, from solid courses of Bible quotes with a thin mortar of her own words. She then reads a grim chapter of the law of Moses as if from Sinai. Tom must learn five verses for Sunday school and picks the shortest he can find, from the Sermon on the Mount. Sid has his lesson by heart days ahead. Readers get Tom's dread of church, a pinch beetle, and a poodle in the aisle.
the-amazing-marriage-volume-2:
Volume two of George Meredith's 1895 novel The Amazing Marriage holds Book Two, running from Small Causes to The Girl Madge. Its chapters track a bride from foreign parts given a taste of old England, a honeymoon in its first stage, and a trip down Whitechapel way.

Chapter Ten opens late at night with Gower Woodseer leaving Fleetwood and a band of late revelers at a hotel door. Under low stars he dwells on the lady's large grey eyes, rimmed dark and ringed with light. Meredith gives her a glamour no courtier can name, part beauty, part daring, part calm that holds men at a distance.
the-armourer-s-prentices-2:
Chapter One of Charlotte M. Yonge's novel of Tudor apprentices opens at the Verdurer's Lodge in the New Forest. A pair of lines from As You Like It stands at its head, about a poor portion left by a father's will, with which a young man means to buy his fortunes.

Forest officers, the chapter begins, have enjoyed some of the pleasantest dwellings in southern England since the days of the Conqueror. The Birkenholt home lies at the foot of a slope crowned with great beeches, their large silver boles rising like columns under a vault of tender green. Below the wood stretches pasture, flecked in season with lady-smocks, all silver white.
the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-of-tw:
Volume two of Gilbert Parker's romance opens at chapter ten with a ship named Narcissus entering rocky waters near the Ecrehos. Its first lieutenant, Philip d'Avranche, is rowed ashore by pilot Jean Touzel. Soundings and shore work have been ordered by the Admiralty.

Philip walks to a ruined chapel on Mattre Ile in a poor mood, bored by dull duty. He has been wrecked at Trinidad, served in America and India, and fought Spanish cruisers off Arabia. Now he waits for command of his own ship. His thoughts turn to Guida, a village beauty in Jersey, whose face he saw the day before.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-3-no-2:
May 1885, volume three, number two, opens with a portrait of Sylvester Marsh and a life by Charles Carleton Coffin. Marsh is named as the projector of the Mount Washington Railroad. He was born on September 30, 1803, the ninth of eleven children, in Campton, New Hampshire.

Coffin describes settlers in the Pemigewasset Valley clearing pine, oak, and elm forest by hard labour before machines were common. Green fields replaced woods on the intervales and hillsides. He also tells of Arthur Scholfield, an English machinist who reached America three years before Marsh was born, forced to leave his tools behind under a British law.
the-boatswain-s-mate-captains-all-book-2:
W. W. Jacobs tells The Boatswain's Mate as part of his Captains All tales. George Benn, an old boatswain now out of the navy, has just asked Mrs. Waters, who keeps a small inn, to wed him. She turns him down with heat. She notes that he asks only after his third mug of ale, and he swears he will ask next time before he drinks a drop.

Benn walks off in gloom, his suit refused five times in two weeks. Two miles on he sits on a bank, lights his pipe, and dozes in the heat. He wakes at steps on the road and sees a tall, keen-eyed man with a pack, plainly an old soldier. The man stops, greets him in a warm way, and asks for a pipe of tobacco. Benn hands over his tin box and starts to chat.
the-boy-slaves-2: Capt. Mayne Reid wrote The Boy Slaves, and this copy is a new form of the book with a memoir by R. H. Stoddard. Thomas R. Knox and Company of 813 Broadway, New York, put it out as heirs to James Miller. A letter from Reid, dated New York, January 1, 1869, is also printed. In it he grants Fields, Osgood and Company the sole right to print his juvenile tales of adventure, called Boys' Novels, in the United States. No tale page is shown.
the-butterfly-s-ball-and-the-grasshopper:
The Butterfly's Ball and the Grasshopper's Feast is a verse tale for children. The heading names R. M. Ballantyne, and William Roscoe, with the date 1802. The verse starts with a call to the ball: come, take up your hats, and away let us haste. The trumpeter Gadfly has summoned his crew, and the revels wait only for the guests.

The ball is set on smooth-shaven grass beside the wood. Under a broad oak, old beyond memory, the children of earth gather with the tenants of air. They meet for an evening's amusement. The Beetle comes, blind and black, carrying the Emmet, his friend, on his back. The Gnat and the Dragonfly come, with all their relations, green, orange, and blue. They promise to lay by their sting for the evening. The Dormouse peeps out and leads his blind cousin the Mole to the feast.
the-castaway-odd-craft-part-2:
The Castaway, a tale from Odd Craft by W. W. Jacobs, opens in Shinglesea at the close of a short day, with Mrs. John Boxer standing at her shop door listening to the beat of the sea half a mile off. The little shop, with its wide-mouthed bottles of sweets, was her childhood home. Her husband was lost with the North Star three years before. Then she gave up her home in Poplar. She came back to help her mother.

Then the shop bell clangs, and she turns to a short, bearded man in the doorway, with oddly shaped shoulders and one leg not a match for the other. In a moment she is in his arms, sobbing and laughing together. The castaway has come home, and her mother, Mrs. Gimpson, wakes to share the uproar.
the-children-of-the-new-forest-2:
Captain Marryat's tale for young readers appears here in a second record, headed with the year 1847, and its opening matches the other edition of the same work word for word. The setting is England in 1647, after nearly five years of civil war. King Charles the First has been defeated and is held prisoner at Hampton Court.

With the Cavalier party dispersed and Cromwell's army gaining control of the Commons, Charles escapes in November. Sir John Berkely, Ashburnham, and Legg ride with him toward the Hampshire coast and the New Forest. A vessel for France was expected but never readied, so the king turns inland toward Titchfield, the Earl of Southampton's seat. Because the two records open with identical text, readers should treat this one as another edition of the same novel, not a sequel or a distinct story.
the-complete-poetical-works-of-percy-bys: Volume 2 of Percy Bysshe Shelley's complete poetical works is shown here in the Oxford Edition of 1914. Thomas Hutchinson edited that edition. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present. The list opens with early poems of 1814 and 1815. Among them stand Mutability, On Death, and A Summer Evening Churchyard. To Wordsworth also appears, with Feelings of a Republican on the Fall of Bonaparte. A note on the early poems by Mrs. Shelley is also listed. No poem text follows.
the-complete-writings-of-charles-dudley-: Volume 2 of Charles Dudley Warner's complete writings reached Project Gutenberg in June 2001 as etext number 2672. Nothing beyond the Gutenberg header is present: the usual copyright warnings, the note that the header must legally be seen first on opening the book, and the donation appeal.A title page and a contents list are all that stand here.
the-confession-of-a-child-of-the-century: Volume 2 of Alfred de Musset's Confession of a Child of the Century, in the French Immortals series, reached Project Gutenberg as etext 3940. Nothing but the header is present, with its April 2003 release date, its September 2001 first posting, and David Widger named as producer.Nothing inside the book follows its front matter.
the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-volum:
Volume 2 of Charles James Lever's Confessions of Harry Lorrequer covers chapters XI to XVII. It was printed at Dublin in 1839. Lever is named in brackets, since the title page names no author. The contents promise Cheltenham, Dublin boarding-house society, a chase, theatricals, a wager, and an elopement. A note flags a printer's slip: chapter XVI appears twice in the print copy.

Chapter XI opens on a cold, raw February evening in the coffee room of the Old Plough at Cheltenham. Harry sits alone, in the Latin tag's phrase, like Lucullus dining with Lucullus, with no companion. The chapter's business is a matrimonial adventure: showing how to make love for a friend. A Dublin chapter recalls Tom O'Flaherty and a reminiscence of the Peninsula. Lever keeps the tone of a mess-room story, where campaigns, matches, and practical jokes share the same breath.
the-diary-and-letters-of-madame-d-arblay: Volume 2 of The Diary and Letters of Madame d'Arblay (Frances Burney), with notes by W. C. Ward and Macaulay's essay as preface, covers 1787 to 1792. It was printed in London by Vizetelly and Company in 1891. An engraving shows George III, Queen Charlotte, and their family. The contents take up her court duties: the Queen's birthday drawing room, the equerries, the Duchess de Polignac, Mrs. Schwellenberg and her frogs, Mrs. Siddons, and Dr. Herschel. Only the title page and contents synopsis are present here.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-p:
Part two of Paradise in Dante's Vision, in the Rev. H. F. Cary's verse, opens at canto fifteen. True love falls silent so that Dante may pray, and a bright spirit runs down a cross of light like flame seen through pale stone. The shade greets Dante as his own blood and speaks of grace that let a living man enter heaven.

Here Dante meets a famed forebear who tells of old Florence and foretells his exile. War, faith, and family pride shape the talk. The sphere of Mars glows red with souls who died for the faith.

Cantos five through ten fill part two of Purgatory in Dante's Vision, in Cary's English verse. A spirit points at Dante, amazed that light breaks below his body, a sign he still lives. His guide rebukes his slow pace and tells him to stand firm as a tower that no blast can shake.

Souls who sang the Miserere draw near, stunned that a living man casts a shadow. Many here died by violence and turned to God at the last hour. Their tales plead for prayers from the living to speed their climb.
the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-2:
Volume two of The Doré Gallery of Bible Illustrations opens with the trial of Abraham's faith. The text retells Genesis in the old wording: God bids Abraham take Isaac to Moriah and offer him there. Abraham rises early, splits the wood, and walks three days to the place. Isaac asks where the lamb is, and his father says God will provide.

Doré's plate shows the altar scene in stark light and shade. Short Bible texts like this fill the volume, each set to face an engraving. Abraham's stayed hand is the volume's strong first note.
the-dwelling-place-of-light-volume-2:
Volume two of Winston Churchill's The Dwelling-Place of Light opens at chapter nine, with Janet Bumpus and her boss Ditmar. Their bond has tightened day by day, and Janet finds a keen, mixed joy in holding such a man on a leash that might snap. Alone, she falls into doubt, torn between new freedoms and old rules.

She fears she may match her wild sister Lise more than she thought. Desire, pride, and shame pull at her as the mill town heats up. Churchill keeps the lens close on a young woman's mind.
the-early-short-fiction-of-edith-wharton:
Volume two of The Early Short Fiction of Edith Wharton holds six tales with their first dates in magazines. Afterward dates to January 1910, The Fulness of Life to December 1893, Xingu to December 1911, and The Reckoning to August 1902. A verse list adds Botticelli's Madonna in the Louvre and The Tomb of Ilaria Giunigi, both from 1891.

Afterward opens with a joke in a bright June garden about a house's one ghost, whom its owners will never know. Mary Boyne recalls the jest in December dusk, and its bite lands. Wharton blends wit with quiet dread.
the-forsyte-saga-volume-2: This Penguin printing of The Forsyte Saga, Volume 2, holds The White Monkey, The Silver Spoon, and Swan Song, and the front matter here is a life of John Galsworthy. It tells of his birth in 1867, Harrow and Oxford, his call to the Bar in 1890, and his turn to writing under Joseph Conrad's sway and his wife's. It dates the three novels to 1924, 1926, and 1928, and notes his Nobel Prize of 1932. No page of the novels can be read here.
the-french-revolution-volume-2:
Hippolyte A. Taine wrote this second volume on the French Revolution as The Jacobin Conquest, part of his Origins of Contemporary France. Two books trace how a small, tight party took hold of a vast land.

The first book studies the Jacobins: their rise, their clubs, their press, and theircast of mind. The second shows the first stage of the conquest, with rigged votes, hunts for foes, and scare tactics. Taine then weighs the Legislative Assembly, its skill, its sessions, and its warring groups. His verdict is cold: a creed, held by few, ruled France by fear and club craft.
the-gaming-table-its-votaries-and-victim:
Andrew Steinmetz wrote The Gaming Table as a two-volume study of gambling in all times and lands, with stress on England and France. This first volume is given to the Duke of Wellington.

In his preface Steinmetz calls the book a set of facts and a slice of social history worth thought. Forty or fifty years before his day, he says, gambling was the rage in London. Squares now full of staid folk once held gaming rooms packed with votaries of chance. Dice, cards, and the turf bred sharpers, ruined lords, and odd codes of honor, and Steinmetz sets out to trace them all.

Andrew Steinmetz wrote this second volume of The Gaming Table on the folk who live by chance and the games they play. The contents run from polite sharpers to fortune telling by cards and amusing card tricks.

The first chapter traces the chevaliers d'industrie, smooth sharpers found in each city. To win trust they pair with men of good name. Or they forge titles of their own. Later heads take up pro game folk and their frauds. They take up duels and deaths among gamblers. They take up the great clubs and the math of chance. They end with the tales of dice and cards, from piquet to faro and hazard.
the-gilded-age-part-2:
Part 2 of The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today is dated 1873. Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner wrote the novel. This part opens with Chapter X. Days after a funeral, papers are found on the dead Major Lackland. Lackland once held a seat in Congress. He lost all trust after he sold his vote for cash.

The papers show a shock. Laura Hawkins was not the child of Mr. and Mrs. Hawkins. The papers name no real parents. Neighbors fill the gap with gossip. Each tale of her birth grows more dark and more wild. Laura soon meets cold looks and turned heads. Her place in the town starts to shift.
the-golden-bowl-volume-2: Henry James wrote The Golden Bowl. This record is Volume II of the novel. Only front matter is present here. It is a Project Gutenberg header. The header gives a long notice on copyright laws. It tells readers to keep the file as it is. It honors the volunteers who made the text. It gives the title and author, a release date of July 2003, and Edition 10. No page of the novel itself is present. Nothing about this volume's own chapters can be told from what is here.
the-great-conspiracy-volume-2:
John Logan wrote The Great Conspiracy: Its Origin and History. This record is Part 2. It opens with Chapter VI, The Great Conspiracy Maturing. The 6th of November, 1860, has come and passed. By the 7th, the conviction that Lincoln would be elected has become a certainty. The fact has been heralded across the Republic.

Logan describes the excitement. Republicans in the North rejoiced. The great wrong of slavery, they felt, was to be placed in the course of ultimate extinction. Douglas Democrats felt gloomy forebodings at their leader's defeat. Much of the Southern Democracy openly exulted. The long-wished-for chance for a revolt of the slave power was at hand. South Carolina rejoiced with bonfires and processions. Fire-eaters were jubilant in Charleston.
the-heart-of-mid-lothian-volume-2:
Walter Scott wrote The Heart of Mid-Lothian, Volume 2. The tale belongs to Tales of My Landlord, second series. The title page credits Jedediah Cleishbotham as collector and arranger. Chapter first opens with lines from Measure for Measure. Mrs. Saddletree then enters a room of hidden misery.

An old man lies in bed after a long swoon. The curtains are drawn around him. Jeanie sits motionless at his side. Mrs. Saddletree is kind but not delicate. She opens the window and draws the curtain back. She urges the old man to bear his sorrow well. Jeanie, pale as ashes, asks if all is over.
the-home-book-of-verse-volume-2:
Burton Egbert Stevenson edited The Home Book of Verse, Volume 2, by various poets. A note states that the contents of the set stand in Volume 1, while the pages present open Part II, Poems of Love. The first poem shown is Eros, by Ralph Waldo Emerson, dated 1803-1882, on how love is a short sense of the world that men and gods have not outlearned.

A second poem, Now What Is Love, follows in question form. Love is called a fountain and a well where pleasure and repentance dwell, a work on holiday, December matched with May, and sunshine mixed with rain. Love poems in many voices fill the part, set for home reading.
the-ink-stain-tache-d-encre-volume-2: Volume two of René Bazin's The Ink-Stain continues a three-part split. The pages present here hold only an old etext header. No chapter of the novel itself appears. The header gives the file as etext 3973. Release came in April 2003. The volume stands sixtieth in the French Immortals series. It stands second among Bazin's works there. Readers seeking the story's middle find only the wrapper. The header names the book, its author, and its place. Nothing more can be read from what is present.
